explanationHtml:
Ophthalmopathy is the specific sign of Graves’ disease.

Glycosaminoglycan deposition, lymphoid infiltrates and fatty infiltration are responsible for ophthalmopathy and dermopathy.

Grave's disease is an autoimmune disorder due to the production of TSH-receptor stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) thereby causing hyperthyroidism.

It is characterized by the triad of:

  • Thyrotoxicosis
  • Infiltrative ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos)
  • Dermopathy (pretibial myxedema)

Ophthalmopathy can sometimes precede or follow thyrotoxicosis, accounting for some cases of euthyroid ophthalmopathy.
question: Which of the following is a specific sign for Graves' disease?

correctAnswer: B. It occurs in more than 50% of patients with Graves' disease.
explanationHtml:
The given scenario along with the image is suggestive of thyroid dermopathy. It occurs in <5% of patients with Graves’ disease. Thyroid dermopathy is almost always associated with ophthalmopathy.

Thyroid dermopathy is most frequently observed over the anterolateral parts of the lower leg. Hence, it is termed pretibial myxedema. Skin changes can occur at other sites, particularly after trauma. The typical lesion is a noninflamed, indurated plaque with a deep pink or purple color and orange peel-textured papules.

Thyroid acropachy refers to a form of clubbing rarely observed in Graves’ disease. It is strongly associated with thyroid dermopathy.

Thyroid dermopathy usually does not need any active treatment, but if necessary, treatment includes topical, high-potency glucocorticoid ointment under an occlusive dressing or octreotide can be useful in some cases.

The following image shows thyroid dermopathy and acropachy:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Acropachy is strongly associated with this condition.
It occurs in more than 50% of patients with Graves' disease.
It occurs almost always in the presence of moderate or severe form of ophthalmopathy.
Skin changes can occur after trauma.

question: A patient with Graves' disease presents with the following finding. Which statement regarding this condition is false?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the Jod-Basedow phenomenon, likely due to the administration of an iodine-containing contrast agent during CECT.

This phenomenon is characterized by hyperthyroidism due to enhanced thyroid hormone production following the administration of contrast agents and other iodine-containing substances. This occurs in:

  • Patients with autonomous thyroid nodules
  • Patients with pre-existing subclinical hypothyroidism (endemic iodine deficiency in hilly areas)

Option B: Wolff-Chaikoff effect is characterized by the transient inhibition of thyroid iodide organification by excess iodine, thereby decreasing thyroid hormone synthesis.

Option C: Basedow disease is another name for Graves' disease.

Option D: Plummer disease is another name for toxic multinodular goitre.
question: A patient from a hilly area was referred with a partial small bowel obstruction confirmed on CECT. Conservative management was tried for a week, but he continued to deteriorate and was taken up for emergency laparotomy. On post-operative day 7, he developed atrial fibrillation. Investigations revealed elevated free T3 and free T4 levels. What is the most probable cause?

explanationHtml:
Hyperactivity and irritability are considered as the most common symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.

The following table summarizes the symptoms and signs of thyrotoxicosis in descending order of frequency:

Symptoms Signs
  • Hyperactivity, irritability, dysphoria
  • Heat intolerance and sweating
  • Palpitations
  • Fatigue and weakness
  • Weight loss with increased appetite
  • Diarrhoea
  • Polyuria
  • Oligomenorrhea, loss of libido
  • Tachycardia, atrial fibrillation in the elderly
  • Tremor
  • Goitre
  • Warm, moist skin
  • Muscle weakness, proximal myopathy
  • Lid retraction or lag
  • Gynecomastia

Rarely, there can be an associated mid-systolic heart murmur called the Means-Lerman scratch. This is heard in the upper part of the sternum caused by the rubbing of the pericardium and the pleura, due to the hyperdynamic circulation.
question: What is the most common symptom of thyrotoxicosis?

correctAnswer: B. The mortality rate is 10% with treatment
explanationHtml:
The mortality rate of thyrotoxicosis crisis is almost 30% even with treatment.

The usual causes for mortality are:

  • Cardiac failure
  • Arrhythmia
  • Hyperthermia

options.text: Symptoms are vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice and altered mentation
The mortality rate is 10% with treatment
High doses of propranolol decrease T4 → T3 conversion

question: Which of the following statements is not true about thyroid storm?

explanationHtml:
Silent thyroiditis is not associated with amiodarone therapy.

Amiodarone has the following effects on the thyroid gland:

  • Acute, transient suppression of thyroid function i.e., Wolff-Chaikoff effect
  • Hypothyroidism in patients susceptible to the inhibitory effects of a high iodine load
  • Thyrotoxicosis may be caused by Jod-Basedow phenomenon due to the iodine load, in the setting of multinodular goitre or incipient Graves’ disease. It can also be caused by a thyroiditis-like condition.

Painless thyroiditis, or silent thyroiditis, occurs in patients with underlying autoimmune thyroid disease and has a clinical course similar to that of subacute thyroiditis.

The condition can occur in up to 5% of women 3–6 months after pregnancy and is then termed postpartum thyroiditis.
question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with amiodarone therapy?

correctAnswer: A. Type 2 AIT is associated with intrinsic abnormalities of the thyroid gland
explanationHtml:
Type 1 AIT is associated with intrinsic abnormalities of the thyroid gland.

Amiodarone is structurally similar to thyroid hormones and contains 39% iodine by weight. Amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis (AIT) is the most common manifestation of the effects of amiodarone on the thyroid.

Type 1 AIT Type 2 AIT

An underlying disease is present.

E.g., Grave’s disease, Multinodular goitre etc

 No underlying disease
Due to the Jod-Basedow phenomenon Due to drug-induced lysosomal destruction of thyroid tissue
Increased vascularity on colour doppler Decreased vascularity on colour doppler

Administration of amiodarone should be stopped if possible.

Near-total thyroidectomy rapidly decreases thyroid hormone levels and may be the most effective long-term clinical solution.

options.text: Type 2 AIT is associated with intrinsic abnormalities of the thyroid gland
Type 2 AIT is due to lysosomal destruction of thyroid gland.
Type 1 AIT is due to Jod-Basedow phenomenon.
Colour flow doppler shows increased vascularity in Type 1

question: Which of the following statements about amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis is false?

correctAnswer: A. It is more commonly observed in women
explanationHtml:
Multinodular goitre (MNG) is more commonly observed in women. It is common in iodine-deficient regions.

Most patients are asymptomatic and euthyroid. Sudden pain may occur due to haemorrhage. TFTs should be performed in all patients to exclude thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism.

The risk of malignancy due to MNG is similar to that due to solitary nodules. Hoarseness, reflecting the involvement of laryngeal nerves implicate malignancy.

Most non-toxic MNGs can be managed conservatively. Levothyroxine if used, should be started at low doses and then increased gradually. Radioiodine therapy is implemented for large goitres as it decreases goitre size and can ablate regions of autonomy.

options.text: It is more commonly observed in women
It does not occur in iodine-deficient regions
Most patients with non-toxic MNG have hypothyroidism
Risk of malignancy is higher than in cases of solitary thyroid nodule

question: Which of the following statements is true about non-toxic multinodular goitre?

explanationHtml:
The major difference between toxic and non-toxic multinodular goiter (MNG) is the presence of functional autonomy in toxic MNG.

The pathogenesis of toxic MNG appears to be similar to that of non-toxic MNG. In both types, many nodules are polyclonal whereas others are monoclonal and vary in their clonal origins.

Most patients with non-toxic MNG are asymptomatic and euthyroid. However, patients with toxic MNG have subclinical or mild hyperthyroidism.
question: What is the major difference between non-toxic and toxic multinodular goitre?

explanationHtml:
Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy.

Prevalence of different types of thyroid malignancies:

Type of malignancy Occurence
Papillary 80-90%
Follicular 5-10%
Medullary <10%
Others 1-2%
question: What is the most common thyroid malignancy?

correctAnswer: A. A 55-year-old woman with no voice abnormalities and nodule size of 3 cms
explanationHtml:
Among the options, the female patient with age between 20 and 65 years and no voice abnormalities and nodule size < 4 cm has the least risk for development of thyroid carcinoma.

Risk factors for the development of thyroid carcinoma in patients with thyroid nodules include:

  • Age less than 20 or greater than 65 years
  • Male gender
  • Increased nodule size > 4 cm
  • Vocal cord paralysis and hoarse voice
  • New or enlarged neck mass
  • Family history of thyroid cancer, MEN2, or other syndromes associated with thyroid malignancy (e.g., Cowden’s syndrome, familial polyposis, Carney complex)
  • Nodule fixed to adjacent structures
  • Exposure to radiation in childhood or adolescence
  • Extrathyroidal extension
  • Lateral cervical lymphadenopathy

options.text: A 55-year-old woman with no voice abnormalities and nodule size of 3 cms
A 65-year-old woman with vocal cord paralysis and hoarse voice and nodule size of 3.5 cms
A 60-year-old man without any voice abnormalities and nodule size of 2.5 cms
A 43-year-old woman with no voice abnormalities and nodule size of 4.5 cm

question: The following patients presented with thyroid nodules. Who has the least risk of developing thyroid carcinoma?

correctAnswer: A. Inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder
explanationHtml:
Thyroid hormone resistance is an autosomal dominant disorder.

It is characterized by elevated thyroid hormone levels and inappropriately elevated or normal TSH levels.

Classic forms of the disease are attributed to the mutation in TR-β gene. Patients with this condition are often asymptomatic, as hormone resistance is partial and compensated by the increase in thyroid hormone levels.

In most patients, no treatment is indicated.

options.text: Inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder
Characterized by elevated thyroid hormone levels and normal or elevated TSH
Classic forms are caused by mutations in TR-β gene

question: Which of the following statements is not true about thyroid hormone resistance?

explanationHtml:
Serum thyroglobulin levels are normal in patients with thyrotoxicosis factitia, as it is caused by the self-administration of thyroid hormone. Its level is elevated in all other types of thyrotoxicosis.

Thyroglobulin (Tg) levels are particularly increased in thyroiditis, implicating destruction of thyroid tissue and release of thyroglobulin.

The primary course of action for determining the thyroglobulin levels, however, is in the clinical follow-up of thyroid cancer patients.

Following total thyroidectomy and radiofrequency ablation, thyroglobulin levels become undetectable. In the absence of anti-Tg antibodies, measurable levels of Tg are indicative of incomplete ablation or recurrent cancer.
question: Patients with what condition present with normal thyroglobulin levels?

correctAnswer: D. It is autoimmune in origin
explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of De Quervain’s thyroiditis, and it is not autoimmune in origin. It is subacute granulomatous thyroiditis that occurs secondary to viral infections.

Many viruses such as mumps, influenza, coxsackie, adenoviruses, and echoviruses have been clinically implicated in this condition. Peak incidence is observed at 30-50 years and women are generally affected three times more often than men.

Clinically, it presents as a painfully enlarged thyroid and is sometimes accompanied by fever.

It has three distinct phases:

  • Thyrotoxic phase
  • Hypothyroid phase
  • Recovery phase

Treatment includes large doses of aspirin, NSAIDs, steroids and/or beta-blockers to relieve the observable clinical symptoms. Antithyroid drugs do not have any role. In case the hypothyroid phase is prolonged - levothyroxine can be used.

options.text: Treatment of choice is supportive care and NSAIDs
Women are generally affected three times more often than men
Both thyrotoxic and hypothyroid phases can be observed

question: A patient presented with fever and painful neck swelling. She gives a history of sore throat and cough one week ago. Lab investigations revealed elevated T3 and T4 levels and elevated ESR. Which of the following statements about this condition is false?

explanationHtml: Graves' disease is not associated with hypothyroidism.
question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with hypothyroidism?

correctAnswer: A. Most common cause is inborn defects in the synthesis of thyroid hormone
explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of congenital hypothyroidism. The most common cause of this condition is thyroid gland dysgenesis, seen in about 80-85% of cases of neonatal hypothyroidism.

In the remaining cases of neonatal hypothyroidism, it is due to inborn defects in thyroid hormone synthesis and rarely due to TSH receptor antibodies. These developmental abnormalities are twice as common in girls.

Clinical features include:

  • Prolonged jaundice
  • Umbilical hernia
  • Enlarged tongue
  • Hypotonia
  • Delayed bone maturation

Permanent neurological damage results if treatment is delayed.

T4 requirements are relatively high during the first year of life. A high circulating T4 level is needed to normalize TSH.

Early treatment with T4 results in normal IQ levels by preventing neurodevelopmental abnormalities.

options.text: Most common cause is inborn defects in the synthesis of thyroid hormone
The developmental abnormalities are more common in girls
High circulating T4 level is needed to normalize TSH

question: A 4-month-old baby presented with a history of constipation, lethargy, and has poor activities. Clinical examination reveals jaundice, hypotonia and there was no palpable goitre. Laboratory investigations revealed low T4 and elevated TSH levels. Which of the following is not true about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Autoimmune hypothyroidism is usually not associated with type II diabetes mellitus.

Genetic risk factors for autoimmune hypothyroidism has been documented with HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, HLA-DR5. A weak association also exists with CTLA4 gene polymorphism.

This may explain the relationship between autoimmune hypothyroidism and type I diabetes mellitus, Addison's disease, pernicious anemia, and vitiligo.

Less commonly encountered clinical associations include:

  • Celiac disease
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis
  • Chronic active hepatitis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Myasthenia gravis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Sjogren's syndrome.
question: Patients with autoimmune hypothyroidism have a higher predisposition for all except:

explanationHtml:
The most common symptom of hypothyroidism is tiredness and weakness.

Symptoms and signs in decreasing order of frequency are given below:

Symptoms

Signs
  • Tiredness, weakness
  • Dry skin
  • Cold intolerance
  • Hair loss
  • Difficulty concentrating and poor memory
  • Constipation
  • Weight gain with poor appetite
  • Dyspnea
  • Hoarse voice
  • Menorrhagia (later oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea)
  • Paresthesia
  • Impaired hearing
  • Dry coarse skin, cool peripheral extremities
  • Puffy face, hands, and feet (myxedema)
  • Diffuse alopecia
  • Bradycardia
  • Peripheral edema
  • Delayed tendon reflex relaxation
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome
  • Serous cavity effusions
question: Most common symptom seen in patients with hypothyroidism is?

explanationHtml:
Hyperthermia is least likely in this patient. Clinical manifestations of myxedema coma include decreased consciousness, seizures and hypothermia.

Myxedema coma is a serious condition with a mortality rate of 20-40%. The clinical outcomes are independent of the detected T4 and TSH levels.

Clinical features of myxedema crisis include:

  • Impaired cognition, ranging from confusion to somnolence to coma (myxedema coma)
  • Convulsions and abnormal CNS signs.
  • Profound hypothermia (can reach 23°C), hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hypotension.
  • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
question: An elderly patient presents to the ER with symptoms suggestive of myxedema coma. Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
explanationHtml:
The presenting symptoms of lethargy, increased sleep, and weight gain are suggestive of hypothyroidism. An increase in TSH on administration of TRH confirms the lack of stimulus for TSH secretion from the hypothalamus.

Although decreased TSH levels can be seen in hyperthyroidism, clinical features such as lethargy, increased sleep and weight gain are not. This pushes the diagnosis in favor of hypothyroidism.

If the disease was in the pituitary, there would be no increase in TSH secretion on administration of TRH (Option B).

Normally, the thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH) is released by the hypothalamus. It stimulates the pituitary gland to release the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T3 and T4 hormones.

Low TSH levels may be seen in the following cases:

Disease Pathogenesis Presentation
Hyperthyroidism Feedback inhibition of TSH release Symptoms of hyperthyroidism
Primary disease of the pituitary Decreased release of TSH, thereby causing a decreased release of thyroid hormones

Symptoms of hypothyroidism.

Administration of TRH does not elevate the TSH levels in this case since the pituitary gland is abnormal
Primary disease of the hypothalamus Decreased release of TRH leading to decreased TSH and hypothyroidism Administration of TRH causes elevation of TSH levels since the pituitary gland is normal.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus

question: A patient came to the hospital with complaints of lethargy, increased sleep, and weight gain. Investigations revealed low plasma TSH concentration.  However, on the administration of TRH, the TSH levels increased. Which of the following conditions is likely in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical history is typical of a case of hypothyroidism and the diagnosis is myxedema coma, which is a serious complication of hypothyroidism.

Myxedema coma is a part of a larger clinical picture of myxedema crisis. Myxedema crisis refers to severe, life-threatening manifestations of hypothyroidism. It is often precipitated by the administration of sedatives, antidepressants, hypnotics, anaesthetics, or opioids.

Clinical features of myxedema crisis :

  • Impaired cognition, ranging from confusion to somnolence to coma (myxedema coma).
  • Convulsions and abnormal CNS signs.
  • Profound hypothermia (can reach 23°C), hypoventilation, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and hypotension.
  • Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury
  • A high mortality rate

Other options:

Option A: Without a history of or focus of infection, septic shock is unlikely.

Option B: Cardiogenic shock would present with symptoms of left heart failure i.e. pitting pedal edema, abdominal distension, prominence of neck veins, and dyspnea.

Option D: Hypoglycemia usually presents with sweating, palpitations, and tachycardia
question: A middle-aged woman with a history of constipation, dry skin and menorrhagia presents to the ER with altered sensorium, non-pitting edema, hypothermia, bradycardia, and hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
In Graves' disease, the level of serum TSH is low, free T4 is high and serum T3 is high. In patients with thyrotoxicosis, the radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) at 24 hours is characteristically elevated.

Grave’s disease is characterized by thyrotoxicosis caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs) synthesized by lymphocytes in the thyroid gland, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies are also seen. This results in excess production of free T3 and free T4 levels and in turn reduces serum TSH levels.

RAIU is used to differentiate Grave’s from other thyroid disorders, here there is diffuse high uptake. Measurement of TRab and TPOs is also done to confirm the diagnosis if the diagnosis clinically is unclear.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) at 24 hours below normal

question: A middle-aged woman who presented with tremors, palpitations, weight loss, and menstrual irregularities is diagnosed with Graves' disease. Which of the following statements would be correct with respect to her thyroid function test?

explanationHtml:
The most common hormone pattern observed in sick euthyroid syndrome (SES) is a decrease in total and unbound T3 levels with normal levels of T4 and TSH. This pattern is called low T3 syndrome.

SES is caused by an acute severe illness in the absence of underlying thyroid disease. T4 to T3 conversion via peripheral deiodination is impaired leading to a fall in T3 corresponding to the severity of illness. There is an adaptive increase in the level of reverse T3 (rT3).

In very sick patients, there can be a dramatic fall in both total T4 and T3 levels. This pattern is called low T4 syndrome and is associated with a poor prognosis.
question:
What is the most common pattern of thyroid hormone levels in a patient with sick euthyroid syndrome?

  1. Decreased T3, Normal T4, Normal TSH
  2. Decreased T3 , Decreased T4, Normal TSH
  3. Normal T3, Normal T4, Increased TSH
  4. Normal T3, Increased T4, Normal TSH

explanationHtml:
An elevated TSH value with low free T4 is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism (Option D).

Option A: In subclinical hypothyroidism, free T4 levels remain normal despite elevated TSH.

Option B: TSH is low in hyperthyroidism.

Option C: The diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism is made along with a deficiency of other pituitary hormones. TSH levels may be low, normal, or slightly increased. The elevation in TSH levels can be attributed to the secretion of immunoreactive but biologically inactive forms of TSH. To confirm the diagnosis, it is essential to detect a low level of unbound T4.

[[figure-1]]
question: On thyroid function test analysis, TSH value was much higher than normal with a low free T4. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image showing localized overactivity (increased uptake) in the left lobe of the thyroid i.e., hot nodule, with suppression of the remainder of the gland, is suggestive of a hypersecreting adenoma.

Other options:

Option B: The likelihood of malignancies like papillary Carcinoma thyroid is low (5%) in the case of a hot nodule.

Option C: Graves disease shows diffusely increased uptake on a thyroid scan.

Option D: Lateral aberrant thyroid presents with swelling of cervical lymph nodes and not thyroid. It is due to skip metastasis from papillary thyroid carcinoma to the ipsilateral cervical lymph nodes.

The thyroid scan appearance in different conditions is shown in the image below:

[[figure-1]]

Diagnostic isotope studies, such as 99mTc-pertechnetate and iodine-123, are becoming less common in thyroid imaging because some warm swellings (5%) which are actually malignant could be mistaken as benign. Isotope scanning is most valuable when assessing a hyperthyroid patient presenting with a nodule or nodularity in the thyroid. It helps to identify overactivity in the gland, which can differentiate between a toxic nodule that suppresses the rest of the gland and a toxic multinodular goitre with multiple areas of increased uptake.
question: The radio-iodine uptake scan of a patient evaluated for swelling of the thyroid is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows the absence of scalp hair and skin, along with calvarial defects(skull bone defects), suggestive of aplasia cutis congenita. This is commonly associated with carbimazole and methimazole.

These drugs can also cause other defects such as:

  • Choanal atresia
  • Tracheoesophageal fistula
  • Fetal goiter
question: Which of the following drugs can cause the condition shown below?

explanationHtml:
Lactating mothers cannot undergo radioiodine therapy. Patients can safely conceive 6 months after undergoing radioiodine treatment.

Absolute contraindications of radioiodine therapy:

  • Active pregnancy
  • Breastfeeding

Radioiodine therapy in patients with severe ophthalmopathy can be given with caution, along with prednisone to prevent exacerbation of ophthalmopathy.
question: Which of the following patients cannot undergo radioiodine therapy?

explanationHtml:
The patient in the given clinical scenario is in the 1st trimester of pregnancy. Propylthiouracil is used in the 1st trimester of gestation because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole.

Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as

  • Aplasia cutis congenita
  • Choanal atresia
  • Treacheosopageal fistula
  • Fetal goiter

However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy.

The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation. This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range.
question: A 25-year-old woman presents with palpitations. She informs you that a urine pregnancy test done one week ago was positive. Her investigations reveal hyperthyroidism. Which of the following antithyroid drugs can be prescribed for her?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of thyroid storm and propylthiouracil is the drug of choice in this patient. This is due to its inhibitory action on peripheral T4 → T3 conversion.

PTU is administered in large doses (500–1000 mg loading dose and 250 mg every 4h) administered orally / via nasogastric tube / per rectum.

Propranolol is also given to reduce symptoms like tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations.
question: A patient undergoing radioactive iodine therapy for a non-toxic multinodular goitre later develops altered sensorium, fever, and vomiting. What is the anti-thyroid drug of choice in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of a non-toxic diffuse goitre. Surgery is rarely indicated in this condition, except for cosmetic reasons, tracheal compression or obstruction of the thoracic inlet.

It is sometimes called simple goitre - because of the absence of nodules, and colloid goitre - because of the presence of uniform follicles that are filled with colloid. It is most commonly caused by iodine deficiency and is often termed endemic goitre.

Most diffuse goitres are benign and asymptomatic. Examination reveals a symmetrically enlarged, non-tender, generally soft gland without palpable nodules. TFTs should be performed in all patients to exclude thyrotoxicosis or hypothyroidism.

If markedly enlarged, it can cause tracheal/oesophagal compression.

Substernal goitre may obstruct the thoracic inlet leading to a positive Pemberton’s sign i.e., facial congestion on bilateral arm elevation due to venous occlusion.

options.text: It is also referred to as simple goitre or colloid goitre
Most commonly caused by iodine deficiency
Thyroid function tests should be performed in all patients with goiter

question: A patient presents with a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. However, she has no features of hyperthyroidism. Which of the following statements about her condition is false?

correctAnswer: B. Glucocorticoids are not indicated for treatment
explanationHtml:
Glucocorticoid treatment is not indicated in silent thyroiditis.

The condition is called silent thyroiditis, as it is painless. When it occurs 3-6 months after pregnancy, it is termed postpartum thyroiditis. The condition is observed in up to 5% of women and it is 3 times more common in women with Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Typically, patients experience a brief phase of thyrotoxicosis lasting 2-4 weeks, followed by hypothyroidism for 4-12 weeks, and then clinical resolution. Often, only one phase is apparent.

In addition to painless goitre, silent thyroiditis can be distinguished from subacute thyroiditis by a normal ESR value and the presence of TPO antibodies.

Severe thyrotoxic symptoms can be managed with a brief course of propranolol, a 20–40 mg dose administered three or four times daily.

Thyroxine replacement may be needed for treating the hypothyroid phase but should be withdrawn after 6–9 months, to enable patient recovery.

explanationHtml:
The clinical effects of levothyroxine replacement are slow to appear. Patients may not experience full relief from symptoms until 3–6 months after normal TSH levels are restored.

If there is no residual function, the daily replacement dose of levothyroxine is usually 1.6 μg/kg body weight (typically 100–150 μg), ideally taken at least 30 minutes before breakfast.

TSH responses are gradual and should be determined 2 months following the initiation of treatment or change in dose. Once the full replacement is achieved and TSH levels are stable, TSH measurement is recommended at annual intervals.

In patients who have developed hypothyroidism following treatment of Graves' disease, lower doses are needed for replacement. This is because there is often underlying autonomous function, necessitating lower replacement doses (typically 75–125 μg/d).

question: Which of the following parameters can help you diagnose a patient with a malignant pheochromocytoma?

explanationHtml:
Norepinephrine is exclusively secreted in patients with extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma.

The PNMT (phenylethanolamine-N-methyl transferase) enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine. This enzyme is absent in extra-adrenal sites. Hence, extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas secrete only norepinephrine and cannot secrete epinephrine.

On the other hand, adrenal pheochromocytomas can secrete norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine in varying amounts depending on the PNMT levels in the tumor.

Extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas or catecholamine-secreting paragangliomas are most commonly found in the abdomen. They commonly arise from the organ of Zuckerkandl.

Cushing's disease is a form of Cushing's syndrome caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor. The high ACTH levels stimulate melanocytes and cause skin hyperpigmentation. This is especially seen over friction-prone areas like knuckles and elbows.

question: You can advise any of the following tests for screening of a patient suspected to be having Cushing's syndrome except:

explanationHtml:
Basal plasma ACTH levels are highest in ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors.

Plasma ACTH > 15pg/ml is suggestive of ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome due to pituitary or ectopic sources. Basal ACTH in pituitary adenoma can be normal or elevated, whereas in an ectopic source the ACTH production is very high. This occurs because a pituitary adenoma retains some sensitivity to the negative feedback mechanism exerted by cortisol, but ectopic tumors remain unaffected.

Plasma ACTH < 5pg/ml is suggestive of ACTH-independent Cushing’s syndrome that can be caused by an adrenal adenoma or exogenous administration of glucocorticoids.
question: In patients with which of the following conditions would you expect to see the highest basal ACTH level?

explanationHtml:

If the MRI brain shows a mass it is suggestive of a pituitary mass of >6 mm in size. However, if the MRI brain does not show a mass it suggests a pituitary tumor of <6mm in size or an ectopic ACTH source.

Note: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test and CRH stimulation test are employed to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH syndrome. A definitive cause can be established only by imaging techniques like MRI for pituitary tumors, CT scan of the chest and abdomen for ectopic ACTH sites. question: Which of the following is the best adrenolytic agent that can be used in the management of patients with adrenocortical carcinoma?

explanationHtml:
Nelson’s syndrome is a rare complication of total bilateral adrenalectomy (TBA). TBA is a procedure used to control hypercortisolism in Cushing's disease (due to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma) when resection of the primary tumor is not possible.

The loss of feedback inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis following TBA increases CRH. This leads to stimulation of ACTH-secreting corticotroph cells, causing enlargement of the original pituitary tumor or the formation of a new one.

Nelson's syndrome is associated with a clinical triad of:

  • Hyperpigmentation
  • Excessive ACTH secretion
  • Corticotroph adenoma

Screening is done with fasting plasma ACTH levels and MRI brain is performed at regular intervals. Prophylactic pituitary irradiation may be recommended to prevent its incidence. The primary treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Patients will also require life-long glucocorticoid replacement, as they do not produce cortisol.

The use of steroidogenic inhibitors in the treatment of Cushing's disease has decreased the need for bilateral adrenalectomy these days.

explanationHtml:
Malignancy does not cause pseudo-Cushing's syndrome. It may cause ectopic ACTH production, leading to true Cushing’s syndrome.

Pseudo-Cushing’s syndrome refers to functional hypercortisolism caused by chronic activation of the HPA axis. It presents with clinical and biochemical features similar to Cushing’s syndrome, making it difficult to differentiate between them. It may occur secondary to the following conditions:

  • Severe major depressive disorder
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome
  • Insulin-resistant obesity
  • Obstructive sleep apnea
  • Chronic alcoholism
  • End-stage renal disease

It usually resolves when the underlying condition is treated.
question: Which of the following is not a cause of pseudo-Cushing's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Primary adrenal insufficiency, also known as Addison’s disease, is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis.

Tuberculous adrenalitis is still a frequent cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developing countries like India. It is characterized by the loss of glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and adrenal androgen secretion.

Glucocorticoid deficiency results in fatigue, lack of energy, weight loss, fever, myalgia, normochromic anemia, and hypoglycemia. Mineralocorticoid deficiency is characterized by nausea, vomiting, low blood pressure, postural hypotension, salt craving, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Adrenal androgen deficiency manifests as a lack of energy, dry itchy skin, loss of libido, and loss of axillary and pubic hair (in women).

Hyperpigmentation is seen in primary adrenal insufficiency due to excess proopiomelanocortin-derived peptides. Hyperpigmentation is not seen in secondary adrenal insufficiency.

The diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency can be made with the short cosyntropin test (cortisol level <450-500nmol/L sampled 30 to 60 minutes after ACTH stimulation is diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency). Plasma ACTH, plasma renin, and serum aldosterone can help differentiate primary from secondary causes. Primary adrenal insufficiency will show elevated ACTH and a compensatory elevation in renin levels due to decreased aldosterone in the body. In secondary adrenal insufficiency, ACTH is low with normal renin and aldosterone.

Treatment includes glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and adrenal androgen replacement.

Other options:

Option B: Patients with adrenocortical carcinoma present with features of glucocorticoid and adrenal androgen excess, and not adrenal insufficiency.

Options C and D: Hypernephroma and medullary carcinoma thyroid are not associated with Addison's disease.
question: Addison's disease is commonly associated with ____

explanationHtml:
Tuberculosis is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in India and other developing countries.

Idiopathic atrophy due to autoimmune conditions is the most common cause in developed countries.
question: What is the most common cause of adrenal insufficiency in India?

explanationHtml:
Elevated ACTH and reduced cortisol levels are seen in primary adrenal insufficiency. It is not a feature of MEN 4 syndrome.

The following syndromes are associated with primary adrenal insufficiency:

  • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1
  • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2
  • Triple-A syndrome
  • Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome
  • Kearns-Sayre syndrome
  • IMAGe syndrome
question: In a patient with reduced cortisol and elevated ACTH, which of the following would not be part of your differential diagnoses?

explanationHtml:
The given image showing skin hyperpigmentation in a patient with severe dizziness and a history of autoimmune thyroiditis points to a diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Hyperglycemia is not a feature of this condition. Hypocortisolism leads to hypoglycemia in these patients.

Addison’s disease is primary adrenal insufficiency characterized by the disruption of glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and androgen secretion. Primary adrenal insufficiency is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis and coincident autoimmune disease occurring in these patients most frequently includes thyroid autoimmune disease, vitiligo, and premature ovarian failure.

question: A 50-year-old woman was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and was started on levothyroxine 2 weeks ago. She now presents to your clinic with abdominal pain and dizziness. The left and right images below show her current appearance and her appearance last month, respectively. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hyponatremia is the most common biochemical abnormality seen at presentation in patients with adrenal insufficiency. It is observed in 80% of the patients at presentation.

Hyponatremia is caused by:

  • Mineralocorticoid deficiency
  • Diminished inhibition of ADH release by cortisol, resulting in mild SIADH during secondary adrenal insufficiency

Hyperkalemia is diagnosed in 40% of the patients during initial diagnosis.

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of adrenal insufficiency. The confirmatory test for diagnosis is the ACTH stimulation test or short cosyntropin stimulation test.

Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia are seen. Plasma levels of ACTH, renin and aldosterone are used to differentiate between primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency.

question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea for the past 3 days. She has been excessively tired and dizzy for the past 2 weeks. On examination, there are patches of hyperpigmented skin. Blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg and blood glucose is 50 mg/dl. How will you confirm the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Normal renin and aldosterone levels
explanationHtml:
Pituitary MRI is indicated in secondary adrenal insufficiency which presents with the following parameters:

  • Low-normal ACTH level
  • Normal renin level
  • Normal aldosterone level

The following findings are seen in primary adrenal insufficiency:

  • High ACTH levels
  • High renin
  • Low aldosterone levels

Pituitary MRIs are not required in primary adrenal insufficiency. The fact that a pituitary MRI is done itself gives a hint towards secondary adrenal insufficiency.

options.text: High renin and low aldosterone levels
Low renin and high aldosterone levels

question: A 20-year-old woman is being evaluated for adrenal insufficiency. You decide to check her serum levels of ACTH, renin, and aldosterone. Which of the following laboratory findings would prompt you to subsequently order a pituitary MRI?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of an adrenal crisis triggered by missed medication. In this patient who is a known case of adrenal insufficiency, IV hydrocortisone is the drug of choice.

However, in patients with newly diagnosed adrenal insufficiency, dexamethasone is used for the treatment of adrenal crisis. This is because dexamethasone is not measured in cortisol assays and would not interfere with the diagnostic tests, whereas hydrocortisone interferes with cortisol assays.

Acute adrenal insufficiency requires the immediate initiation of the following therapeutic strategies:

  • Rehydration - saline infusion at an initial rate of 1 L/h with continuous cardiac monitoring.
  • Glucocorticoid replacement - bolus injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone, followed by the maintenance dose of 100–200 mg over 24h.
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement - initiated once the daily hydrocortisone dose has been reduced to <50 mg as higher doses of hydrocortisone have sufficient mineralocorticoid action.
question: A 33-year-old man collapses during a family vacation. At the hospital, blood pressure is found to be 86/52 mm Hg, and random blood sugar is 49 mg/dl. His wife says that he has been on treatment for Addison's disease for two years but had forgotten to pack his medication for the trip. What is the drug of choice for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Hyperkalemia will not improve following administration of dexamethasone. Dexamethasone is a long-acting steroid with glucocorticoid action. It has no effect on hyperkalemia, which is mediated by mineralocorticoids.

Hyponatremia is chiefly due to mineralocorticoid deficiency, however, hypocortisolism causes hyponatremia due to loss of feedback inhibition of ADH resulting in SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion).

Hypocortisolism can also cause postural hypotension as cortisol regulates vascular tone by potentiating the effects of vasoconstrictors. Thus on administration dexamethasone hyponatremia and postural hypotension will improve as dexamethasone has glucocorticoid action but hyperkalemia will not improve.

Dexamethasone is used in patients with newly diagnosed adrenal insufficiency as it does not interfere with serum cortisol measurement.

question: A patient who presented with an adrenal crisis is undergoing treatment with dexamethasone. Which of the following abnormalities will not improve with this treatment?

explanationHtml:
A non-functioning pituitary adenoma causes hypopituitarism due to compression of the pituitary stalk. This results in secondary adrenal insufficiency. Hyperpigmentation is not a feature.

This condition is characterized by an alabaster-like paleness due to the lack of ACTH secretion. In primary adrenal insufficiency, hyperpigmentation occurs as a result of elevated ACTH.
question: A 62-year-old woman who was diagnosed with a non-functioning pituitary adenoma develops features of adrenal insufficiency. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Does not affect the oral mucosa
explanationHtml:
Addison's disease causes patchy hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa.

A characteristic sign of primary adrenal insufficiency is hyperpigmentation, which becomes more prominent in friction-prone areas such as the palmar creases, dorsal feet, and nipples due to ACTH-driven melanocyte activation.

options.text: Does not affect the oral mucosa

question: Which of the following  is incorrect with respect to Addisonian pigmentation?

explanationHtml:
Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is the most common cause of mineralocorticoid excess. It causes primary hyperaldosteronism. Other causes of primary hyperaldosteronism are:

  • Conn’s syndrome – Unilateral adrenal adenoma
  • Glucocorticoid-remediable hyperaldosteronism (< 1%)

Other causes of mineralocorticoid excess are as follows:

  • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
  • Syndrome of apparent mineralocorticoid excess (SAME)
  • Adrenocortical carcinoma
  • Progesterone-induced hypertension
  • Cushing’s syndrome

Liddle’s syndrome is due to a mutation of ENaC subunits. This results in reduced degradation of ENaC channels, causing prolonged mineralocorticoid action.
question: What is the most common cause of mineralocorticoid excess?

explanationHtml:
Features of Primary Hyperaldosteronism:

  • Hypokalemia
  • Hypertension
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Polyuria (due to ANP)
  • Polydipsia (consequence of polyuria)
  • Muscle weakness

In Conn’s syndrome, volume expansion occurs, but a salt-escape mechanism prevents the development of pedal edema. Hypernatremia-induced volume expansion causes right atrial dilation, which triggers atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) release, promoting compensatory diuresis and preventing fluid accumulation and edema despite sodium retention.
question: Which of the following clinical features will you not expect to see in a patient with Conn's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Conn syndrome is a cause of primary hyperaldosteronism that presents with hypertension and low levels of renin.

Elevated aldosterone levels cause negative feedback in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and results in decreased renin production.
question: A 39-year-old man is referred for evaluation of severe hypertension that has not improved despite being on 3 anti-hypertensive drugs. The presence of decreased plasma renin activity in this patient would point to which of the following diagnoses?

explanationHtml:
Hypokalemic hypertension is suggestive of hyperaldosteronism. The screening test of choice is a measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone levels to calculate the aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR).

ARR must be estimated in patients with hypertension and any one of the following features:

  • Drug resistance
  • Hypokalemia
  • Adrenal mass
  • Onset before 40 years of age

Prior to the determination of ARR, hypokalemia correction must be done. If the patient is on spironolactone, it must be stopped 4 weeks prior to testing. Other blood pressure medication may be continued.

ARR screen is considered positive when:

  • ARR > 750 pmol/L : ng/mL per hour
  • Aldosterone > 450 pmol/L

Option A: ACTH stimulation test is used for the diagnosis of Addison’s disease. It presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia.

Options B and C: If ARR is positive, CT abdomen and adrenal vein sampling are used for confirmation of the diagnosis.
question: Which of the following is the best initial investigation in a patient with hypokalemic hypertension?

explanationHtml:
An elevated aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR) is indicative of primary hyperaldosteronism. Metyrapone stimulation test is used in the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency, not hyperaldosteronism.

A failure of suppression of aldosterone levels below 140 pmol/L indicates autonomous aldosterone production, which is the hallmark of primary hyperaldosteronism. This principle is used in the following tests:

  • Saline infusion test - IV administration of 2L of physiological saline over 4 hours
  • Oral sodium loading test - oral sodium given over 3 days
  • Fludrocortisone suppression test - given IV over 4 days

These tests may be used to confirm the diagnosis in patients with elevated ARR, but are not necessary in cases of overt hypokalemic hypertension, strongly positive ARR, and high aldosterone.
question: Which of the following tests is not performed in patients with an elevated aldosterone-renin ratio?

explanationHtml:
Weight loss is a clinical feature of diabetes mellitus, not weight gain.

Diabetes mellitus refers to a group of common metabolic disorders that result in hyperglycemia. It causes the following classical triad of symptoms:

  • Polyuria - due to osmotic diuresis
  • Polydipsia - triggered by the resulting hypovolemia
  • Weight loss - due to catabolic state

Note: Obesity is a risk factor, not a symptom of type 2 diabetes mellitus and plays a role in its pathogenesis. Increase in the adipocyte mass leads to an increase in the level of circulating free fatty acids. Free fatty acids impair glucose utilization in skeletal muscles, promote glucose production by the liver, and impair beta-cell function.

question: Which of the following is not a clinical feature of diabetes mellitus?

correctAnswer: A. Antibodies against zinc transporters may be present
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is an autoimmune disease associated with the following immunologic markers:

  • Antibodies against zinc transporter (ZnT-8)
  • Islet cells antibodies (ICA)
  • Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GAD)
  • Insulin autoantibodies (IAA)

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the OPD by his worried mother as he urinates more than ten times a day and is always drinking water. She also reports that despite eating more than his brother did at that age, he is not gaining any weight. Random blood glucose is 252 mg/dl. Which of the following statements is true about this condition?

explanationHtml:
The major susceptibility gene for type 1 diabetes mellitus is located in the HLA region of chromosome 6.

Type I diabetes mellitus occurs in genetically susceptible individuals and is usually triggered by infections. The HLA complex is most commonly involved. The common HLA associations include:

  • Causative - HLA-DQA1*0501 and DQB*0201
  • Protective - HLA-DQA1*0102, DQB1*0602, DRB1*1501

Other genomic associations of type I diabetes mellitus include the CTLA-4 gene and IL-2 receptor.

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is associated with mutations in the calpain-10 gene on chromosome 2. It results in insulin resistance.

question: Which chromosome contains the major susceptible gene for type 1 diabetes mellitus?

explanationHtml:
In type 2 diabetes mellitus increased fasting blood sugar is predominantly due to increased hepatic gluconeogenesis.

In the postprandial period, there is a rise in peripheral blood glucose levels. Due to insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes mellitus, there is reduced peripheral uptake of glucose by insulin-sensitive tissues like the liver and skeletal muscles. This results in reduced glucose utilization by skeletal muscles as well as reduced glycogenesis in the liver and skeletal muscles. This results in increased postprandial plasma glucose levels.
Increased hepatic glucose output predominantly accounts for increased FPG levels, whereas decreased peripheral glucose utilization results in postprandial hyperglycemia.

question: Which of the following mechanisms is predominantly responsible for an increase in the fasting plasma glucose level of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus?

correctAnswer: B. Maturity-onset diabetes of the young
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY).

MODY is a monogenic form of diabetes mellitus that is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion. It affects young adults < 25 years of age. It occurs due to reduced insulin secretion. Etiological factors of type 1 and 2 diabetes such as insulin resistance, obesity, and antibodies are not associated with this condition.

Stable hyperglycemia is usually seen, hence complications like diabetic ketoacidosis are uncommon. Macrovascular complications like hyperlipidemia or hypertension are not seen. It is treated with sulfonylureas.

Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA) is a form of type 1 diabetes that occurs between 30-50 years of age.

question:
A 22-year-old woman presents with fatigue and weight loss for the past 6 months. She tells you that her father is also a diabetic. Further evaluation reveals the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Body mass index - 21 kg/m2

Fasting blood sugar - 252 mg/dl

Glycosylated hemoglobin - 8.2%

Urinalysis for ketones - Negative

correctAnswer: B. MODY 4 is the most common form
explanationHtml:
MODY 3 is the most common form of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), accounting for two-thirds of all the cases.

MODY is a monogenic form of diabetes mellitus that is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion. It affects young adults <25 years of age. There are a total of 11 types of MODY based on mutations involves. Some of the affected genes include:

  • Types 1,3,5: HNF (Hepatocyte nuclear transcription factor) mutation
  • Type 2: Glucokinase mutation
  • Type 4: IPF 1 (Insulin Promotor Factor-1) mutation

These mutations result in impaired glucose-induced insulin secretion resulting in insulinopenia.

options.text: MODY 4 is the most common form

question: All of the following are true about maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) except:

correctAnswer: D. Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults
explanationHtml:
Type 1 diabetes mellitus in an adult is suggestive of latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA).

LADA is common in thin-built adults between 30-50 years and is associated with autoantibodies. As the progression of the disease is less rapid than in children, clinical features may mimic type 2 diabetes. However, patients usually require insulin treatment within 5 years.

Option A: Patients with latent diabetes become diabetic under stressful conditions. However, upon removal of stress, they become non-diabetic.

Option B: MODY or maturity-onset diabetes of the young is a monogenic form of diabetes that occurs < 25 years. There is impaired insulin secretion, but no antibodies.

Option C: Brittle diabetes is seen in children with type 1 DM. It presents with wide fluctuation in blood sugar levels.

question: Which of the following would cause type 1 diabetes in an adult patient?

explanationHtml:
Fragile X syndrome is not associated with diabetes mellitus.

Genetic syndromes associated with diabetes include:

  • Prader-Willi syndrome
  • Friedreich’s ataxia
  • Wolfram’s syndrome
  • Down’s syndrome
  • Klinefelter’s and Turner’s syndrome
  • Huntington’s chorea
  • Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome
  • Myotonic dystrophy
  • Porphyria

Diseases of the exocrine pancreas causing diabetes:

  • Hemochromatosis
  • Pancreatitis
  • Neoplasia
  • Cystic fibrosis

Endocrinopathies causing diabetes:

  • Acromegaly
  • Cushing’s syndrome
  • Glucagonoma
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Hyperthyroidism

question: Which of the following patients can be diagnosed with diabetes mellitus?

explanationHtml:
HbA1c and fasting blood glucose are used for screening diabetes mellitus in asymptomatic individuals.

HbA1c refers to glycated hemoglobin and it serves as a long-term indicator for blood glucose levels (8 to 12 weeks).

  • Normal < 5.7 %
  • Abnormal glucose homeostasis: 5.7 to 6.4 %
  • Diabetes mellitus: ≥ 6.5%

HbA1c also serves as a prognostic indicator for glycemic control.

A 46-year-old man presents to his physician for a routine health evaluation. He is concerned that he might have diabetes as his three brothers have all been diagnosed with diabetes. He does not have any complaints. Which of the following tests can be employed in this patient?

  2. Random blood glucose

  4. Glycosylated hemoglobin level
  5. Postprandial blood glucose

correctAnswer: C. Blood glucose levels between 140 and 199 mg/dL following oral glucose tolerance test
explanationHtml:
Impaired glucose tolerance is defined as blood glucose levels between 140-199 mg/dL following an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).

Impaired fasting glucose is when the fasting blood glucose is between 100 to 125 mg/dL.

question: Which of the following can be termed impaired glucose tolerance?

correctAnswer: A. All individuals > 35 years must undergo screening every 3 years
explanationHtml:
The ADA recommends screening for type 2 diabetes mellitus in all asymptomatic individuals > 35 years every 3 years.

The tests used for screening are:

  • HbA1c levels
  • Fasting blood glucose levels

Individuals can be screened earlier if they are overweight with BMI >25 kg/m2 and have one of the following risk factors:

  • Family history of diabetes
  • History of cardiovascular diseases
  • History of gestational diabetes mellitus or delivery of a baby > 4 kg
  • Obesity (BMI ≥25 kg/m2)
  • Physical inactivity
  • Hypertension (≥140/90 mm Hg)
  • HDL cholesterol < 35 mg/dL
  • Triglycerides >250 mg/dL
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome or acanthosis nigricans

Note- If an individual has a test result near the margins of the diagnostic threshold, a close follow-up should be done and repeat the test in 3–6 months.

explanationHtml:
Insulin is the best initial drug of choice when HbA1c is > 9% at diagnosis.

Insulin is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes in the following cases:

  • Inadequate glycemic control with 2 or more oral agents
  • HbA1c > 9% at diagnosis

In patients with HbA1c < 9%, metformin is the drug of choice.

They tell you that she is taking an oral medication for diabetes. On examination, the patient was disoriented, and CBG was 45 mg/dl. Which of the following drugs most likely played a role in the patient’s current presentation?

explanationHtml:
Hydrochlorthiazide belongs to the thiazide group of diuretics, that can cause dyslipidemia and hyperglycemia. Hence they are not preferred for use in diabetic hypertensives.

The antihypertensive drug of choice in diabetes mellitus include angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs).

question: A 40-year-old male patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus is now diagnosed with hypertension. Which of the following antihypertensive drugs will you not prefer in this patient?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a urinary tract infection (UTI). This adverse effect occurs as a result of dapagliflozin use.

The group of sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 or SGLT-2 inhibitors includes drugs like dapagliflozin and canagliflozin. These drugs prevent glucose reabsorption in the renal tubules and cause loss of sodium and glucose.

question: A type 2 diabetic patient who was recently started on treatment complains of frequent urination, fever, and burning micturition. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these symptoms?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario describes the sliding scale method. Rapid-acting insulins such as glulisine are used.

Sliding scale refers to the administration of insulin as a bolus dose based on the blood sugar level before the meal. Using this principle, the insulin dose is titrated every time according to pre-meal glucose levels to determine insulin requirement. Hence, rapid-acting insulin is preferred.

This method requires a fixed carbohydrate intake at every meal. It is used for the short-term management of hospitalized patients, especially when the frequency or quantity of food intake is very variable.

It does not deliver insulin in a physiological manner, hence is not a preferred long-term strategy for glycemic control.

question: A 65-year-old man is hospitalized with pneumonia. He is a known patient of type 2 diabetes. During the hospital stay, his appetite is poor and his oral intake is irregular. The physician decides to administer rapid-acting insulin based on high blood sugar values. Which of the following would he use?

correctAnswer: C. It does not cause hypoglycemia
explanationHtml:
Afrezza is an inhalational form of insulin that can cause hypoglycemia.

It is a rapid-acting form of insulin that is administered at the beginning of each meal. Peak levels are achieved 12-15 minutes later.

Adverse effects include hypoglycemia, cough, throat pain, or irritation. It may cause acute bronchospasm in patients with asthma, COPD, as well as active smokers. Hence, it is contraindicated in these condition.

question: Which of the following is incorrect about Afrezza?

explanationHtml:

Non-diabetic clinical applications of insulin include:

  • To examine the completion of truncal vagotomy

question: A 60-year-old man presents to the casualty with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain. His blood sugar levels are 421 mg/dl and urine ketones are 3+. He is started on IV normal saline and insulin infusion. Which of the following should he be monitored for?

correctAnswer: C. Early morning hyperglycemia with normal blood glucose levels at 3 am
explanationHtml:
Dawn phenomenon refers to normal blood glucose levels at 3 am followed by early morning hyperglycemia.

This occurs due to an early morning surge in plasma growth hormone and cortisol levels, which have an insulin-antagonistic action. In normal individuals, this is countered by increased early morning insulin secretion. However, in diabetic patients, insulin secretion is disrupted which results in the unopposed action of growth hormone. Hence, there will be resulting hyperglycemia.
