Early morning hyperglycemia with normal blood glucose levels at 3 am
Early morning hypoglycemia with hyperglycemia at 3 am

question: Dawn phenomenon is clinically suspected when a patient shows which of the following findings?

explanationHtml:
When a patient needs > 200 units of insulin per day, they are said to have developed insulin resistance.

Some causes of insulin resistance are as follows:

  • Werner syndrome
  • Lipodystrophy syndrome
  • Ataxia-telangiectasia
  • Polycystic ovarian disease

Insulin resistance can present as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Types, Clinical Features And Management
question: A patient is said to have developed insulin resistance when the required insulin dosage is which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and the first step is to assess the arterial blood gas (ABG) levels. This precedes correction of fluid balance, as assessment of the current status of the patient is necessary before beginning treatment. A baseline pH and electrolyte level must be obtained.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the most serious complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. The symptoms include dehydration, nausea, vomiting, confusion, drowsiness, and coma in severe cases.

In DKA, the insulin-to-glucagon ratio is decreased which promotes gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketone body formation in the liver. Ketone bodies exist as ketoacids at physiological pH which are neutralized by bicarbonate. As bicarbonate stores are depleted, metabolic acidosis ensues. Increased lactic acid production also contributes to the acidosis.

The diagnostic biochemical criteria for DKA includes:

  • Hyperglycemia (>250 mg/dL)
  • Venous pH <7.3
  • Plasma/serum bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L
  • Increased anion gap
  • Ketonemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate [BOHB] >3 mmol/L) and ketonuria

Signs of ketoacidosis:

  • Kussmaul breathing (deep, heavy, non-labored rapid breathing)
  • Fruity breath odor (acetone)
  • Prolonged Q-T interval
  • Diminished neurocognitive function
  • Coma

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Types, Clinical Features And Management

options.text: 2-3 L of normal saline over 1-3 hours
Insulin bolus of 0.1 units/kg given IV

question: A 12-year-old child who is known to have type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with confusion and drowsiness. Her mother says that she seems to be breathing very fast. On examination, mucous membranes are dry and blood pressure is 70/50 mm Hg. Random blood glucose is 415 mg/dl and urine ketones are 4+. What is the next best step in management?

correctAnswer: B. Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
explanationHtml:
The elevated levels of triglycerides (TG) and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) in diabetes mellitus (DM) are due to decreased activity of lipoprotein lipase (LpL) and increased activity of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL).

Insulin normally has an inhibitory action on HSL and induces LpL on capillary walls. There is an absolute or relative deficiency of insulin in DM. In DM, the activity of LpL is decreased and HSL is increased.

The increased activity of HSL results in increased mobilisation of fat stores towards lipolysis releasing fatty acids. These fatty acids are partly cleared by the liver, resulting in increased synthesis of VLDL and TG, resulting in dyslipidemia. They can accumulate in the liver, resulting in steatosis (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease).

The reduced activity of LpL prevents the clearing of TG and VLDL in the bloodstream and their levels remain elevated.

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Types, Clinical Features And Management

options.text: Increased activity of lipoprotein lipase and decreased activity of hormone sensitive lipase
Increased activity of hormone sensitive lipase and decreased lipoprotein lipase activity
Increase in peripheral function of LDL receptors
Increased in activity of hepatic lipase

question: Which of the following is responsible for the elevated levels of TG and VLDL in diabetes mellitus?

explanationHtml:
Fasting blood sugar >126 mg/dL and 2-hour postprandial blood sugar >200 mg/dl can be used as screening tests for diabetes in a primary health center (PHC).

HbA1c estimation is usually unavailable for screening at many PHCs due to low resources. In India, facilities for HbA1c estimation are usually available only at tertiary centers.

Random blood sugar >200 mg/dL can be used for diagnosis only if the patient presents with symptoms of diabetes, hence it is not a useful screening test.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Types, Clinical Features And Management
question:
In a PHC, which of the following initial screening tests are used to diagnose diabetes?

  1. HbA1c >6.5
  2. Fasting blood sugar >126mg/dL
  3. Random blood sugar >200mg/dL
  4. 2 hour post glucose load blood sugar

explanationHtml:
In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), serum bicarbonate is usually < 15. Serum HCO3 > 15 meq/L is suggestive of alcoholic ketoacidosis.

DKA is an acute complication of type 1 diabetes mellitus. It is usually precipitated by absolute or relative insulin deficiency caused by increased metabolic demand (infections) or insulin noncompliance.

The common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain. The common signs include Kussmaul breathing, fruity odor of the breath, dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, and delirium.

The diagnosis of DKA is made based on the following parameters:

  • Hyperglycemia > 250 mg/dl
  • Ketosis or ketones in urine
  • Metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.3
  • HCO3 < 15-18 mEq/L
  • High anion gap due to ketoacids and lactic acidosis

Hyponatremia is seen as a result of hyperglycemia (osmotic shift causes dilutional hyponatremia). Normal sodium levels on admission indicate severe dehydration. Despite a total-body potassium deficit, the serum Potassium at presentation may be mildly elevated, secondary to the acidosis and volume depletion.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following is not a feature of diabetic ketoacidosis?

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice for controlling hyperglycemia in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is short-acting insulin, preferably regular insulin.

Intermediate (such as lente insulin and NPH), long-acting insulins, and oral hypoglycemic agents are never used in the initial management of DKA.

The mainstay of treatment is the administration of normal saline followed by infusion of short-acting insulin. The precipitating event must be identified and treated. Careful monitoring of K+ levels and replacement in the later stages is required, as insulin therapy causes hypokalemia.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A 19-year-old woman with a history of type 1 diabetes is brought to the ER with confusion, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Investigations show blood glucose of 520 mg/dl and urine positive for ketone bodies. Which of the following is the drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
Cerebral edema is the leading cause of mortality in children with diabetic ketoacidosis.

The osmolar gradient generated due to the high blood glucose level results in water shift from the intracellular fluid (ICF) to the extracellular fluid (ECF) space and leads to the contraction of cell volume. Correction with insulin and intravenous fluids can result in a rapid reduction in effective osmolarity, reversal of the fluid shift, and result in cerebral edema.

Complications of diabetic ketoacidosis include:

  • Cerebral edema – especially in children
  • Cardiac arrhythmia - due to electrolyte imbalance
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
  • Venous thrombosis
  • Acute gastric dilation
  • Acute kidney injury
  • Intestinal necrosis
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Mucormycosis
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following is the leading cause of death in children with diabetic ketoacidosis?

explanationHtml:
In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), severe abdominal pain can mimic acute pancreatitis. Serum lipase is the best test to rule out this condition. It must then be confirmed by imaging (USG or CT abdomen).

Serum amylase is an unreliable indicator as DKA is associated with hyperamylasemia of salivary origin.

Serum and urine trypsinogen may be elevated in early pancreatitis but are not used for diagnosis. Fecal elastase is elevated in chronic pancreatitis.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has severe abdominal pain. Which of the following is the recommended test to rule out acute pancreatitis?

correctAnswer: C. Start IV fluids and correct hypokalemia first, then administer IV regular insulin
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). On confirming the diagnosis, IV fluids must be started. If the initial serum potassium < 3.3 meq/L, insulin should be administered only after the correction of hypokalemia.

This is because treatment with insulin and fluids can worsen hypokalemia by the following mechanisms:

  • Insulin causes the shift of K+ ions into cells
  • Resolution of the acidosis also promotes K+ entry into cells
  • Urinary loss of K+ salts of organic acids

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management

options.text: Start IV fluids, administer IV regular insulin, and then correct hypokalemia
Start IV fluids, administer subcutaneous bolus of insulin and correct hypokalemia concurrently
Start IV fluids and correct hypokalemia first, then administer IV regular insulin
Administer IV regular insulin with KCl first , then start IV fluids once the K+ level is corrected

question:
A 15-year old boy presents with persistent vomiting for one day. Laboratory investigations reveal the following. What is the best sequence of management?

Random blood glucose: 400 mg/dl

Serum sodium: 133 mEq/L

Serum potassium: 3 mEq/L

Urine ketone bodies: 4+

explanationHtml:
Hypotension and tachycardia are common features of both hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS) and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

In DKA, insulin deficiency and an increase in counter-regulatory hormones lead to shunting of free fatty acids to form ketone bodies. The ketoacids increase the anion gap and cause low pH. In HHS, there is still some insulin available. Hence, there are no ketones formed, and the patient has normal pH and pCO2.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Distinguishing features between hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state and diabetic ketoacidosis include all  of the following except:

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS). Kussmaul's breathing is not a feature of HHS.

HHS is commonly seen in older adults suffering from type 2 diabetes mellitus. Patients can present with the following features:

  • Polyuria
  • Polydipsia
  • Lethargy
  • Altered sensorium, coma
  • Seizures
  • Severe dehydration

The following lab values are seen:

  • Blood glucose of 600-1200 mg/dl
  • Serum osmolality > 350 mOsm/L
  • Prerenal azotemia due to dehydration
  • Pseudohyponatremia may be seen due to hyperglycemia
  • Normal pH and ketones

The mainstay of management is fluid replacement, IV regular insulin, along with potassium replacement.

Heparin can be given prophylactically as volume contraction can increase the risk of venous thrombosis.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: An elderly man is brought to the hospital with confusion and drowsiness. His son says that he has been urinating more frequently than normal and eating very little over the past 1 week. Capillary blood glucose is 800 mg/dl.  Which of the following would not be seen in this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Increased triglycerides and decreased HDL
explanationHtml:
Dyslipidemia commonly occurs as a complication of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The most common pattern is as follows:

  • Increased triglyceride levels - due to increased glucose and free fatty acids, decreased lipolysis of VLDL.
  • Decreased HDL levels

Though diabetes does not increase LDL levels, there is increased atherogenicity as the existing LDL molecules are more easily glycated and susceptible to oxidation.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: What is the most common pattern of dyslipidemia associated with diabetes mellitus?

explanationHtml:
Dyslipidemia is more commonly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

It is less common in type 1 and gestational diabetes. Maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY) is not associated with dyslipidemia.

Note: Saroglitazar is a more advanced drug that reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients. It acts on PPAR alpha and gamma receptors.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management

options.text: Maturity onset diabetes of the young

question: Dyslipidemia is more commonly associated with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
According to the ADA guidelines, a treatment goal of postprandial plasma glucose < 180 mg/dL must be followed in adults with diabetes.

In younger individuals or those with other cardiovascular risk factors, the target blood pressure is < 130/80 mm Hg. Although not a treatment goal, the ADA also recommends triglyceride levels be maintained at < 150 mg/dl.

Note: Saroglitazar is a more advanced drug that reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients. It acts on PPAR alpha and gamma receptors.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: You have started a 40-year-old man on treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia. Which of the following is not an appropriate target for this patient?

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice in this diabetic patient with hypertension is losartan.

Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE inhibitors) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are the first-line drugs in diabetic hypertensives. Among ARBs, the drug of choice is telmisartan (acts on PPAR receptor).

They reduce both macrovascular and microvascular complications and have a nephroprotective effect. However, they are contraindicated in chronic kidney disease as they can cause a further decline in GFR.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A middle-aged patient with type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with essential hypertension. What is the antihypertensive drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
The earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy is an increase in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

It occurs as a result of glomerular hyperperfusion and renal hypertrophy. The following sequence of changes are seen in diabetic nephropathy:

  • Increased GFR
  • Incipient diabetic nephropathy - microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day albumin)
    • Diagnostic marker to detect early diabetic nephropathy
    • Indicator of long-term cardiovascular disease
  • Overt diabetic nephropathy - macroalbuminuria ( >300 mg/day albumin)
  • End-stage renal disease

[[figure-1]]
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following is the earliest manifestation of diabetic nephropathy?

explanationHtml:
Albumin of 30-300 mg/day refers to microalbuminuria. It can be unreliable in the diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy.

It is not required to diagnose nephropathy as it is very variable. Non-albuminuric diabetic nephropathy may occur in some patients and regression of albuminuria may be seen in type 1 diabetics.

Diabetic nephropathy can be diagnosed if the following are satisfied:

  • Reduced GFR (< 60 mL/min/1.73 m2) with or without persistent albuminuria (> 30 mg/day or urine PCR > 30 mg/g)
  • Long duration of diabetes or established diabetic retinopathy
  • Other etiologies are ruled out

Long duration in type 1 diabetes refers to 5 years after diagnosis. On the other hand, patients with type 2 diabetes are exposed to hyperglycemia and prediabetes for a long time even before diagnosis. Hence, at the time of diagnosis, patients with type 2 diabetes are considered to have had the disorder for a duration sufficiently long to produce kidney disease.

However, a clinical diagnosis of diabetic nephropathy can be made in patients with established retinopathy, even if the duration of diabetes is short.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A 15-year-old boy has been on treatment for type 1 diabetes mellitus since the age of 10 years. His physician decides to begin screening for diabetic nephropathy. Which of the following is not always a reliable indicator of this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Pancreatic transplantation can improve proteinuria at an early stage
explanationHtml:
Pancreatic transplantation can help improve proteinuria at an early stage. Successful pancreatic transplantation can have the following effects:

  • Prevention of diabetic nephropathy and regression of albuminuria in early stages.
  • Stabilization and improvement of diabetic neuropathy and retinopathy
  • Increase in HDL with reduction in LDL and triglycerides

Option B: Strict glycemic control can prevent or revert microalbuminuria.

Option C: The ADA does not suggest restrictions of protein intake in diabetic patients with albuminuria because studies have failed to prove its benefits.

Option D: Microalbuminuria is an indicator of long-term cardiovascular morbidity.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management

options.text: Pancreatic transplantation can improve proteinuria at an early stage
Strict glycemic control is unlikely to prevent microalbuminuria
Dietary protein restriction can benefit diabetic patients with albuminuria
Microalbuminuria is not an indicator of long-term cardiovascular morbidity

question: Which of the following statements about diabetic nephropathy is true?

explanationHtml:
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACEI) inhibitors or angiotensin-receptor blockers (ARB) are recommended to reduce the progression of diabetic nephropathy. It has the following effects:

  • Reduction of albuminuria
  • Reduces the associated decline in GFR

The mainstay of management of diabetic nephropathy includes control of blood sugar and blood pressure, inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone(RAAS) system, and inhibitors of SGLT2 to halt the progression of the disease.

RAAS inhibitors include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or direct renin inhibitors.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is found to have a 24-hour urinary albumin of 250 mg. Which of the following drugs may be prescribed to reduce the progression of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The characteristic lesion of diabetic nephropathy is nodular or intercapillary glomerulosclerosis, also called Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules. It is pathognomonic for this condition.

The following image shows Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.

[[figure-1]]

Other non-specific findings seen on biopsy include:

  • Glomerular basement membrane (GBM) thickening - highly sensitive
  • Diffuse glomerulosclerosis - most common pattern, due to diffuse mesangial thickening
  • Fibrin cap - accumulation of hyaline material within the capillary loop
  • Capsular drop - accumulation of hyaline material attached to the Bowman's capsule
  • Armani-Ebstein reaction - collection of glycogen clumps within the renal tubules due to tubular injury

Renal biopsy is done to rule out other causes of renal failure. The indications for renal biopsy in diabetic nephropathy are:

  • Absence of diabetic retinopathy
  • Absence of edema
  • Absence of frothing and proteinuria
  • Absence of hypertension
  • Presence of microscopic hematuria or features of nephritic syndrome
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A pathologist is studying a renal biopsy sample from a patient with suspected diabetic nephropathy. Which of the following biopsy findings is pathognomonic for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Type IV renal tubular acidosis (RTA) may occur in individuals with diabetes mellitus types 1 and 2.

Type IV RTA occurs due to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism. Low plasma renin activity is common in diabetic patients due to:

  • Impaired conversion of prorenin to renin
  • Volume expansion in diabetic nephropathy suppresses renin release

These individuals have a tendency to develop hyperkalemia and acidemia, which can be exacerbated by the use of ACEI and ARBs. Hence, these drugs should be avoided.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following types of renal tubular acidosis can develop in individuals with diabetes mellitus?

correctAnswer: B. Immediately at the time of diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Patients with type 2 diabetes should undergo a comprehensive ophthalmological examination to screen for diabetic retinopathy at diagnosis, followed by an annual examination of the fundus.

In patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, screening for retinopathy is recommended 3 to 5 years after diagnosis. Annual fundal examination is recommended thereafter.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management

options.text: Immediately at the time of diagnosis

question: A 45-year-old man has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus. When should you refer him to an ophthalmologist?

explanationHtml:
Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Guidelines:

  • Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus: Screening should commence 3-5 years after diagnosis.
  • Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Screening is recommended at the time of diagnosis. This is due to the often prolonged asymptomatic period of hyperglycemia in Type 2 diabetes, which increases the likelihood of complications being present at diagnosis.

Diabetic retinopathy frequently occurs in individuals diagnosed with diabetic nephropathy. It is also commonly observed in many individuals who have had diabetes for over 20 years.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question:
Which of the following patients would you screen for diabetic retinopathy?

  1. A 10-year-old boy on treatment for type 1 diabetes for the past 2 years
  2. A 48-year-old man newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes
  3. A 25-year-old primigravida with gestational diabetes mellitus
  4. A 62-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy
  5. A 22-year-old woman with prepubertal onset of type 1 diabetes

explanationHtml:
The most common form of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy. It presents with distal sensory loss and pain in a stocking-and-glove distribution and is a risk factor for foot ulceration.

Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication and results in the following features:

  • Postural hypotension
  • Silent myocardial infarction
  • Hypoglycemia unawareness
  • Erectile dysfunction
  • Overflow incontinence
  • Gastroparesis
  • Enteropathy with constipation or diarrhea

Isolated loss of funtion of peripheral or cranial nerve (called peripheral mononeuroplathy or cranial mononeuropathy), although of lesser incidence as compared to polyneuropathy, can also be seen in diabetics. Of the mononeuropathies seen in diabetics, occulomotor nerve is the most commonly affected and clinically presents with diplopia. Peripheral mononeuropathy can be seen occuring in median, ulnar and radial nerves.

Diabetic polyradiculopathy is characterized by severe pain along the distribution of one or more nerve roots.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: What is the most common clinical presentation of diabetic neuropathy?

explanationHtml:
Amyotrophy refers to weakness of hip extensors and flexors secondary to polyradiculopathy involving the lumbar plexus and femoral nerve. It is associated with severe pain along the distribution of the nerve roots. It is self-limiting and resolves over 6-12 months.

Strict glycemic control can reduce the incidence and prevent the progression of macular edema, peripheral neuropathy, and macroalbuminuria. However, once developed, they cannot be reversed. Intermittent microalbuminuria with normal GFR can be reversed with strict glycemic control.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following findings in a diabetic patient is self-limiting?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of silent hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient. The most likely cause is autonomic neuropathy.

Hypoglycemia presents with symptoms like palpitation, tremors, and sweating as a result of sympathetic stimulation. These symptoms are protective and provide advance warning before progression to neuroglucopenia.

However, in autonomic neuropathy, there is a reduced release of counterregulatory hormones like catecholamines. Hence, the classical symptoms of hypoglycemia do not occur and the patient directly presents with features of neuroglucopenia. This is called hypoglycemia unawareness.

The use of beta-blockers can also cause hypoglycemia unawareness.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management

options.text: Medication change from metformin to insulin

question: You are evaluating a 65-year-old diabetic woman who has been admitted following a seizure. On admission, she was unconscious, and random blood glucose at admission was 37 mg/dl. The hypoglycemia was corrected and she regained consciousness. The woman says that she had felt normal and had no other symptoms prior to the onset of seizures. What is the likely cause of this presentation?

explanationHtml:
In patients with longstanding diabetes mellitus, tight glycaemic control is beneficial for microvascular complications. However, it has no effect on macrovascular complications like peripheral vascular disease (PVD), myocardial infarction, and stroke.

Good glycemic control improves microvascular complications through primary and secondary prevention. It reduces the incidence of complications as well as stabilizes and prevents further progression in affected individuals. Intermittent microalbuminuria with normal GFR can even be reversed with tight glycemic control.

Complication

Retinopathy

47 %

Microalbuminuria

39 %

Nephropathy

54%

Neuropathy

60 %
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: You are counselling a patient with longstanding, poorly-controlled diabetes mellitus. Advising tight glycemic control in this patient would not improve which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Legacy effect or metabolic memory can be observed in relation to glycemic control during early disease in patients with diabetes mellitus.

Intensive glycemic control during the early stages of the disease has a positive effect on long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications (statement 1) even if this intensive glycemic control is not maintained long term. Similarly, uncontrolled blood glucose levels in the early stages causes an increased risk of these complications (statement 5). This phenomenon is called legacy effect and is attributed to metabolic memory.

In patients with longstanding diabetes, intensive glycemic control at later stages can improve microvascular complications but has no effect on macrovascular complications.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question:
Which among the following statements explains Legacy effect and metabolic memory?

  1. Intensive glycemic control in early disease
  2. Early detection and management of dyslipidemia
  3. Good glycemic control in longstanding disease
  4. High HbA1c values in longstanding disease
  5. Uncontrolled blood glucose levels in early disease

explanationHtml:
Venous stasis is not a cause of diabetic foot ulcers and gangrene. They are usually caused by a combination of three factors:

  • Ischemia - secondary to atheroma
  • Peripheral neuropathy - leads to trophic skin changes
  • Immunosuppression - due to excess sugar deposition in tissues, predisposing diabetic patients to infection

Common sites of ulcers include:

  • Great toe
  • Metatarsophalangeal areas.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A patient with chronic diabetes presents to the OPD for his annual checkup. A small painless ulcer is noted over his right foot. His BMI is 33 kg/m2. All of the following factors can be implicated in the causation of his foot ulcer except:

explanationHtml:
The given image showing irregular plaques with yellowish discoloration and telangiectasias are suggestive of necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum.

It is an inflammatory granulomatous disorder of the skin due to collagen degeneration and lipid deposition. It is usually seen in young women with diabetes mellitus.

The lesions usually begin in the pretibial region. It begins as papules that gradually enlarge and darken to form erythematous plaques with irregular margins, atrophic centers, and central ulceration.

Option A: Necrolytic migratory erythema is a feature of glucagonoma. It is a waxing and waning rash that appears as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Diabetic dermopathy or shin spots are commonly seen in elderly men. It presents as pigmented pretibial papules as shown below.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Granuloma annulare presents with small papules arranged in an annular pattern. There is no yellowish discoloration or telangiectasias, as shown below.

[[figure-3]]
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A 25-year-old diabetic woman presents to the OPD with the following skin lesions. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Emphysematous appendicitis is not a complication of diabetes mellitus. The potentially fatal infectious complications of diabetes include:

  • Malignant otitis externa
  • Rhinocerebral mucormycosis
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis
  • Emphysematous cholecystitis
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Patients with diabetes mellitus are at a higher risk of developing all of the following infections except:

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, canagliflozin (Option C) is the most suitable treatment. It is an oral drug belonging to the class SGLT-2 inhibitors and causes weight loss. Although it increases the risk of urogenital infections, it has no risk of pancreatitis or bladder cancer.

Option A: Sitagliptin, a DPP-IV inhibitor, is associated with the risk of acute pancreatitis.

Option B: Pioglitazone, a thiazolidinedione, can increase the risk of bladder cancer and can cause weight gain and congestive cardiac failure.

Option D: Liraglutide is an injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist. Pancreatitis is a serious adverse effect of this drug. Hence, it is contraindicated in individuals with a history of pancreatitis and should be permanently discontinued if pancreatitis develops.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: A morbidly obese diabetic woman is not responsive to metformin therapy. She has a history of pancreatitis and family history of bladder cancer. She does not want to take injections. Which of the following would be suitable to reduce her glucose levels?

explanationHtml:
Metformin should be stopped in case of elevated creatinine levels (renal insufficiency) > 1.5 mg/dl in men and >1.4 mg/dl in women.

Metformin acts by reducing hepatic glucose production and improves peripheral glucose utilization. Lactic acidosis and Vitamin B12 deficiency are specific adverse effects of metformin. It is not used in patients with a glomerular filtration rate <30 mL/min (moderate renal insufficiency), acidosis, unstable congestive cardiac failure, liver disease, severe hypoxemia, and patients undergoing contrast studies.
lessonTitle: Diabetes Mellitus Complications And Their Management
question: Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs should be stopped in a patient with a creatinine of 5.6 mg/dL?

explanationHtml:
11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency is associated with metabolic alkalosis, not metabolic acidosis.

It is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia that presents with the following features:

  • Glucocorticoid deficiency:
    • Hypoglycemia
    • Hyperpigmentation around the genitals due to excess adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion
  • Mineralocorticoid excess:
    • Hypokalemia
    • Hypertension
    • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Adrenal androgen excess
    • Virilization in females
    • Precocious puberty in males
question: Which of the following is not a feature of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario with ambiguous genitalia in a male neonate is suggestive of 17 alpha-hydroxylase deficiency. It causes hypertension and hypokalemia due to the accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, which is a mineralocorticoid causing sodium retention.

11-hydroxylase deficiency also leads to the accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone.
question: A neonate with ambiguous genitalia undergoes karyotyping and is confirmed to have a 46XY genotype. His blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg and serum potassium is 1.9 mEq/L. Which of the following is responsible for these findings?

explanationHtml:
Hypoglycemia is a feature of salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH).

It is due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. It results in hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Males typically present with salt-wasting crises as they often go undiagnosed at birth due to the presence of normal genitalia.
question: Which of the following abnormalities will you see in a child with salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia?

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice for the prenatal treatment of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency is dexamethasone, as it readily crosses the placenta.

It is an experimental approach aimed at reducing the virilization of 46XX fetuses by suppressing fetal adrenal steroid and androgen secretion. It may be considered when there is a high risk of CAH due to strong family history. It is effective only when started before 4 weeks of gestation.

Hydrocortisone is given in the children at divided doses of 1–1.5 times the normal cortisol production.
question: Which of the following is the drug of choice for the prenatal treatment of congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Ambiguous genitalia, elevated 17-(OH)-progesterone, and hypoglycemia are suggestive of 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The drug of choice is hydrocortisone.

Hydrocortisone acts as a potent glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid action and thus increases salt absorption from the kidneys as well.

Betamethasone, beclomethasone, and dexamethasone have negligible effects as mineralocorticoids.
question: A female neonate is noted to have ambiguous genitalia at birth. Further testing reveals elevated 17-(OH)-progesterone levels and a blood glucose of 40 mg/dl. What treatment will you recommend?

explanationHtml:
Galactorrhea or pathological production of milk is not associated with lactation, which is a physiological condition.

Galactorrhea is the inappropriate discharge of milk-containing fluid from the breast. It may be unilateral or bilateral. It is associated with acromegaly and hyperprolactinemia.

Treatment is with dopamine agonists like bromocriptine or cabergoline if it is due to hyperprolactinemia.
question: Which of the following is incorrect about galactorrhea?

explanationHtml:
Determination of prolactin level is not useful in patients with gynecomastia.

For the diagnosis of gynecomastia, serum levels of the following hormones must be checked:

  • Testosterone
  • LH
  • FSH
  • Estradiol
  • hCG
question: In a patient with gynecomastia, you will order all of the following tests except:

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario of gynecomastia with low LH and testosterone is suggestive of a sertoli cell tumor.

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is also a possible diagnosis with the above clinical presentation and must be ruled out before diagnosing a Sertoli cell tumor.

The differential diagnosis of gynecomastia is as follows:

  • High LH and low testosterone
    • Testicular failure
  • Low LH and low testosterone
    • Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
    • Sertoli cell tumor - increased primary estrogen production
  • High LH and high testosterone
    • Androgen-resistant state
    • GnRH-secreting tumor
question: A 32-year-old man is being evaluated for gynecomastia. Laboratory investigations reveal low levels of serum testosterone and luteinizing hormone. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome.

Clinical features:

  • Female phenotype
  • Normal breast development
  • Blind-ended vagina with absent uterus and ovaries
  • Presence of testes in the abdomen or inguinal region
  • Scanty pubic and axillary hair
  • Primary amenorrhea in late adolescence

Option A: In Turner’s syndrome, breasts are infantile.

Option B: Stein Leventhal syndrome or polycystic ovarian disorder presents with hirsutism and anovulatory menstrual cycles.

Option C: Premature ovarian failure presents with secondary amenorrhea.
question: A mother brings her 17-year-old daughter to the gynecologist as she has not started menstruating yet. Examination reveals well-developed breasts and the absence of pubic and axillary hair.  Pelvic examination reveals a short, blind-ended vagina. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical picture is suggestive of androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS). Affected children have a male karyotype or 46 XY with a female phenotype.

46XY individuals with complete AIS (formerly called testicular feminization syndrome) have the following features:

  • Female phenotype
  • Normal breast development
  • Blind-ended vagina with absent uterus and ovaries
  • Scanty pubic and axillary hair

Most patients present with

  • Inguinal masses in infancy - Due to undescended testes or hernias containing testes
  • Primary amenorrhea in late adolescence

Gonadectomy is a recommended course of treatment due to the possible risks of malignancy.
question: A baby girl is referred to a pediatric surgeon for suspected bilateral inguinal hernias. Further evaluation reveals the masses to be testes in the inguinal canal. Which karyotype would you expect to find in this child?

explanationHtml:
Anosmia and absent secondary sexual characteristics in this patient are suggestive of Kallman syndrome.

It is an X-linked disorder that causes isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism due to defective development of the olfactory bulb. This results in:

  • Defective migration of GnRH-producing neurons that originate from the olfactory epithelium
  • Aplasia or hypoplasia of olfactory bulb

The clinical features include:

  • Cryptorchidism
  • Absent or delayed pubertal changes due to GnRH deficiency
  • Anosmia or hyposmia

Options A and B: Klinefelter syndrome is a cause of primary or hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.

Option D: Hyperprolactinemia can cause hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, but is also associated with gynecomastia, galactorrhea, and bitemporal hemianopia.
question: An 18-year-old boy is brought to the casualty with minor burns following a house fire. He tells you that he did not even smell the smoke. Further probing reveals a history of bilateral orchidopexy at the age of 7. Examination findings include eunuchoid habitus, prepubertal testes, and microphallus. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism in males is Klinefelter’s syndrome

It occurs in males with a 47 XXY karyotype and is associated with testicular dysfunction and male infertility.

Causes of hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism in males and females:

  • Congenital
    • Klinefelter's syndrome
    • Turner's syndrome
    • Swyer's syndrome
    • Premature ovarian failure associated with fragile X syndrome and galactosemia
  • Acquired
    • Mumps orchitis
    • Testicular torsion, trauma
    • Liver cirrhosis
    • Ketoconazole
    • Premature ovarian failure
question: What is the most common cause of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism in males?

explanationHtml:
Gonadectomy is clinically recommended in all patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) or testicular feminization syndrome due to the risk of malignancy arising from the abnormally located testes.

Options B, C, D: These treatment options may be offered to patients with AIS, but it depends on personal preference and whether they identify as males or females.
question: Which of the following will you recommend in all patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Decreased levels of estrogen, FSH, and LH are suggestive of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, which is caused by Kallman syndrome.

It is an X-linked disorder (KAL gene) that causes isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and anosmia.

Causes of hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism:

  • Congenital
    • Kallman's syndrome
    • Isolated hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism (IHH)
    • Prader-Willi syndrome
    • CHARGE syndrome
  • Acquired
    • Pituitary tumors, apoplexy
    • Hyperprolactinemia
    • Anorexia nervosa, excess exercise
    • Irradiation
    • Infection
    • Trauma

Option A: Asherman syndrome causes secondary amenorrhea due to intrauterine synechiae.

Option B: Müllerian agenesis presents with primary amenorrhea with normal levels of all hormones.

Option D: Turner's syndrome causes primary amenorrhea due to hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism.
question: A 19-year-old patient is being evaluated for primary amenorrhea. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased estrogen, FSH, and LH. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Hypercalcemia is associated with all of the following conditions except hypothyroidism. Hyperthyroidism is however associated with hypercalcemia.

Other options:

1) Multiple myeloma is a hemotological malignancy associated with hypercalcemia.

2) Hyperparathyroidism is associated with sub-periosteal bone resorption resulting in hypercalcemia.

3) Sarcoidosis is associated with hypercalcemia due to increased activity of 1 alpha hydroxylase activity in the macrophages.

question: Hypercalcemia is associated with all of the following medical conditions except:

explanationHtml:
Vitamin A intoxication can cause hypercalcemia. This is due to high bone turnover. Ingestion of 50,000–100,000 units of Vitamin A daily can increase calcium levels up to 12–14 mg/dL.

Note: Vitamin D intoxication also leads to hypercalcemia.

question: Which of the following can cause hypercalcemia in a patient?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario with severe hypercalcemia (> 14.8 mg/dl) is suggestive of a hypercalcemic crisis. Pancreatitis causes hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

Hypercalcemic crisis is often caused by malignancies due to an acute rise in calcium levels following bone resorption due to metastases. It is a medical emergency that presents with polyuria, severe dehydration, gastrointestinal symptoms, and altered consciousness. It can lead to cardiac arrest and coma.

question: A 66-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found unconscious by her neighbors. She is found to have marked dehydration and serum calcium levels of 16 mg/dl. All of the following can cause this presentation except:

explanationHtml:
Hypercalcemia is associated with constipation and not diarrhea.

Clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia include:

System Clinical features
Renal Renal stones (Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate)
Nephrocalcinosis
Polyuria and dehydration
Renal failure
Musculoskeletal Bone pain, bone cysts
Myalgia and arthralgia
Osteopenia, osteoporosis
GIT Constipation
Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
Abdominal pain
Peptic ulcer disease
Acute pancreatitis
Neuropsychiatric Anxiety, depression, fatigue
Cognitive dysfunction
Drowsiness, obtundation, coma
Cardiac Short QT interval, bradycardia
Hypertension
Others Ectopic calcification

The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic 'stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychic moans'.

question: Which of the following will not be seen in a patient with hypercalcemia?

explanationHtml:
Excess calcium ingestion is not associated with restrictive cardiomyopathy. It results in milk-alkali syndrome, commonly associated with excessive intake of absorbable antacids such as milk or calcium carbonate.

In susceptible individuals, there is a loss of negative feedback, leading to excess calcium absorption when there is excess intake. It results in the following triad of clinical features:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Alkalosis - due to HCO3 reabsorption caused by PTH suppression, natriuresis, and water depletion.
  • Renal failure - due to damage to renal tubules.

It is reversible once ingestion of antacid is stopped. However, in severe cases, a chronic form called Burnett’s syndrome can develop. It is associated with irreversible renal damage.

question: Which of the following is not seen in patients following excessive intake of calcium?

explanationHtml:
Parathyroid adenomas are the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.

Causes of primary hyperparathyroidism:

  • Parathyroid adenomas: These maybe
    • Solitary (more common)
    • Multiple
    • Part of MEN-1, MEN-2A or MEN-4
  • Chief cell parathyroid hyperplasia
  • Parathyroid gland carcinoma
  • Lithium use
  • Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumor (HPT-JT) syndrome

question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?

explanationHtml:
Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD will cause decreased calcium and increased levels of PTH, phosphate, and ALP.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD due to resistance to the normal level of PTH is a major factor contributing to the development of hypocalcemia, which, in turn, is a stimulus to parathyroid gland enlargement. In CKD, there is elevated phosphate levels due to decreased ability of phosphate excretion by renal tubules.

Other causes of secondary hyperparathyroidism includes vitamin D deficiency, gastrointestinal malabsorption, liver disease.

Option B: Secondary hyperparathyroidism secondary to Vitamin D deficiency, initially elevated parathormone (PTH) will compensate and keep calcium level normal by increasing bone turn-over which will lead to elevated ALP and phosphate excretion which will lead to decrease in phosphate level. In long-term cases, hypocalcemia may occur.

question: Which of the following sets of lab values will be seen in a patient with secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD?

correctAnswer: A. It causes prolongation of QT interval
explanationHtml:
Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) causes shortening of the QT interval.

Majority of the patients are asymptomatic in the western population, whereas patients are commonly symptomatic in developing countries. The classical symptoms and signs of PHPT are due to hypercalcemia as well as increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels.

The features of hypercalcemia are as follows:

System Clinical features
Musculoskeletal
  • Bone pain
  • Skeletal deformities
  • Pathological fractures
  • Myalgia and arthralgia
Renal
  • Renal stones(Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate)
  • Nephrocalcinosis
  • Polyuria and dehydration
  • Renal failure
GIT
  • Constipation
  • Nausea, vomiting, anorexia
  • Abdominal pain
  • Peptic ulcer disease
  • Acute pancreatitis
Neuropsychiatric
  • Anxiety, depression
  • Cognitive dysfunction
  • Irritability
  • Hallucinations
Cardiac
  • Short QT interval
  • bradycardia
  • Hypertension
Ectopic calcification
  • Cornea: Band keratopathy
  • Extravascular tissues: calcinosis
  • Small arteries: calciphylaxis

The features of elevated PTH levels are as follows:

  • Osteitis fibrosa cystica
  • Osteopenia/osteoporosis
  • Hyperuricemia and gout
  • Pseudogout
  • Increased production of calcitriol
  • Nephrolithiasis
  • Hypophosphatemia
  • Anemia

The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic - “bones, stones, groans, moans with fatigue overtones”

explanationHtml:
Neuropsychiatric changes are seen in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT).

question: Which of the following would you expect in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism?

explanationHtml:
Calcitonin levels are increased in hyperparathyroidism.

Due to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels in hyperparathyroidism, there is osteoclast activation. This leads to increased calcium levels in plasma. As a response to this, there is an increase in the level of calcitonin to regulate the high calcium levels.

Calcitonin is secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland. Its principal effects are to lower serum calcium and phosphate by its action on bone and kidney. In bone, calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts and reduces bone resorption. In the kidney, it inhibits the reabsorption of both calcium and phosphate.

Other options

Option A: In hyperthyroidism, the direct effect of thyroid hormones can lead to bone resorption and mild hypercalcemia. However, hyperparathyroidism is a better answer.

Options B and D: Hypoparathyroidism and Cushing’s syndrome will have low serum calcium and hence, will not have increased calcitonin levels.

question: Calcitonin levels are increased in:

explanationHtml:
The above x-ray shows a rugger jersey spine which is a distinct feature of hyperparathyroidism. It is associated with elevated ALP.

It refers to the prominent hyperdensities at the endplates of successive vertebrae, which mimics the striped appearance of a rugby jersey.

Option A: Paget's disease causes cortical thickening, which results in increased opacity on all sides of the vertebral body. These are called picture frame vertebrae.

Option C: Osteopetrosis presents with normal ALP levels. It results in sclerotic endplates of vertebrae that are termed sandwich vertebrae. Though this finding is similar to rugger jersey spine, it is denser and more sharply defined than rugger jersey spine. In addition, there is sclerosis of inner margins of vertebral bodies, resulting in a bone within a bone appearance.

Option D: Ankylosing spondylitis produces a bamboo spine appearance due to fusion of vertebral bodies.

question: The spinal x-ray of a patient with elevated ALP levels is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml: This clinical scenario is suggestive of a pathological fracture of the tibia. The given x-ray shows brown tumors or osteitis fibrosa cystica, which are characteristic of hyperparathyroidism.

question: A middle-aged woman presents with worsening pain and an inability to bear weight on her left leg. She says that she had banged her leg against a chair 3 days ago. X-ray reveals a fracture of her left tibia. In view of this finding, a skeletal survey was performed and reveals the following additional finding. What is the likely cause?

explanationHtml:
The arrows in this x-ray point to arrow-headed fingers or the spade phalanx sign. It is pathognomonic of acromegaly.

Acromegaly is the result of excessive growth hormone (GH) production, most commonly from a macroadenoma of the pituitary. There is osseous enlargement, presenting with spade-like hands and widening of the terminal phalangeal tufts, giving an arrow-head appearance.

Other features in the hand include:

  • Widened joint spaces (due to cartilage hypertrophy)
  • Generalized osteoporosis and cystic changes in the carpal bones

Option A: Hyperparathyroidism causes subperiosteal bone resorption, which is marked along the radial aspect of the middle phalanges of the index and middle fingers.

Option B: Down's syndrome can cause hypoplasia of the middle phalanx of the 5th finger.

Option C: Psoriasis causes a pencil-in-cup appearance of the distal phalanx.

question: This x-ray finding in a patient is characteristic of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Glucocorticoids have no effect on the serum calcium concentration in primary hyperparathyroidism and normal individuals.

They are effective in the treatment of hypercalcemia when associated with the following conditions:

  • Malignancy
  • Vitamin D intoxication
  • Sarcoidosis

Initial medical management of hypercalcemia involves the following:

  • Normal saline (200-500 ml/hour): It is the mainstay treatment to correct dehydration, and titrated to maintain a urine output of >100 ml/hour
  • Pamidronate or zoledronate: These are bisphosphonates and are considered as the drug of choice in primary hyperparathyroidism
  • Cinacalcet: This is a calcimimetic that increases the affinity of the glands to extracellular calcium, thereby decreasing parathyroid hormone secretion
  • Denosumab: This inhibits RANK-ligand, which acts on osteoclasts
  • Calcitonin: This is an activated vitamin D analog that may be used to reduce calcium levels. It should be used within the first 24 hours

Forced diuresis refers to aggressive fluid hydration with loop diuretic administration. Although this is an effective method to reduce calcium levels, it requires careful monitoring for adverse effects like fluid overload, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesia. Due to this reason as well as the availability of more effective treatment modalities, forced diuresis is not preferred any longer.

The definitive management of primary hyperparathyroidism is the surgical removal of the parathyroid gland.
lessonTitle: Disorders Of Parathyroid And Calcium Homeostasis
question: Which of the following is not used to treat a patient with hypercalcemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism?

explanationHtml:
In patients with hypercalcemia due to vitamin D toxicity, glucocorticoids like dexamethasone are the preferred therapy as they ultimately decrease intestinal calcium absorption and increase urinary excretion of calcium by decreasing 1,25 (OH2) vitamin D (calcitriol) production.

Hydroxychloroquine, chloroquine, and ketoconazole may also decrease calcitriol production and are used occasionally. But the preferred therapy is steroids.

Vitamin D toxicity presents acutely with features of hypercalcemia such as confusion, polyuria, polydipsia, anorexia, vomiting, and muscle weakness. Chronic intoxication may cause nephrocalcinosis, bone demineralization, and pain.

Lab features include elevated 25 (OH) vitamin D, high calcium, and suppressed PTH.

Dexamethasone can also be used in the treatment of hypercalcemia caused by the humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (due to PTHr) and sarcoidosis.
lessonTitle: Disorders Of Parathyroid And Calcium Homeostasis
question: Which of the following is used in the treatment of hypercalcemia due to Vitamin D toxicity?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a hypercalcemic crisis. The next best step in management is saline hydration.

Correcting dehydration remains as the principle focus in treating hypercalcemic crisis and is achieved by administering fluids at a rate of 200-500 mL/hr. Once hydration is established, it becomes essential to maintain a urine output of more than 100mL/hour according to which, the rate of fluid administration is adjusted.

Hypercalcemic crisis is a medical emergency associated with serum calcium >14 mg/dl. It is often caused by conditions causing an acute rise in calcium levels such as malignancies or lithium overdose.

It presents with oliguria, severe dehydration, gastrointestinal symptoms, and altered consciousness. It can lead to cardiac arrest and coma.

Initial medical management of hypercalcemia involves the following:

  • Fluids are the mainstay treatment
  • Bisphosphonates
  • Cinacalcet
  • Denosumab
  • Calcitonin

question: A patient is brought to the emergency department with confusion, drowsiness, and multiple episodes of vomiting. His family members say that he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder several years ago and has been on medication ever since. Further evaluation reveals a serum calcium level of 16 mg/dl. What should be the next step in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is associated with hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia

Hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia is observed in the following conditions:

  • True hypoparathyroidism
    • Hereditary hypoparathyroidism
    • Acquired hypoparathyroidism – following surgery
    • Hypomagnesemia
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • DiGeorge syndrome

question: In a patient with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, which of the following will you not suspect?

explanationHtml:
Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism is not associated with hyperphosphatemia. The phosphate levels in pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism are normal.

Hyperphosphatemia is seen in conditions like:

  • Chronic renal failure (Option A)
  • Prolonged phosphate intake (Option B)
  • Pseudohypoparathyroidism (Option D)

Pseudohypoparathyroidism (type 1a) is an autosomal dominant condition due to mutations in the GNAS1 gene. Here, the mutation is on the maternal chromosome. Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP) is a variant of pseudohypoparathyroidism wherein the GNAS mutation occurs on the paternal chromosome.

The patient is functionally hypoparathyroid in pseudohypoparathyroidism, but the levels of parathyroid hormone (PTH) are high due to end-organ resistance. Presence of hypocalcemia and hyperphosphataemia is seen in this condition, whereas the levels of calcium and phosphorus are normal in PPHP.

Association with Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (short stature, round facies, short 4th metacarpal) is seen in both pseudo and pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.

question: All of the following medical conditions are associated with hyperphosphatemia except:

correctAnswer: A. Decrease in parathyroid hormone level
explanationHtml:
The image shows a windswept deformity in the legs, with one limb deviating outward (valgus) while the opposite deviating inward (varus).

In the presence of low vitamin D levels, this presentation is suggestive of rickets due to vitamin D deficiency, which is usually associated with secondary elevation of parathyroid hormone (PTH).

question: A 5-year-old boy is brought by his mother with with the following abnormality. Serum levels of vitamin D are found to be low. Which of the following would not be seen in this boy?

correctAnswer: D. Not a feature of secondary hyperparathyroidism
explanationHtml:
Hypocalcemia is a feature of secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT).

Hypocalcemia refers to total serum calcium ≤8.4 mg/dl. The causes include:

  • Low PTH
    • Hypoparathyroidism
  • High PTH (SHPT)
    • Chronic kidney disease
    • Vitamin D deficiency
    • Pseudohypoparathyroidism
    • Hyperphosphatemia
  • Loop diuretics, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
  • Massive blood transfusions
  • Hyperventilation
  • Hypomagnesemia - Mg is essential for PTH release
  • Severe hypermagnesemia (Option A) - higher Mg levels suppress PTH secretion

Hypocalcemia causes tetany or increased neuromuscular excitability. It can cause paresthesias, cramps, spasms, and seizures. Latent tetany (Option B) can only be detected by performing Chvostek and Trousseau's signs. A prolonged QT interval (Option C) is seen on ECG.

options.text: Not a feature of secondary hyperparathyroidism

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to hypocalcemia?

explanationHtml:
The above image indicates Trousseau's sign or carpopedal spasm classically seen in patients with hypocalcemia.

Trousseau's sign is elicited by making the forearm ischemic by applying a sphygmomanometer cuff to the arm and keeping the pressure above systolic blood pressure (SBP) for 5 minutes. The hand goes into a painful carpopedal spasm and assumes the accoucheur’s hand position.

Hypocalcemia results in tetany or increased neuromuscular irritability. It leads to paresthesia and tingling of extremities and perioral area. Severe hypocalcemia can cause seizures.

Option A: Chvostek's sign is also seen in hypocalcemia. Tapping the facial nerve in front of the tragus will cause spasms of the facial muscles.

Option C: Tinel's sign is seen in carpal tunnel syndrome. It refers to a tingling sensation on tapping over the median nerve.

Option D: Troisier's sign refers to left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in metastatic abdominal malignancy.

question: The following sign is elicited in a patient. What is it called?

explanationHtml:
Etidronate is not used in the management of hypocalcemia. It is a bisphosphonate used in the management of hypercalcemia.

The goal in the management of hypoparathyroidism is to restore the calcium-phosphate balance. The mainstay is calcium and vitamin D supplements. Other underlying conditions must also be treated.

Instead of loop diuretics, thiazides can be administered on a low sodium diet as they enhance urinary calcium reabsorption.
lessonTitle: Disorders Of Parathyroid And Calcium Homeostasis
question: Which of the following agents cannot be used to manage a patient with chronic hypocalcemia?

explanationHtml:
Leptin is an adipocyte-derived hormone.

It acts through brain circuits (predominantly in the hypothalamus) to influence appetite, energy expenditure, and neuroendocrine function. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure.

The arcuate nucleus in the hypothalamus plays an important role in the regulation of appetite.
question: The hormone leptin is derived from which of the following?

explanationHtml: In the fasting state, high levels of ghrelin are seen. It is a gut-peptide produced in the stomach and stimulates hunger and appetite.
question: A 25-year-old woman has been fasting all day as part of a new diet. Which of the following is a gut peptide that will be increased in this woman?

explanationHtml: This boy is likely to have high levels of α-Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH). It is a hypothalamic peptide that decreases appetite and hence would be increased in the fed state.
question: A 16-year-old boy ate two pieces of cake, a sandwich, and two scoops of ice cream at his friend's birthday party an hour ago. Levels of which of the following are likely to be high in this boy?

explanationHtml:
One of the key transcription factors involved in the differentiation of mesenchymal preadipocytes to adipose cells is the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ). It is a nuclear receptor that also binds the thiazolidinedione class of insulin-sensitizing drugs used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Note: Saroglitazar has a dual action on PPARα and PPAR𝝲 receptors. It reduces blood sugar and lipid levels in diabetic patients.
question: Which of the following is a key transcription factor involved in the differentiation of mesenchymal preadipocytes to adipose cells?

correctAnswer: A. Its levels are increased in obesity
explanationHtml:
Adiponectin levels are reduced in obesity.

It is an abundant adipose-derived protein with the following characteristics:

  • Its levels are reduced in obesity
  • It enhances insulin sensitivity and lipid oxidation
  • Has vascular-protective effects

On the other hand, resistin and RBP4 levels, which are also secreted by adipocytes, may induce insulin resistance.

options.text: Its levels are increased in obesity

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding adiponectin?

explanationHtml:
The most prominent neuroendocrine abnormality seen in obese individuals with inactivating mutations in the leptin (ob gene) or leptin receptor (db gene) is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Leptin mutations are responsible for a rare form of obesity that runs in families. These mutations prevent leptin from delivering satiety signals. Hence, the brain perceives starvation despite adequate nutrition. It results in morbid, early-onset obesity.

Mutations in the following genes can cause obesity in humans:

  • Lep (ob)
  • LepR (db)
  • POMC
  • PC-1
  • MC4R
question: A 2-year-old girl is referred to an endocrinologist with severe obesity and insatiable hunger despite adequate nutrition. Due to the early-onset severe obesity, genetic testing was done and revealed inactivating mutations in the leptin gene. Which of the following neuroendocrine abnormalities is this child most likely to develop?

explanationHtml:
Cachexia is not a feature of mutations of the pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) gene. It is associated with the following characteristics:

  • Absence of α-MSH
    • Severe obesity - α-MSH inhibits appetite in the hypothalamus
    • Pale skin and red hair
  • Absence of ACTH
    • Secondary adrenal insufficiency
question: Genetic mutations causing pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) deficiency presents with all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
Insulin levels are increased in obesity. It stimulates the synthesis of fatty acids and TAG and decreases the rate of lipolysis. Thyroxine, growth hormone, and adiponectin have lipolytic effects, hence their levels are reduced in obesity.

Hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance are consistent features of obesity. Insulin resistance is more strongly linked to intra-abdominal fat than to fat in other areas.

Adiponectin (Option D) is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that is produced by adipocytes. It performs vital functions that are reduced in obesity - like, increasing insulin sensitivity and the inhibition of gluconeogenic enzymes. It also enhances fatty acid oxidation.

Insulin resistance in obesity occurs as a result of the following:

  • Insulin receptor downregulation
  • Increased FFA (free fatty acids) and capable of impairing insulin action
  • Intracellular lipid accumulation
  • Circulating peptides produced by adipocytes such as TNF-α, IL-6, RBP4, and resistin modify insulin action.
question: The production of which of the following hormones is increased in obesity?

explanationHtml:
Children with Angelman syndrome present with mental retardation but do not have obesity and hypogonadism. It occurs due to the deletion of band q12 of the maternal chromosome 15.

The following syndromes present with obesity, hypogonadism, and mental retardation

  • Prader-Willi syndrome - deletion of band q12 of the paternal chromosome 15.
  • Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome
  • Carpenter syndrome
  • Cohen syndrome

question: A known patient of type 2 diabetes mellitus on oral medication presents to your OPD for review. His blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg and his BMI is 28.4 kg/m². His fasting glucose is 118 mg/dl and postprandial glucose is 154 mg/dl. He consumes a low-calorie diet and exercises regularly. How will you manage his obesity?

explanationHtml: Orforglipron is a non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist with oral bioavailability. It is the first non-peptide oral GLP-1 agonist approved for chronic weight management and type 2 diabetes. It promotes weight loss by activating GLP-1 receptors, which stimulate insulin secretion, inhibit glucagon secretion, delay gastric emptying, enhance satiety, and improve glycemic control.
question: Which of the following anti-obesity drugs is an orally active non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist?

correctAnswer: D. Direct bilirubin <15% of total bilirubin
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario describes recurrent hemolysis in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis leading to jaundice. In hemolytic conditions, only the unconjugated/ indirect bilirubin is raised and conjugated/direct bilirubin remains normal i.e. <15% of total bilirubin.

Bilirubin is synthesized from heme which is released primarily from the breakdown of old RBCs. This bilirubin is in its unconjugated form. It enters the circulation and reaches the liver. It is converted to conjugated bilirubin which is then secreted into the biliary tree.

Therefore, in a healthy person, most of the circulating bilirubin is unconjugated/indirect bilirubin. Hence, the normal liver function tests show indirect bilirubin >85% and direct/conjugated bilirubin <15% of the total bilirubin. The normal bilirubin values are as follows:

  • Total bilirubin levels - 1 to 1.5 mg/dL
  • Direct bilirubin - <0.3 mg/dL

question: A 4-month-old child was brought with a history of recurrent episodes of jaundice. Blood investigations were suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis.  Which of the following liver function test findings is likely to be seen here?

explanationHtml:
The raised direct bilirubin levels indicate conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Among the given options, biliary atresia causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Biliary atresia is a disorder characterised by destruction or absence of bile ducts in a newborn. It leads to obstruction to the flow of bile thereby causing leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation.

Option B: Physiological jaundice of the newborn occurs due to immaturity of the newborn's liver. It is not able to conjugate the excess bilirubin produced after birth. It leads to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Option C: Breast milk may contain certain factors that inhibit the conjugation of bilirubin leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Option D: Hemolytic disease of the newborn causes excess production of bilirubin due to hemolysis leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function
question: A 2-week-old baby presented with yellowish discoloration of the skin. Investigations revealed markedly elevated direct bilirubin levels. Which of the following conditions should be suspected in the newborn?

explanationHtml:
The presence of urinary bilirubin and increased total bilirubin indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Among the given options, Dubin Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Only conjugated bilirubin can appear in the urine because it is water-soluble and filterable by the kidney. Unconjugated bilirubin is water-insoluble and bound to albumin, hence it cannot be filtered by the kidney.

Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is caused by:

  • Where bilirubin production is increased -
    • Anemias due to hemolysis
    • Hematoma reabsorption
  • Where bilirubin uptake and conjugation is impaired-
    • Gilbert syndrome
    • Crigler Najjar syndrome
  • Certain medications-
    • Probenecid
    • Rifampin

Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is caused by:

  • Hereditary cholestatic syndromes
  • Dubin Johnson syndrome
  • Rotor syndrome
  • Biliary obstruction

question:
Investigations performed in a patient with recurrent jaundice gave the following results. What is the possible cause of jaundice in this patient?

Total bilirubin - 4 mg/dL

Urine bilirubin +

explanationHtml:
Probenecid causes impaired hepatic uptake of bilirubin which leads to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate, acute hepatitis and stone in the common bile duct are causes that lead to mixed hyperbilirubinemia (both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin elevated) or predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemias.

Levels of conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin are useful in determining pre-hepatic causes of jaundice but are not useful in differentiating between intrahepatic and post-hepatic causes of jaundice.

options.text: Stone in the common bile duct

question: Which of the following is a cause of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Dubin Johnson syndrome (DJS). The LFT describes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzyme levels. The given image of microscopic examination of liver biopsy shows an accumulation of dark melanin-like pigment in the hepatocytes which is seen in this condition.

DJS is an autosomal recessive condition causing defective expression of MRP 2 protein which is important for the biliary excretion of conjugated bilirubin. The patient has icterus but is otherwise asymptomatic.

DJS also impairs biliary excretion of various compounds like epinephrine metabolites. The dark melanin-like pigment is derived from these metabolites causing the liver to appear black.

Rotor syndrome is also an autosomal recessive condition causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia but it does not present with pigmentation of the liver.

Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes are characterized by unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

question:
A 24-year-old woman presents with jaundice. She had been on OCPs for the past month. Her LFT and liver biopsy findings are given below. What is the probable diagnosis?

Total bilirubin - 12 mg/dL

Direct bilirubin - 10 mg/dL

AST - 28 IU/L

ALT - 30 IU/L

GGT - 20 IU/L

correctAnswer: B. Mutation in organic anion transport protein
explanationHtml:
Rotor syndrome occurs due to mutation in OATP (organic anion transport protein) 1B1 and 1B3.

Rotor syndrome is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. It is a benign disorder with mild elevation of bilirubin levels. It is similar to Dubin Johnson syndrome but the liver does not show any black pigmentation. No treatment is required for these patients.

question: While evaluating a patient with jaundice, all of the following investigations would help you to differentiate between Dubin Johnson syndrome and Rotor syndrome except:

explanationHtml:
Kernicterus is seen in Crigler-Najjar syndrome but not in Gilbert syndrome. Gilbert syndrome does not cause a significant elevation in unconjugated bilirubin to cause kernicterus.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome and Gilbert syndrome are both caused by various mutations in the UGT1A1 gene. This leads to decreased activity of bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase enzyme leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Both are predominantly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

These syndromes present with jaundice in infants. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in these syndromes is not associated with any hemolysis. All the other liver function tests are usually normal.

Crigler Najjar syndrome may lead to kernicterus causing severe brain damage. Liver transplantation is required without which the infant may not survive beyond 1-2 years of age. Whereas, Gilbert syndrome is a benign asymptomatic condition that does not need any intervention.
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function
question: In a patient with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which feature helps confirm the diagnosis of Crigler- Najjar syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario with poor feeding and seizures is indicative of kernicterus. This accompanied with unconjugated hyperbilrubinemia is highly suggestive of Crigler-Najjar syndrome type 1.

No improvement in bilirubin levels following the administration of phenobarbital further supports the diagnosis.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome is of two types with type 1 having absent/trace enzyme activity and type 2 having <10% of the normal enzyme activity. Hence, type 1 is far more severe and leads to kernicterus and neurological damage. Type 2 may also lead to kernicterus occasionally.

Kernicterus occurs because the unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and hence crosses the blood-brain barrier.

Phenobarbital is an enzyme inducer. Its administration can be used to differentiate between type 1 and type 2 Crigler-Najjar.

  • Enzyme induction by phenobarbital leads to improved conjugation of bilirubin leading to a reduction in total bilirubin level in type 2 Crigler-Najjar syndrome.
  • No improvement is seen in type 1 as the enzyme activity is absent and therefore cannot be induced.

Inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinemias (Autosomal Recessive) include:

Crigler-Najjar type I

Crigler-Najjar type II

 Gilbert Syndrome
UDP-GT Activity Absent Markedly reduced Reduced
Serum bilirubin 20 - 45 mg/dl <20 mg/dl Generally <3 mg/dl
Pheno-barbital effect on serum bilirubin No effect Reduction Reduction
Outcome Kernicterus Usually benign, kernicterus is rare Benign
Prevalence Rare Rare Common

Note: Rotor syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

The normal serum bilirubin (between 1 and 1.5 mg/dL) present in serum represents a balance between input from the production of bilirubin and hepatic/biliary removal of the pigment.

Isolated elevation of the bilirubin:

  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia- >15% conjugated bilirubin
  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia- <15% conjugated bilirubin

question: An infant presented with yellow discolouration of the skin, poor feeding, and seizures. Investigations revealed total bilirubin- 40 mg/dL and unconjugated bilirubin- 34 mg/dL. Phenobarbitone was administered while blood was being arranged for an exchange transfusion. However, there was no improvement. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemolytic jaundice. It can present with the following features:

  • Low hemoglobin
  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
  • Pigment gall stones - excess bilirubin in bile
  • Development of cholestasis when the gall stones obstruct the flow of bile. This would result in the elevation of conjugated bilirubin and LFTs show a cholestatic picture.

Hepatic and obstructive causes of jaundice are not likely as the other liver function tests are normal. The various causes of jaundice can be differentiated as follows:

Jaundice Pre hepatic Hepatic Post hepatic
Cause

Excessive amount of bilirubin is presented to the liver

Impaired cellular uptake/ defective conjugation/ defective secretion of bilirubin

 Defective excretion due to mechanical obstruction to the flow of bile

Elevated conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin

Marked elevated levels of AST and ALT (>1000U/L)

Elevated conjugated bilirubin

Elevated levels of ALP and GGT
Example Hemolytic anaemia Hepatitis Choledocholithiasis

Inherited hyperbilirubinemias like Gilbert syndrome are suspected when there is no associated hemolysis. It is unlikely in this patient because there are clear hemolytic features.

An 8-year-old child presents with jaundice and easy fatiguability. He had a history of ear infection which was treated with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Investigations done are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hemoglobin - 8 g/dL

Enzymes elevated in cholestasis are :

  • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
  • 5ʹ-nucleotidase
  • γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)
