question: Which of the following conditions is associated with increased activity of 5’- nucleotidase?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, alanine aminotransferase is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury.

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are indicators of liver cell injury. This is because ALT is found primarily in the liver, whereas, AST is found in the liver, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, brain, pancreas, etc.

GGT and ALP are enzymes that primarily reflect cholestasis.
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function
question: Which among the following is the most specific indicator of liver cell injury?

explanationHtml:
In a patient with acute viral hepatitis, serum transaminases are elevated to >1000 IU/L

The normal levels of serum transaminases are 10-40 IU/L. Minor elevations of serum transaminase levels up to 300 IU/L are non-specific and can be found in any liver disease however significant increase of levels >1000 IU/L is seen in conditions with severe liver disease and hepatocellular injury. These include:

  • Viral hepatitis
  • Ischemic hepatitis due to hypoperfusion (eg. in acute heart failure)
  • Hepatotoxicity caused by toxins or drugs
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function
question: In a patient with acute viral hepatitis, what level of serum transaminases will you expect?

correctAnswer: D. Suggestive of cholestatic liver disease
explanationHtml:
An increase in serum ALP (alkaline phosphatase) by x4 the normal value is suggestive of cholestatic liver disease, but extrahepatic and intrahepatic cholestasis cannot be differentiated by measuring serum ALP levels.

The normal range for serum ALP is considered 40-125 IU/L. Serum alkaline phosphatase is found in the liver, bone, small intestines, and placenta. Hence, a mild increase in ALP, i.e., 1 - 1.5 times normal, can be seen in these conditions:

  • Following a fatty meal intake - influx of intestinal alkaline phosphatase into the blood. Hence, the patient is advised to fast before the blood sample is collected for the test.
  • In pregnancy - placental ALP
  • In children - rapid bone growth
  • In elderly people over 60 years of age

ALP can be raised even in conditions like metastatic bone disease, inflammatory bowel disease, Hodgkin's lymphoma, etc. Hence, it needs to be correlated with raised levels of gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) and 5' nucleotidase which are more specific for liver disease.
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function

options.text: Could be due to fatty meal intake

question: A 64-year-old man with jaundice and abdominal pain was found to have an ALP level of 200 IU/L. His LFT reports from a month ago had shown an ALP level of 50 IU/L. What is your inference?

correctAnswer: C. AST:ALT ratio <1 is seen in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
explanationHtml:
AST:ALT ratio <1 is seen in NAFLD (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease).

The AST:ALT ratio can be interpreted as follows:

AST:ALT Condition
<1 Chronic viral hepatitis, Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
>1 Cirrhosis
>2:1

Suggestive of alcoholic liver disease

Alcohol intake is associated with the deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate which in turn leads to decreased levels of ALT enzyme. So, AST>ALT.
>3:1 Highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease.

Option A: Patients with cirrhosis have only mildly elevated or even normal levels of serum transaminases.

Option B: Absolute levels of aminotransferases are not used for predicting prognosis. This is because there is a poor correlation between the degree of liver cell damage and the levels of aminotransferases.

question: Which of the following statements regarding liver enzymes is true?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, penicillin does not lead to elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) levels.

GGT is a microsomal enzyme. Hence, drugs that are microsomal enzyme inducers can lead to an increase in GGT levels. However, other liver enzyme levels will be normal. Therefore, an isolated rise in GGT level does not indicate cholestatic liver disease.

Drugs that increase levels of GGT are:

  • Barbiturates
  • Carbamazepine
  • Ethanol
  • Griseofulvin
  • Rifampicin
  • Phenytoin

question: Liver function tests of a patient show isolated elevation of gamma-glutamyltransferase with other liver enzymes within normal limits. All of the following drugs could be responsible for this finding except:

correctAnswer: C. Measures factors II, V, VIII, X
explanationHtml:
Prothrombin time (PT) can help in estimating the levels of factors II, V, VII, and X.

PT evaluates the extrinsic and the common pathway of coagulation. Factor VII is required in the extrinsic pathway and factors II, V, X are required in the common pathway.

Coagulation factors are produced by the liver (except factor VIII) and they have a short half-life. Hence, they indicate the synthetic function of the liver and are very useful in assessing acute hepatic dysfunction. Factor VIII is produced by vascular endothelial cells.

Prolonged PT that is not corrected by vitamin K administration indicates poor prognosis in both acute and chronic liver disease.

question: Which of the following statements regarding prothrombin time is false?

explanationHtml:
Serum albumin is a marker of chronic liver disease because it is synthesized by the hepatocytes and has a long half-life of 18–20 days. Serum albumin is not a good indicator of acute or mild hepatic dysfunction.

Hypoalbuminemia is more common in chronic liver disorders such as cirrhosis and usually reflects severe liver damage. In hepatitis, albumin levels <3 g/dL should raise the possibility of chronic liver disease.

Prothrombin time is used to assess acute parenchymal liver disease. 5' nucleotidase is elevated in cholestasis. Elevation of ALP (<3 fold) is not specific to liver diseases.
lessonTitle: Hyperbilirubinemias And Tests Of Liver Function
question: Which among the following is a marker of chronic liver disease?

explanationHtml:
Chronic liver disease is associated with hypergammaglobulinemia. Chronic liver diseases with hypergammaglobulinemia include autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, and alcoholic liver disease.

The liver produces all globulins except gamma globulin which are produced by B cells. In chronic liver diseases like liver cirrhosis, there is impaired reticuloendothelial function in hepatic sinusoids. Hence the liver fails to clear the bacterial antigens. This causes an increased production of gamma globulin.

explanationHtml:
Telopeptide is not a marker for liver fibrosis. It is a marker for bone resorption.

question: Which of the following is not a marker for liver fibrosis?

explanationHtml:
Liver biopsy can be performed in a patient with splenomegaly via the percutaneous approach.

When the percutaneous approach is not advisable, liver biopsy can be performed via the transjugular approach. In this approach, a cannula is inserted via the jugular vein which is then passed into hepatic veins through which the biopsy sample is taken. Therefore, any bleeding resulting from the procedure will drain into the hepatic veins.

Indications of transjugular liver biopsy:

  • Percutaneous approach contraindicated
    • Significant ascites
    • Prolonged INR
    • Coagulopathies
  • Difficulty in accessing the liver via the percutaneous route
    • Morbid obesity

question: In which of the following patients planned for a liver biopsy, would you not be required to use the transjugular approach?

explanationHtml:
Alcoholic liver disease is the most common cause of cirrhosis in India.

The most common cause of cirrhosis worldwide is chronic viral hepatitis - Hepatitis C and B. MASH is expected to be one of the leading cause of liver cirrhosis in upcoming years. MASH (Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) is the updated term for NASH, shifting focus from alcohol exclusion to underlying metabolic conditions like diabetes, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension.

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of cirrhosis in India?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, the average amount of ethanol required to be consumed by a man to be at increased risk for alcoholic liver disease is >40g/day.

While there is no strict linear relationship between the dose of alcohol and the risk of developing alcoholic liver disease, the average amount of ethanol that leads to an increased risk in men is usually >40g/day. Heavy drinking with ethanol content >80g/day in men causes significant risk of advanced liver disease.

The risk factors for alcoholic liver disease are:

  • Quantity of alcohol consumption - The risk of developing alcoholic liver disease increases when alcohol consumption is around 40-80g/day in men and around 20-40g/day in women.
  • Gender - Women have increased susceptibility to alcoholic liver disease
  • Hepatitis C infection - Increases the severity and decreases survival in alcoholic liver disease
  • Genetics - A variation in patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 3 (PNPLA3) gene confers an increased risk of progressive liver disease
lessonTitle: Alcoholic Liver Diseases And Non Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
question: What is the average amount of ethanol a man must have consumed for him to be at increased risk for alcoholic liver disease?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of alcoholic liver disease. It is usually characterized by an AST: ALT > 2. This is because there is a deficiency of pyridoxal 5'- phosphate that is a cofactor for the enzymatic activity of ALT. Therefore, ALT levels fail to rise and there is a reversal of the AST: ALT ratio.

Prothrombin time (PT) is prolonged due to the deficiency of coagulation factors and, usually, does not respond to the administration of parenteral vitamin K. Platelet counts are often reduced early in the disease, which is reflective of portal hypertension with hypersplenism.

Elevated ALP levels are seen due to enzymatic induction by alcohol and mild cholestasis.
lessonTitle: Alcoholic Liver Diseases And Non Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease
question: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and nausea. His ultrasound abdomen revealed grade 2 fatty liver. Which among the following findings is unlikely to be seen in his condition?

explanationHtml:
Zieve's syndrome is not associated with thrombocytosis.

Zieve's syndrome is a rare syndrome occurring due to severe alcoholic hepatitis characterized by a triad of:

  • Cholestatic jaundice
  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Transient hyperlipidemia

It resolves with abstinence from alcohol.

question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in patients with Zieve's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The most specific marker for alcoholism is GGT (Gamma Glutamyl Transferase). It is a microsomal enzyme concentrated in the liver.

The markers with maximum sensitivity and specificity for alcohol consumption are:

  • Gamma Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
  • Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT)

  • Ischemic liver injury
  • Drug-induced liver injury

  • <1 in chronic viral hepatitis

  • Drugs like phenytoin, barbiturates

ALP

question: Which of the following is the most specific marker for alcoholism?

correctAnswer: A. C - drink to calm your nerves
explanationHtml:
C stands for feeling the need to cut down your drinking in the CAGE questionnaire.

The CAGE questionnaire is used for identifying alcohol abuse. It can be expanded as below:

  • C - Have you ever felt you ought to cut down on your drinking?
  • A - Have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking?
  • G - Have you ever felt guilty or bad about your drinking?
  • E - Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover (eye-opener)?

One 'yes' response raises a suspicion of an alcohol use problem and more than one is a strong indication of abuse or dependence.

question: You are using a CAGE questionnaire to screen a patient for alcohol abuse. Which of these is not the correct expansion of this questionnaire?

explanationHtml:
Discriminant function (DF) is calculated using prothrombin time and bilirubin level. It is also known as the Maddrey score and it assesses the severity and mortality risk in alcoholic hepatitis.

DF = 4.6 X (the prolongation of the prothrombin time above control [seconds]) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL)

DF ≥ 32 indicates severe disease and is an indication for starting glucocorticoids.

Note: MASH (Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) is the updated term for NASH, shifting focus from alcohol exclusion to underlying metabolic conditions like diabetes, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. The first virologic marker to rise in acute hepatitis B is HBsAg i.e., Hepatitis B surface antigen. It is detectable in serum within 1–12 weeks of infection. Usually, HBsAg becomes undetectable 1–2 months after the onset of jaundice. If it persists beyond 6 months, it indicates chronic hepatitis B.

However, very rarely, patients may have an HBsAg negative status even during active infection due to infection with escape mutant HBV. These escape mutants have mutations within the S gene and they are known to be responsible for occult hepatitis B infections.

question: What is the first marker to rise in a patient with acute hepatitis B?

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis of acute hepatitis B in the window period or serological gap can be made by the detection of the anti-HBc antibody.

Infection with hepatitis B mutants is difficult to treat and causes infections of prolonged duration. They have a higher risk of progressing to liver cirrhosis.

question: A patient with acute hepatitis B has recovered from the infection. Identify the serological marker marked in the image:

explanationHtml:
The most reliable indicator of recent HBV infection is IgM anti-HBc in serum. However, the first virologic marker to rise in acute hepatitis B is HBsAg i.e. surface antigen.

HBsAg is detectable in serum within 1–12 weeks of infection. Anti-HBc is demonstrable in the serum about 1-2 weeks after this, and may sometimes persist in the serum even longer than an anti-HBs antibody. IgM anti-HBcAg is seen early in the infection and persists for about 6 months. It indicates a recent infection. IgG anti-HBcAg antibody is seen later i.e. after 6 months and indicates remote infection.

HBcAg is not detectable in the serum of patients with HBV infection as it is present intracellularly.

Note: The risk of transmission of HBV from percutaneous routes (eg., needle prick) is about 6-30% and it is about 100 times more infectious than HIV.

Antiviral therapy is not indicated in acute hepatitis B infection. It is only indicated in chronic hepatitis B.

The majority of acute hepatitis (A, B, and E) infections are self-limiting, resulting in viral elimination and complete healing within 6 months. Hence, they need only supportive management. Only 5% of acute hepatitis infections become chronic.

In acute hepatitis C infection, recovery is rare, and the risk of progression to chronic hepatitis is high(∼85%). Thus antiviral therapy is started irrespective of the disease stage.

explanationHtml:

The decision to initiate antiviral therapy is primarily based on the presence or absence of cirrhosis, and parameters such as HBeAg, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level, and HBV DNA level.

The following are the indications for starting antivirals in chronic hepatitis B:

  • Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL
  • Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis

Recommended first-line antiviral drugs:

  • Entecavir
  • Tenofovir alafenamide
  • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate

Pegylated interferon alfa can also be used. Treatment is aimed at HBeAg seroconversion, but most patients may need to continue antiviral therapy indefinitely.

question: A 35-year-old male comes to the OPD with intermittent jaundice for the past 2 months. You suspect acute viral hepatitis. Which of the following will you not evaluate in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The investigations to be done to rule out acute viral hepatitis in this patient are anti-HAV, HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, and anti-HCV.

In the given clinical vignette, the features of fever, fatigue, yellow-coloured urine, clay-coloured stools, and icterus, along with raised bilirubin levels, increased levels of SGOT and SGPT, suggest a diagnosis of acute viral hepatitis.

For the evaluation of acute viral hepatitis, a panel of five serological tests is recommended. These include:

  • HBsAg
  • IgM anti-HAV
  • Anti-HCV
  • HCV RNA
  • IgM anti-HBc

In a setting of acute hepatitis, the tests are directed at recognising hepatitis A, B, and C. A negative serology for hepatitis B excludes the possibility of hepatitis D infection, as hepatitis D is dependent on the hepatitis B virus for its establishment in a host. Hepatitis E is not routinely tested, as it is usually associated with predisposing conditions such as pregnancy, and it resolves spontaneously in most cases.

question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen as an extrahepatic manifestation in patients with hepatitis C infection?

explanationHtml:
While HCV RNA is considered the gold standard for establishing a diagnosis of hepatitis C, it has no role in determining the progression of liver disease in patients with chronic hepatitis C.

The likelihood of progression of liver disease in patients with chronic hepatitis C is increased by:

  • Longer duration of infection - most important determinant
  • Older age
  • Obesity - patients with a high body mass index are at an increased risk of developing fibrosis
  • Diabetes mellitus and insulin resistance
  • Concomitant liver disorder (eg., alcoholic liver disease, chronic hepatitis B, hemochromatosis)
  • Concomitant HIV infection.

The best prognostic indicator in chronic hepatitis C is the rate of fibrosis and baseline inflammation seen in liver histology.

explanationHtml:
Presence of viral markers is not a part of the simplified scoring system for diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis.

The simplified scoring system includes four variables. They are:

  1. Presences of autoantibodies like anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti–smooth muscle actin (ASMA)
  2. Serum IgG level showing elevation
  3. HPE features that are typical or compatible with autoimmune hepatitis
  4. Viral hepatitis markers absent

The clinical presentation in autoimmune hepatitis shares features with acute and chronic hepatitis of other aetiologies and is usually variable. It presents with an insidious onset of non-specific symptoms such as fatigue, anorexia, and eventually jaundice. It can then progress to extensive liver necrosis and liver failure.

Autoimmune hepatitis is associated with several autoimmune diseases such as:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus

question: Which of the following drugs is associated with Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH)?

explanationHtml:
cANCA is not seen in autoimmune hepatitis. It is positive in Wegner's granulomatosis. pANCA is what is seen in autoimmune hepatitis.

There are 2 types of autoimmune hepatitis:

Type I (classic) autoimmune hepatitis is often seen in young women. It is linked to HLA-DR3 or HLA-DR4. It responds well to steroids and has a better prognosis. The autoantibodies that are seen in type I are:

  • ANA - antinuclear antibodies
  • ASMA - anti-smooth muscle actin
  • pANCA - perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic
  • anti-SLA - anti-soluble liver antigen

Type II autoimmune hepatitis is often seen in children. It is linked to HLA-DRB1 or HLA-DQB1. It usually leads to fibrosis, cirrhosis and liver failure. The autoantibodies that are seen in type II are:

  • Anti-LKM 1 - anti-liver kidney microsomes
  • Anti-liver cytosol 1

The mainstay of management in autoimmune hepatitis is glucocorticoid therapy.

Glucocorticoids are started at high doses and tapered down to a low maintenance dose. The dose of glucocorticoids is often reduced by combining with azathioprine.

The benefits of glucocorticoid + azathioprine combination therapy are:

  • Reduction in the duration of therapy.
  • Avoid life-threatening complications of steroids (e.g., cushingoid features, hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis).

  • An increase in serum albumin.
  • A decrease in serum bilirubin, globulins and aminotransferases.
  • Improvement of symptoms.

Histopathologic improvement can often take months to years.
question: A young lady has been on treatment for autoimmune hepatitis for 2 weeks, she has now come for follow-up investigations. Which of the following suggests a poor prognosis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The most common symptom of primary biliary cholangitis(PBC) is fatigue.

Primary biliary cholangitis(PBC) is a granulomatous autoimmune condition characterized by the destruction of interlobular hepatic bile ducts.

Most patients with PBC are asymptomatic at the time of the diagnosis. Fatigue and pruritus are both common presenting symptoms. However, the most common symptom is fatigue.

Other symptoms and signs are -

  • Right upper quadrant pain
  • Hyperpigmentation
  • Xanthomas and xanthelasma
  • Jaundice
  • Hepatosplenomegaly.
question: The most common symptom of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is

explanationHtml:
Anti-LKM 2 antibodies are not seen in primary biliary cholangitis. They are seen in drug-induced hepatitis.

The laboratory findings of primary biliary cholangitis include :

  • Liver function tests
    • Elevated ALP
    • Elevated GGT and 5'- nucleotidase
    • Elevated ALT and AST
  • Serology -
    • Antimitochondrial antibodies - positive in 95% of patients. These are mostly directed against the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
    • Antinuclear antibodies
  • Elevated HDL, LDL, and VLDL
  • Elevated serum IgM

Hyperbilirubinemia is seen once cirrhosis has developed.
question: A 44-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is now diagnosed with primary biliary cholangitis. Which of the following is false regarding her lab values?

explanationHtml:
The presence of ascites and variceal bleeding suggest decompensated liver disease and the appropriate treatment is liver transplantation.

The first-line drug in primary biliary cholangitis is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). It only slows the rate of progression of the disease. It does not provide any symptomatic benefit or cure the disease.

Obeticholic acid is another drug used in PBC as monotherapy or in combination with UDCA. It is a farnesoid X receptor agonist.

Liver transplantation is considered when there are signs of decompensation or portal hypertension such as ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, or malnutrition.

options.text: Add obeticholic acid to the treatment

question: A patient with a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis has been taking ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) twice daily. She now presents with ascites and variceal bleeding. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Florid duct lesion is characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). It is the lymphocytes and plasma cells all centered around bile ducts.

[[figure-1]]

Primary sclerosing cholangitis has the characteristic "onion-skin" concentric fibrosis surrounding the bile ducts.

[[figure-2]]
question: A middle-aged woman presented with fatigue, pruritis, and xanthomas over the elbows. A biopsy of her bile duct revealed florid duct lesions. What is the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Liver biopsy definitively establishes the diagnosis
explanationHtml:
Liver biopsy does not establish the diagnosis in primary sclerosing cholangitis. The diagnosis requires imaging with MRCP.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a chronic progressive disorder characterized by inflammation and fibrosis of intra and extrahepatic biliary ducts resulting in strictures and cholestasis. The cause is unknown. Most patients have underlying ulcerative colitis. It has an association with HLA DRw52. Patients present with symptoms of cholestasis such as fatigue and pruritus.

The laboratory findings include:

  • Liver function tests - Elevated ALP and aminotransferases.
  • Increased serum IgM levels
  • Positive p-ANCA

MRCP is the investigation of choice. It shows multiple strictures in intra and extrahepatic bile ducts. Liver biopsy reveals a concentric "onion skin" fibrosis. This is however not pathognomic of PSC.

There is no definitive treatment. It involves the administration of UDCA and liver transplantation.

PSC can lead to the development of cholangiocarcinoma

The image below shows onion-skin fibrosis in PSC.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Affects both intra and extrahepatic bile ducts
Liver biopsy definitively establishes the diagnosis

question: Which of the following statements about primary sclerosing cholangitis is false?

explanationHtml:
In acute liver failure, encephalopathy occurs within 4 weeks of the development of the clinical symptoms.

Acute liver failure is the rapid worsening of the liver function in patients without cirrhosis or any preexisting liver disease. The patient initially suffers from an acute injury to the liver by viruses, drugs, etc. Following this, the function of the liver rapidly worsens and patient develops coagulopathy and encephalopathy within 4 weeks of the development of jaundice or other clinical symptoms.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: In acute liver failure, encephalopathy occurs within ______ of the development of clinical symptoms.

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of acute liver failure (ALF) in India is a viral infection. Among the viruses, hepatitis E virus is the most common cause of acute liver failure.

In developed countries, acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: What is the most common cause of acute liver failure in India?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Amanita phalloides (wild mushrooms) toxicity causing acute liver failure. Hypoglycemia is seen in acute liver failure and not hyperglycemia. It occurs due to impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis.

Features of acute hepatic failure are:

  • Hepatic encephalopathy and cerebral edema- There are increased levels of ammonia (neurotoxin) in the body as a result of decreased elimination by the liver.
  • Coagulopathy- There is a decrease in the synthesis of coagulation factors leading to the elevated prothrombin time and INR.
  • Increased risk of infections- It occurs as a result of decreased reticuloendothelial activity, decreased synthesis of complements, acute phase reactants, etc.
  • Renal failure- This is more commonly seen in drug/toxin-induced hepatic failure.
  • Metabolic complications like hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A small child was rushed to the ED by his parents. He had accidentally consumed wild mushrooms while they were trekking. Examination showed features of encephalopathy and his liver function tests were deranged. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Hyperacute liver failure is defined as the development of encephalopathy within 7 days of the appearance of symptoms.

Acute liver failure can be subcategorized into three groups depending on the time interval between the onset of jaundice and encephalopathy.

  • Hyperacute- encephalopathy develops within 7 days or less than 7 days
  • Acute- encephalopathy develops between 8-28 days
  • Subacute- encephalopathy develops between 28 days to 6 months

Patients with hyperacute liver failure are more likely to develop coagulopathy and cerebral edema, but most of the patients will recover without the need for liver transplantation. On the other end, patients with subacute liver failure have less severe coagulopathy and cerebral edema, but most of them will need liver transplantation.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A patient is said to have hyperacute liver failure if encephalopathy occurs within?

explanationHtml:
In a patient with acute liver failure, MELD score and King's College Hospital criteria can be used to assess the prognosis.

Option A: Pitt score is used used to predict mortality in patients having bloodstream infections.

Option B: The child-Pugh score is used to assess the severity of cirrhosis.

Option D: Maddrey's Discriminant Function (MDF) score suggests which patients with alcoholic hepatitis may have a poor prognosis and benefit from steroid administration.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A young patient with Hepatitis E virus infection develops acute liver failure. Which of the following scores can be used in assessing the prognosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Serum bilirubin is not included in King's College Hospital criteria in acute liver failure due to paracetamol overdose.

The King's College Hospital Criteria is an adverse prognostic tool for patients with acute liver failure (ALF). The criteria is divided into acetaminophen and non-acetaminophen causes of liver failure and is used to determine possible indications of liver transplantation.

Acetaminophen-induced ALF

Non-acetaminophen causes of ALF
  • Arterial pH <7.25
  • Prothrombin time >100 sec or INR >6.7
  • All of the following
    • Prothrombin time >100 sec or INR >6.5
    • Serum creatinine level >3.4 mg/dL (300 μmol/L) or anuria
    • Grade 3-4 encephalopathy
  • Any three of the following
    • Seronegative hepatitis or idiosyncratic drug reaction
    • Age <10yrs or >40 yrs
    • Acute or subacute category (duration of jaundice >7 days)
    • Serum bilirubin level >17.5 mg/dL (300 μmol/L)
    • Prothrombin time >50 sec or INR >3.5
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A young patient is admitted to the hospital after ingestion of a large number of acetaminophen tablets. To predict the prognosis using King's College hospital criteria in this patient, which of the parameters are not used?

explanationHtml:
Portal vein thrombosis is not an absolute contraindication to liver transplantation. This is because portal vein thrombosis can be overcome by constructing a graft from the donor liver portal vein to the recipient’s superior mesenteric vein.

Absolute contraindications of liver transplantation are:

  • Uncontrolled extra-hepatobiliary infection or untreated sepsis
  • Uncorrectable life-limiting congenital anomalies
  • Active substance or alcohol abuse
  • Malignancies- Hepatocellular carcinoma with metastatic spread, incurable malignancies outside the liver, cholangiocarcinoma
  • AIDS
  • Advanced cardiopulmonary disease

Note: Milan criteria- Patients with primary hepatocellular malignancy can be considered for liver transplantation if there is:

  • A single lesion ≤5 cm.
  • Up to three separate lesions all <3 cm without any evidence of gross vascular invasion, nodal or distant metastases.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: For patients with acute liver failure, which of the following is not an absolute contraindication for liver transplantation?

explanationHtml:
Biliary atresia is the most common indication of liver transplantation in children.

Indications of liver transplant in children:

  • Biliary atresia
  • Neonatal hepatitis
  • Congenital hepatic fibrosis
  • Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
  • Wilsons disease
  • Glycogen storage disorders
  • Lysosomal storage disorders

The most common indication of liver transplant in an adult is the cirrhotic liver. Cirrhosis may be the consequence of viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, chronic use of alcohol, or biliary cirrhosis.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: Which among the following is the most common indication of liver transplantation in children?

correctAnswer: A. When he develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
explanationHtml:
Liver transplant assessment should be considered in a patient with cirrhosis of the liver when he develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Cirrhosis is the most common indication of liver transplantation in adults. However, not all cases of cirrhosis require liver transplantation. It is considered

1. When the patient either develops the complication of cirrhosis like:

  • Persistent hepatic encephalopathy
  • Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
  • Portal hypertensive bleeding
  • Diuretic resistant ascites
  • Hepatorenal syndrome

2. Or has a poor liver function

  • MELD score > 12
  • Child-Pugh grade C
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation

options.text: When he develops spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
When he has ascites which responds to diuretics

question: When should a liver transplant assessment be considered in a patient with cirrhosis of the liver?

explanationHtml:
Mannitol is not a component of the University of Wisconsin (UW) solution. It is the most commonly used preservation solution during the transplantation of the liver and kidneys. The organ can be stored in this solution for up to 20 hours.

Components of UW solution are:

  • Lactobionate- Prevents cellular swelling and reperfusion injury
  • Raffinose and hydroxyethyl starch- Prevents endothelial injury
  • Glutathione and allopurinol- free radical scavengers
  • Adenosine- required for regeneration of ATP
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A surgeon has removed a part of the liver from the live donor and has stored it in the University of Wisconsin (UW) solution. Which of the following is not a component of this solution?

correctAnswer: D. Reduced size LT involves dividing the whole liver into right lobe for an adult patient and left lateral segments for pediatric patients.
explanationHtml:
The false statement regarding liver transplantation is option D. Reduced-size liver transplantation involves the resection of a full-size liver to appropriately fit in the abdominal cavity of small adults/adolescents. It is reserved only for urgent transplantation. On the contrary, split LT involves dividing the whole donor liver into a left lateral segment (segments II and III) for a pediatric patient and an extended right lobe (segments I, IV-VIII) for an adult patient.

Option A: The required graft volume in a living donor transplant is measured by graft weight to recipient weight ratio (GRWR) or ratio of graft volume (GV) to recipient standard liver volume (SLV). The ideal GRWR is >0.8 % or GV/SLV is > 35%. The remnant donor liver mass is kept at >30% for safe regeneration.

Option B: Domino liver transplant involves transplanting a liver from a donor with metabolic disease (eg: familial amyloid polyneuropathy) to a recipient with end-stage liver disease (eg: hepatocellular carcinoma). The donor also receives an LT (healthy donor) and is prioritized over the end-stage liver disease recipient. As a liver with metabolic diseases is structurally and functionally normal, it can prolong the recipient’s life by at least 15-20 years as they will not develop the metabolic disease immediately.

Option C: Extended criteria donors/ECDs (liver grafts extracted from donors after circulatory death) and paired-exchange technique are used to decrease waitlist mortality. However, ECDs have poor graft function due to prolonged hypoxia and are associated with higher infection transmission and biliary complications.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation

options.text: The ideal graft weight to recipient weight ratio (GRWR) in living donor transplant is &gt;0.8 %.
In domino LT, liver grafts with metabolic diseases is used as they are structurally and functionally normal.
Extended criteria donors and paired-exchange LT decrease waitlist mortality.
Reduced size LT involves dividing the whole liver into right lobe for an adult patient and left lateral segments for pediatric patients.

question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding liver transplantation (LT)?

explanationHtml:
Auxiliary liver transplantation is beneficial in acute liver failure.

Auxiliary liver transplantation involves implanting a healthy liver graft heterotopically or orthotopically while leaving the whole or part of the native liver intact. The auxiliary partial orthotopic LT (APOLT) technique is used in patients with acute liver failure and metabolic diseases (primary hypercholesterolemia, glycogen storage disorders, organic acidemia, etc). In acute liver failure, this technique helps in native liver regeneration and immunosuppression withdrawal. In children with metabolic liver diseases, this technique helps in future gene therapy.

Options B, C, and D are chronic liver diseases not suitable for auxiliary liver transplantation.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: Auxiliary liver transplantation is beneficial in which of the following conditions:

correctAnswer: B. Left lateral lobe is donated to the paediatric recipient
explanationHtml:
In a split liver transplant, the left lateral lobe is donated to the pediatric recipient.

Split liver donation: This method is done when the liver from the deceased donor is suitable for transplant in an adult as well as a pediatric recipient. The liver is split into two. The left lateral segment (2 and 3) is donated to the pediatric recipient, left medial and extended right segments (1 and 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8) is donated to the adult recipient.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation

options.text: It is done in living donor
Left lateral lobe is donated to the paediatric recipient
It is the most common type of liver transplant
Caudate lobe is donated to the adult recipient

question: Which of the following sentences is true regarding split liver transplantation?

explanationHtml:
In a patient who is on tacrolimus, the addition of fluconazole may lead to toxicity of the tacrolimus.

Tacrolimus and cyclosporine are calcineurin inhibitors and are the common agents used for the immunosuppression following liver transplantation. They are metabolized by the CYP3A enzyme. Fluconazole can inhibit this enzyme and lead to increased levels of tacrolimus and cyclosporine.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation

options.text: No effect on both the drugs

question: A patient who underwent liver transplantation is started on tacrolimus for immunosuppression. His family physician prescribed him fluconazole for the treatment of a fungal infection. This will lead to

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of peritonitis due to hepatic artery thrombosis. Sirolimus is known to cause hepatic artery thrombosis in liver transplant recipients.

Sirolimus is an mTOR inhibitor and prevents T cell activation. It is not used commonly in liver transplant recipients because of the increased frequency of hepatic artery thrombosis in the first month posttransplantation. However, they can be used in patients with calcineurin inhibitor-related nephrotoxicity.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A patient presented with fever and pain abdomen. He had undergone liver transplantation a month ago and is taking immunosuppressants. On examination, abdominal guarding was present and on auscultation, no bowel sounds were heard. Doppler showed hepatic artery thrombosis. Which of the following medications is he most likely on?

explanationHtml:
Patients with liver transplantation are more likely to develop B cell lymphomas and not T cell lymphoma.

Complications of liver transplantation

  • Rejection of the transplanted liver
  • Hepatic artery thrombosis
  • Posttransplantation lymphoproliferative disorders- It can range from a mild polyclonal proliferation of B cells to B cell lymphomas.
  • Congestive heart failure and arrhythmias
  • Increased susceptibility to infections as a result of immunosuppression
  • Renal dysfunction due to acute tubular necrosis or nephrotoxicity of the tacrolimus and cyclosporine
  • Seizures are commonly associated with cyclosporine or tacrolimus toxicity.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: All of the following complications can be seen in patients with liver transplantation except

explanationHtml:
The presence of endotheliitis confirms the presence of acute rejection of the liver transplant.

Rejection following liver transplantation can be acute or chronic.

Patients usually present with

  • Malaise
  • Fever
  • Right upper quadrant pain

Laboratory investigations will show

  • Elevated levels of serum bilirubin
  • Aminotransferases
  • Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidases
  • Liver biopsy- for confirming the diagnosis and planning the treatment

Liver biopsy of the acute rejection is characterized by the presence of mixed portal cellular infiltrate, bile duct injury, and endothelial inflammation (endotheliitis).

Chronic rejection is characterized by the presence of focal parenchymal necrosis, mononuclear cell infiltration, progressive cholestasis, and fibrosis. In some patients, this process will lead to the loss of intrahepatic bile ducts, which is called vanishing bile duct syndrome.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A liver biopsy is performed in a patient who is suspected to have acute rejection following liver transplantation. Which of the following findings in the biopsy will confirm the presence of acute rejection?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of post-solid transplant infection most likely due to cytomegalovirus(CMV). It is the most common cause of post-solid organ transplants in India. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), herpes, and varicella are also known to cause infection post-solid organ transplantation but to a lesser extent.

CMV disease in recipients can present with fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, malaise, and arthralgia. They usually present within 1-4 months after transplant. The diagnosis of CMV infection is established by nucleic acid testing (NAT) using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Management includes the use of anti-viral drugs like ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, cidofovir and intravenous immunoglobulins.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: A 40-year-old male patient developed fever, malaise, and anorexia after a month of liver transplantation. On evaluation, he has leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and deranged liver function tests. Which of the following organisms is most likely to have caused this?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, autoimmune hepatitis has the highest chance of recurrence after liver transplantation.

Although some cases of sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cirrhosis recur, data for recurrence of autoimmune hepatitis is more supportive.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency does not recur after liver transplantation.
lessonTitle: Acute Liver Failure And Liver Transplantation
question: Which of the following primary diseases has the higher chance of recurrence, after liver transplantation?

explanationHtml:
The most common mutation seen in hemochromatosis is a cysteine to tyrosine substitution at position 282 (C282Y) in the HFE gene.

HFE mutations are the most common cause of hereditary hemochromatosis and are inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
question: What is the most common gene mutation associated with hemochromatosis?

explanationHtml: Thalassemia minor does not result in iron overload. Secondary hemochromatosis or iron overload is characterized by the deposition of iron in parenchymal cells.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to develop iron overload?

explanationHtml:
Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, impotence, amenorrhea) in hemochromatosis occurs as a result of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. This is due to iron deposition in the pituitary gland, not testes.

Iron deposition occurs in the following sites:

Organ Manifestation
Liver Hepatomegaly
Skin

Slate-grey or bronze skin hyperpigmentation: increased melanin synthesis due to iron deposition
Pancreas pancreatic diabetes/type 3C diabetes
Pituitary

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

Secondary hypothyroidism
Heart

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Congestive heart failure

Arrhythmias
Joints

Arthropathy is due to:

  • Iron deposition
  • Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (pseudogout)
question:
Which of the following clinical manifestations of hemochromatosis is incorrectly matched with its mechanism of onset?

Clinical feature Mechanism
1. Hypothyroidism - Iron deposition in pituitary
2. Arthropathy - Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals
3. Skin hyperpigmentation - Increased melanin production
4. Sexual dysfunction - Iron deposition in testes

explanationHtml:
Serum ferritin > 1000 μg/L is the strongest predictor of disease expression among individuals homozygous for the C282Y mutation.

Many patients with C282Y mutations are initially asymptomatic and do not show features of iron overload. In such patients, serum ferritin can indicate whether they are likely to develop the disease as ferritin levels reflect the total iron stores.

As ferritin levels may be high following inflammatory conditions, combined measurement of ferritin and transferrin saturation is done in a practical setting to avoid false positives. It is also repeated once inflammation subsides. If these tests are abnormal, genetic testing for HFE mutations is done.
question: A 7-year-old boy undergoes genetic testing as his brother has been diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. He is found to be homozygous for the C282Y mutation. Which of the following is the strongest indicator that he will develop symptoms of the disease?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of hemochromatosis. The treatment of choice is the removal of excess iron by phlebotomy.

Phlebotomy is an inexpensive, convenient, and safe method of treatment. In this process, 500 mL of blood is removed 1-2 times weekly which removes 200-250 mg of iron. Weekly phlebotomy should be continued until the serum ferritin level is ≤100 μg/L and every 3 months thereafter. It is contraindicated in severe anemia and hypoproteinemia.

Chelating agents bind to iron to form complexes that get excreted and are the drugs of choice. Drugs such as deferoxamine and deferasirox are commonly used. However, they are less effective and more expensive than phlebotomy.

Liver transplantation is indicated either in end-stage liver disease or in refractory cases.

Supportive management includes avoiding iron-containing substances such as red meat, multi-vitamin tablets, etc. Alcohol should be completely avoided as it can aggravate the disease.
question: A 47-year-old diabetic man is worried as the skin over his face, neck, and dorsum of hands has turned greyish over the past two months. He also complains of abdominal and joint pain. On examination, gynecomastia and hepatomegaly are noted. What is the treatment of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml: In hemochromatosis, removal of excess iron through phlebotomy has no effect on arthropathy and hypogonadism.
question: A 30-year-old man with hereditary hemochromatosis has been started on weekly phlebotomy. All of the following features will improve with this treatment except:

explanationHtml:
Wilson’s disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene on Chr.13q. The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions:

  • Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin
  • Helps excrete free copper in bile.

Thus, an ATP7B deficiency leads to excess deposition of free copper within tissues. It is an autosomal recessive condition. So, siblings of affected children have a 1 in 4 chance.

Intracellular trafficking of ATP7B (Wilson's disease) and ATP7A (Menke's disease) genes are regulated by an adaptor protein encoded by the AP1S1 gene. Mutations in this gene result in a syndrome with features of both Wilson's and Menke's diseases. It is called MEDNIK syndrome:

  • Mental retardation
  • Enteropathy
  • Deafness
  • Neuropathy
  • Ichthyosis
  • Keratodermia.

options.text: AP1S1 gene is essential for normal functioning
Siblings of affected children have 1 in 4 risk of the disease

question: Which of the following is incorrect about Wilson's disease?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, statements 1 and 5 are true.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings are seen in almost 95% patients of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement. It initially appears as a crescent in the superior pole of Descemet's membrane and gradually extends inferiorly, eventually becoming circumferential in shape.

KF rings occur due to copper deposition in Descemet's membrane. They are golden-brown to greenish-brown in colour and can be visualised by slit-lamp examination.

While it is a characteristic sign of Wilson’s disease (statement 2), it can also be seen in:

  • Primary biliary cholangitis
  • Liver disease
  • Neonatal cholestasis

KF rings are present in almost 95% of patients with Wilson's disease with neuropsychiatric symptoms compared to around 65% of those with hepatic presentations (statement 4). They disappear on treatment with copper-chelating agents like d-penicillamine (while desferrioxamine is an iron chelating agent) and may reappear as the disease progresses (statement 3).

The image below shows a KF ring :

[[figure-1]]
question:
Which of the following are true regarding KF ring?

  1. Seen in 95% patients of Wilson's disease with neurological involvement
  2. Is seen only for Wilson's disease
  3. Resolves with desferrioxamine
  4. Seen in all patients with hepatic involvement
  5. Seen in superior and inferior pole of Descemet's membrane

explanationHtml:
The presence of the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring in Wilson's disease is most commonly associated with neuropsychiatric manifestations such as dystonia.

In majority of the cases, neuropsychiatric manifestations follow hepatic manifestations. It is due to the deposition of free copper in the basal ganglia (leading to bilateral degeneration and atrophy) and cortex. The features include:

  • Dysarthria (most common): Irregular word spacing, hypophonic or spastic speech
  • Dystonia: Vacuous smile i.e mask-like face with an open mouth
  • Parkinsonism: Bradykinesia, postural instability, rigidity
  • Subcortical dementia: Slow mental processing, memory loss
  • Psychiatric symptoms: Loss of emotional control, depression, hyperactivity
  • Decreased scholastic performance: Deterioration in handwriting, clumsiness
  • Autonomic symptoms: Excessive sweating and salivation, sexual dysfunction
  • Wing beating tremors (seen in advanced disease): High amplitude tremor that is prominent with arms abducted, elbows flexed and palms facing downward.
question: In patients with Wilson's disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings are most commonly associated with:

explanationHtml:
The given laboratory values indicate hepatic disease and hemolytic anemia (low Hb with high reticulocyte count). These lab findings along with clinical features point to a diagnosis of Wilson's disease.

The clinical features of Wilson’s disease include:

System Clinical features
Hepatic
(most common)

Jaundice
Abdominal pain
Hepatomegaly
Fatigue
Ascites
Variceal bleed
Coagulation defects

High AST & ALT with low ALP
Neurological Dysarthria
Dystonia
Parkinsonism
Subcortical dementia
Depression
Wing beating tremors
Decreased scholastic performance
Ophthalmic Kayser-Fleischer (KF) rings
Sunflower cataract
Others Hemolytic anemia (Coombs negative)
Acute pancreatitis
Fanconi's syndrome
Hypoparathyroidism
Cardiomyopathy
Spontaneous abortions
Infertility

Option A: Hemochromatosis presents with clinical features of iron overload. Serum ferritin and total iron are elevated.

Option B: Acute viral hepatitis presents with positive HbsAg, whereas anti-Hbs IgG indicates past infection. There is tender hepatomegaly with very high levels of transaminases (>1000 IU/L).

Option C: Primary biliary cirrhosis presents with jaundice, severe itching, and pale stools. There are high levels of direct bilirubin, ALP, and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies.
question:
A 22-year-old woman is being evaluated in the emergency department for a 3-day history of dark-colored urine and abdominal distension. On examination, she is conscious and oriented. Icterus is present. The following investigations are done. Which of the following would you suspect?

Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dl
Hematocrit 26%
Reticulocytes 5%
Platelets 1.3 x 105/mm3
Serum total iron Reduced
Serum ferritin Normal
Serum ALT 110 IU/L
Serum AST 240 IU/L
Serum ALP 30 IU/L
Total bilirubin 13 mg/dl
Anti-Hbs IgG Positive
USG Abdomen Nodular liver and enlarged spleen

explanationHtml:
The clinical features of hepatitis, progressive neurological degeneration, and the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image are suggestive of Wilson's disease. The initial step regarding investigations done for the diagnosis is the measurement of serum ceruloplasmin levels.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is a golden to greenish-brown ring of deposition of copper in the Descemets membrane of the peripheral cornea. Patients with neurological manifestations manifest with KF ring in >95% of cases.

Lab investigations in Wilson's disease would show:

Lab markers Change in Wilson's disease Reason
Serum ceruloplasmin ↓↓↓ ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper
24h urinary copper ↑↑ (>100 μg/24h) Excess free copper excreted in urine
Total serum copper ↓ Due to marked reduction in ceruloplasmin

The gold standard technique for diagnosis of Wilson’s disease is percutaneous needle liver biopsy for measurement of hepatic copper levels >200 μg/g of dry weight.

Option B: The role of total serum copper in the diagnosis of Wilson's disease is limited. Measurement of serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper is preferred.

Option C: ATP7B enzyme assays have shown promise in early studies as a neonatal screening test for Wilson's disease. However, it is not yet part of routine clinical practice.

Option D: Karyotyping is done for every asymptomatic 1st and 2nd degree relative of a patient with Wilson’s disease. This helps differentiate the carriers (heterozygous) from the patients (homozygous) and can lead to early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms.
question: A child presents with hepatitis and progressive neurological degeneration. A picture of his eye has been provided below. Among the following options, what would be the initial step regarding the investigations done for this child's diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The following findings will be seen in a patient with Wilson's disease:

  • Decreased total serum copper
  • Decreased serum ceruloplasmin
  • Increased urinary copper
Lab markers Change in Wilson's disease Reason
Serum ceruloplasmin ↓↓↓ ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper

This clinical scenario is suggestive of Wilson's disease with predominantly neurological features. The safest drug that can be initiated for this patient is trientine. This is because D-penicillamine can worsen neurological symptoms and would not be tolerated by this patient.

The copper chelating agents, D-penicillamine and trientine are the first-line drugs in the management of Wilson's disease. D-penicillamine is the recommended drug due to its availability and cost-effectiveness compared to trientine.

However, D-penicillamine can precipitate various adverse effects including aplastic anemia, myasthenia gravis and membranous nephropathy. It can also worsen neurological symptoms. Hence, trientine is administered in those who cannot tolerate D-penicillamine.

Elemental zinc is commonly used as a maintenance therapy along with chelating agents. It can also be used as first-line therapy in pregnancy.

Tetrathiomolybdate is currently under phase 2 clinical trials. It has been identified to be effective in patients with neuropsychiatric manifestations but is not approved for clinical use.

Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment for advanced liver disease.

explanationHtml:
Low serum copper level attributed to the ATP7A gene is due to Menke's disease (Option C).

Menke's disease or Menke-Kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition occurring due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper-containing enzymes. It presents within 3 years of age and is characterized by:

  • Depigmented kinky hair
  • Failure to thrive
  • Neurodegenerative symptoms like loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, epilepsyLoose, wrinkled skin
  • Multiple fractures
  • Poor visual acuity
  • Recurrent infections.

Lab investigations show low serum copper (<65 μg/dL) and low ceruloplasmin(<20 mg/dl). The disease is fatal as it has no curative treatment. But, administration of L-histidine and copper chloride injections may be beneficial, if started early.

Aceruloplasminemia is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by tissue iron overload, mental deterioration, microcytic anemia, and low serum iron and copper concentrations.

Option B: Low serum copper and low ceruloplasmin is also seen in Wilson’s disease, but is associated with the gene defect ATP7B on chromosome 13. It is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism with features of hepatolenticular degeneration and Kayser Fleischer ring.

Option A: Dubin Johnson Syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired canalicular excretion of bilirubin due to mutation in MRP-2 protein leading to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Option D: Gilbert’s Syndrome is characterized by decreased UDP glucuronyl transferase activity leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, which can be autosomal recessive or dominant.

Budd-Chiari syndrome is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension.

Budd Chiari syndrome is a congestive hepatopathy characterized by the obstruction of hepatic venous outflow. The most common cause is due to hepatic vein thrombosis. Obstruction of two or more major hepatic veins causes Budd-Chiari syndrome. It is characterized by hepatomegaly, ascites, and abdominal pain.

SAAG helps distinguish ascites caused by portal hypertension from other causes of ascites.
question: Ascitic tap done on a patient with abdominal distention revealed a SAAG of 1.4g/dL. What is the likely cause of his ascites?

explanationHtml:
The likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) >1.1g/dL [calculated as serum albumin level - ascitic fluid albumin level, which in this case is 3-1=2g/dL] and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL is late Budd Chiari syndrome.

Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) can be used to differentiate between ascites due to portal hypertension and non-portal hypertensive ascites. It represents the pressure within the hepatic sinusoids and correlates with the hepatic venous pressure gradient.

It is given by the formula: SAAG = Serum albumin level - Ascitic fluid albumin level

Interpretation of SAAG:

  • SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is due to increased pressure in the hepatic sinusoids. It reflects the presence of portal hypertension.
  • SAAG <1.1 g/dL indicates that the ascites is not related to portal hypertension. It may be due to infection or malignancy.

In cases with high-SAAG (≥1.1), ascitic protein level analysis further helps in identifying the etiology:

  • ≥2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids are normal and are allowing the passage of protein into the ascites as in early Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • <2.5 g/dL indicates that the hepatic sinusoids have been damaged and scarred and no longer allow passage of protein as in late Budd-Chiari syndrome

SBP is the spontaneous infection of the ascitic fluid without an intraabdominal source. Infection with E.coli and other gut bacteria is most commonly seen. explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with ANC ≥ 250 cells/μl in ascitic fluid is suggestive of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Daily antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended in patients who have had an episode of SBP to prevent a recurrence.

SBP is the spontaneous infection of the ascitic fluid without an intraabdominal source. The most common causative organisms are E.coli and other gut bacteria. The diagnosis of SBP is made when the ascitic fluid has an absolute neutrophil count >250/μl.

According to the latest recommendations, weekly antibiotic prophylaxis is no longer recommended. For patients with low protein ascites (<1.5 g/dL [15g/L]) along with either impaired renal function or liver failure, we use prolonged outpatient trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (one double-strength tablet daily). Alternatives include ciprofloxacin 500 mg per day or norfloxacin 400 mg per day.

For patients on chronic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy, renal function should be monitored by checking serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine every one to six months depending on the stability of patient. If there is worsening renal function, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should be discontinued.

Hepatopulmonary syndrome is characterized by a triad of liver disease, hypoxemia, and intrapulmonary vascular dilatations. Most patients have dyspnea on exertion. The classic clinical manifestations are:

  • Platypnea - Increase in dyspnea when the patient moves from supine to upright position
  • Orthodeoxia - Decrease in arterial oxygen tension when the patient moves from supine to upright position

The hypoxemia is due to a ventilation-perfusion mismatch which causes an increased alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient. The most sensitive test for diagnosis is contrast bubble echocardiography.

Liver transplantation is the definitive treatment of this condition following which the symptoms subside.

MELD (Model for End-stage Liver Disease) score is used to prioritize patients awaiting liver transplantation. However, there are patients whose condition might be worse than what their MELD score suggests. There might also be certain diseases or certain complications of liver disease which may affect patient survival. Such conditions are not accounted for in the MELD score. Hence, such patients are given an upgraded score to accurately represent the mortality risk. These conditions are called MELD exceptions.

The MELD exceptions include:-

  • Portopulmonary hypertension
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Familial amyloid polyneuropathy
  • Primary hyperoxaluria (necessitating liver-kidney transplantation)

explanationHtml:
Restitution is an epithelial mucosal defense mechanism. It is the process by which healthy surface epithelial cells from the adjoining areas migrate to restore a damaged region of the gastric mucosa.

The gastric mucosa has well-established mucosal defense mechanisms against various assaults like HCl, pepsin, alcohol, etc. These include:

  • Pre-epithelial defense: A layer of mucous over the surface epithelium. This is secreted by the surface epithelium and contains HCO3- which maintains neutral pH at the cell surface
  • Epithelial defense: It is constituted by the surface epithelial cells and their intercellular tight junctions that perform the following functions
    • Act as a physical barrier
    • Restitution is the migration of healthy cells to damaged areas
    • Rapid renewal of surface epithelial layer
    • Generating factors that prevent cellular damage such as heat shock proteins
  • Sub-epithelial defense:
    • Rich microvascular bed of the gastric submucosa that provides HCO3- and washes away the toxic metabolites.
    • Alkaline tide- It is caused by the release of HCO3- into the gastric capillaries by the parietal cells. This HCO3- helps in the quick neutralization of HCl.

question: Which of the following is an epithelial mucosal defense mechanism of the gastric mucosa?

explanationHtml:
The NSAIDs impair the mucosal defense mechanism primarily by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

NSAIDs also decrease nitric oxide synthesis and have an irritant effect on the gastric mucosa but inhibition of COX enzymes/ prostaglandin synthesis is the most prominent factor.

Almost all the mucosal defense mechanisms are primarily mediated by prostaglandins synthesized by the gastric mucosal cells. Apart from the prostaglandins, the other factors that play a role in mucosal defense include:

  • Nitric oxide (NO)- Causes vasodilation thereby increasing the mucosal blood flow.
  • Several growth factors like EGF, TGF, FGF- Play a role in epithelial regeneration and restitution.

question: All of the following are true about the risk factors of NSAIDs associated peptic ulcer disease except:

explanationHtml:
Antral predominant gastritis is associated with duodenal ulcers. Antral predominant gastritis is associated with increased acid production by the parietal cells. This subjects the duodenum to increased acid exposure, leading to the formation of duodenal ulcers.

H. pylori infection may result in the following patterns of gastritis:

  • Non-atrophic pangastritis- mostly asymptomatic and sometimes associated with MALToma.
  • Corpus predominant gastritis- affects the corpus and causes atrophy. This leads to the loss of acid-producing parietal cells that are primarily found in the corpus. Hence, it is associated with decreased acid production. This is also a predisposing factor for the development of gastric cancer.
  • Antral predominant gastritis- spares the parietal cells. Hence, it is associated with increased acid production.

Option A: Autoimmune gastritis is caused due to autoantibodies against the parietal cells. It is not associated with H. pylori.

Option C: Granulomatous gastritis is characterized by the presence of granulomas It is associated with Crohn's disease and sarcoidosis.

question: What pattern of gastritis is most common in patients with H.pylori-related duodenal ulcers?

explanationHtml:
Epigastric pain with a burning sensation that usually occurs 2-3 hours after a meal and is relieved by taking food suggestive of duodenal ulcer.

The following patterns of pain are usually seen in peptic ulcer disease:

  • Duodenal Ulcer- Pain occurs 1.5 to 3 hours after a meal and is frequently relieved by antacids or food. Pain may awaken the patient from sleep.
  • Gastric Ulcer- Pain/discomfort may be precipitated by food. Nausea and weight loss are common.
  • Perforated ulcer- The bed of the ulcer tunnels through the entire thickness of the gastric wall and opens into the peritoneum. This presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain and leads to peritonitis. Radiography shows gas under the diaphragm.
  • Penetrating ulcer- It is a type of perforation where the ulcer tunnels into an adjacent organ like the pancreas/liver. In this case, the pain won't subside with food or antacid administration and might radiate to the back.

A large majority of patients (especially in NSAID-induced ulcers, elderly or immunocompromised) do not show symptoms like epigastric pain and directly present with complications like perforation or bleeding.

question: A patient presents with frequent epigastric pain with burning sensation for the past 2 years. The pain usually occurs 2-3 hours after a meal and is relieved by taking food. He also says that he sometimes wakes up at night because of severe pain. The most probable cause for his symptoms is:

explanationHtml:
Gastric ulcers are associated with low basal acid production and low stimulated acid production.

Gastric acid secretion occurs in two patterns:

  • Basal acid output- Occurs in a circadian pattern. It is mediated by ACh from the vagus and histamine.
  • Stimulated acid production- Occurs in response to food. It is mediated by gastrin in addition to other factors.

question: You are a first-year resident. You are asked to prescribe an H.pylori eradication regimen to a patient with peptic ulcer disease. Which of the following drugs will you not include in it?

explanationHtml:

H pylori eradication therapy is offered to patients diagnosed with peptic ulcer disease (PUD) as it greatly decreases the recurrence of ulcers. In addition to this, it should also be offered to patients at increased risk of PUD and gastric cancer such as:

  • Patients with long-term NSAIDs usage. Eg. Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Patients taking gastric acid inhibitors for >1 year
  • Patients with increased exposure to risk factors of gastric cancers. Eg. heavy smokers, exposure to dust, coal
  • Patients with previous history/family history of gastric neoplasm

question: Eradication of H.pylori infection in patients with peptic ulcer disease is determined by?

explanationHtml:
H.pylori increases the risk of gastric MALT lymphoma.

H.pylori is protective against the following:

  • GERD
  • Barrett's esophagus
  • Adenocarcinoma of esophagus

H. pylori are inversely related to gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and its sequelae, which include Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

H.pylori strains positive for Cag A may be particularly protective against the development of esophageal adenocarcinoma. Thus, colonization with H. pylori, particularly Cag A strains, may be protective against the more severe forms of GERD.

Eradication of H. pylori is associated with mild worsening of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in patients with corpus-dominant or pangastritis. It improves symptoms in those with antral-dominant gastritis.

H. pylori has not been found to be a contributing factor to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

question: The most common complication in patients with peptic ulcer disease is:

explanationHtml:
The given clinical features indicating hypercalcemia and investigations showing renal insufficiency, metabolic alkalosis are suggestive of milk-alkali syndrome. Long-term use of calcium carbonate can lead to this condition.

In susceptible individuals, there is a loss of negative feedback, leading to excess calcium absorption when there is excess intake. It results in the following triad of clinical features:
  • Hypercalcemia
  • Alkalosis- due to HCO3 reabsorption caused by PTH suppression, natriuresis, and water depletion
  • Renal failure- due to damage to renal tubules
It is reversible once ingestion of antacid is stopped. However, in severe cases, a chronic form called Burnett’s syndrome can develop. It is associated with irreversible renal damage.

question:
A 47-year-old woman presented to the ER with an altered sensorium. Her husband reported that she has had abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation for the past 4 days. She has been self-medicating for gastritis. Her lab investigations are as shown. Which of the following drugs is she most likely on that could have caused her symptoms?

Renal function test:

explanationHtml:
The gastric ulcers associated with head trauma are Cushing ulcers. Head trauma leads to vagal stimulation which in turn leads to increased gastric acid production.

Option A: Curling ulcers are seen in severe burns.

Option C: Stress ulcers are seen in conditions like shock, sepsis, etc. They are thought to be caused by local ischemia and splanchnic vasoconstriction.

Option D: Refractory ulcers are those that do not heal even after adequate medical therapy.

question: A patient is admitted to the ICU after he suffered trauma to his head. This patient is prone to develop what type of gastric ulcers?

explanationHtml:
A gastric ulcer is said to be refractory if it fails to heal after 12 weeks.

Refractory gastric ulcers may indicate the presence of complicating factors, including persistent infection, continued NSAID use, severe comorbidities, or malignancy.

Management of refractory peptic ulcer disease (PUD) involves first identifying and addressing underlying causes such as persistent Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use. This is followed by high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy to promote healing. Surgery is reserved for ulcers that remain unhealed or develop complications like bleeding, perforation, or obstruction.

A duodenal ulcer is said to be refractory if it fails to heal after 8 weeks.

question: You would diagnose a patient to have a refractory gastric ulcer if the ulcer fails to heal after:

explanationHtml:
The given scenario of symptoms not improving with antacids, associated diarrhea, and the unusual location of ulcers are highly suggestive of Zollinger Ellison syndrome.

Zollinger Ellison syndrome (ZES) is a peptic ulcer disease caused by unregulated gastrin release from a neuroendocrine tumor/gastrinoma. About 60% of the tumors are malignant, hence, it is important to identify ZES.

The clinical presentation of ZES is very similar to that of peptic ulcer disease. The features which help in suspecting ZES include:

  • Unusual locations- the second part of the duodenum and beyond
  • Refractory to medical therapy
  • Recurrence after acid-reducing surgery
  • Presenting with complications like bleeding and perforation
  • Not associated with H. pylori or NSAID ingestion

Patients of ZES often have associated diarrhea and involvement of the esophagus (esophagitis, ulceration, or stricture).

question: A middle-aged woman presents with acidity, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss for the past few months. Her symptoms are not relieved by taking antacids. An endoscopic evaluation shows ulcers on the second part of the duodenum. Which of the following conditions should be suspected in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Zollinger Ellison syndrome (ZES). The next appropriate step to evaluate the patients for ZES is by measuring the serum gastrin levels. History of hyperparathyroidism and transsphenoidal prolactinoma resection indicates MEN1 syndrome. ZES is commonly associated with MEN1.

The normal gastrin levels are <150 pg/mL. An increase of >10 times the normal levels is highly suggestive of ZES.

Secretin test is a gastrin provocative test. It is done when the gastrin levels and the acid secretory studies are inconclusive for ZES. It is the most sensitive and specific gastrin provocative test for the diagnosis of gastrinoma.

Endoscopic ultrasound is done to localize the tumor. It is done after the diagnosis of ZES has been established.

question: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent duodenal ulcers with poor response to medical therapy. He had a history of hyperparathyroidism and transsphenoidal prolactinoma resection. Which among the following is the next appropriate step?

explanationHtml:
OctreoScan detects gastrinomas using their property of uptake of somatostatin analogues.

OctreoScan detects endocrine tumors that express receptors for somatostatin in conditions such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) and multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes.

Other modalities used for localizing the tumor in ZES include:

  • Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)
  • PET/CT with Ga-DOTATATE is the investigation of choice when available.

Note: PET/CT with Ga-DOTATATE is the gold-standard test for localizing tumors in pheochromocytoma.

question: Which of the following viruses cause infectious gastritis in immunocompromised patients?

explanationHtml:
The given peripheral smear findings and serology are suggestive of pernicious anemia. It is usually seen in type A gastritis.

Type A autoimmune gastritis is caused by circulating antibodies against the parietal cells. The destruction of parietal cells leads to the deficiency of intrinsic factor that is necessary for the absorption of vitamin B12. The resulting B12 deficiency causes pernicious anemia.

question: An anemic patient on evaluation showed macrocytes with hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear. Serology revealed anti-parietal cell antibodies. Which of the following is most likely to be associated with her condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with her endoscopy findings are suggestive of phlegmonous gastritis. It is caused due to E.coli.

Phlegmonous gastritis is a potentially life-threatening disorder characterized by marked and diffuse acute inflammatory infiltrates of the entire gastric wall accompanied by necrosis. It usually affects the immunocompromised and elderly individuals.

Organisms associated with phlegmonous gastritis are:

  • E.coli
  • Streptococci
  • Staphylococci
  • Proteus
  • Haemophilus species

Other uncommon forms of gastritis are:

  • Eosinophilic gastritis: Presents as intestinal obstruction
  • Russel’s body gastritis: Pseudotumor on endoscopy
  • Granulomatous gastritis is seen in Crohn’s disease
  • Lymphocytic gastritis is seen in celiac disease
