question:
An 84-year-old woman living in an assisted care facility is rushed to the hospital with an upper GI bleed. On arrival, she is febrile and the nurse notes a sudden spurt of blood from her nasogastric tube. The following investigations are done. Which of the following is responsible for this patient's condition?

CRP- 23 mg/L

Upper GI endoscopy- Extensive gastric ulceration with necrotic tissue and edematous mucosa

CT abdomen- Thickened gastric wall

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of steatorrhoea, which is seen in short bowel syndrome.

Steatorrhoea is defined as excess fat in stools (>7g/day) due to poor absorption of lipids. It is characterized by stools are bulky, pale, foul-smelling, and difficult to flush.

Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorption disorder caused by a lack of functional small intestine. It can lead to the typical features of malabsorption such as abdominal pain, diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, weight loss and anaemia.

Option B: Primary lactase deficiency leads to defective absorption of lactose. It does not affect lipid absorption.

Option C: Pernicious anemia is due to an absence of gastric parietal cell-intrinsic factor which is necessary for the absorption of vitamin B12.

Option D: Wilson's disease is associated with increased absorption of copper and is not a part of malabsorption syndrome.
question: A patient presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating sensation, and weight loss. History is significant for stools that are bulky, pale, foul-smelling, and difficult to flush. Further testing reveals fecal fat excretion of  8.2g/day. Which of the following would be a differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Yogurt is the least likely to cause symptoms of lactose intolerance. It contains lactobacillus that produces lactase and is generally well tolerated.

Lactase is a brush border enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. In lactase deficiency, patients have great variability in clinical symptoms, depending on both the severity of lactase deficiency and the amount of lactose ingested.

The goal of treatment in patients with isolated lactase deficiency is achieving patient comfort through the elimination of dietary lactose.

Foods that are high in lactose include milk (12 g/cup), ice cream (9 g/cup), and cottage cheese (8 g/cup). Aged cheese has lower lactose content. Most people can tolerate up to 12g of lactose a day without significant symptoms.
question: A 22-year-old man presented with diarrhea and intolerance to dairy products. On investigation, he was found to have a lactase deficiency. Which of the following agents is least likely to cause symptoms of lactose intolerance?

correctAnswer: D. Rapid small-intestinal transit time decreases the symptoms
explanationHtml:
Rapid small-intestinal transit time increases the symptoms of lactose intolerance.

Lactose intolerance can be due to:

  • Primary lactase deficiency- a genetically determined deficiency or absence of lactase enzyme
  • Secondary lactase deficiency- due to small intestinal mucosal diseases such as celiac disease

Factors affecting symptoms of lactose intolerance:

  • Amount of lactose in the diet.
  • Rate of gastric emptying- symptoms are more likely when gastric emptying is rapid (post-gastrectomy and skimmed milk intake).
  • Small intestinal transit time- more rapid small intestinal transit time makes symptoms more likely.
  • Antibiotic use- results in decreased colonic microflora which in turn decreases the production of easily absorbed short-chain fatty acids from non-absorbed lactose. This can worsen the symptoms.

options.text: It may be seen in celiac disease
It can mimic irritable bowel syndrome
Delayed gastric emptying decreases the symptoms
Rapid small-intestinal transit time decreases the symptoms

question: Which of the following is incorrect about lactose intolerance?

explanationHtml:
Small bowel diarrhea is associated with steatorrhea, not large bowel diarrhea.

Features Small bowel Large bowel
Volume of stools Large Small
Frequency of stool No change Increased
Blood and mucus in stools Absent Present

Tenesmus refers to the constant urge to defecate with little or no stool passed.
question: Which of the following is unlikely to be present in a patient with large bowel diarrhea?

correctAnswer: D. Are associated with enterotoxigenic E. coli
explanationHtml:
Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is associated with secretory diarrhea.

Feature Osmotic diarrhea Secretory diarrhea
Definition Diarrhea due to poorly absorbed osmotically active substances in the colonic lumen. Diarrhea due to excessive secretion of NaCl, HCO3-, and water into the gut.
Fasting Improves symptoms No effect
Stool osmolar gap (mOsm) >100 <50
Causes Malabsorption syndrome

Tumors - VIPoma

Toxins - ETEC, V. cholera

Stool osmolar gap = measured osmolality - calculated osmolality

= (290 to 300) - 2 (stool Na+ + stool K+)

options.text: Increased osmolarity of stool is due to unabsorbed dietary nutrients
Are associated with enterotoxigenic E. coli

question: All are true regarding osmotic diarrhea except :

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is factitious diarrhea.

Factitious diarrhoea is a form of Münchausen's syndrome. The normal stool osmolality is about 290 mOsm/kg H2O. Very low (<250 mOsm/kg) or very high (>400 mOsm/kg) values of stool osmolality can indicate intentional tampering of the sample by the patient by adding diluted or concentrated urine to it.

The stool osmolar gap is calculated using the amount of electrolytes Na+ and K+ in the stool sample. This value helps in differentiating between osmotic (gap >100) and secretory (gap <50) diarrhea. A very high or very low osmotic gap indicates diarrhea induced by the consumption of laxatives.

In the given scenario, the values of both the stool osmolality and the osmolar gap are suspiciously low, which indicates a high likelihood of intentional tampering of the sample, making factitious diarrhea the most likely diagnosis.
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with complaints of abdominal pain and recurrent diarrhea for several months. History reveals that she regularly goes on camping trips. Stool osmolality was 200 mOsm/kg H2O and the stool osmolar gap was 20 mOsm/kg H2O. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Good response to low fat diet
explanationHtml:
Bile acid diarrhea has no response to a low-fat diet.

explanationHtml:
The most common viral cause of diarrhoea in adults (and overall) is norovirus (Norwalk virus).

In children, the most common cause is rotavirus.
question: Which of the following is the most common viral cause of diarrhea in adults?

explanationHtml:
Yersinia enterocolitica causes diarrhea with symptoms resembling appendicitis, also called pseudoappendicitis.

The patients present with abdominal pain which can be localized to the right iliac fossa, thus mimicking appendicitis. USG shows a normal appendix and may show enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes.

Appendectomy is not indicated for Yersinia infection pseudoappendicitis.

question: A father brings his 12-year-old son with complaints of severe abdominal pain and diarrhea. The pain is localized to the right iliac fossa. USG abdomen reveals enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes and a normal appendix. Which of the following is the likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
Enterovirus is not an etiological agent for travelers' diarrhea.

The various causes of travelers' diarrhea are as follows:

  • Bacterial
    • Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)- most common
    • Shigella
    • Salmonella
    • S. aureus
    • B. cereus
  • Viral
    • Norovirus
    • Rotavirus
  • Parasite
    • Giardia lamblia
    • Entamoeba histolytica.
question: Which of the following is not associated with travellers' diarrhoea?

explanationHtml:
The image shows the characteristic fish in stream appearance of Vibrio, suggestive of cholera. Diarrhea due to Vibrio cholerae results in hypokalemic acidosis.

Cholera exotoxin activates adenylate cyclase (↑ cAMP) leading to loss of bicarbonate, water, and electrolytes leading to hypokalemic acidosis.

Note: The other cause for hypokalemic acidosis is renal tubular acidosis.
question: A child was brought with complaints of watery diarrhea for 48 hours. On examination, tachycardia and decreased skin turgor were present. Stool microscopy revealed the following organisms. Which of the given findings is likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of acute onset gastroenteritis. Since the symptoms appeared shortly after ingestion, they are caused due to preformed toxins. From the given options, Staphylococcus aureus is associated with preformed toxins.

Etiology of gastroenteritis are as follows :

1. Preformed toxin:

  • Staphylococcus aureus
  • Bacillus cereus
  • Clostridium perfringens

2. Toxin forming:

  • Vibrio cholerae
  • Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC)

3. Invasive:

  • Shigella
  • Salmonella
  • Yersinia
  • Campylobacter
question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the ER with complaints of acute onset nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She gives a history of consumption of street food earlier the same day. Which of the following organisms is likely to be responsible for her condition?

correctAnswer: B. Persistent diarrhoea after a 48 hour fast
explanationHtml: Persistent diarrhoea after a 48-hour fast is not a diagnostic criteria for IBS.

question: Which of the following is not a diagnostic criterion for irritable bowel syndrome?

correctAnswer: D. Constipation alternating with episodes of diarrhoea
explanationHtml:
The most common pattern in IBS patients is constipation alternating with episodes of diarrhoea.

Based on bowel movement patterns, IBS is classified as:

  • IBS-C: Irritable bowel syndrome-constipation predominant
  • IBS-D: Irritable bowel syndrome-diarrhoea predominant
  • IBS-M: Irritable bowel syndrome-mixed

The majority of patients change subtypes over the course of illness.

Note: Abdominal pain is a pre-requisite for the diagnosis of IBS. This means that for the diagnosis of IBS, recurrent abdominal pain must be present.

options.text: Constipation alternating with episodes of diarrhoea

question: The most common pattern seen in irritable bowel syndrome patients is _______

correctAnswer: D. Onset of symptoms during a period of stress
explanationHtml:
The onset of symptoms during a period of stress or emotional upset is a feature that supports a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

Features in favour of IBS:

  • Abdominal pain that improves/worsens with defecation
  • Association with stress or emotional symptoms
  • Small volume of stools

Features not in favour of IBS:

  • Onset of symptoms in old age
  • Presence of fever and weight loss
  • Persistent diarrhoea after a 48h fast
  • Nocturnal diarrhoea
  • Steatorrhoea

options.text: Persistent diarrhoea after a 48 hour fast
Onset of symptoms during a period of stress

question: A patient presents with a 3-month history of crampy abdominal pain associated with diarrhea. Which of the following features, if present, will support a diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Decreased colonic motor potentials are not implicated in the pathogenesis of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). On the contrary, increased colonic motor potentials are seen.

The pathogenesis of IBS is poorly understood. However, the following have been implicated in its pathogenesis:

  • Increased colonic motor potentials lead to increased high-amplitude propagating contractions (HAPCs) which causes diarrhea.
  • Visceral hypersensitivity leads to exaggerated sensory responses to visceral stimulation by food. This explains the postprandial symptoms in IBS.
  • CNS dysregulation - dysfunctional activation of the mid-cingulate cortex and prefrontal lobes leads to increased perception of visceral pain.
  • Abnormal serotonin pathways - serotonin-containing enterochromaffin cells are increased in IBS patients.
  • Altered gut flora
question: Which of the following is not implicated in the pathogenesis of irritable bowel syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Serotonin is associated with irritable bowel syndrome diarrhoea type (IBS-D).

Abnormal serotonin pathways is one of the causes for symptoms in IBS. The serotonin containing enterochromaffin cells are increased in a subset of IBS-D patients. This provides a rationale for the use of serotonin antagonists in the treatment of this condition.
question: A 35-year-old housewife has been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome - diarrhea predominant. Which neurotransmitter is associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Mid cingulate cortex and prefrontal lobe are associated with IBS.

Mid cingulate cortex: Modulation of this region is associated with changes in the subjective unpleasantness of pain.

Prefrontal lobe: Dysfunction of this area leads to the increased perception of visceral pain.
question:
Which of the following parts of the brain are associated with irritable bowel syndrome?

  1. Paracentral lobule
  2. Mid cingulate cortex
  3. Prefrontal lobe
  4. Temporal cortex

explanationHtml:
Male gender is not a risk factor for post-infectious IBS.

Post-infectious IBS develops following a gastrointestinal infection with microbes such as Campylobacter, Salmonella and Shigella.

Risk factors for developing post-infectious IBS:

  • Young age and female gender
  • Prolonged duration of illness
  • Toxicity of infecting bacterial strain
  • Smoking
  • Depression
  • Hypochondriasis
question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome?

explanationHtml:
A stool fat test is not recommended in a suspected case of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

IBS is a clinical diagnosis that can be made without performing many tests if the patient presents with typical symptoms. However, it is recommended to perform the following tests in most patients to rule out other conditions:

  • Complete blood count
  • Sigmoidoscopic examination
  • Stool examination for ova and parasites
  • 3-week lactose-free diet

In patients >40 years, air-contrast barium enema or colonoscopy should also be performed.

options.text: Stool examination for ova and parasites

question: In a suspected case of irritable bowel syndrome, which of the following investigations is not recommended?

explanationHtml:
Fecal lactoferrin is the marker of IBD that is used to rule out irritable bowel syndrome. Fecal lactoferrin is a highly sensitive and specific marker for detecting intestinal inflammation.

Fecal calprotectin is another marker of IBD and it is used to rule out irritable bowel syndrome and bacterial overgrowth. It correlates well with histologic inflammation, predicts relapses, and detects pouchitis.

Option A: Fecal fat is normally digested by pancreatic lipase and absorbed from the jejunum. In disorders of exocrine pancreatic function, fat absorption decreases, resulting in steatorrhea and increased fecal fat.

Options C & D: Fecal trypsin, chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes, therefore a decrease in fecal levels below normal suggests a disorder of the exocrine pancreas.
question: Which of the following is a marker of inflammatory bowel disease, which helps to rule out irritable bowel syndrome?

correctAnswer: D. FODMAPs are highly absorbed by the small intestine
explanationHtml:
FODMAPs are poorly absorbed in the small intestine.

FODMAPs stands for Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, And Polyols. Foodstuff containing lactose, fructose, and sorbitol are some examples of FODMAPs.

Since FODMAPs are poorly absorbed, they are fermented by gut bacteria in the colon to produce gas and osmotically active carbohydrates. So, a diet low in FODMAPs is recommended to reduce symptoms in IBS patients.

options.text: Diet low in FODMAPs reduces symptoms in IBS patients
Sorbitol is an example of FODMAP
FODMAPs are highly absorbed by the small intestine

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the FODMAPs diet recommended for a patient with irritable bowel syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Lubiprostone is used in the treatment of constipation-predominant IBS.

Lubiprostone eases the passage of stools and improves symptoms of constipation-predominant IBS by activating chloride channels on the apical surface of enterocytes which promotes the secretion of water and chloride into the bowel.

Loperamide, alosetron, and eluxadoline (opioid mu receptor agonist) are used in the treatment of diarrhea-predominant IBS.
question: A 35-year-old woman with constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome presents with worsening abdominal pain and bloating. Which of the following drugs can be prescribed for her condition?

explanationHtml:
Paroxetine is most effective in treating constipation. It is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that accelerates oro-caecal transit.

Note: Citalopram is an SSRI that is effective in the management of pain in IBS. It blunts perception of rectal distension and reduces the magnitude of gastrocolic reflex.
question: You have prescribed paroxetine to a patient with irritable bowel syndrome. This medication is most effective in reducing which of the following symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Alosetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist used in the treatment of IBS–D.

Options B and C: Tegaserod and lubiprostone are used in the treatment of constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS–C).

Option D: Ondansetron is used in the treatment of nausea and vomiting.
question: Drug 'X', a 5 HT3 receptor antagonist, is prescribed to treat a patient with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome. Identify the drug 'X'.

explanationHtml:
Ischaemic colitis is a side-effect of alosetron.

Alosetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist that is used to reduce diarrhoea in irritable bowel syndrome.

Option A: Lubiprostone is associated with nausea and diarrhea.

Option B: Linaclotide is associated with diarrhea.

Option D: Tegaserod is associated with cardiac toxicity.
question: A patient with irritable bowel disease was started on a drug. A few days after administration of the drug, the patient complained of acute GI distress suggestive of ischemic colitis. What was the drug taken by the patient?

explanationHtml:
The best time to take antispasmodics for postprandial pain is 30 min before meals.

Antispasmodics such as dicyclomine inhibit the gastrocolic reflex and thus reduce pain due to intestinal spasms. It is best taken 30 min before meals so that the effective blood levels are achieved shortly before the anticipated onset of pain.
question: A 28-year-old female patient comes to you for advice. She is a known case of irritable bowel syndrome. She asks you when is the best time to take antispasmodics for her postprandial abdominal pain. What would you suggest?

explanationHtml:
The gene associated with Crohn's disease is the NOD2 gene. It is present on chromosome 16.

Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain 2 (NOD2) acts as a cytoplasmic sensor of microbial products. Defective NOD2 gene results in defective innate immunity. When the innate immunity is unable to clear the bacteria, there is an exaggerated response of the immune system (T-cells) resulting in damage to the host tissue.

Option B: JAK2 mutation is associated with polycythemia vera.

Option C: BRAF V600E mutation is associated with melanoma, papillary thyroid cancer, and serous ovarian cancers.

Option D: STAT3 mutations are associated with the autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome.

question: Which of the following genes is associated with Crohn's disease?

explanationHtml:

The genetic disorders associated with IBD are:

  • Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  • Immunodysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy X-linked (IPEX) syndrome
  • Turner's syndrome
  • Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome
  • Glycogen storage disease

question: Which of the following conditions are not associated with inflammatory bowel disease?

question: In patients who have undergone an appendectomy, there is a lower risk for developing which of the following diseases?

question: Early-onset inflammatory bowel disease is associated with:

correctAnswer: B. Due to FOXP3 gene mutation
explanationHtml:
IPEX (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, and X-linked) syndrome is caused by mutations in the FOXP3 gene, which leads to a deficiency of T-regulatory cells, resulting in immune dysfunction.

IPEX is associated with:

  • Ulcerative colitis-like autoimmune enteropathy
  • Neonatal type 1 DM
  • Thyroiditis
  • Dermatitis

question: Which of the following is true about immune dysregulation polyendocrinopathy enteropathy X-linked (IPEX) syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Campylobacter enteritis should be ruled out before diagnosing a patient with IBD.

Campylobacter enteritis can mimic the clinical presentation and biopsy appearance of ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease (IBD). Hence, it should be ruled out, especially in persons with a history of:

  • Foreign travel
  • Significant animal contact
  • Immunodeficiency
  • Exposure incurring a high risk of transmission.

It can also cause a relapse of established ulcerative colitis.

A definitive diagnosis of campylobacter infection can be made by culture or real-time PCR.

question: Which of the following sites is most commonly involved in Crohn’s disease?

explanationHtml:
The above specimen of the small bowel shows creeping fat which is a feature of Crohn's disease (CD).

Mesenteric fat is normally seen along the longitudinal axis of the intestine. However, in Crohn's disease, excessive fibrofatty proliferation results in mesenteric fat wrapping around the inflamed bowel. This is called creeping fat.

Strictures and fistulae are the commonly associated complications of long-standing Crohn's disease. Strictures can cause bowel obstruction.

Other gross features seen in Crohn's disease are:

  • Transmural inflammation- full-thickness inflammation involving all the layers of the bowel
  • Aphthous ulcers- small, shallow ulcers surrounded by erythema
  • Longitudinal ulcers- linear or serpiginous deep ulcers
  • Skip lesions- involvement of discontinuous segments of the bowel with intervening normal mucosa
  • Cobblestone appearance- deep, longitudinal ulcerations interlaced with intervening normal mucosa

The image below shows cobblestone appearance in Crohn's disease.

question: A patient presented with acute severe small bowel obstruction to the ER. An emergency small bowel resection was done. The resected specimen is shown below. What could be the likely diagnosis?

The clinical presentation along with the endoscopy image showing a cobblestone appearance are suggestive of Crohn's disease (CD).

Endoscopic findings in Crohn's disease include:

  • Aphthous ulcers - small, shallow ulcers surrounded by erythema
  • Longitudinal ulcers - linear or serpiginous deep ulcers
  • Cobblestone appearance - deep, longitudinal ulcerations interlaced with intervening normal mucosa
  • Strictures
  • Fistulas

Strictures and fistulae are the commonly associated complications of long-standing Crohn's disease.

Option C: Ulcerative colitis (UC) can be a differential diagnosis based on the history of bloody stools, however, Crohn's disease can mimic UC by presenting with bloody stools, if it extends to cause colitis involving the rectum. In UC there is inflamed mucosal projections present on a background of continuous inflammation, as compared to discontinuous lesions with intervening areas of normal or edematous mucosa in CD.

question: A 28-year-old man presented with diarrhea, bloody stools, weight loss, and intermittent fever for the past 2 months. Endoscopy revealed the following. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of Crohn's disease presenting as jejunoileitis. This is evidenced by the presence of features of malabsorption such as steatorrhea, chronic diarrhea, and vitamin B12 deficiency anemia.

The fecal calprotectin and lactoferrin are elevated in inflammatory conditions like inflammatory bowel disease, but not in irritable bowel syndrome.

The stool guaiac test or guaiac fecal occult blood test (gFOBT) reveals the presence of microscopic levels of blood suggesting Crohn's disease. Gross bleeding per rectum is more characteristic of ulcerative colitis.

Additionally, smoking is a risk factor for Crohn's disease. However, it is a protective factor in ulcerative colitis.

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of Crohn's disease presenting as ileocolitis. Fine granular mucosa is seen in ulcerative colitis, not Crohn's disease.

Ileocolitis presents as right lower abdominal pain, fever, and diarrhea. Pain is usually colicky and is relieved by defecation. It may mimic acute appendicitis in the early stages.

Endoscopic findings in Crohn's disease include:

  • Aphthous ulcers - Small, shallow ulcers surrounded by erythema

question: A young man presents to the OPD with complaints of chronic diarrhea, right lower abdominal pain, and weight loss. On examination, you note a low-grade fever and a palpable mass in the right lower quadrant. Colonoscopy revealed sparing of the rectum. The following endoscopic findings may also be seen in his condition except:

explanationHtml:
Aphthous ulcers seen in Crohn's disease are the earliest radiological signs on small bowel follow-through study.

They are shallow ulcers that are often multiple and separated by normal intervening mucosa. They are also the earliest macroscopic findings of Crohn's disease.

Features on barium small bowel follow-through in Crohn's disease include:

  • Mucosal ulcers:
    • Aphthous ulcers initially
    • Deep ulcers (more than 3 mm depth)
    • Longitudinal fissures
    • Transverse stripes
    • Severe mucosal ulcers lead to cobblestone appearance
  • Sinus tracts and fistulae
  • Creeping fat: widely separated loops of the bowel due to fibrofatty proliferation
  • Thickened folds due to edema
  • Pseudo-diverticula formation: due to contraction at the site of ulcer with ballooning of the opposite site
  • String sign of Kantor: tubular narrowing due to spasm or stricture depending on the chronicity
  • Rose thorn appearance
  • Partial obstruction.

CT and MR enterography have a higher sensitivity for the diagnosis of Crohn’s disease. They may reveal additional features such as:

  • Fat halo sign - submucosal fat deposition
  • Comb sign - engorgement of the vasa recta.

In gastric Crohn's disease, conical narrowing of the antrum may be seen. This is called Ram’s horn sign.

[[figure-1]]

The image below shows the string sign of Kantor:

The image below shows rose thorn appearance:

[[figure-3]]

question: What is the earliest radiographic feature of Crohn's disease?

explanationHtml:
The earliest radiological change of ulcerative colitis seen on barium enema is fine mucosal granularity.

Double-contrast barium enema allows for exquisite detail of the colonic mucosa and also allows the bowel proximal to strictures to be assessed. It is however contraindicated if acute severe colitis is present due to the risk of perforation.

Early changes in ulcerative colitis:

  • Mucosal granularity
  • Fine granular pattern
  • Mucosal stippling
  • Collar button ulcers
  • Deep collar stud ulcers.

The below contrast radiograph shows granular mucosa typical of ulcerative colitis.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Collar button ulcers are small deep ulcers in which the button surface corresponds to the eroded ulcer base and the button neck corresponds to the undermined and preserved mucosa. They are also seen in ulcerative colitis.

Option C: String sign represents circumferential inflammation and fibrosis, resulting in long segments of luminal narrowing as shown below. It is more characteristic of Crohn's disease.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Ram's horn sign is seen in gastric Crohn's disease.

Other gross findings in ulcerative colitis include:

  • Fine mucosal granularity
  • Collar button ulcers

Rose thorn appearance, skip lesions, and pseudodiverticula are features of Crohn's disease.

Fistula is not a complication of ulcerative colitis. It is seen in Crohn’s disease.

Hemorrhage, malignant change, and toxic megacolon are complications of ulcerative colitis.

question: Which of the following complications is unlikely to occur in a patient with ulcerative colitis?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows pyoderma gangrenosum. It is very difficult to treat and often requires IV antibiotics and IV glucocorticoids. Other drugs used in its management include dapsone, cyclosporine, and infliximab.

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a dermatological extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease. It begins as a pustule and progresses to an ulcer with necrotic tissue and exudates. It may occur years before the onset of bowel symptoms and is usually associated with severe disease.

Lesions are commonly found on the dorsal surface of the feet and legs but may occur on the arms, chest, and even the face. It responds poorly to colectomy and may even develop years after the surgery.

Other dermatological manifestations associated with IBD include:

  • Erythema nodosum
  • Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis)
  • Perianal skin tags
  • Psoriasis
  • Metastatic Crohn's disease (cutaneous granulomas).

question: A patient with inflammatory bowel disease presents with the following lesion. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given urinary crystal is the bipyramidal or envelope-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate dihydrate. Calcium oxalate stones are more commonly associated with Crohn's disease.

In Crohn's disease (especially post small bowel resection), fatty acids are not absorbed because of ileal dysfunction. These fatty acids in the gut lumen bind to calcium. Because of this, the dietary oxalates which normally bind to the calcium are now left unbound. This leads to increased absorption of dietary oxalates leading to hyperoxaluria and oxalate stones.

Note: Celiac disease is also associated with calcium oxalate stones.

question: A 28-year-old man was brought to the casualty with a high fever and abdominal pain for the past 2 days. His history is significant for bloody diarrhea over the past few months. The abdominal radiograph of this patient is given below. Identify the condition.

explanationHtml:
Uveitis is the most common cause of the given symptoms in a patient with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Uveitis is an ophthalmic manifestation of IBD. It is associated with both ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. It can develop during remission and is seen even after bowel resection. Prompt intervention with glucocorticoids is required to prevent scarring and visual impairment.

The other common ophthalmic manifestations in IBD are conjunctivitis and episcleritis. Episcleritis, more common in Crohn's, is a benign disorder presenting with mild ocular burning.

Patients with Crohn's disease on infliximab are at increased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) and hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (HS-TCL).

Infliximab is the first biologic therapy approved for Crohn's disease. It is an IgG1 antibody against TNF-alpha.

question: A patient with IBD was brought to the ER with acute epigastric pain radiating to the back. His lab investigations revealed elevated serum amylase and lipase. He gives a history of being started on a new drug for maintenance therapy of his IBD 2 weeks back. The causative drug is most likely to be:

correctAnswer: C. Inducing remission in Crohn's disease
explanationHtml:
Nutritional therapy is used for inducing remission in Crohn's disease.

Dietary antigens may stimulate an immune response. Hence, nutritional therapies like total parenteral nutrition, enteral nutrition (peptide-based preparations), etc. can be used to provide bowel rest in active Crohn's disease. These interventions cannot be used for maintaining remission.

Ulcerative colitis does not respond to dietary intervention.

Drugs used in treatment of Crohn’s disease:

  1. Oral budesonide (mainly for mild to moderate)
  2. Oral prednisolone
  3. Methotrexate
  4. Anti TNF alpha

question: What is nutritional therapy in inflammatory bowel disease used for?

correctAnswer: A. Procto-colectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis
explanationHtml:
The treatment of choice for refractory ulcerative colitis is proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) performed in an elective setting.

This procedure is ideal as it removes the entire colon and rectum, which eliminates the disease and prevents the recurrence of colorectal cancer while preserving the anal sphincter.

A pouch (reservoir) is created by anastomosing the distal ileum with the anal canal. This maintains bowel continuity and continence, preventing the need for a permanent stoma and preserving the overall quality of life.

Other options:

Option B: Proctectomy involves the surgical removal of the rectum. Therefore, an ileorectal anastomosis (joining the ileum to the rectum) cannot be performed if the rectum has already been resected.

Option C: Subtotal (abdominal) colectomy with end ileostomy is the procedure of choice in an emergency setting (such as for acute fulminant colitis, toxic megacolon, or impending perforation) or for severely malnourished, unstable patients. It rapidly removes the source of sepsis and avoids complex, time-consuming pelvic dissection in critically ill patients. However, it is not the preferred definitive treatment because it requires a stoma and leaves a diseased rectal stump.

Option D: Total colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis leaves a diseased rectum intact, which is generally contraindicated in ulcerative colitis because it leaves the patient at a high risk for intractable symptoms (bleeding, urgency, tenesmus) and future malignant transformation (dysplasia or carcinoma) in the retained rectal mucosa.

question: What is the treatment of choice in a patient with refractory ulcerative colitis?

explanationHtml:
Constipation is not a feature of malabsorption syndrome.

Malabsorption syndrome refers to a spectrum of conditions of various etiologies that arises due to diminished absorption of one or more dietary nutrients.

The general features of malabsorption syndrome are abdominal pain, diarrhea, steatorrhea, and weight loss.

Anemia may be present when there is defective absorption of iron, folate, or vitamin B12. Hypocalcemia and tetany can be seen due to defective absorption of vitamin D.
question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in patients with malabsorption syndrome?

explanationHtml:
D-xylose test is useful for the assessment of intestinal mucosal function.

D-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the intestinal mucosa without undergoing enzymatic digestion.

The test is performed by administering 25g of D-xylose orally followed by the collection of urine 5h later. The test is considered abnormal (positive) if urinary D-xylose is <4.5g. A positive D-xylose test indicates abnormal small intestinal mucosa.
question: Which of the following tests is useful for the assessment of intestinal mucosal function in a patient presenting with symptoms of malabsorption?

explanationHtml:
A urinary D-xylose <4.5g after 5 hours of oral D-xylose (abnormal) can be seen in Crohn’s disease.

D-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the small intestinal mucosa without undergoing enzymatic digestion. An abnormal (positive) D-xylose test indicates abnormal small intestinal mucosal absorption.

A positive D-xylose test is seen in:

  • Celiac disease
  • Whipple’s disease
  • Tropical sprue
  • Short bowel syndrome
  • Crohn’s disease

The test is of limited clinical value today and mostly has been replaced by small intestinal biopsy.
question: The result of a D-xylose test showed urinary excretion of the monosaccharide at 3.6g after 5 hours. Which of the following can be a differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
A small bowel diverticulum can result in malabsorption.

A small bowel diverticulum is a blind pouch protruding from the small intestine that communicates with the lumen of the gut. It becomes a potential site for bacterial overgrowth, which causes malabsorption by depleting vitamin B12 and deconjugating bile acids, which thereafter causes steatorrhea, diarrhea, and macrocytic anemia.

Anterior colon resection, ulcerative colitis, and sigmoid volvulus affect the large intestine and therefore do not cause malabsorption.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are likely to suffer from malabsorption?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of short bowel syndrome in adults is Crohn's Disease.

Short bowel syndrome (SBS) is a malabsorption disorder caused by a lack of functional small intestine. In adults, the common causes are :

  • Crohn's Disease
  • Mesenteric vascular disease (e.g: mesenteric vascular occlusion.)
  • Operations without any preexisting small-intestinal disease (e.g: after trauma)

In children, necrotizing enterocolitis is the most common cause.

explanationHtml:
Homocystinuria is not a protein malabsorption disorder. It is a disorder of methionine metabolism that leads to increased homocysteine levels.

Proteins are broken down by pancreatic enzymes and are absorbed as amino acids and peptides. So, protein malabsorption usually occurs only in pancreatic insufficiency. Additionally, there are three rare genetic disorders that lead to protein malabsorption. They are:

  • Enterokinase deficiency- Defective conversion of the proenzyme trypsinogen to trypsin. It is characterised by:
    • Diarrhoea
    • Growth retardation
    • Hypoproteinemia
  • Hartnup disease- Defective transport of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids. It is characterised by:
    • Pellagra-like rash
    • Neuropsychiatric symptoms
  • Cystinuria- Defective transport of cystine and other dibasic amino acids. It is characterised by:
    • Renal calculi
    • Chronic pancreatitis

question: A Schilling test was performed on a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency and the results are given below. What is the inference?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario describes a case of malabsorption syndrome (chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea), a normal xylose test and normal duodenal biopsy with abnormal schilling test points towards pancreatic insufficiency.

A normal xylose test and normal duodenal biopsy rules out small intestinal pathologies like celiac disease (option A) and intestinal lymphangiectasia (option C), presence of steatorrhea rules out ulcerative colitis (option B) as it affects the large bowel which is not the main site of absorption of fat.

Ileal disease is also characterized by normal xylose test, normal duodenal biopsy and steatorrhea and abnormal schilling test but among the given options the most appropriate answer would be pancreatic insufficiency due to chronic pancreatitis.

Pancreatic insufficiency is characterised by the deficiency of exocrine pancreatic enzymes that result in maldigestion and malabsorption.

The features in favor of the diagnosis:

  • Steatorrhea - a deficiency of pancreatic lipases can lead to undigested fat in stools.
  • D-xylose test - d-xylose is a monosaccharide that is directly absorbed by the intestinal mucosa without undergoing any enzymatic action. Normal d-xylose test denotes intact mucosa.
  • Schilling test - it is abnormal as pancreatic enzymes are required for the absorption of vitamin B12.

Ileal disease Normal Normal Abnormal

question: A patient presented with chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea. D-xylose test was normal and the Schilling test was abnormal. A duodenal biopsy was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

It presents in early childhood with steatorrhoea and diarrhea, hypolipidemia, failure to thrive, ataxia, sensory and motor neuropathies.

question: All are true about the types of celiac disease except :

explanationHtml:
The most significant extraintestinal manifestation of celiac disease is dermatitis herpetiformis (DH).

DH is characterized by intensely pruritic small papules and vesicles on the extensor surfaces of extremities, buttocks, and neck. It can be considered a celiac disease of the skin.

Other extraintestinal manifestations of celiac disease are:

  • Anemia
  • Low bone density
  • Ataxia
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Infertility

Celiac disease is often associated with other conditions such as type 1 diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease, IgA deficiency, bird fancier's lung, and Down syndrome.

question: Which of the following extraintestinal manifestations has the most significant association with celiac disease?

explanationHtml:
The presence of fatigue, chronic diarrhea, weight loss and abdominal distention along with investigations showing features of malabsorption (iron deficiency) lead to the diagnosis of celiac disease or gluten sensitive enteropathy. The single best test for which is checking serum for the presence of IgA tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG) antibodies (Option D).

Celiac disease is a disorder characterized by an immunological response to gluten causing damage to the proximal intestinal mucosa (villous atrophy) and malabsorption of nutrients.

Symptoms usually begin 6 to 24 months from the introduction of gluten into diet, although most patients go undiagnosed.

The common manifestations are - irritability, abdominal distention, chronic diarrhea, weight loss or muscle wasting and extra-intestinally, the symptoms observed are aphthous ulcers, delayed puberty, iron deficiency anemia and short stature.

Screening for celiac disease is by testing for tissue transglutaminase IgA, endomysial, and deamidated antigliadin antibodies. IgA levels in serum are measured to detect false-negative results because of IgA deficiency.

Small intestinal biopsy shows characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

The treatment involves the exclusion of gluten-containing food from diet.

Long term complications observed are osteoporosis, anemia, infertility and malignancy (enteropathy related-T cell lymphoma is the most common association)

The Marsh classification is used to categorize celiac disease into different types and to quantify severity of disease involvement.
question: A 15-year-old girl presented with fatigue, chronic diarrhoea,  weight loss, bone pain, and abdominal distension.  Investigations revealed iron deficiency anemia and osteoporosis. Which of the following is the single best test to be done for her evaluation?

explanationHtml:
In this patient with positive serology, a biopsy should be done next, to confirm the diagnosis of celiac disease.

Tissue transglutaminase Ab (tTG-IgA) is the best screening test. IgA endomysial antibodies (EMA) are most specific.

But a small-intestinal biopsy is required to establish a diagnosis of celiac disease, before starting treatment.
question: A patient who presented with severe malabsorption is found to be positive for IgA tissue trans-glutaminase antibodies. What will be the next best step?

explanationHtml:

The complications of celiac disease are:

  • Intestinal lymphomas
  • Intestinal ulcers- also known as ulcerative jejunoileitis
  • Collagenous sprue- development of a subepithelial collagen layer

explanationHtml:

Whipple's disease is a chronic multisystem disorder caused by the gram-positive bacteria Tropheryma whipplei. It primarily causes malabsorption along with central nervous system & cardiac problems. It mostly affects men and presents with fever, diarrhea weight loss, and arthralgia.

The diagnosis of Whipple's disease is made through a biopsy which shows the presence of PAS-positive macrophages in the small intestine and other organs with evidence of disease.

question: All are true about Whipple's disease except :

explanationHtml:
The most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple’s disease is progressive dementia.

Other important CNS manifestations in Whipple's disease are:

  • Personality and mood changes
  • Progressive supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
  • Focal neurologic presentations
  • Oculomasticatory myorrhythmia - an unusual combination of rhythmic eye and jaw movements which is pathognomonic of Whipple's disease.

Whipple's disease associated with CNS symptoms has a poor prognosis.

Note: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with neuroblastoma.
question: What is the most common CNS manifestation associated with Whipple’s disease?

Other cardiovascular findings include:

Treatment of Whipple's disease:

  • Induction phase- ceftriaxone or meropenem or penicillin G + streptomycin - 2 weeks
  • Maintenance phase- One of the following regimens may be used

question: A 38-year-old man presented with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and joint pains. A duodenal biopsy was done. Which of the following drug is used in the maintenance phase of treatment of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The history of malabsorptive symptoms, a negative celiac serology, and the biopsy findings are suggestive of tropical sprue.

Improvement in symptoms after folic acid intake is a hallmark of tropical sprue.

Tropical sprue is an acquired malabsorptive condition of probable infectious aetiology. It is seen in people from the tropics such as India, Southeast Asia and South America.

Tropical sprue and celiac disease have similar clinical, endoscopic and histologic findings. However, a positive celiac serology (anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies) can be used to rule out tropical sprue.
question: A 42-year-old man presented with diarrhea, floating stools, and weight loss for 3 months. Celiac serology was negative. Biopsy of the small intestinal mucosa revealed villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia with normal mucosal thickness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Because of marked folate deficiency, folic acid is most often given together with broad spectrum antibiotics for up to 6 months.

Pancreatic rests are not a differential diagnosis for hypertrophied gastric folds. These usually present as a single lump in the stomach and are formed by ectopic pancreatic tissue.

Thickened gastric folds can represent a local malignant process, inflammatory process, or hormonal response. The differential diagnoses of large gastric folds include:

  • Menetrier's disease
  • Zollinger–Ellison syndrome - hypergastrinemia leads to parietal cell hyperplasia and prominent folds
  • Malignancy- lymphoma, infiltrating gastric cancer
  • Infections- histoplasmosis, tuberculosis.
question: An upper GI endoscopy is performed in a patient with dyspeptic symptoms. It shows the presence of thickened gastric folds. Which of the following differential diagnoses would you not consider in this patient?

The antrum is usually spared in Menetrier's disease.

Foveolar hyperplasia results in the development of large rugal folds in the body and fundus of the stomach, sparing the antrum. These hypertrophied rugal folds give a cobblestone or cerebriform appearance to the gastric mucosa.

question: Which part of the stomach is usually spared in Menetrier's disease?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario and endoscopy image showing large, rugal gastric folds are suggestive of Menetrier's disease. Among the given options, hematemesis is least likely to occur in this patient.

Large, gastric rugal folds in Menetrier's disease occur due to massive overgrowth of mucous cells (foveolar cells) lining the stomach.

Patients usually present with epigastric pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia, peripheral edema, and weight loss. Occult gastrointestinal bleeding may occur, but overt bleeding is unusual. If overt bleeding is seen, it is usually due to superficial mucosal erosions.

They develop protein-losing gastropathy, leading to hypoproteinemia as a result of increased secretion of gastric mucus. There is also a decrease in the number of parietal cells which leads to decreased acid secretion (hypochlorhydria) in the stomach. They are at an increased risk of developing gastric carcinoma.
question: A 46-year-old man presented with a history of diarrhea for 5 months, occasional abdominal pain, and weight loss. Upper GI endoscopy showed the following finding. Which of the following is least likely to occur in this patient?

question: A 6-year-old child with vomiting, abdominal pain, weight loss, and peripheral edema underwent an upper GI biopsy. Histology showed foveolar hyperplasia and glandular atrophy within the gastric mucosa. Which of the following is most commonly associated with this condition?

explanationHtml: Overexpression of TGF-α (transforming growth factor-alpha) causes Menetrier's disease. This overexpression results in overstimulation of the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway and increased proliferation of mucous cells, resulting in mucous cell (foveolar) hyperplasia.
question: Overexpression of which of the following causes Menetrier’s disease?

explanationHtml:
Menetrier's disease is confirmed by endoscopic full-thickness biopsy.

A full-thickness biopsy allows for the visualization of the cells on the surface as well as the pits of the gastric glands. The histopathological specimen shows the following features:

  • Foveolar hyperplasia - hyperplasia of surface and glandular mucosa
  • Reduction in oxyntic glands, parietal cells, and chief cells
  • Dilated, tortuous gastric glands
  • Elongation of pits of gastric glands
  • Eosinophilic infiltration in lamina propria

A punch biopsy can only sample the surface of the gastric gland and hence is not preferred.

question: A 24-year old woman underwent extensive workup for unexplained weight loss, vomiting, and diarrhea. She was suspected to have Menetrier's disease. Which of the following investigations will confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing foveolar hyperplasia are suggestive of Menetrier's disease. The treatment of choice is cetuximab.

Increased epidermal growth factor receptor(EGFR) signaling has been implicated in the pathogenesis of Menetrier's disease. Cetuximab is an EGFR inhibitor, and blocks this signaling pathway and helps in the improvement of the symptoms. Therefore, it is the first line of treatment.

Medical therapy with proton pump inhibitors (lansoprazole) and somatostatin analogues (octreotide) may also be tried to manage symptoms. If the patient continues to have protein loss despite medical therapy, then total gastrectomy is indicated.

question: A middle-aged man presented with a history of dyspepsia. He has been taking pantoprazole for the last few months, however, his symptoms persisted. The most common site for mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma or MALToma is the stomach.

MALToma is a type of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma that most commonly occurs in the stomach and to a lesser extent in the salivary glands, lungs, small intestine, etc. It occurs as a result of the malignant proliferation of B cells in the marginal zone of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT).
question: What is the most common site for a MALToma?

explanationHtml:
MALToma arises from B lymphocytes present in the marginal zone of the lymphoid tissue.

The majority of the cases of MALToma are associated with H. pylori induced chronic gastritis. This infection results in an increased proliferation of lymphocytes in the mucosa of the stomach causing MALToma. It is initially low grade and if the infection is not treated, it later progresses to high grade.

The patients usually present with non-specific symptoms like epigastric pain and discomfort. It is usually diagnosed in patients around 60 years of age. It is also associated with autoimmune diseases like Sjogren's syndrome and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and lymphoepithelial lesions seen in the gastric glands is suggestive of MALToma. The diagnosis is confirmed by immunophenotyping.

Histopathological examination of a MALToma shows the presence of lymphoepithelial lesions. These are caused due to the invasion of gastric glands and crypts by the neoplastic lymphocytes. These lymphocytes are positive for CD19, CD20 and negative for CD5 and CD10. Biopsy or aspiration of the bone marrow is also done to see the bone marrow involvement.

Radiological investigations like CT scans, MRIs, and PET scans are useful in identifying the extent of the tumor and infiltration of the tumor to the adjacent organs.

Note: Cytogenetic testing will be helpful in identifying chromosomal abnormalities.

question: A 62-year-old woman underwent an endoscopic biopsy of a gastric tumor. The biopsy shows dense lymphocytic infiltration with lymphoepithelial lesions in the gastric glands. Which of the following investigations will confirm your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of a low-grade gastric MALToma. The treatment of choice for this condition is H. pylori eradication therapy which can be done with the OCM regimen (omeprazole, clarithromycin and metronidazole).

Immunophenotyping in MALTomas shows positive staining for CD19 and CD20 which is suggestive of a B-cell neoplasm. Negative staining for CD5 and CD10 is seen, suggesting it arises from the marginal zone of lymphoid tissues.

Chronic infection with H. pylori leads to the development of MALTomas. When these lesions are limited to the mucosa, treatment of the infection alone is sufficient to cause regression of the tumour.

In high-grade tumors or the tumors which invade into the adjacent or distant organs, radiotherapy and chemotherapy are required to treat the tumor. Radiotherapy is usually three-dimensional conformal radiotherapy. The chemotherapeutic agents used in the treatment of MALToma are rituximab, cyclophosphamide, fludarabine, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. Radical gastrectomy has a limited role and is done when the disease is confined to the stomach.

The given case scenario is suggestive of chronic mesenteric ischemia.

Chronic mesenteric ischemia occurs due to atherosclerotic disease affecting the superior mesenteric artery and celiac arteries. Risk factors include old age, female gender, and smoking. Patients with comorbidities like coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, renal or liver disease, and aortic insufficiency are at higher risk.

The important clinical features of chronic mesenteric ischemia are:

  • Postprandial abdominal pain presents as an acute, dull cramping pain because of inadequate blood supply, also known as intestinal angina
  • Weight loss- The patient restricts food intake to avoid abdominal pain
  • Diarrhea- Occurs as a result of decreased absorption
  • Epigastric bruit

The gold standard investigation to diagnose the blockade is mesenteric angiography. Once the disease is confirmed, the patients have to be started on antiplatelets, and mesenteric angioplasty and stenting should be performed.

Option A: Acute mesenteric ischemia presents with acute abdomen, bloody diarrhea, and nausea. Angiography will show occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery.

Option C: Wilkie's syndrome occurs due to compression of the third portion of the duodenum by the superior mesenteric artery. It can present similarly, however is associated with vomiting and rapid weight loss. It usually occurs in young, asthenic women.

Option D: Nutcracker syndrome - The aorta and the superior mesenteric artery compress the left renal vein passing in between them. It presents with varicoceles and hematuria.

question: A 42-year-old man presented with complaints of fever, malaise, and weight loss. His lab investigations showed mild anemia, elevated ESR, and serology was positive for cANCA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Giant cell arteritis is common in older women (>50 years of age).

Giant cell arteritis is an inflammatory vasculitis of the large vessels, commonly seen in females over 50 years of age. It usually involves the temporal artery.

It is characterized by fever, anemia, and headache. Depending on the artery involved, the patient may have tenderness over the affected artery, scalp pain, tongue and jaw claudication. Untreated patients may develop ischemic optic neuropathy.

Laboratory investigations reveal elevated ESR and normochromic normocytic anemia. It shows good response to glucocorticoid therapy.

options.text: May lead to ischemic optic neuropathy

question: Which of the following is not true about giant cell arteritis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation of headache, jaw claudication, and painless visual loss is suggestive of giant cell arteritis. The best investigation for the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis is temporal artery biopsy.

Histopathology shows panarteritis with the presence of mononuclear cells and giant cells. The biopsy may not be positive in all patients due to patchy histologic findings. Since involvement of the vessel may be segmental, positive yield is increased by obtaining a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens.

Note : According to the 21st edition of Harrison's Medicine, as involvement of the vessel may be segmental, getting a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens would help to increase a positive yield. And Robbin's 10th edition mentions that an adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment.
question: A 65-year-old woman came with complaints of headache for the past 1-month. She also reported aching of the jaw during her meals. Over the last week, she has experienced episodes of painless visual loss which lasted for around 10 minutes. Which of the following is the best investigation for the diagnosis of her condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation of painful, tender, and stiff shoulders with restricted movement points toward a diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica, which is closely associated with giant cell arteritis.

Polymyalgia rheumatica is characterized by pain and stiffness (worst in the morning) in the muscles of the neck, shoulder, back, hips, and thigh. On examination, diffuse tenderness is present without localization to any specific structures. Pain restricts the active range of motion but passive range of motion and muscle strength are normal.

ESR and CRP are typically elevated in polymyalgia rheumatica whereas creatine phosphokinase (CPK) lies within the normal range. It shows a good response to prednisone therapy.
question: A 50-year-old woman presents to your OPD with complaints of pain and stiffness of the shoulders which is worse in the morning. She works as a bus conductor and tells you that she has difficulty raising her shoulders to ring the bell. On examination, there is diffuse tenderness over the shoulders. Which of the following vasculitis is closely associated with her presentation?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation of headache and symptoms suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica with raised ESR points towards a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis (GCA), for which the next best step is initiation of steroids (prednisone).

Although temporal artery biopsy is the diagnostic investigation for GCA, it should not delay the initiation of steroids as it helps in reducing symptoms and preventing visual loss. The biopsy findings usually remain positive for at least 1 month after initiation of steroids.

Newer drugs used in the treatment of giant cell arteritis are tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) and abatacept (CTLA4-Ig).
question: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe right-sided throbbing headache. She also gives history of pain and stiffness of the shoulders and hips. Her lab values show an ESR of 80 mm/hr. What is the next best step in her management?

explanationHtml:
The most common artery involved in Takayasu arteritis is the subclavian artery.

Patients present with pain, claudication, and weakness of the affected limb. The arterial pulse in the affected limb may be weak or absent.

The order of arteries affected in Takayasu arteritis is subclavian artery > common carotid artery > abdominal aorta > renal artery > aortic arch = vertebral > coeliac axis > iliac > pulmonary > coronary artery.
question: Which is the most common artery involved in Takayasu arteritis?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical features with a marked weakening of pulse in the upper extremities and laboratory findings of elevated ESR are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis. It is also known as pulseless disease.

Takayasu arteritis is a systemic disease and may present with generalized and vascular symptoms. It commonly affects adolescents or young females. Generalized symptoms like fever, night sweats, weight loss, malaise, arthralgias, and anorexia may occur long before vascular symptoms.

Vascular symptoms depend on the vessel involved:

  • Arch of the aorta and its branches:
    • Subclavian artery (most commonly affected) - It leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities. Hence, it is also known as pulseless disease. It may also lead to Raynaud’s phenomenon.
    • Carotid arteries- It leads to weak pulses, blindness, and neurological deficits.
    • Aortic arch- It may lead to congestive heart failure.
  • Abdominal aorta, celiac axis, and superior mesenteric artery - leads to abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting
  • Iliac vessels - leads to claudication of the legs
  • Renal arteries - leads to systemic hypertension
  • Pulmonary artery - leads to pulmonary hypertension
  • Coronary arteries (least commonly affected) - lead to myocardial infarction

Investigations:

  • Laboratory tests reveal an elevated ESR level, anemia, and elevated immunoglobulin levels.
  • Arteriography is done as a confirmatory test.

question: Which of the following is a medium vessel vasculitis?

explanationHtml:
The most probable diagnosis is polyarteritis nodosa.

The image shows the gangrene of the fingers. The presence of myalgia, the involvement of cutaneous vessels (gangrene with palpable peripheral pulses), renal vessels causing hypertension and serology negative for ANCA make polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) the most probable diagnosis.

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is necrotizing arteritis of the medium-sized blood vessels. It can affect the skin, peripheral nerves, renal vessels, mesenteric vessels, heart, and brain. Lungs are usually spared in PAN.

The disease initially starts with non-specific symptoms like fever, malaise, arthralgia, and myalgia. Later, depending on the artery involved, patients may develop the following symptoms:

  • Skin findings - ulcers, digital gangrene, and livedo reticularis
  • Renal arteries - hypertension and renal failure
  • Mesenteric arteries - abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, bleeding, and a bowel perforation

Other options:

1) Takayasu arteritis- It is a large vessel vasculitis. Also known as pulseless disease as it may be associated with weak upper extremity pulses.

2) Microscopic polyangiitis- It is a small vessel vasculitis. It is positive for p-ANCA. Presentation is similar to granulomatosis with polyangiitis but without upper airway involvement.

3) Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis- It is frequently associated with hepatitis C. Circulating cryoglubulins and rheumatoid factor can be found in blood. Most common clinical manifestations are cutaneous vasculitis, peripheral neuropathy, glomerulonephritis and arthritis.
question: A 47-year-old man presented to the hospital with the findings shown in the image below. He also complained of pain in the upper and lower limbs. On examination, his BP was 160/100 mmHg and his peripheral pulses were palpable. Serology was negative for ANCA. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Pulmonary arteries are characteristically spared in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN). PAN mainly involves renal and visceral arteries.

Histopathology of the involved arteries usually shows the following findings:

  • Transmural necrotizing vasculitis of the arteries and adjacent veins. Venules are spared.
  • Renal arteries - arteritis without glomerulonephritis
  • Fibrinoid necrosis
  • Absence of granuloma and eosinophilia
question: In a patient diagnosed with polyarteritis nodosa which of the following arteries are characteristically spared?

correctAnswer: D. 30% is associated with Hepatitis B
explanationHtml:
One-third of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) cases are associated with Hepatitis B.

Other options:

Option A: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic vasculitis which is associated with necrotizing inflammation of small and medium-sized muscular arteries.

Option B: Patients show hypergammaglobulinemia.

Option C: PAN is rarely associated with ANCA positivity. There is no serological test for PAN. Most patients exhibit an elevated leukocyte count with a predominance of neutrophils.

PAN is usually seen in young adults, characterized by rapidly accelerating hypertension, abdominal pain, bloody stools, myalgias, and peripheral neuropathy.

Arterial inflammation is segmental, necrotizing, and transmural, leading to aneurysms and thrombosis.

The involved vessels are typically found at arterial bifurcations, spreading to veins but sparing venules. The most commonly affected organs are the kidney, heart, liver, and gastrointestinal tract, in that order. Pulmonary arteries are not involved. Inadequate blood flow leads to ischemia, ulcers, infarcts, atrophy, or hemorrhage.

Diagnosis relies on histopathological findings from organ biopsies or the demonstration of aneurysms in small to medium-sized arteries of the renal, hepatic, and visceral vasculature.

Untreated PAN has an extremely poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of only 10 to 20%. Common causes of death include gastrointestinal complications, such as bowel infarcts and perforation, as well as cardiovascular issues. Timely treatment is vital for improved outcomes.

Combining prednisone and cyclophosphamide has shown significant benefits in survival rates. Glucocorticoids alone may be sufficient for milder cases. In PAN cases associated with hepatitis B or C, antiviral therapy is combined with glucocorticoids and plasma exchange. Managing hypertension effectively can help reduce vascular complications. Despite successful treatment, relapses occur in approximately 10-20% of patients.

  • Upper respiratory tract- presenting with sinusitis, otitis media, and nasal septal perforation.
  • Lower respiratory tract- presenting with hemoptysis.
  • Kidney (glomerulonephritis)- presenting with proteinuria, hematuria, and hypertension.

explanationHtml:
Wegener's granulomatosis is associated with necrotizing vasculitis.

Wegener's granulomatosis predominantly affects the small blood vessels of the upper respiratory tract, lungs, and kidneys. Lung involvement will show multiple, bilateral cavitating nodules and pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray.

The radiograph below shows cavitating nodules in a patient with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis).

Renal involvement initially appears as focal or segmental glomerulonephritis on biopsy. If left untreated, it can lead to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). Patients with Wegener's granulomatosis have an increased incidence of venous thrombosis, like deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.

The diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis on biopsy. This finding is commonly seen in the tissues obtained from lungs, skin, upper airways, and rarely kidneys.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical presentation along with pANCA positivity and biopsy findings of leukocytoclastic (neutrophil infiltration) vasculitis point towards a diagnosis of microscopic polyangiitis. It is associated with fibrinoid necrosis.

Microscopic polyangiitis, also known as hypersensitivity vasculitis, causes segmental fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles and venules. It is associated with neutrophil infiltration, and hence also called leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Histopathology of the affected tissue will show necrotizing vasculitis of arterioles, venules, and capillaries without any granulomas. It is caused by ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) and is not mediated by the immune complex. It primarily affects the kidneys and lungs.
question: A 57-year-old man presented with complaints of fever, weight loss, and hemoptysis. His serology was positive for pANCA and biopsy showed small vessel vasculitis with neutrophil infiltration. Which of the following is a feature associated with his condition?

explanationHtml:
A triad of skin lesions, asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex, and eosinophilia is seen in Churg–Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

It is a necrotizing vasculitis of the small-to-medium-sized vessels and in order to be diagnosed with Churg-Strauss, a patient should have evidence of asthma, peripheral blood and tissue eosinophilia (>1000 cells/μL), extravascular granuloma formation and clinical features consistent with vasculitis.

Common presenting symptoms of this condition are lower respiratory tract symptoms such as severe attacks of asthma, upper respiratory tract symptoms such as allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and nasal polyps, mono neuritis multiplex (a type of peripheral neuropathy affecting at least two nerves) which presents with a complaint of pain, numbness, or weakness in the affected areas and skin lesions like palpable purpura and subcutaneous nodules.

Renal involvement is less common and less severe than other small vessel vasculitis.

P-ANCA antibodies are present in Churg Strauss syndrome.

  • Severe attacks of asthma
  • Mononeuritis multiplex: a type of peripheral neuropathy affecting at least two nerves. Patients will complain of pain, numbness, or weakness in the affected areas.
  • Skin lesions like palpable purpura and subcutaneous nodules.

Glucocorticoids show effective responses in these patients. Other drugs that have been tried are mepolizumab and rituximab.

For fulminant multisystem disease, daily cyclophosphamide with prednisolone followed by azathioprine or methotrexate is used.

Option A: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis presents with palpable purpura, arthralgia, neuropathy, and glomerulonephritis. It is most commonly associated with Hepatitis C.

Option D: Giant cell arteritis manifests with the cardinal symptom of headache localized to the temporal region. Common symptoms include headache, polymyalgia rheumatica , jaw claudication, fever, and decrease in body weight. Laboratory results show increased ESR, CRP levels, normochromic or mildly hypochromic anemia.

Laboratory investigations will show peripheral blood eosinophilia. Some patients may be positive for pANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies). Histopathology will show the presence of necrotizing vasculitis, tissue eosinophilia, and extravascular granulomas.

Histopathology of ANCA associated vasculitides can be remembered as:

  • Microscopic polyangiitis: necrotizing vasculitis
  • Wegener's granulomatosis: necrotizing vasculitis with granulomas
  • Churg Strauss syndrome: necrotizing vasculitis with extravascular granulomas and eosinophilia
question: A 47-year-old housewife presented with recurrent attacks of asthma and pain and numbness along the distribution of the median and ulnar nerve. Her serology was positive for pANCA. Further evaluation is unlikely to reveal which of the following findings?

  • Abdominal pain

Cryoglobulins are the immunoglobulins that precipitate at temperatures less than 37°C, the presence of these cryoglobulins in serum leads to Cryoglobulinemia, which is characterized by cutaneous vasculitis, palpable purpura, arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, and glomerulonephritis.

Defects of tubular function, including renal tubular acidosis, uricosuria, and phosphaturia, are often seen and are associated histologically with tubulointerstitial nephritis.

Lacrimal and salivary glands are the major targets of this disease, while the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and the vagina may also be involved. The characteristic decrease in tears and saliva (sicca syndrome) is the result of lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis of the lacrimal and salivary glands. The infiltrate contains predominantly activated CD4+ helper T cells and some B cells, including plasma cells.

Antibodies detected are:

  • Rheumatoid factor - seen in 75% of patients, whether or not coexisting rheumatoid arthritis is present
  • Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs)
  • SS-A (Ro) - associated with early disease onset, longer disease duration, and extra-glandular manifestations, such as cutaneous vasculitis and nephritis
  • SS-B (La)

These patients are at high risk for the development of B-cell lymphomas. About 60% of patients have another accompanying autoimmune disorder, such as rheumatoid arthritis, and these patients also have the symptoms and signs of that disorder.

Biopsy of the lip (to examine minor salivary glands) is essential for the diagnosis of Sjögren's syndrome.

Note: Mikulicz syndrome is characterized by lacrimal and salivary gland enlargement from any cause, including sarcoidosis, lymphomas, and other tumors.

The most common extracutaneous manifestation of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is Raynaud's phenomenon.

Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by episodes of reversible vasoconstriction in the fingers and toes on exposure to cold. Rarely, it affects the lips, tip of the nose, and earlobes. These episodes classically occur in the following sequence:

  • Affected part turning pale due to vasoconstriction.
  • Blue due to ischemia, often associated with numbness or pain.
  • As blood flow returns, the area turns red with a burning sensation.

Raynaud phenomenon is manifested as episodic vasoconstriction of the arteries and arterioles of the extremities, causing pallor of extremities followed by pain and cyanosis. It is seen in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis or scleroderma and precedes other symptoms in 70% of cases.

Focal, and sometimes diffuse, subcutaneous calcifications may develop, especially in patients with CREST syndrome. The most ominous manifestation is malignant hypertension.

Scleroderma renal crisis is a medical emergency characterized by acute onset malignant hypertension and kidney failure, usually in the absence of previous evidence of significant kidney disease. The use of steroids is associated with an increased risk of scleroderma renal crisis.

Clinical features of scleroderma renal crisis are:

  • Accelerated hypertension - headache, vomiting, blurring of vision, hypertensive retinopathy, and hypertensive encephalopathy.
  • Acute kidney injury - oliguria, mild proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, renal failure.
  • Pulmonary edema, congestive heart failure.
  • Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia.

In patients with persistent hypertension, the addition of angiotensin II receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, and direct renin inhibitors should be considered.

Squeezing of the relaxed calf muscles from side to side is painful as the thrombosed deep veins in the calf are always tender. This test is known as Moses’ sign.

The clinical manifestations in APS occur due to the activation of coagulation and thrombus formation. Therefore, anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents are the mainstays in the treatment. Important drugs used are:

  • Aspirin- is an antiplatelet agent.

The above image shows flexion at the PIP joint and extension in the DIP joints which is known as boutonniere deformity which is seen in rheumatoid arthritis(RA).

If the patient gives a history of pain/stiffness in the joints in the early hours of the day which usually decreases as the day progresses suggesting inflammatory arthritis and if it presents with predominant involvement of smaller joints, it is most likely a case of RA(option A).

It occurs due to the accumulation of inflammatory mediators which on increased joint mobility are flushed out due to increased blood supply.

Pain and stiffness in osteoarthritis (Option B) usually increase as the day progresses due to an increase in the activity of the joint. They typically present with nodules around the distal interphalangeal joint (Heberden nodes) and proximal interphalangeal joint (Bouchard nodes).

Patients who have a history of cigarette smoking had early onset arthritic manifestations and tested positive for RA factor or ACPA are more likely to develop extra-articular manifestations. Other common extra-articular manifestations include secondary Sjogren's syndrome, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary nodules, and anemia. question: Which of the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis?

explanationHtml:
For further management of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with worsening disease activity, the preferred therapy is a step-up to oral triple therapy with methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine. The addition of leflunomide or a biological (anti - TNF) to methotrexate is another alternative.

Ideally, the approach to a patient with early RA is aggressive. Methotrexate is always the first DMARD that the patient is started on, and if an adequate response is not observed within 3-6 months, a step up in therapy is made by adding on drugs.

For assessment of progression, composite indices like Disease Activity Score - 28 (DAS-28) can used.

Other options:

Option A: Changing the route of administration of methotrexate from oral to parenteral is not a part of step up

Option C: Priority is given to minimising the duration the patient is on steroids.

Option D: Anti -TNF agents (adalimumab, etanercept) are not recommended as a monotherapy, and are reserved for treatment in combination with DMARDs. This is due to the fact that the efficacy of monotherapy is lesser than that of DMARDs, and the adverse effects include increased risk of serious infections, re-activation of latent TB and opportunistic fungal infections. They are reserved for cases where there is a lack of response with the first line agents.

explanationHtml:
The rise in post-bronchodilator FEV1>12% is a feature of asthma, not COPD. It suggests reversible airflow obstruction.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the presence of airflow obstruction that is partially reversible.

Cigarette smoking is the most common cause of COPD. Cigarette smoke exposure affects large airways, small airways, and alveoli:

  • Changes in large airways cause cough and sputum
  • Changes in small airways (≤2mm) and alveoli are responsible for physiologic alterations

The major site of increased resistance in most individuals with COPD is in airways ≤2 mm diameter.

Characteristic cellular changes include goblet cell metaplasia. Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells that replace surfactant-secreting Club cells.

Nonuniform ventilation and ventilation-perfusion mismatching are characteristic of COPD.
