explanationHtml:
The clinical picture is highly suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD). An increase in the residual volume is a feature of COPD.

COPD is defined as a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the presence of airflow obstruction that is partially reversible.

COPD is the clinical expression of abnormalities of airways and/or alveoli and includes:

  • Emphysema is defined pathologically as the abnormal and permanent dilation of airways distal to the terminal bronchiole, along with the destruction of their walls.
  • Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically as the presence of persistent cough with sputum production on most of the days for ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years.

explanationHtml:
Body plethysmography is the best investigation to measure lung volume in an emphysematous patient with bullous lesions as seen on the X-ray.

To measure absolute lung volumes, two techniques are used:

  1. Body plethysmography: It is used to measure the volume of any gas containing space in the thorax including bullae. It is accurate in both obstructive and restrictive diseases.
  2. Inert gas dilution technique: It is used to measure the volume of regions that are well ventilated which excludes trapped gas or bullae. It is accurate in restrictive diseases only.

The amount of gas trapped in bullae can be measured by subtracting lung volumes measured by inert gas dilution technique from lung volume measured by body plethysmography.

Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FENO) is a non-invasive test used in the diagnosis and monitoring of bronchial asthma. NO levels are increased in asthmatics and related to the eosinophilic inflammation in the airways.

Glucocorticoids are used during an exacerbation of COPD. They hasten recovery and reduce the chances of future exacerbations.

Exacerbations are episodes of increased dyspnoea and cough, with a change in the amount and character of sputum. They are often triggered by an infection with one-third of cases having a viral etiology. They may or may not have other signs of illness such as fever, myalgias, and sore throat. question: Which of the following is false regarding acute exacerbations in COPD patients?

correctAnswer: A. Non-Invasive PPV should be given
explanationHtml:
Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV) should be the first mode of ventilation used in COPD patients with acute respiratory failure provided there are no absolute contraindications. This approach improves gas exchange, reduces work of breathing and the need for intubation, decreases hospitalization duration and enhances overall survival outcomes.

Invasive positive pressure ventilation is only considered after failure of NIPPV, resulting in severe respiratory distress, life threatening hypoxemia, severe hypercarbia and/or acidosis, markedly impaired mental status, respiratory arrest or hemodynamic instability (Option B).

Apart from NIPPV, short-acting inhaled beta 2 agonists (albuterol, salbutamol) with or without short-acting anticholinergics (ipratropium) and Long-acting anticholinergics (tiotropium) are recommended as the initial bronchodilators. Maintenance therapy with long-acting beta 2 agonists (formoterol) must be started as soon as possible.

Systemic corticosteroids are useful in the treatment of acute exacerbations of COPD as they reduce airway inflammation and improve lung function over time. However, the effects are not immediate. NIPPV on the other hand provides immediate relief to the patient and reduces the work of breathing. Therefore, it would not be the best choice in this case. (Option C)

Antibiotics can also be considered, as they reduce duration of hospitalisation. Treatment is given for 5 days.

Permissive hypercapnia refers to a ventilation strategy where tidal volume is reduced in order to avoid hyperinflation-associated lung trauma. It is not preferred at the initial presentation. It is only permitted once invasive PPV is started following NIPPV failure (Option D)

An exacerbation of COPD is defined as an event characterized by dyspnea and/or cough and sputum that worsen over < 14 days. Exacerbations of COPD are often associated with increased local and systemic inflammation caused by airway infection, pollution, or other insults to the lungs.

A 45-year-old obese chronic smoker is rushed to the ER with difficulty in breathing and a productive cough. He has a past history of two similar episodes this year. On examination, RR- 34/min, with use of accessory muscles and central cyanosis is present. ABG is as shown. Chest X-ray shows increased vascular markings. What is the best initial step of management?

ABG Analysis:

pH- 7.33

PaO2- 50 mmHg

PaCO2- 48 mmHg

HCO3‾- 27 mEq/L

explanationHtml:
Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) is contraindicated in cardiovascular instability. NIPPV can impede venous filling of the heart, decrease cardiac output, and worsen/precipitate hypotension. Moreover, in unstable states with impending cardiovascular collapse, invasive ventilation is preferred.

Indications of NIPPV:

  • Apnea - central and obstructive
  • Central hypoventilation syndrome
  • Neuromuscular and chest wall disorders
  • Respiratory failure - PaCO2 >45 mmHg

Contraindications of NIPPV:

  • Cardiovascular instability
  • Impaired mental status or inability to cooperate
  • Copious secretions or the inability to clear secretions
  • Craniofacial abnormalities
  • Trauma precluding effective fitting of the mask
question: In patients with which of the following conditions is NIPPV contraindicated?

explanationHtml:
Oral glucocorticoids are not used in the long-term treatment of COPD because of an unfavorable benefit/risk ratio.

Chronic use of glucocorticoids is associated with significant side effects, including osteoporosis, weight gain, cataracts, glucose intolerance, and increased risk of infection.

Treatment of COPD:

  • Smoking cessation
  • Anticholinergic agents- Ipratropium bromide
  • Beta Agonists- Long-acting inhaled β agonists, such as salmeterol or formoterol are commonly used.
  • Methylxanthines- theophylline produces improvements in expiratory flow rates and vital capacity.
  • Phosphodiesterase inhibitors - roflumilast is used when FEV1<50%.
  • Antibiotics- macrolides like azithromycin reduce exacerbations when used over one year
  • N-acetylcysteine has been used in patients with COPD for both its mucolytic and antioxidant properties
  • Oxygen therapy

Non-pharmacologic therapies:

  • Lung volume reduction surgery
  • Lung transplantation

question: Which of the following organisms can cause both typical and atypical pneumonia?

explanationHtml:
Home split air-conditioners are least likely to cause an outbreak of Legionella pneumonia.

Legionella outbreaks occur most commonly due to aerosol droplets of contaminated water. Another source of contamination is hot water systems, as they have the ideal temperature supporting the growth of Legionella.

Therefore, systems using aerosols, such as cooling towers, and hot water systems such as evaporative condensers, humidifiers, etc, pose a high risk of causing an outbreak.
question: Which of the following is least likely to cause an outbreak of Legionella pneumonia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of atypical pneumonia caused by legionella.

Clinical features of Legionnaire's disease:

  • Cough with scanty sputum
  • Extrapulmonary manifestations involve

explanationHtml:
A urinary antigen detection test is recommended for the diagnosis of Legionella pneumonia. The sensitivity (70%) and specificity (99%) of the test are high.

The test can detect antigen even after the initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy. Urinary antigen detection test can also be used for Streptococcus pneumonia but is not used due to the availability of better alternatives.

Other investigations for Legionella:

  • DFA (direct fluorescent antibody)- is highly specific but not sensitive
  • Culture- Gold standard, BCYE media is used
  • DNA detection with PCR

Treatment: Drugs of choice are azithromycin and respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin).

The given clinical scenario along with chest X-ray and lab values is suggestive of atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae. The blood investigations show decreased hemoglobin, elevated LDH, and elevated unconjugated bilirubin suggestive of hemolytic anemia.

Mycoplasma is the most common bacteria causing atypical pneumonia and the second most common cause of pneumonia.

Clinical Presentation:

correctAnswer: C. Cefotaxime is the drug of choice
explanationHtml:
Cefotaxime is not the drug of choice for the treatment of Mycoplasma pneumonia. Cefotaxime is a cell-wall synthesis inhibitor, hence it is not effective on M.pnemoniae as they lack a cell wall.

Investigations:

  • PCR of respiratory secretions
  • Chest X-ray shows-
    • Patchy consolidation at the hilum and fanning to the periphery
    • Diffuse peribronchial and perivascular interstitial infiltrates
    • Airspace consolidation
    • Reticulonodular opacification
  • HRCT shows- areas of ground-glass attenuation
  • On PPLO agar (Dienes method) shows- fried-egg appearance.

The diagnosis is made by serology/PCR. Azithromycin is the drug of choice for management. Doxycycline is the second-best drug for the management of atypical pneumonia.

Klebsiella pneumonia is associated mostly with alcoholics and shows upper lobe involvement. The patients present with red-currant jelly sputum.

It is seen in any space-occupying process in the lung such as pulmonary hemorrhage, lung abscess, and lung tumors.

question: A chronic alcoholic presents to the OPD with fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, and productive cough. On examination, there is bronchial breathing on the right side and a dull note on percussion. A chest x-ray is done. What is the most likely causative agent?

explanationHtml:
The most likely causative agent of pneumonia in an infant with X-ray showing pneumatoceles (air-filled cysts within lung parenchyma) is Staphylococcus aureus.

In newborns and infants, S. aureus is a significant cause of severe respiratory tract infections, presenting with dyspnea, fever, and respiratory failure. Community-acquired infections are often preceded by viral infections, most commonly influenza. Among adults, nosocomial S. aureus pulmonary infections are frequently observed in intubated patients within intensive care units.

S. aureus often causes necrotizing pneumonitis that may be associated with complications such as pneumothorax and empyema.

Pneumatocoele can also be caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, E. coli, group A streptococci, Klebsiella pneumoniae, etc. However, Staphylococcus aureus is most commonly implicated.

Other options:

Option A: Klebsiella pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia in alcoholics and diabetics. Patients present with fever, dyspnea, and a productive cough with red currant jelly sputum. Classic chest X-ray findings include upper lobe consolidation, classically on the right side, cavitation, and bulging fissure sign.

The following image shows bulging fissure sign:

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Streptococcus pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia. Patients with pneumococcal pneumonia present with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. On examination, the involved lobes are dull to percussion, bronchial breath sounds, and crackles are heard on auscultation.

The following image shows right lower lobe consolidation:

[[figure-2]]

Option C: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia. Patients present with dry cough, fever, chills, malaise, and upper respiratory tract symptoms. On auscultation, wheezes or rales are heard. Chest X-ray shows peribronchial pneumonia with prominent bronchial markings, interstitial infiltration, and atelectasis.

The below chest X-ray shows patchy consolidation at the hilum and fanning to the periphery:

question: A 3-month-old male child was brought with a history of fever and respiratory distress. Suspecting pneumonia, a chest X-ray was ordered. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

explanationHtml:
The best biomarker for lobar pneumonia is procalcitonin.

The most commonly used biomarkers of severe inflammation are C-reactive protein (CRP) and procalcitonin (PCT). Levels of these acute phase reactants increase in the presence of bacterial pathogens. PCT testing distinguishes between bacterial (mostly lobar pneumonia) and viral infection to decide the need for antibacterial therapy or discontinuation of treatment.

CRP, fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A are other acute phase reactants.
question: Which of the following is the best biomarker for lobar pneumonia?

correctAnswer: D. Systolic blood pressure less than 100 mm Hg
explanationHtml:
Among the options, systolic blood pressure less than 100 mm Hg (Option D) is not a component of CURB-65. CURB65 includes blood pressure, systolic ≤90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg.

CURB-65 criteria is used to assess the severity of illness in a case community-acquired pneumonia. It includes confusion (C), urea >7 mmol/L (U), respiratory rate ≥30/min (R), blood pressure systolic ≤90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg (B) and an age of ≥65 years.

Pneumonia severity index (PSI) is another index to assess the severity of illness and the risk of mortality in the case of pneumonia. It includes 20 variables and depending on the score, patients are assigned into one of the 5 classes.
Class, I, II, III - at low risk of death and can be treated on an outpatient basis
Class IV & V require hospitalization

question: A patient in the ICU is diagnosed with community acquired-MRSA. What is the best line of management?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia due to aspiration. The drug of choice is clindamycin as anaerobes are implicated.

Anaerobes play a significant role only when an episode of aspiration has occurred days to weeks before presentation for pneumonia. The combination of an unprotected airway (e.g., in patients with alcohol or drug overdose or a seizure disorder) and significant gingivitis constitutes the major risk factor.

Anaerobic pneumonia is often complicated by abscess formation and significant empyemas or parapneumonic effusions.
question: An epileptic patient presented with fever, breathlessness, and productive cough for 2 days. The last episode of seizures occurred a week ago. On examination, PR-102/min, RR-30/min, and oral cavity revealed a gingival infection. Bronchial breath sounds were heard on auscultation on the right side. What is the drug of choice for his condition?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis in a case of pneumonia in a HIV positive patient, along with the presence of fever, and non-productive cough with radiographic findings of diffuse interstitial infiltrates and symmetric perihilar involvement is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). A characteristic feature of PCP is retrosternal chest pain, which worsens on inspiration and is described as sharp or burning.

It is important to note that even though the incidence of PCP is the highest at CD4+ counts of <200/μL (80%), it can be seen in patients with higher counts.

Other options:

Option D: Tuberculosis (TB) should be considered as a possibility in cases of pneumonia in people living with HIV. However, the absence of hilar lymph node involvement, non-productive cough, and no extrapulmonary (pleural, pericardial, lymphatic) features are not consistent with tuberculosis.

TB can occur at any stage of HIV infection. In the early stages, pulmonary TB appears typically with upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation. In advanced HIV infection, with CD4+ T-cell count below 200/μL, TB presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates, minimal cavitation, pleural effusion, and lymphadenopathy. Extrapulmonary TB is fairly common in HIV, with it being documented in 40-60% of cases.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Staphylococcal pneumonia most commonly presents with a productive cough, and radiologically presents with pneumatoceles (cavitations)

[[figure-2]]

Option B: Patients with pneumococcal pneumonia also present with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. Imaging usually shows lobar involvement.

question: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with fever for 3 weeks, dry cough, and significant weight loss. He complains of retrosternal chest pain that is worse on inspiration. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole combination (commonly known as cotrimoxazole) is the first-line drug for both prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis jirovecii infections in immunocompromised patients.

Cotrimoxazole acts by causing a sequential block of folate metabolism. CD4+ T cell counts below 200 cells/μL are an indication to start prophylaxis.
question: In an immunocompromised patient, which of the following is the drug of choice for prophylaxis of pneumocystis jirovecii?

correctAnswer: D. Aerosolized pentamidine is used in the treatment
explanationHtml:
Aerosolised pentamidine is not used in the treatment of PCP. It is used in PCP prophylaxis.

Diagnosis of PCP:

  • Histopathological staining of induced sputum examination
  • Bronchoscopy with BAL (most sensitive)
  • Elevated LDH

Treatment and Prophylaxis:

  • Drug of choice- trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)
  • IV pentamidine- treatment of choice for severe disease in the patient unable to tolerate TMP-SMX
  • Glucocorticoids- indicated if PaO2 <70 mmHg or with an A–a gradient >35 mmHg
  • Other drugs used- dapsone/pyrimethamine + leucovorin, clindamycin/primaquine, and atovaquone
  • Aerosolised pentamidine is an alternative used in PCP prophylaxis.

Prophylaxis is indicated when CD4+ T cell count <200/uL ( CD4 cell %<15), recent oropharyngeal candidiasis, and prior PCP infection.

options.text: Glucocorticoids are indicated if Pao2 &lt;70 mmHg
Recent oropharyngeal candidiasis is an indication for prophylaxis
Elevation of LDH is a common finding
Aerosolized pentamidine is used in the treatment

question: Which of the following is false regarding patients with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the chest X-ray and gram-staining is suggestive of Nocardiosis. The drug of choice is cotrimoxazole.

Nocardia is a gram-positive and acid-fast bacteria. Nocardia pneumonia has a sub-acute presentation with mostly cough with thick sputum and fever. Generally, hemoptysis is uncommon. Chest radiography shows nodular infiltrations involving bilateral lung fields.

Extrapulmonary manifestations are common, the brain is the most commonly involved organ. It is associated with dense bilateral infiltrates with cavitating nodules and subacute brain abscesses.

The drug of choice is cotrimoxazole. Severe disease is treated with a combination of cotrimoxazole, amikacin, and ceftriaxone, or imipenem.

Note: Mnemonic SNAP:

Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (Cotrimoxazole) is the drug of choice for Nocardia.

For Actinomyces, Penicillins are the drugs of choice.
question: A 36-year-old male HIV patient presents to the ED with a cough with bloody sputum. He also has night sweats, chills, and difficulty in breathing. A chest X-ray and examination of the sputum show the following findings. Which of the following is the drug of choice for his condition?

explanationHtml:
Azithromycin is the drug of choice for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in an OPD setup.

Outpatient management of CAP:

1. For previously healthy patients who have not taken antibiotics within the past 3 months:

  • A macrolide – Azithromycin, 500 mg orally as a first dose and then 250 mg orally daily for 4 days, or 500 mg orally daily for 3 days, or
  • Clarithromycin, 500 mg orally twice a day; or
  • Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day

2. For patients with such comorbid medical conditions as chronic heart, lung, liver, or kidney disease, diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, malignancy, asplenia, immunosuppressant conditions or use of immunosuppressive drugs or use of antibiotics within the previous 3 months:

  • A respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin, 400 mg orally daily; gemifloxacin, 320 mg orally daily; levofloxacin, 750 mg orally daily) or
  • A macrolide (as above) plus a beta-lactam (amoxicillin, 1 g orally three times a day; amoxicillin-clavulanate, 2 g orally twice a day; cefuroxime, 500 mg orally twice a day).

3. In regions with a high rate (> 25%) of infection with high level (MIC ≥ 16 mcg/mL) macrolide-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae, consider the use of alternative agents listed in (2) for patients with comorbidities.

Other options: Vancomycin, Ceftriaxone, and Streptomycin are administered parenterally, and hence, not appropriate for outpatient management.
question: Which of the following drugs is commonly used for treating community-acquired pneumonia in OPD?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, Acinetobacter species is the most commonly isolated organism in cases of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP).

Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) develops in hospitalized patients, usually after 48 hours of being placed on invasive mechanical ventilation.

The causative organisms vary in different hospitals. However, the frequently found organisms are Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter sp., Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and gram-negative rods (Enterobacter species, K. pneumoniae, and Escherichia coli).

Three factors distinguish nosocomial pneumonia from community-acquired pneumonia:

  1. Different infectious agents
  2. Different antibiotic susceptibility patterns, specifically, a higher incidence of drug resistance
  3. Poor underlying health status of patients puts them at risk for more severe infections

Within 48 hours of admission, 75% of seriously ill hospitalized patients have their upper airway colonized with organisms from the hospital environment. Impaired cellular and mechanical defense mechanisms in the lungs of hospitalized patients raise the risk of infection after aspiration has occurred.

VAP patients may be infected with Acinetobacter species and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia. Anaerobic organisms (Bacteroides, anaerobic streptococci, Fusobacterium) may also cause pneumonia in the hospitalized patient.
question: What is the most likely causative organism of ventilator-associated pneumonia among the following?

correctAnswer: C. Pleural fluid protein >4 gm/dL is an indication of tube thoracostomy
explanationHtml:
Pleural Fluid Protein >4 gm/dL is not an indication of tube thoracostomy.

Parapneumonic effusion is pleural effusion associated with bacterial pneumonia, lung abscess, or bronchiectasis. When it worsens, it can result in the collection of frank pus in the pleural space. This is known as empyema.

Risk factors include diabetes, immunosuppression, alcoholism, cancer, and poor dental hygiene.

Investigations:

  • Chest X-ray:
    • Loculations or encystments (complicated parapneumonic effusion)
    • Intrapleural air-fluid level (bronchopulmonary fistula)
    • Parenchymal infiltrations (underlying pneumonia)
  • Ultrasound: Shows echogenic pleural fluid with septations and helps in characterizing the effusion
  • Pleural fluid analysis:
    • Exudative neutrophilic effusion
    • Low pH <7.2, low glucose <60 mg/dL, high LDH >1000 IU/L in complicated parapneumonic effusion
  • CECT: Split pleura sign seen in empyema

Treatment:

  • Antibiotics: Tailored according to the microorganism
  • Therapeutic thoracocentesis
  • Tube thoracostomy is indicated if:
    • Pleural fluid pH <7.2
    • Frank pus
    • Microorganism isolated in Gram stain or culture of pleural fluid

Pleural fluid protein &gt;4 gm/dL is an indication of tube thoracostomy
USG is helpful in characterizing the effusion

explanationHtml:
The most common interstitial lung disease (ILD) is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

ILD refers to the remodeling of interstitial space, the region between the epithelium and endothelium. The main pathology is fibrosis, mediated by TGF-ß and platelet-derived growth factor.

Classification of Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)

ILDs of known etiology

  • Occupational: Coal worker's pneumoconiosis, silicosis
  • Treatment-related: Radiation, drug-induced
  • Connective tissue disease-related: Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren's syndrome, scleroderma

ILDs of unknown etiology

  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF): Most common type
  • Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)
  • Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP)
  • Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP)/Hamman-Rich syndrome
  • Respiratory bronchiolitis associated ILD (RBILD)
  • Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)
  • Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia (LIP)
  • Pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis

Granulomatous

  • Sarcoidosis
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Other forms

  • Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)
  • Pulmonary Langerhans' cell histiocytosis (PLCH)
  • Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP)
question: Which of the following is the most common interstitial lung disease?

explanationHtml:
The above HRCT shows a honeycomb appearance of lung parenchyma due to interstitial fibrosis in a restrictive lung disorder that is suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD). Inspiratory coarse crackles are not a feature of interstitial lung disease.

Auscultating a patient with ILD will reveal bilateral basal end-inspiratory fine crackles also called velcro crackles or rales.

Patients with interstitial lung disease usually present with a non-productive cough and breathlessness on exertion. Clubbing may be seen on examination, especially in advanced cases.
question: An 80-year-old woman was found to have a restrictive disease with reduced lung volumes on a pulmonary function test. A high-resolution CT of the thorax was done and is shown below.  Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

correctAnswer: C. FEV1/FVC ratio >0.7 and DLCO decreases
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the HRCT findings are suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD). FEV1/FVC ratio >0.7 and decreased DLCO are likely to be seen in the PFT. A history of swollen joints and early morning stiffness hints at rheumatoid arthritis. It is associated with the usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern of ILD.

In ILD, restrictive pattern is seen on pulmonary function test, which is characterized by:

  • Decreased total lung capacity (TLC)
  • Decreased forced vital capacity (FVC)
  • Decreased residual volumes (RV)
  • Decreased DLCO (diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide)
  • FEV1/FVC ratio - normal or increased, >0.7
question: A 70-year-old woman presents with breathlessness on exertion and dry cough for 4 weeks. She has swollen joints and early morning stiffness for which she is on treatment for a few years. On auscultation, inspiratory fine crackles were heard. An HRCT was ordered and it showed bilateral, subpleural and basilar honeycombing pattern. PFT of the patient is likely to show which of the following patterns?

explanationHtml:
Ground-glass opacities on HRCT are not a characteristic finding in UIP.

Honeycombing, loss of lung architecture, traction bronchiectasis, and basilar subpleural reticular opacities are seen in UIP pattern of ILD on HRCT.

options.text: Honeycombing and loss of lung architecture

question: Which of the following is not a characteristic HRCT finding of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)?

explanationHtml:
Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) is also known as Hamman–Rich syndrome.

AIP is a rare, idiopathic, fulminant interstitial lung disease (ILD) that is similar in presentation to ARDS. It is often preceded by a viral upper respiratory tract infection.

Histologically, it shows diffuse alveolar damage. HRCT shows bilateral patchy, ground-glass opacities. Lung biopsy shows diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline formation.
question: Which of the following conditions is also known as Hamman-Rich syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the image showing sclerodactyly suggestive of scleroderma along with the HRCT findings point to a diagnosis of non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP). It is characterized by homogeneous interstitial involvement.

NSIP is often associated with connective tissue disease but can also be drug-induced. The common drugs implicated in NSIP are:

  • Bleomycin
  • Busulfan
  • Methotrexate
  • Amiodarone

It usually affects middle-aged woman who have never smoked. There is uniformity of interstitial involvement across the biopsy section, and this may be predominantly cellular or fibrosing. HRCT shows homogenous involvement with symmetrical ground-glass opacities.

Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) responds to steroids. Other treatment modalities include cytotoxic drugs like azathioprine or cyclophosphamide and also biologics like rituximab.
question: A 52-year-old woman presented with dyspnoea. General physical examination revealed deformity of the hand as shown below. There is restricted mobility in the small joints and loss of wrinkle lines on the facial skin. An HRCT of the thorax showed diffuse subpleural, symmetric, ground-glass opacities of the lungs. Which of the following histopathological finding is likely to be seen in the lung biopsy of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is not related to smoking.

It is usually seen in young females with tuberous sclerosis. LAM can lead to pneumothorax or chylous effusions.

Pulmonary function testing usually reveals an obstructive or mixed obstructive-restrictive pattern. HRCT shows thin-walled cysts surrounded by normal lung parenchyma.

The smoking-related ILDs are:

  • DIP - Desquamating interstitial pneumonia.
  • RB-ILD - Respiratory bronchiolitis associated ILD.
  • LCH - Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
question: Which of the following is not a smoking-related interstitial lung disease (ILD)?

correctAnswer: D. It typically affects elderly smokers
explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH), an interstitial lung disease associated with smoking. It commonly occurs in younger adults. Cessation of smoking often leads to improvement in the condition.

The specific immunohistochemical markers for LCH are CD1a and langerin (CD207). On electron microscopy, the presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is characteristic (as shown below).

[[figure-1]]

High-resolution CT scans show bilateral nodules and irregular cystic changes, primarily in the upper lobes. The rupture of these cysts can lead to spontaneous pneumothorax.

options.text: They may present with spontaneous pneumothorax
Cysts and nodules are seen on HRCT
It is a smoking related interstitial lung disease

question: A man presented with progressively worsening cough with sputum, breathlessness, easy fatiguability, and loss of appetite for 6 months. PFT was suggestive of a restrictive disorder.  Trans-bronchial biopsy showed cells positive for CD1a and langerin (CD207). Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Chunky, gelatinous, PAS-positive sputum is a feature of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP).

PAP is a condition characterized by the accumulation of surfactants in alveoli and terminal airways. It can be due to impaired clearance or abnormal production of surfactants.

PAP can be of three forms:

  • Primary (most common): There is impaired GM-CSF-dependent surfactant clearance by the alveolar macrophages. It can be due to:
    • Autoantibodies against GM-CSF (acquired/idiopathic/autoimmune PAP)
    • Mutation in GM-CSF receptors (hereditary PAP)
  • Secondary: There is a reduction in the number or ability of alveolar macrophages that causes impaired surfactant clearance. It can be due to:
    • Silicosis
    • Immunodeficiency disorders
    • Hematopoietic disorders and malignancies
  • Congenital: It affects neonates and children. There is abnormal surfactant production due to mutation in the genes coding for:
    • Surfactant protein B
    • Surfactant protein C
    • ATP binding cassette protein member 3

About 30% of patients are asymptomatic. Symptomatic patients can have persistent dry cough, progressive dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain

X-ray shows bilateral, diffuse opacities and HRCT shows a crazy-paving pattern (as shown below). The treatment is whole lung lavage.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Acquired due to antibodies formed against GM-CSF

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding pulmonary alveolar proteinosis?

explanationHtml:
The given X-ray shows irregular opacities, which appear to be pleural thickenings i.e., pleural plaques. The sign along with a history of working in the cement industry suggests a diagnosis of asbestosis.

Workers of the cement, shipping, and textile industries are at a higher risk of developing asbestosis. Asbestos tends to involve the pleura first.

The earliest manifestation is benign asbestosis-related pleural effusion. With time, the plaques calcify resulting in the formation of thick pleural plaques. The pleural thickenings can be seen on the X-ray. This is the “holly leaf sign”.

Lung parenchymal involvement occurs after years of exposure (at least 10 years). They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea. It predominantly affects the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

The image below shows thick plueral plaques.

question: A daily-wage worker from the cement industry got a chest X-ray as a part of his routine health check-up. What could be the cause of the findings shown below?

explanationHtml:
Workers in the roofing industry are exposed to asbestos. Lung cancer (of all histologic types) is the most common cancer associated with asbestos exposure.

Smoking along with asbestos exposure multiplies the risk to a great extent. Cough and hemoptysis are common presentations.

Pleural mesothelioma is the most specific cancer associated with asbestos exposure, but not the most common. Smoking does not seem to be associated with mesothelioma. Pleuritic chest pain or a mass on the radiographic image are common presentations.
question: A woman has been working for a company that manufactures roofing sheets for 12 years, but the company does not provide her with personal protective equipment. Which of the following cancers is commonly seen in such individuals?

explanationHtml:
Silicosis is a common concern for people working in granite mining industries.

Silica is found in rock, granite, slate, and sandstone. People working in mining, stone cutting, sandblasting, glass and cement manufacturing, and quarrying are exposed to silica. The active molecule that causes silicosis is free silica or crystalline silica (quartz).

Silicosis can present as:

  • Acute silicosis - due to heavy exposure in closed spaces and they manifest within 2 years.
  • Chronic silicosis (simple silicosis) - due to long-term (10 to 30 years), less intense exposure.
  • Complicated silicosis- simple silicosis may progress to complicated silicosis that presents with chronic cough and progressive dyspnoea on exertion.

Note: Silicosis is the most common pnemoconiosis in the world.
question: Which among the following is a common concern for a patient presenting with chronic dry cough, working in the granite mining industry?

explanationHtml:
A history of working in the sandblasting industry for about a year without PPE suggests a heavy exposure to silica. This along with the CT finding of bilateral nodules, interstitial fibrosis, and crazy pavement pattern suggests a diagnosis of acute silicosis.

Acute silicosis is seen rarely. It manifests within 2 years of heavy exposure. Common presentations are dyspnoea and hypoxemia.

The X-ray may show diffuse miliary infiltrates or consolidation. HRCT may also show bilateral centrilobular nodules and ground-glass opacification. Bronchoalveolar lavage yields a PAS-positive milky white fluid.
question: A 45-year-old man comes to the emergency room with an acute onset of dyspnoea. He tells you that he has been working in the sandblasting industry for about a year and the company does not provide personal protective equipment. He also gives a history of on and off dry cough. CT scan shows the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Small round opacities in upper lobes
explanationHtml:
In this scenario, the man works in the stone cutting industry, indicating exposure to silica. He is expected to have less intense, long term exposure owing to a few but substandard measures to control exposure to silica. Such individuals are more likely to develop simple silicosis. These patients are asymptomatic, and HRCT shows small round opacities in the upper lobes.

This can progress to complicated silicosis. Here, the nodules coalesce and form masses leading to impairment of lung function. They present with chronic cough and progressive dyspnoea on exertion. This may progress further to cause progressive massive fibrosis.

PFT shows a mixed obstructive and restrictive pattern. Calcification of hilar lymph nodes is seen in a few cases, called eggshell calcification. This is depicted in the image below.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: A crazy pavement pattern is seen with acute silicosis.

Option C: Thin-walled cysts surrounded by normal lung parenchyma are seen in pulmonary lymphangiomyomatosis (LAM).

Option D: Pleural plaques are seen in patients suffering from asbestosis.

question: A 30-year-old man has recently started work in the stone cutting industry. The company provides him with a respirator mask but they do not use dust control measures. If he works in similar conditions for 20 more years, which of the following will you most likely see in his HRCT scan image?

explanationHtml:
Silicosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis.

Silica causes pulmonary alveolar macrophage dysfunction and hence, patients with silicosis have a higher risk of developing lung infections from organisms like M. Tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria and fungi.

Radiographic imaging of silicotuberculosis shows cavitation.
question: Which of the following pneumoconiosis is associated with an increased incidence of tuberculosis?

explanationHtml:
Caplan's syndrome also called rheumatoid pneumoconiosis, is a combination of rheumatoid arthritis and pneumoconiosis.

It manifests as pneumoconiotic nodules along with features of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis. Caplan syndrome was first described in coal miners and later in patients with silicosis too.

Option C: Hilar adenopathy, polyarthritis, and erythema nodosum are characteristic of Lofgren syndrome.

Option D: Arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis are characteristic of Reiter syndrome.
question: Choose the correct option with respect to Caplan’s syndrome.

explanationHtml:
The above characteristic pattern of symptoms is called Monday fever or Monday chest tightness and is due to byssinosis.

Byssinosis is seen commonly in cotton factory workers due to cotton dust exposure. It is also caused due to flax, hemp, and jute dust.

It is due to occupational hypersensitivity reaction with symptoms occurring (or recurring) on the first day of the workweek and diminishing by the weekend due to development of tolerance.
question: A factory worker presents to the clinic with fever, tiredness, and a chronic dry cough. He says his symptoms are worst on the first day of the week, improve by the end of the week, and are almost non-existent over the weekends. What could be the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) pattern of ILD is the most common pulmonary manifestation in systemic sclerosis.

The CT scan of NSIP shows ground-glass opacities. It responds to steroids given along with azathioprine or cyclophosphamide.

Other connective tissue diseases associated with ILD:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Sjögren syndrome
  • Dermatopolymyositis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
question: Which interstitial lung disease is likely to be seen in a patient suffering from systemic sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the microscopic image showing abundant black-colored pigment within the macrophages of lung parenchyma is characteristic of pulmonary anthracosis/coal worker's pneumoconiosis. It may give rise to centrilobular emphysema.

The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages. They accumulate in the connective tissue along lymphatics or in lymphoid tissue along the bronchi or the hilum, which causes the blackening of the tissues. Aggregates of carbon dust are present as coal macules or nodules which consist of carbon-laden macrophages.

It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles, such as coal mines. It is usually benign and less than 10% of the cases develop progressive massive fibrosis which may lead to pulmonary dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, and cor pulmonale. Coal workers may also develop emphysema or chronic bronchitis, independent of smoking.

Unlike asbestosis, this condition does not predispose to cancer.
question: A 45-year-old man who has worked as a miner for the past 25 years, comes to the OPD with complaints of dyspnoea and cough. Pulmonary function tests and a lung biopsy are done. The histopathology of the sample is shown below. Which type of emphysema can this condition give rise to?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and the CT showing signet ring sign is suggestive of bronchiectasis which can be due to cystic fibrosis.

A history of repeated chest infections is an indication of cystic fibrosis and a major risk factor for the development of bronchiectasis.
question: A 30-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital with a fever and cough. She has a history of repeated chest infections for several years and coughs up yellow-green purulent sputum with some streaky hemoptysis. What could be the underlying condition based on the CT given below?

explanationHtml:
Lung cancer is not a known complication of bronchiectasis.

Complications of bronchiectasis include:

  • Massive hemoptysis
  • Empyema and lung abscess
  • Respiratory failure
  • Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
  • Secondary amyloidosis (AA type)

Chronic and recurrent infections lead to secondary amyloidosis (AA type) and involve the kidneys.
question: Which of the following is an unlikely complication in patients with bronchiectasis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiectasis secondary to a non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infection. Mucolytic dornase is recommended routinely in cystic fibrosis (CF)-related bronchiectasis but not in non-CF bronchiectasis.

Macrolides (azithromycin or clarithromycin) combined with rifampicin and ethambutol are used in the treatment of non-CF bronchiectasis.

Treatment of bronchiectasis:

  1. Antibiotic therapy: This is used to treat exacerbations and is given for 10-14 days. Commonly administered antibiotics include:
    • Amoxicillin or clarithromycin: First-line drugs
    • Ciprofloxacin: For Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  2. Airway clearance:
    • Postural drainage: This is done by gravity-assisted positioning of the patient and chest physiotherapy.
    • Mucolytic treatment: only in cystic fibrosis patients
      • Normal or hypertonic saline (≥3%) nebulization
      • Humidified air inhalation
      • Drugs like N-acetylcysteine or carbocysteine
  3. Others:
    • Inhaled bronchodilators like long-acting β2 agonists and anticholinergics
    • Long-term oxygen therapy: In patients with chronic respiratory failure
    • Pulmonary rehabilitation
    • Adequate hydration
    • Resection of a focal area of suppuration, lung transplantation: In refractory cases
question: A 58-year-old white man presents with a 6-month history of productive cough, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. HRCT shows a cluster of grapes appearance. A biopsy shows features of a non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection. Cystic fibrosis is ruled out. Which of the following drugs is not to be used in the treatment regimen?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchiectasis. High resolution CT (HRCT) is the best answer among the other given options.

Bronchiectasis is a suppurative lung disease with abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchi. It is an end-stage condition of various diseases (infections, congenital or autoimmune disorders) that result in the destruction of the bronchial wall and its surrounding supporting tissues. Ried’s classification divides bronchiectasis into 3 types based on the phenotype of the affected bronchi, cylindrical or tubular (most common), saccular or varicose and cystic

Traction bronchiectasis is a type of bronchiectasis seen in conditions causing extensive pulmonary fibrosis (tuberculosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis). The mechanical traction due to fibrosis pulls apart the adjacent bronchi, making them distorted and abnormally dilated. There is no destruction of the bronchial wall. Clinically, they have a chronic productive cough, clubbing, crackles, and rhonchi.

Multidetector CT (MDCT) with thin collimation has gained greater advantages by overcoming the limitations of HRCT. Hence it is the most preferred investigation to asses the presence and extent of bronchiectasis, followed by HRCT.
question: An old woman presents with a persistent productive cough and clubbing. On auscultation, wheeze and crackles are present. There is no history of fever. Which of the following is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Abnormality in CFTR gene leads to defective calcium transport
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Abnormalities in cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein (CFTR) gene lead to defective chloride transport and not calcium transport.

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting the epithelial cells of various exocrine glands of the body. It is caused by mutations in the gene coding for CFTR protein. The most common CFTR mutation is F508 deletion.

The most prominent clinical features of cystic fibrosis are chronic respiratory diseases (fever, productive cough, recurrent lung infections) and pancreatic insufficiency (steatorrhea).

Male patients with cystic fibrosis usually have infertility due to congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in azoospermia.

Most common mutation is F508 deletion

question: A college student presents with complaints of fever, chronic productive cough, steatorrhea. There is a past history of recurrent lung infections and multiple hospitalizations with similar complaints. Which of the following is false about this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cystic fibrosis. In these patients, sperm count is most likely to be decreased.

Male patients with cystic fibrosis usually have infertility due to congenital absence of bilateral vas deferens and defective sperm transport, resulting in obstructive azoospermia.

Option A: Sweat chloride levels are elevated (≥60 mEq/L) due to abnormalities in the CFTR protein leading to defective chloride transport.

Option B: Serum bicarbonate levels are increased due to excessive loss of salt in the sweat resulting in hypochloremic alkalosis.

Option D: Immunoreactive trypsinogen levels are increased due to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. Measurement of these levels is a diagnostic screening test in newborns.
question: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with an acute respiratory tract infection. He has a history of asthma associated with recurrent respiratory tract infections and sinusitis. Genetic testing in childhood had revealed CFTR mutations. Which of the following is likely to be decreased in this patient?

explanationHtml:
DNA analysis is used to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis in patients with equivocal (one normal and one abnormal value) or frankly normal sweat chloride values.

The diagnosis is confirmed if both of the following criteria are met:

  • Presence of
    • Clinical symptoms affecting at least one organ system (respiratory, gastrointestinal, or genitourinary) or
    • Positive newborn screening or
    • A sibling with cystic fibrosis
  • Evidence of dysfunction of the CFTR gene by
    • Two positive sweat chloride test results obtained on separate days or
    • Identification of two CFTR mutations by genetic testing or
    • An abnormal measurement of nasal potential difference

Option A: 72-hour fecal fat is not used in the diagnosis of CF.

Option B: Measuring the levels of immunoreactive trypsinogen is a screening test in newborns.

Option D: Trans epithelial nasal potential difference measurement can be used as an adjunct to sweat test, but it has limited availability and is predominantly used as a research tool.
question: A young boy is being evaluated for cystic fibrosis. Sweat chloride shows values of 38 and 44 mEq/L (normal<40). What is the next best test to confirm the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis?

explanationHtml:
Male infertility is typical in Kartagener syndrome, but not a component of the triad.

Kartagener’s syndrome is primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of:

  • Situs inversus
  • Chronic sinusitis
  • Bronchiectasis

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis.

As ciliary function is necessary to ensure proper rotation of the developing organs in the chest and abdomen, its absence, will lead to situs inversus or a partial lateralizing abnormality.

Male patients with this condition tend to be infertile, due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).
question: A 15-year-old boy has been having recurrent hospitalizations for infections, since 2 years of age. After a detailed evaluation, a diagnosis of Kartagener's syndrome was made. Which of the following features is not a component of the triad seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Infertility in Kartagener syndrome is due to asthenospermia. Asthenospermia refers to immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella.

Kartagener’s syndrome is a type of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterised by the classical triad of

  • Situs inversus
  • Chronic sinusitis
  • Bronchiectasis

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (also called immotile cilia syndrome) is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility. It occurs due to ultrastructural defects in the dynein arm of cilia. This causes the retention of secretions due to a failed mucociliary clearance mechanism. Clinically, this manifests as chronic sinusitis and recurrent infections that ultimately lead to bronchiectasis.
question: Infertility in Kartagener’s syndrome is due to which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of lung abscess is aspirated oropharyngeal secretion.

Necrosis and cavitation of the lung caused due to a microbial infection constitutes a lung abscess.

It can broadly be classified into two categories:

  1. Primary lung abscesses: Aspiration of gastric contents into the respiratory tract ultimately leading to an anaerobic bacterial infection is the most common cause of primary lung abscess.
  2. Secondary lung abscesses: It is caused due to an underlying condition rather than a direct bacterial infection. Such underlying contributing factors can be an obstruction which reduces oropharyngeal clearance as seen in bronchial foreign body or tumor or it can be due to a systemic cause like HIV infection or other immunosuppressant conditions which increase the susceptibility of the patient to various opportunistic infections.
question: Which is the most common cause of lung abscess?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a primary lung abscess. Staphylococcus is involved in the formation of secondary lung abscess, not primary.

Microbial pathogens causing lung abscess:

Clinical conditions

Pathogens

Anaerobes (e.g., Peptostreptococcus spp., Prevotella spp., Bacteroides spp., Streptococcus milleri), microaerophilic streptococci

Secondary lung abscess (due to underlying conditions)

Staphylococcus aureus, gram-negative rods (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Enterobacteriaceae), Nocardia spp., Aspergillus spp., Legionella spp., Pneumocystis jirovecii

Embolic lesions

question: A bed-ridden patient with a Ryles tube tried to pull out the tube. This led to aspiration following which he developed fever with chills and cough. X-ray findings were suggestive of lung abscess. Which of the following pathogens is unlikely to have caused it?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a primary lung abscess due to aspiration. Most common lobes involved in primary lung abscess are posterior upper lobes and superior lower lobes, given the predisposition of aspirated materials to be deposited in these areas.

The right lung is affected more commonly than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated.

In secondary abscesses, the location of the abscess may vary with the underlying cause.
question: A 64-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department after being found unconscious due to alcohol intoxication. On physical examination, his dental hygiene was poor. Chest auscultation revealed fixed amphoric breath sounds over the right hemithorax. Which of the following lung lobes is most likely to be affected?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario described along with the chest X-ray image showing air-fluid level is suggestive of a lung abscess.

The patients usually present with complaints of fever, cough with sputum production, and chest pain. Patients with putrid lung abscesses may report foul-smelling sputum. Patients with chronic lung abscesses usually have a history of night sweats, fatigue, and anemia.

On physical examination:

  • Poor dentition/gingival disease
  • Amphoric and/or cavernous breath sounds on lung auscultation
  • Digital clubbing
  • The absence of a gag reflex

CXR features of lung abscess:

  • A lung cavity with an air-fluid level
  • The cavity wall is thick and irregular, and a surrounding pulmonary-infiltrate is often present
  • Computed tomography (CT) is more sensitive than chest radiography and is used to detect small cavities

The two x-ray images given below show thick-walled cavities with air-fluid levels on lateral and PA views respectively.

question: A middle-aged man presents with persistent fever and productive cough for 6 weeks with night sweats and anemia. The following is his CXR. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, the patient most likely has a lung abscess as depicted by the radiograph. Clindamycin is the drug of choice in the treatment of lung abscesses.

When there are contraindications to clindamycin, a combination of penicillin and metronidazole is likely to be as effective as clindamycin.

Anaerobes of oral origin are the most common causative organism and require broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage. Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and cephalexin have no significant activity against anaerobes.

question: A 60-year-old male patient presented with 2 weeks of productive cough, fever, and shortness of breath. A chest radiogram was done as shown below. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for him?

explanationHtml:
Lung carcinoma is unlikely in patients with lung abscesses. Lung carcinoma may cause lung abscess (in 10-15% of cases) but lung abscess is not a premalignant condition.

Complications of lung abscess:

  • Empyema
  • Pneumatocele
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Metastatic infections like brain abscess
  • Life-threatening hemoptysis

question: A patient with fever, productive cough, night sweats, and clubbing is diagnosed with lung abscess. Which of the following is an unlikely complication of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The most common presentation of inhalational anthrax is haemorrhagic mediastinitis, which is seen in 38% of the patients.

Inhalational anthrax, also known as wool sorter's disease, is caused by Bacillus anthracis. Infection usually occurs among workers handling contaminated animal wool, hair, and skin in the textile and tanning industries.

Patients present with malaise, fever, cough, shortness of breath & headache. Lymph nodes in the mediastinum are infected by the spores phagocytosed in the lung. Necrotic changes in these lymph nodes result in haemorrhagic mediastinitis. Other findings include:

  • Pulmonary infiltrates
  • Mediastinal widening
  • Pleural effusion

Treatment of inhalation anthrax includes a combination of intravenous ciprofloxacin and clindamycin for at least 14 days, antitoxins (Raxibacumab, Obiltoxaximab), anthrax immunoglobulins and steroids (if associated meningitis is present).

Prophylaxis with ciprofloxacin (500 mg twice daily for 2 months) is recommended for anyone at high risk of inhalational exposure to anthrax spores.
question: What is the most common presentation of inhalational anthrax?

explanationHtml:
Distal bronchiectasis is not a common feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).

ABPA is caused by an exaggerated immune response to airway infection caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. Asthma and cystic fibrosis are predisposing factors for this condition.

Patients with ABPA present with cough, wheezing, and breathlessness. Investigations reveal raised serum IgE levels and a positive skin prick test. Proximal (central) bronchiectasis is seen in this condition.

ABPA is diagnosed serologically, based on the presence of:

  • Serum IgE > 1000 IU/ml
  • Positive skin prick test or IgE levels against A. fumigatus extract
  • Detection of Aspergillus-specific antibodies
  • Eosinophilia >500 cells/μL

The use of systemic glucocorticoids is indicated for ABPA, but the course should be tapered by 3-6 months. Antifungal agents like itraconazole, voriconazole, and newer azoles can be used for over 4 months to control disease activity. Monoclonal antibodies against IgE, IL-4, and IL-5 receptors can be used for severe, refractory cases.
question: Which of the following is not a common feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?

correctAnswer: D. Culture of Aspergillus fumigatus from sputum
explanationHtml:
The culture of Aspergillus fumigatus from sputum is not a diagnostic criterion for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The sensitivity of sputum culture in ABPA is low.

ABPA is diagnosed serologically, based on the presence of:

  • Serum IgE > 1000 IU/ml.
  • Positive skin prick test or IgE levels against A. fumigatus extract.
  • Detection of Aspergillus-specific antibodies.
  • Eosinophilia >500 cells/μL.

question: Which of the following tests is not used to diagnose a patient with suspected allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?

correctAnswer: A. Fungal hyphae are broad and aseptate
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of aspergillosis. Fungal hyphae of Aspergillus species are narrow, septate, and have branching at 45o.

Yeast forms of Aspergillus are not seen in infected tissue.

Exposure to the high number of conidia that are found in construction sites, hay barns, moldy barks, and composts is a risk factor.

Clinical features:

  • Most of the patients are asymptomatic
  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Chest discomfort
  • Trivial hemoptysis
  • Shortness of breath

Halo sign-on HRCT refers to a localized ground glass appearance representing an area of hemorrhagic infarction surrounding a nodule. It is seen in invasive aspergillosis, a distinct entity where there is a direct invasion of hyphae into the lung tissue.

The air crescent sign describes the crescent of air that can be seen in invasive aspergillosis. It usually heralds recovery and is the result of increased granulocyte activity.

Monod sign refers to the gas that surrounds a mycetoma (most commonly an aspergilloma) in a pre-existing pulmonary cavity.

options.text: Fungal hyphae are broad and aseptate
Yeast forms are not seen in infected tissue
Most of the patients are asymptomatic
Exposure to hay barns is a risk factor.

question: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia underwent induction therapy. Within the next few days, he developed a cough and fever. On evaluation, HRCT showed a halo sign. Eventually, the patient deteriorated and died due to respiratory compromise. On autopsy, lung histopathology showed infarction and invasion of blood vessels by Aspergillus hyphae. Which of the following is not true about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Reduction in FEV1/FVC is characteristic of obstructive lung disease.

Forced vital capacity (FVC) is the volume of expired air recorded when a person inhales to the total lung capacity and exhales as hard and as completely as possible. The volume of air expired in the first second is called the forced expiratory volume 1 (FEV1).

Given below is a graphical representation of FEV and FEV1:

[[figure-1]]

FVC is reduced in both obstructive and restrictive lung diseases. In obstructive diseases, the slope of FVC is steady, therefore the FEV1 value is low and the FEV1/FVC ratio decreases. In restrictive diseases, the airflow is fast in the beginning leading to a higher value of FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio increases.
question: On performing a pulmonary function test, reduction in FEV1/FVC is characteristic of:

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). It is characterized by an increased residual volume.

According to Uptodate, decreased vital capacity and increased total lung capacity is indicative of hyperinflation seen in COPD. FVC can be used a proxy for VC in normal individuals but in COPD FVC is less than VC due to air trapping, airflow limitation, and small airway collapse.
question: A 66-year-old smoker presented with chronic productive cough and shortness of breath. Physical examination revealed a barrel chest and an expiratory wheeze on auscultation. All of the following findings would be seen in his pulmonary function tests except?

explanationHtml: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of asthma. The diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) tends to be normal or high in these patients.

question: An 8-year-old boy presents with intermittent wheeze and cough. His mother reports that these episodes are precipitated by physical exercise. There is a history of atopic dermatitis in his mother. Pulmonary function tests are performed. Which of the following findings are least likely to be seen in him?

explanationHtml:
Decreased maximum mid-expiratory flow rate (MMFR) is seen in obstruction of small airways.

MMFR is the average expiratory flow rate during the middle 50% of the vital capacity i.e., forced expiratory flow rate between 25 and 75% of the vital capacity.

This is the most sensitive measurement of early airflow obstruction, particularly in small airways.
question: Decreased maximum mid-expiratory flow rate is seen in obstruction of:

Low FEV1 and FVC with a high FEV1/FVC ratio are characteristics of restrictive lung disease. Among the options, pleural effusion is a restrictive lung disease.

    • Asthma
    • COPD
    • Bronchiectasis
    • Bronchiolitis
  • Restrictive lung diseases
    • Intrinsic
      • Interstitial lung disease
    • Extrinsic
      • Myasthenia gravis
      • Kyphoscoliosis
      • Pleural effusion

question: A 76-year-old retired worker from a granite quarry presents with progressive dyspnea and a chronic cough. He has never smoked cigarettes. His chest X-ray is shown below. Which of the following patterns would you see on his pulmonary function tests?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario along with the honeycomb pattern of lung parenchyma due to interstitial fibrosis is suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD). The alveolar-arterial gradient (PAO2-PaO2) is increased in ILD. It is a restrictive lung disease.

In ILD, the alveolar-capillary bed is damaged and thus there is a decrease in diffusion capacity. Therefore, while the PAO2 (Alveolar O2) remains normal, the PaO2 (arterial) decreases, and the alveolar-arterial difference increases.

[[figure-1]]
question: An elderly woman presents with breathlessness on exertion. On auscultation, bilateral basal rales are heard. A chest CT is done and is shown below. Which of the following is likely to be increased in her?

explanationHtml:
Diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO) is decreased in patients with emphysema.

DLCO indicates the effectiveness of gaseous exchange from alveoli to the RBCs.

DLCO is decreased in patients with:

  • Interstitial lung disease
  • Emphysema (DLCO is usually normal in COPD)
  • Bronchiolitis obliterans
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Thromboembolic disease
  • Chronic congestive heart failure

DLCO is increased in patients with:

  • Alveolar hemorrhage

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with shortness of breath and fatigue. She has a medical history of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Her pulmonary function test results are given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?

A normal flow-volume loop begins on the X-axis (Volume axis): at the start of the test, both flow and volume are equal to zero. After the starting point, the curve rapidly mounts to a peak: Peak expiratory flow (PEF).

Then, the PEF the curve descends (=the flow decreases) as more air is expired. A normal, non-pathological F/V loop will descend in a straight or a convex line from the top (PEF) to the bottom (FVC).

The forced inspiration that follows the forced expiration has roughly the same morphology, but the PIF (Peak Inspiratory Flow) is not as distinct as PEF.

question: An elderly man was rushed to the ED with confusion and multiple episodes of vomiting. His wife reported that he had increased frequency of urination and constipation for the past 3 days. The various types of proteinuria are:

  1. Glomerular - increased filtration of proteins due to disruption of basement membrane
  2. Tubular - damage to tubules prevents protein reabsorption in the PCT
  3. Overflow - excess production of low molecular weight proteins such as light chains
  4. Postrenal - infections or stones can lead to secretion of IgA and IgG by the urinary tract

options.text: Proteinuria is always due to glomerular pathology
Albuminuria upto 150 mg/day is considered normal
Proteins are reabsorbed in the DCT

question: Which of the following is true about proteinuria?

explanationHtml:
Non-glomerular proteinuria is characterized by the presence of N-acetyl glucosaminidase (NAG).

This form of proteinuria occurs as a result of tubular injury. N-acetyl glucosaminidase (NAG) is a lysosomal enzyme present in the proximal tubular cells and is released into the urine following any injury to the tubules.

Low-molecular-weight proteins such as β2-microglobulin are normally reabsorbed in the PCT. When there is tubular injury, the proportion of these proteins in urine increases. This lowers the albumin: β2-microglobulin ratio in urine.

In glomerular proteinuria, there is increased filtration of macromolecules like albumin across the glomerular capillary wall. NAG is absent as there is no tubular injury.

Glomerular proteinuria Non-glomerular proteinuria

Type of protein excreted

24 hr protein excretion

RBC casts

 1000:1 10:1

N-acetyl glucosaminidase (NAG)

 Absent Present

question: All of the following findings in a patient are suggestive of non-glomerular proteinuria except:

explanationHtml:
The image shows a hexagonal crystal, suggesting cystine stones. These stones are a recurrent feature in patients with cystinuria.

Crystals in urine are usually associated with kidney stones. Crystals are formed in the urine when the constituent molecules are present in sufficient concentration and the pH is favorable.

Calcium oxalate and uric acid crystals can sometimes be found in normal urine that has been left to stand, due to crystal formation ex vivo.
question: A patient presents with recurrent kidney stones. The microscopic examination of urine is shown below. What is the type of stone seen in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Site of formation is proximal convoluted tubule
explanationHtml:
The sites of formation of casts are the collecting ducts and DCTs (distal convoluted tubules).

Casts are cylindrical structures formed by the aggregation of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein or uromodulin. This protein is secreted in the thick ascending loop of Henle. The casts usually take the shape and size of the lumen of the tubule where they originate.

Factors favoring cast formation:

  • Concentrated urine
  • Low pH
  • Urinary stasis

Casts are the only elements in urine sediments that are specifically of renal origin.

options.text: Width of cast depends on the size of tubule in which it is formed
Casts in urine are specific to kidneys
Site of formation is proximal convoluted tubule
Casts are made up of uromodulin

question: Which of the following is incorrect about casts in urine?

explanationHtml: Muddy-brown granular casts are seen in acute tubular necrosis, a type of intrinsic renal failure. ATN can occur secondary to nephrotoxicity or hypovolemia.
question: A patient with cryptococcal meningitis was started on amphotericin B. Two days later, he is found to have decreased urine output. Urinalysis reveals granular casts. What could be the possible diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Broad casts are associated with a poor prognosis.

They refer to wider waxy casts that are seen in advanced chronic kidney disease. It implies dilation of the tubules.
question: Which of the following casts are associated with a poor prognosis?

correctAnswer: D. Large for gestational age at birth
explanationHtml:
Small for gestational age (SGA) at birth is a risk factor for chronic kidney disease (CKD), not LGA.

Important risk factors for CKD or chronic renal failure are:

  • SGA
  • Childhood obesity
  • Hypertension
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Autoimmune disease
  • Family history of kidney disease
  • Previous episode of acute kidney injury
  • Structural abnormalities of the urinary tract
  • Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease

options.text: Large for gestational age at birth

question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for chronic kidney disease?

explanationHtml:
Diabetic nephropathy is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD).

The leading causes of CKD in decreasing order of frequency are as follows:

  • Diabetic nephropathy
  • Glomerulonephritis
  • Hypertension-associated CKD
  • ADPKD (Adult or autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease)
question: What is the most common cause of chronic kidney disease?

explanationHtml: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is least likely to cause chronic renal failure. It is a rapidly progressive condition and a cause of acute renal failure.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to develop chronic renal failure?

explanationHtml:

question: Which of the following parameters are used in the staging of chronic kidney disease?

explanationHtml:
The features of kidney failure become prominent as the GFR progressively declines to stages 3 and 4. The following complications occur as a result of loss of kidney function:

  • Volume overload
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Hyperphosphatemia
  • Mineral and bone disorders
  • Hypertension
  • Anemia
  • Dyslipidemia

explanationHtml:
Clinical features of uremia start to appear in patients with GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2 or end-stage renal disease (ESRD). By this stage, renal clearance is severely impaired and the accumulation of uremic toxins leads to several complications including:

  • Pruritus
  • Malnutrition
  • Anorexia, nausea, fatigue
  • Platelet dysfunction
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Pericarditis, pleuritis
  • Peripheral neuropathy

question: A 66-year-old woman is being evaluated for new-onset uremic encephalopathy. What is her GFR likely to be?

correctAnswer: D. Can be eliminated by removing urea through intensive dialysis
explanationHtml:
Uremic syndrome cannot be eliminated by removing urea alone. It is a complex condition occurring due to the accumulation of multiple toxins.

The pathophysiology of uremic syndrome involves the following:

  • Accumulation of toxins (uremia) - urea, creatinine, other products of protein metabolism like urates, hippurates, polyamines, indoles.
  • Loss of kidney function leading to fluid and electrolyte imbalance and hormone dysregulation.
  • Progressive systemic inflammation with vascular and nutritional impairment.

Clinical features secondary to loss of kidney function tend to develop in parallel with declining GFR. However the features of uremia and, hence, uremic syndrome, usually occur only in stage 5 or ESRD.
