question:
Match the following:

Disease Gene
1. Medullary cystic kidney disease-1 (MCKD-1) a. UMOD
2. Medullary cystic kidney disease-2 (MCKD 2) b. PKHD1
3. Adolescent nephronophthisis c. MUC1
4. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) d. NPHP2

explanationHtml:
Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive renal cystic disease.

It belongs to a category of conditions called ciliopathies. It occurs due to an underlying defect in the primary cilia of the tubular epithelial cells. The cilia play an important role in cell signaling and maintenance of cell growth, proliferation, and secretion.

Other ciliopathies include autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, and medullary cystic kidney disease.
lessonTitle: Cystic And Inherited Disorders Of The Kidney
question: Which of the following is an autosomal recessive renal cystic disease?

explanationHtml:
The most common inherited cause of kidney failure in childhood is nephronophthisis.

Nephronophthisis (NPHP) refers to a group of related, but genetically distinct, autosomal recessive disorders. Mutations are seen in the NPHP genes 1-20. These genes code for nephrocystins which are expressed on the kidney tubules.

NPHP is classified into infantile, juvenile, and adolescent forms. The juvenile form is the most common form. Common features include tubulointerstitial fibrosis, renal cysts, and chronic kidney disease.
lessonTitle: Cystic And Inherited Disorders Of The Kidney
question: What is the most common inherited cause of  kidney failure in children?

explanationHtml:
Joubert’s syndrome is defined by the presence of juvenile nephronophthisis (NPHP) and multiple neurologic findings.

Some additional examples of multiorgan syndromes linked to nephronophthisis include:

  • Senior-Loken syndrome: characterized by nephronophthisis combined with retinitis pigmentosa.
  • Bardet-Biedl syndrome: involves nephronophthisis along with truncal obesity, cognitive deficits, retinal dystrophy, and polydactyly.
lessonTitle: Cystic And Inherited Disorders Of The Kidney
question: A child with Joubert syndrome will have which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a paintbrush or bouquet of flowers appearance on intravenous pyelography (IVP). It occurs in medullary sponge kidney (MSK).

MSK is a sporadic benign condition that is often diagnosed incidentally. It is a developmental defect affecting the formation of collecting tubules and results in cystic dilatation of the medullary and papillary portions of collecting ducts. It is characterized by medullary cysts that are of variable size. It is associated with distal RTA which leads to hypercalciuria. The hypercalciuria leads to a tendency to form calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones. The patients can also have recurrent UTIs and hematuria.

CT urography has largely replaced intravenous pyelography as the investigation of choice.
lessonTitle: Cystic And Inherited Disorders Of The Kidney
question: The following finding on intravenous pyelography is seen in which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: A. Normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
explanationHtml:
In renal tubular acidosis (RTA), there is normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

RTA refers to a group of disorders in which there is impaired tubular transport of H+ and/or HCO3- despite relatively well-preserved renal function. There are 4 types:

  • Type I - impaired H+ secretion (distal), leading to decreased HCO3- production
  • Type II - impaired HCO3- reabsorption (proximal)
  • Type III - carbonic anhydrase deficiency causing defects in the transport of both H+ and HCO3- (mixed)
  • Type IV - hypoaldosteronism (hyperkalemic)

The overall deficiency of HCO3- in all the types is compensated by Cl- retention to maintain charge neutrality. Hence, the serum anion gap remains normal.

options.text: Normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
High anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
Normal anion gap hypochloremic metabolic acidosis
High anion gap hypochloremic metabolic acidosis.

question: What acid-base disturbance is seen in patients with renal tubular acidosis?

explanationHtml: The most common type of renal tubular acidosis (RTA) is the type 4 or hyperkalemic type.
question: What is the most common type of renal tubular acidosis?

explanationHtml:
Type 4 renal tubular acidosis can be a congenital or acquired disorder.

It is caused by conditions that result in hypoaldosteronism or hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism including:

  • Diabetic nephropathy - most common
  • Tubulointerstitial disease
  • Addison's disease
  • Obstructive uropathy
  • Drugs like NSAIDs, ACEI, ARBs can increase the risk
  • Psuedohypoaldosteronism type 1 (due to aldosterone resistance)
  • Psuedohypoaldosteronism type 2/ gordons syndrome (due to defects in Na-Cl cotransporter)
  • Congenital isolated hypoaldosteronism (due to enzyme deficiency)

options.text: The most common cause is diabetes mellitus
It can occurs in patients with interstitial renal diseases
It is caused by hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism

question: Which of the following is incorrect about type 4 renal tubular acidosis?

explanationHtml:
Hyperkalemia is a characteristic feature of type 4 RTA or generalized distal RTA. It commonly occurs in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).

In CKD patients, renal dysfunction results in hyperkalemia only when the GFR is severely impaired (stage 5). Hyperkalemia in the earlier stages of CKD is suggestive of type 4 RTA.

In CKD, volume overload leads to low levels of renin and, hence, aldosterone. This leads to Na+ loss and K+ retention in the distal tubule. The resultant hyperkalemia causes impaired NH3 synthesis in the proximal tubule. Hence, H+ cannot be excreted as NH4+ ions. Retained H+ ions lead to reduced HCO3- production and acidosis.
question: A 52-year-old man presented with dizziness and infrequent urination. He was diagnosed with stage 4 chronic kidney disease last month.  Investigations reveal metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Urinary pH is < 5.5 after acid loading
explanationHtml:
Urinary pH will be > 5.5 after acid loading in RTA type 1.

In this condition, there is a defect in H+ secretion by the distal tubules. Hence, there is a failure of urine acidification. H+ combines with NH3 to form NH₄⁺ and thus in RTA type 1, NH4+ excretion is reduced. In the acid loading test, acidosis is induced by the administration of NH4Cl (releases H+). In normal individuals, this results in increased excretion of H+, leading to acidic urine (pH < 5.5). However, this fails to occur in RTA type 1.

Impaired secretion of H+ leads to potassium wasting and hypokalemia (via the H+/K+ATPase antiporter). The resulting metabolic acidosis causes bone demineralization and resorption.

options.text: Urinary pH is &lt; 5.5 after acid loading

question: Which of the following would not be seen in patients with type 1 renal tubular acidosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of type 1 RTA. In this condition, calcium phosphate and oxalate stones are formed in the distal convoluting tubules (DCT).

In this condition, there is a defect in H+ secretion by the distal tubules. This leads to:

  • Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • Urinary pH > 5.5
  • Hypokalemia
    • Impaired H+ secretion causes K+ wasting
    • It improves following alkalinization therapy with NaHCO3

Acidemia increases cell citrate utilization which leads to hypocitraturia, hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria. Normally, citrate in the urine binds to calcium and increases its solubility. In the absence of citrate in the urine, calcium begins to precipitate. This leads to nephrocalcinosis and calcium phosphate and oxalate stones.
question:
A 6-month-old infant is being evaluated for failure to thrive. Lab investigations are as follows. Hypokalemia is found to improve following alkalinization therapy. What type of renal stones is this infant at a higher risk of developing?

Investigation Value
Serum sodium 136 mEq/L
Serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Serum pH 7.1
Serum anion gap 11
Urinary pH 6.4

explanationHtml:
Hypertonia is not a feature of Lowe's syndrome or oculo-cerebro-renal syndrome. The following clinical features are seen in this condition:

  • Hypotonia
  • Cataract
  • Glaucoma
  • Intellectual disability
  • Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) type 2
question: Which of the following would you not expect in a patient with Lowe's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Dent's disease is an inherited cause of type 2 RTA. A proximal renal tubular defect is seen in this condition, not a distal tubular defect.

It is an X-linked recessive condition. It is caused by inactivating mutations in CLCN5, a chloride transporter expressed in endosomes of the proximal tubule. The resulting dysfunction of the proximal convoluted tubule and failure of reabsorption of substances leads to:

  • Hypercalciuria
  • Hypophosphatemia
  • Recurrent kidney stones
question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in patients with Dent's disease?

explanationHtml:
Medullary sponge kidney is a cause of RTA type 1, not type 2.

The causes of RTA type 2 include:

  • Amyloidosis
  • Wilson's disease
  • Galactosemia
  • Hereditary fructose intolerance
  • Cystinosis
  • Lowe syndrome
  • Drugs - tenofovir, acetazolamide, topiramate

The causes of RTA type 1 include:

  • Familial defects
  • Autoimmune conditions - SLE, Sjogren syndrome
  • Drugs - amphotericin, lithium, aminoglycosides, ifosfamide
  • Medullary sponge kidney
question: Patients with which of the following are not at risk of developing type 2 renal tubular acidosis?

correctAnswer: C. Renal stones may occur in patients
explanationHtml:
Renal stones are not a feature of type 2 or proximal RTA. This is because high levels of citrate in the urine bind with calcium and prevent stone formation.

In this condition, the cells of the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) fail to reabsorb HCO3-. In the initial stages, this HCO3- loss leads to a urine pH > 5.5. However, as the body's HCO3- stores are depleted, the urinary pH falls to < 5.5 as the secretion of H+ in the DCT remains intact. Hence, the minimum urinary pH is < 5.5.

It can be caused by Lowe's syndrome but a majority of type 2 RTA cases are associated with Fanconi's syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by a generalized defect of reabsorption of various substances at the PCT. This leads to loss of HCO3-, glucose, amino acids, phosphate, citrate, and calcium in the urine. Loss of phosphate leads to vitamin-D resistant hypophosphatemic rickets /osteomalacia.

Note: An exception is Dent's disease, a genetic cause of RTA type 2 in which renal stones are present.

options.text: It can be caused by Lowe's syndrome
Renal stones may occur in patients

question: Which of the following is incorrect about renal tubular acidosis type 2?

explanationHtml:
Pathological fractures and a bone-in-bone appearance point towards a diagnosis of osteopetrosis. The lab values are significant for hypokalemia with normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. These findings are suggestive of renal tubular acidosis (RTA) type 3.

Type 3 RTA is a rare condition that is commonly seen in neonates and infants. It is an autosomal recessive disorder, in which there is a deficiency of carbonic anhydrase-2 (CA-2) enzyme. The pathology is a hybrid of type 1 RTA and type 2 RTA:

  • Failure to reabsorb HCO3 at PCT
  • Failure to excrete H+ at DCT

This results in the following findings:

  • Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
  • Hypokalemia
  • Urinary pH > 5.5
  • Positive urine anion gap

CA-2 enzyme deficiency occurs due to a loss of function mutation in the gene encoding it. It leads to a condition called the marble bone disease presenting with the following clinical findings:

  • Cerebral calcifications
  • Mental retardation
  • Type 3 RTA
  • Osteopetrosis
question:
A 14-month-old baby was brought with complaints of refusal to walk after a minor fall while playing. Imaging revealed a left tibial fracture along with generalized sclerosis and a bone-in-bone appearance. Additionally, his developmental milestones were found to be delayed. Investigations are as follows. What is the likely renal tubular defect present in this patient?

Serum sodium - 137 mEq/L

Serum potassium - 2.9 mEq/L

Serum pH - 7.1

Serum bicarbonate - 15 mEq/L

Serum anion gap - 9

Urine pH - 5.7

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario with hypertension and metabolic alkalosis is suggestive of Liddle's syndrome.

It is an autosomal dominant condition due to a gain of function mutation in the ENaC gene. This gene codes for the epithelial sodium channels present in the kidney. This leads to increased sodium retention and results in a state of pseudo-hyperaldosteronism. The following findings are seen:

  • Hypertension
  • Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Normal-low aldosterone
  • Low renin

Treatment is with diuretics that directly block the ENaC channels, like amiloride and triamterene. Spironolactone is not effective as it is an aldosterone-receptor antagonist.
question: A 30-year-old man is being evaluated for high blood pressure noted on multiple occasions. Investigations reveal metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin levels, and high urine chloride levels. What is the likely cause?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of Bartter syndrome. It occurs due to a defect in the Na+/K+/Cl- channel in the thick ascending loop of Henle.

A defect in the Na+/K+/Cl- channel impairs the transport functions of the thick ascending loop of Henle. It results in the following features:

  • Polyuria and polydipsia
  • Natriuresis with high aldosterone (due to RAAS activation)
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypocalcemia and hypercalciuria

The clinical features of this condition are similar to the effects of loop diuretics. These drugs also act on the Na+/K+/Cl- channel. Hence, response to loop diuretics may be blunted. Treatment is with potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone and amiloride. NSAID's like indomethacin are second line drugs however they can reduce renal function.

Option A: Defect in the proximal tubule results in Fanconi's syndrome. These patients have acidosis, with glycosuria, generalized aminoaciduria, and phosphaturia.

Option B: Defect in the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in distal convoluted tubule (DCT) results in Gitelman syndrome. These patients also present with hypokalemic alkalosis and hypomagnesemia. However, they also develop, hypocalciuria, and chondrocalcinosis.

Option D: Increased activation of the epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) channels results in Liddle syndrome. This causes increased reabsorption of Na+ exchanged for K+ causing hypokalemia. Increased Na absorption leads to hypertension.
question: A young patient presented with polyuria and polydipsia. His BP is 130/80 mm Hg. Laboratory parameters revealed serum K+ of 3.2 mmol/L, blood pH of 7.46, and hypomagnesemia. Urinary calcium was elevated. He is not on any medications. This condition is likely due to a defect in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Chvostek's sign (spasm of facial muscles on tapping the facial nerve) indicates tetany. In this patient with hypercalcemia, it is likely due to hypomagnesemia. These clinical features are suggestive of Gitelman syndrome.

This condition occurs due to a mutation of Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal collecting tubule (DCT). The resulting impairment of the tubular transport leads to the following features:

  • Mild natriuresis with normal-low BP
  • Increased renin and aldosterone
  • Hypokalemia
  • Metabolic alkalosis
  • Hypercalcemia and hypocalciuria
  • Hypomagnesemia

The clinical features of this condition are similar to the effects of thiazide diuretics. These drugs also act on the Na+/Cl- cotransporter. Hence, response to thiazide diuretics may be blunted. Treatment is with potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone and amiloride.

Option A: Bartter syndrome affects the Na+/K+/Cl- channels. It causes hypocalcemia and hypercalciuria.

Option C: Liddle syndrome causes increased activation of ENaC channels. It results in hypokalemia and hypertension.

Option D: Fanconi's syndrome occurs due to a defect in proximal tubular function. It results in metabolic acidosis.
question: A 17-year-old boy is being evaluated for fatigue and muscle weakness for 3 months. On examination, Chvostek's sign is positive and BP is 90/60 mm Hg. Investigations show hypokalemia and hypercalcemia with metabolic alkalosis. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Most common cause in elderly is renal cell carcinoma
explanationHtml:
The most common cause of renal vein thrombosis in the elderly is renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

The most common causes of renal vein thrombosis in different age groups are as follows:

  • Children - Dehydration, followed by sepsis
  • Adults - Nephrotic syndrome (most commonly membranous glomerulonephritis)
  • Elderly - Renal cell carcinoma

The left renal vein is more commonly involved and 2/3rd of cases are bilateral. Doppler USG is used for screening but the investigation of choice is CT angiography.

options.text: Right renal vein is more commonly involved
Most common cause in children is nephrotic syndrome
Investigation of choice is doppler ultrasound of renal vein
Most common cause in elderly is renal cell carcinoma

question: Which of the following is true regarding renal vein thrombosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of renal vein thrombosis secondary to dehydration.

Hematuria in children following diarrhea can be due to the following:

Hemolytic uremic syndrome Renal vein thrombosis
Onset 5-10 days after diarrhea Depends on severity of dehydration
Renal failure Present Present
Hematuria + +
Peripheral smear fragmented RBCs + +
Platelets Decreased Decreased
USG kidney Normal Enlarged due to congestion by renal vein thrombosis (bilateral in 67% cases)

Henoch-Schonlein purpura would present 1-3 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. It causes hematuria, non-blanching rash over the buttocks, and abdominal pain.
question: A 10-year-old child develops hematuria after 4 days of severe diarrhea. Peripheral smear shows fragmented RBCs and thrombocytopenia. Ultrasound reveals the enlargement of both kidneys. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) globally is Escherichia coli O157:H7.

The causes of HUS are as follows:

  • Infections: Usually occur 5-10 days after diarrheal diseases due to bacterial exotoxins.
    • E.coli O157:H7 - Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin)
    • Shigella dysenteriae type I - Shiga toxin
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Autoimmunity
  • Complement activation (in atypical HUS)
question: What is the most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome globally?

correctAnswer: D. Coomb's positive hemolytic anemia is seen in HUS
explanationHtml:
The hemolytic anemia in hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) occurs as a result of mechanical RBC destruction caused by microthrombi. Hence, Coomb's test is negative.

There are two types of HUS, namely typical and atypical.

Typical HUS Atypical HUS
  • 5-10 days after diarrheal illness
  • E.coli O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae type I
  • Mutation in genes encoding complement regulatory protein
  • Shiga-like toxins produced cause endothelial damage.
  • This leads to platelet activation and thrombi.
  • Uncontrolled activation of the complement system
  • No specific treatment
  • Supportive management of renal failure
  • Plasma exchange to replace the deficient proteins
  • Eculizumab, a C5 inhibitor

options.text: Symptoms and signs of HUS develops as diarrhea begins to improve
Only supportive managment of acute renal failure is done in typical HUS
Eculizumab improves microangiopathic hemolytic anemia in atypical HUS
Coomb's positive hemolytic anemia is seen in HUS

question: Which of the following is false about hemolytic uremic syndrome?

correctAnswer: D. Mainstay of treatment is blood transfusion
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and image showing schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) in a woman are suggestive of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Blood transfusion is not preferred in TTP as it can aggravate the condition.

TTP is a type of thrombotic microangiopathy that occurs due to deficiency or autoantibodies against the ADAMTS13 metalloprotease, which is responsible for cleaving von Willebrand factor multimers. In the absence of this protein, vWF multimers aggregate and form thrombi. It presents with a classical pentad of clinical features:

  1. Fever
  2. Thrombocytopenia
  3. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
  4. Renal failure
  5. Neurological manifestations

It is treated with plasmapheresis and rituximab.

options.text: It is caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency
20% patients will have falsely positive RA factor
Arrhythmias are a frequent cause of death
Mainstay of treatment is blood transfusion

question:
A 56-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset headache and photophobia. On examination, she is disoriented and febrile. The investigations and peripheral smear are given below. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this disease?

Hemoglobin - 11.2 g/dl

Platelet count - 32,000/uL

Serum creatinine - 3.9 mg/dl

Blood urea nitrogen - 38 mg/dl

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of clinically significant renal artery stenosis is atherosclerosis.

Renal artery stenosis is a relatively common finding in older patients with chronic essential hypertension. However, it is considered clinically significant only when renovascular hypertension develops. It occurs in the case of:

  • > 70% stenosis in both renal arteries
  • > 50% stenosis with post stenotic dilatation

The causes of renal artery stenosis are:

  • Atherosclerosis (most frequent): typically occurs in older individuals having cardiovascular risk factors.
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia: usually affects young white women and often involves both sides.
  • Less common causes include:
    • Thromboemboli
    • External compression by tumors
    • Systemic vasculitis
    • Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
    • Transplant renal artery stenosis
    • Infrarenal aortic aneurysms and dissections

The investigation of choice for renal artery stenosis is renal angiography.
question: What is the most common cause of clinically significant renal artery stenosis?

correctAnswer: C. Most commonly affected peripheral artery is subclavian artery
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario and the string of beads appearance on CT angiography is characteristic of fibromuscular dysplasia. The most common peripheral (limb) arteries affected are the iliac arteries.

Fibromuscular dysplasia is a segmental, non-atheromatous, dysplastic type of angiopathy that predominantly affects females. The most common subtype is medial fibroplasia. It is one of the major causes of renovascular hypertension. The most common sites of involvement in decreasing order of frequency are as follows:

  1. Renal arteries
  2. Carotid arteries
  3. Peripheral (limb) arteries - most commonly iliac arteries

On angiography, a string of beads appearance is seen as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: String of beads appearance on angiography
Most commonly affected peripheral artery is subclavian artery

question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about fibromuscular dysplasia?

explanationHtml:
Atheroembolic kidney disease is associated with decreased complement levels.

Atheroembolic kidney disease is more frequent in males with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease. Most clinical atheroembolic events follow angiographic procedures, often of the coronary vessels.

It is associated with aortic aneurysms and renal artery stenosis. Systemic embolic manifestations such as fever, abdominal pain, and weight loss are also present, although cutaneous manifestations are more common like livedo reticularis and localized toe gangrene.

The lab findings include:

  • Rising serum creatinine
  • Transient eosinophilia
  • Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate
  • Hypocomplementemia

Definitive diagnosis depends on kidney biopsy which demonstrates microvessel occlusion with cholesterol crystals that leave a cleft in the vessel as shown below.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following is unlikely in patients with atheroembolic kidney disease?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of renal artery stenosis. Renal intra-arterial angiography is the gold standard for diagnosis.In a patient with hypertension and increased creatinine, an ultrasound of the abdomen must be performed first to visualize the renal size and morphology to look for a unilateral shrunken kidney and thereby renal artery stenosis.

Option A: MR angiography is less preferred as gadolinium contrast can lead to nephrogenic fibrosis, particularly in patients with reduced kidney function.

Option C: CT scan with image reconstruction provides an excellent image but also carries a risk of contrast nephropathy.

Option D: Renal arterial doppler ultrasound measures renal artery velocities and can predict hemodynamically important lesions. However, it is not the gold standard test. Duplex ultrasonography is used as a screening investigation.
question: A 50-year-old patient is being evaluated for uncontrolled hypertension despite being on 3 antihypertensive drugs. He has a history of myocardial infarction which was managed with percutaneous intervention last month. On examination, an abdominal bruit is noted. Lab values indicate elevated serum urea and creatinine. Which of the following investigations is the gold standard test to diagnose this condition?

explanationHtml:
ACE inhibitors must be avoided in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (RAS).

In renal artery stenosis, blood flow to the kidney is reduced, thereby reducing blood flow to the afferent arterioles. Hence, constriction of efferent arterioles is needed to maintain hydrostatic pressure within the glomerulus in order to maintain GFR.

ACEIs and ARBs inhibit efferent renal arteriolar vasoconstriction. In bilateral RAS, this causes a decline in the GFR within a few days of starting the drug.

Note: Bilateral renal artery stenosis has been classically considered as an absolute contraindication to the use of ACE inhibitors. However, new studies show that they may be used in some cases with careful monitoring.
question: Which of the following drugs must be avoided in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis?

explanationHtml:
The "a" wave in jugular venous pressure (JVP) is a positive wave, which corresponds to right atrial contraction.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

  • a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
  • c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
  • x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
  • v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
  • y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

[[figure-1]]
question: 'a' wave in JVP corresponds to?

correctAnswer: A. Bulging of tricuspid valve into the right atrium
explanationHtml:
The c-wave in a JVP waveform represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.

JVP measured in the internal jugular vein is a reflection of the right atrial pressure.

The waveforms seen in a normal JVP are:

  • a wave corresponds to atrial contraction and occurs just after the P wave (on ECG) and just before the first heart sound.
  • c wave represents the bulging of the tricuspid valve into the right atrium during ventricular systole.
  • x descent corresponds to the atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.
  • v wave represents atrial filling during ventricular systole and peaks at the second heart sound.
  • y descent represents passive emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle after tricuspid valve opening.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Bulging of tricuspid valve into the right atrium
Venous filling of the right atrium
Emptying of the right atrium into the right ventricle

question: The c wave seen in a normal JVP waveform represents?

explanationHtml:
The given waveform shows a cannon ‘a’ wave seen in ventricular tachycardia. It occurs since atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve in ventricular tachycardia.

JVP measured in the internal jugular vein is a reflection of the right atrial pressure.

Note: Giant/prominent a-waves occur during every beat while cannon a-waves result from arrhythmias, therefore, are usually intermittent. The ECG is helpful to look for rhythm disturbances that are associated with cannon a-waves whereas echocardiography can be used to assess structural defects (of right atrium) that are associated with giant a-waves.

[[figure-1]]
question: The following abnormality on a JVP waveform can be seen in which of the given conditions?

explanationHtml:
Hypotension, soft or absent heart sounds, and jugular venous distention (Beck’s triad) are the three principal features of cardiac tamponade. The typical JVP finding here is absent y-descent.

JVP is usually raised, and the waveform shows a prominent x (early systolic) descent and an absent y (early diastolic) descent because of the ventricle's limited or absent early diastolic filling.

There may be reductions in the amplitude of the QRS complexes and electrical alternans of the P, QRS, or T waves in cardiac tamponade.

Note: Alternation of QRS complexes, usually in a 2:1 ratio, on ECG is called electrical alternans. It is caused by the movement of the heart in the pericardial space. Electrical alternans is also seen in patients with myocardial ischemia, acute pulmonary embolism, and tachyarrhythmias.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 37-year-old male patient comes to the clinic with complaints of weakness, restlessness, and chest pain. On examination, his blood pressure is found to be 90/60 mmHg, his heart sounds are muffled, and his neck veins are distended. What is the typical JVP finding in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The y-descent in jugular venous pulse (JVP) corresponds to the fall in right atrial pressure after the tricuspid valve opening in the early diastolic phase of the right ventricle. Y-descent is attenuated or absent in cardiac tamponade because of resistance to ventricular filling in the early diastole.

Other options:

Options B and C: Restrictive cardiomyopathy and constrictive pericarditis can have deep y descent due to rapid filling of the right ventricle during early diastole.

Option D: In patients with tricuspid regurgitation, increased blood flow to the right atria through the incompetent tricuspid valve during ventricular systole results in a prominent v wave. When the tricuspid valve opens during ventricular diastole, this increased blood in the right atria enters rapidly into the right ventricle during early diastole resulting in deep y-descent.
question: Deep y descent in JVP is seen in all except:

explanationHtml:
Orthostatic hypotension is a sustained reduction within 3 min of standing or head tilt test in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg.

On standing, blood is displaced to the lower extremities, causing a drop in the venous return to the heart. This drop leads to a decrease in cardiac output and stimulation of compensatory mechanisms which trigger a reflex increase in sympathetic (vasoconstrictor) outflow. Orthostatic hypotension is a manifestation of sympathetic (autonomic) failure.

Manifestations consist of giddiness, dizziness, and near-syncope (almost fainting) triggered by abrupt changes in posture.

explanationHtml:
Pulsus bisferiens is seen in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not pulsus paradoxus.

Pulsus paradoxus refers to the fall in systolic pressure by > 10 mmHg with inspiration. It is an exaggeration of the normal response. It is seen in the following conditions:

  • Cardiac tamponade
  • Massive pulmonary embolism
  • Hemorrhagic shock
  • Obstructive lung disease
  • Tension pneumothorax
question: Pulsus paradoxus is seen in all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
Pulsus alternans (characterized by alternating strong and weak beats) is seen in left ventricular dysfunction.

Pulsus bisferiens is a bifid pulse with two systolic peaks. It is seen in the following conditions:

  • Advanced aortic regurgitation (AR)
  • Aortic stenosis (AS) with AR
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

[[figure-1]]
question: Pulsus bisferiens is seen in all of the following conditions except:

explanationHtml:
Water hammer pulse, also known as Corrigan’s pulse, is characterized by a sharp rise and a rapid fall-off and is seen in aortic regurgitation (AR) due to the fact that arterial pressure falls rapidly in late systole and early diastole.

In AR, the pulse pressure is widened due to systolic hypertension and decreased diastolic pressure. The diastolic pressure is measured at Korotkoff phase IV. In certain patients with AR or a combination of aortic stenosis (AS) and AR, the carotid arterial pulse may exhibit a bisferiens pattern, characterized by two systolic waves separated by a trough.

The apical impulse is heaving and displaced inferiorly. A diastolic thrill may be palpable along the left sternal border.

A2 is usually absent in AR. An early diastolic murmur can be auscultated in chronic AR. It is best heard in the third intercostal space along the left sternal edge.

[[figure-1]]

Severe AS (Option A) would show pulsus parvus et tardus, characterized by the carotid pulse rising slowly to a delayed peak.

Chronic mitral regurgitation (Option D) shows a sharp, low volume upstroke due to reduced cardiac output and acute mitral regurgitation demonstrates narrow pulse pressure.
question: Water hammer pulse is seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Rheumatic mitral stenosis is associated with loud S1.

The greater the distance the valve travels to close, the louder is the sound. Increased left atrial pressures in rheumatic mitral stenosis force the mobile portion of the mitral valve leaflets far apart such that they are forced closed from a relatively far distance, resulting in a loud S1. In calcific mitral stenosis, leaflet mobility is poor, and they are not separated by a large distance, resulting in a soft S1.

Loud S1 is heard in the following:

  • Short PR intervals
  • Early stages of mitral stenosis as long as the valves are pliable
  • Atrial myxoma
  • High output states
  • Tachycardia

Soft S1 is heard in the following:

  • Mitral regurgitation
  • Aortic regurgitation
  • Long PR intervals
  • Calcified Mitral stenosis
  • Left ventricular contractile dysfunction
  • Beta-receptor blockers
  • Due to decreased conduction of sound waves through the chest wall as seen in:
    • Pericardial effusion
    • Obesity
    • COPD
question: A loud S1 is associated with?

explanationHtml:
Reversed (or paradoxical) splitting refers to the situation when P2 is heard before A2. This is seen in the following:

  • LBBB
  • HOCM
  • Right ventricular pacing
  • Severe AS
  • Acute myocardial ischemia
question: A hypertensive patient presented with chest pain and was found to have dilated cardiomyopathy on an echocardiogram. On auscultation, a reversed splitting of second heart sound was heard. Which of the following could most likely be responsible for the same?

explanationHtml:
Loud S1 is heard in mild mitral stenosis (MS).

The intensity of S1 depends on the distance over which the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve moves, leaflet mobility, LV contractility, and PR interval. It is independent of the severity of MS.

Loud S1 is seen in early rheumatic MS, short PR interval, and hyperdynamic circulatory states.

S1 becomes soft in case of calcified leaflets, long PR interval, associated aortic regurgitation and LV dysfunction.
question: Disappearance of loud S1 in mitral stenosis occurs in all except:

explanationHtml:
A wide split of S2 is not seen in the left bundle branch block (LBBB), however paradoxical splitting is seen.

S2 is normally heard as A2-P2. This split is exaggerated in conditions that cause early aortic valve closure or delayed pulmonary valve closure.

Option A: In atrial septal defect (ASD), left ventricle (LV) ejection time decreases due to the shunting of the blood from the left atrium (LA) to the right atrium leading to early aortic valve closure.

Option B: In mitral regurgitation (MR), due to the regurgitation of blood from the LV to the LA, the LV ejection time decreases leading to early aortic valve closure.

Option C: In pulmonary stenosis (PS), the delayed closure of pulmonary valves leads to the splitting of S2.

Wide splitting of S2 is also heard in RBBB and LV pacing.
question: While examining a patient, you hear a widely split S2 on auscultation. Which of the following is not a possible diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Fixed wide splitting of S2 is seen in atrial septal defect (ASD).

The ASD creates a left to right shunt that increases the blood flow to the right side of the heart. This causes the pulmonary valve to close later than the aortic valve independent of inspiration/expiration.
question: Which of the following conditions is associated with a fixed wide splitting of S2?

correctAnswer: C. S4 is heard during the ventricular-filling phase
explanationHtml:
S4 is heard during the ventricular-filling phase.

S3 and S4 are diastolic sounds that are low pitched, and best heard with the bell of the stethoscope at the cardiac apex in the left lateral decubitus position.

S3 - Ventricular gallop S4 - Atrial gallop


Occurs during early ventricular diastole

Occurs near the end of ventricular diastole

During the first rapid ventricular filling

 During active ventricular filling (filling by atrial contraction)

Due to a sudden rush of blood entering a volume-depleted ventricle (normal ventricular compliance)

Due to vibration of the ventricular wall during atrial contraction because of increased stiffness of ventricular walls (decreased ventricular compliance)
It can be physiological in children and young adults. Always pathological
In older patients, it indicates systolic heart failure Indicates diastolic heart failure

The presence of an S3 and S4 heart sound is called a summation gallop and sounds like a galloping horse.

options.text: S3 and S4 are high pitched systolic sounds
S4 is heard during the ventricular-filling phase
S3 occurs due to rapid filling of the ventricles during atrial systole

question: Which of the following statements is true?

correctAnswer: A. The split increases with inspiration
explanationHtml:
In a patient with a right bundle branch block (RBBB), there's a widely split S1 which increases with inspiration.

S1 is normally heard as a single sound. Any delay in the closure of the tricuspid valve or early closure of the mitral valve produces a split in S1. During inspiration, venous return to the right atrium increases. Therefore, the atria take a longer time to empty into the ventricles delaying the closure of the tricuspid valve. This increases the split in S1 during inspiration. In a patient with an RBBB, the tricuspid valve closure is further delayed leading to a wide split in S1.

options.text: The split remains constant with inspiration and expiration
The change in split depends on the degree of bundle branch block

question: An ECG of a patient who underwent pulmonary artery catheterization showed a right bundle branch block. On auscultation, a widely split S1 was observed. Which of the following is true regarding this auscultatory finding?

explanationHtml:
The probable diagnosis of the above scenario is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS).

EDS is a group of clinically and genetically heterogeneous connective tissue disorders. Typical presenting features include joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility. EDS type 6 is also characterized by scoliosis. Gorlin’s sign refers to the ability of patients of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome to touch the tip of the nose with the tip of their tongue.

Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is a frequent finding in patients with EDS. An early systolic click which may be followed by a late systolic murmur is the auscultatory finding heard in MVP.
question: A 23-year-old woman presents with a history of occasional palpitations. She has no history of chest pain or dyspnea. On examination, blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, the pulse is 82/min and regular. Joint hypermobility and thoracolumbar scoliosis are present. Gorlin's sign is positive. On auscultation, a click is heard after S1, followed by a late systolic murmur.  What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The ejection click is a systolic sound.

Ejection clicks are high-pitched sounds that occur at the moment of the maximal opening of the aortic or pulmonary valves. They are heard just after the first heart sound.

Ejection clicks occur in:

  • Non-calcific aortic or pulmonary stenosis
  • Aortic or pulmonary root dilatation
  • Congenital bicuspid aortic or pulmonary valves

Nonejection clicks, which occur after the onset of the carotid upstroke, are related to the mitral valve prolapse.
question: Which of the following is not a diastolic sound?

explanationHtml:
A murmur occurring between S1 and S2 is a systolic murmur. Pulmonary regurgitation produces a diastolic murmur.

The causes of systolic murmurs are as follows:

  • Mid-systolic- aortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, ASD, HOCM.
  • Holosystolic/pansystolic- mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation, VSD.
  • Late systolic- mitral valve prolapse.

The causes of diastolic murmurs are as follows:

  • Early diastolic- aortic regurgitation, pulmonic regurgitation.
  • Mid/late diastolic- mitral stenosis, tricuspid stenosis, Austin-Flint.

The causes of continuous murmurs are as follows:

  • Patent ductus arteriosus (machinery or Gibson's murmur).
  • Venous hum
  • AV fistula
  • Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
question: On auscultation of a patient, you hear a murmur between S1 and S2. Which of the following conditions is not likely to be associated with this finding?

explanationHtml:
A mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation and an opening snap is typically seen in mitral stenosis.

The presystolic accentuation is due to the atrial contraction forcing blood through the stenosed mitral valve. The presystolic accentuation disappears in atrial fibrillation.

Option A: Mitral regurgitation presents with a holosystolic murmur, best heard at the apex with radiation to the left axilla.

Option B: Mitral valve prolapse presents with an early systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is heard.

Option C: Aortic stenosis presents with a harsh crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border, with radiation of the murmur to the carotid arteries.
question: While examining a patient, you hear a mid-diastolic murmur with presystolic accentuation on auscultation of the precordium. Which of the following condition is associated with this finding?

explanationHtml:
The above image shows the Valsalva maneuver. The murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) increases in intensity while performing the Valsalva maneuver.

The murmurs produced by TR (tricuspid regurgitation), AS (aortic stenosis), and MR (mitral regurgitation) decrease in intensity while performing the Valsalva maneuver.

Note: Valsalva maneuver decreases the intensity of all murmurs except MVP (mitral valve prolapse) and HCM.
question: You are a part of a health camp conducting check-ups for cardiovascular ailments. On auscultation of a patient's precordial area, you hear a systolic murmur. On asking the patient to perform the following maneuver, the intensity of the murmur increased. Which of the following conditions is associated with this finding?

explanationHtml:
The above image shows a sustained handgrip maneuver. The murmur of aortic stenosis decreases in intensity during sustained handgrip.

Maneuvers like sustained handgrip, simultaneous inflation of blood pressure cuffs above the systolic in both upper limbs, and infusion of vasopressors increase the systemic vascular resistance (afterload). Since increasing afterload will prevent blood from flowing in a normal forward path, it will increase any murmurs that are due to backward flowing blood and decresase the ones due to forward blood flow.

Murmurs that increase in intensity on sustained handgrip:

  • Mitral regurgitation
  • Ventricular septal defect
  • Aortic regurgitation

Murmurs that decrease in intensity on sustained handgrip:

  • Aortic stenosis
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
question: While auscultating a patient's precordium, a murmur was heard that decreased in intensity on performing the following sustained maneuver. Which of the given condition is associated with this finding?

explanationHtml:
The murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HOCM) increases with standing, as there is a reduction in preload. In conditions of reduced preload, there is lesser end diastolic volume in the left ventricle, leading to a narrower outflow tract, and a louder murmur is heard.

The murmur heard in HOCM is a mid-systolic murmur, which is loudest along the left sternal border. It increases in conditions of decreased preload and afterload (standing, valsalva, vagal maneuvers) or conditions of increased contractility (inotropic stimulation) and decreases when preload and afterload are increased (squatting, vasopressors).

Most murmurs decrease in intensity with reduced preload and afterload except HOCM and mitral valve prolapse (MVP).
question: Which of the following murmur increases on standing?

correctAnswer: A. Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation
explanationHtml:
The murmur described above is a continuous murmur.

A continuous murmur is produced when there is a pressure gradient between the cardiac chambers or the blood vessels throughout the systole and diastole. Continous murmurs are characterised by the flow of blood in the same direction and through the same channel during systole and diastole. These murmurs begin in systole, envelope the second heart sound (S2), and continue through some portion of diastole.

Conditions producing a continuous murmur:

  • Patent ductus arteriosus
  • Venous hum
  • AV fistula
  • Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm

Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation does not produce a continuous murmur. It produces a systolic-diastolic murmur as the blood flows through different channels during systole and diastole. These murmurs do not envelope S2.

options.text: Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation

question: A child was being evaluated for an underlying cardiac defect. On auscultation, a murmur was heard which began in systole, enveloped the second heart sound, and continued through some portion of the diastole. Which of the following condition is not associated with this finding?

correctAnswer: B. It is seen in aortic stenosis
explanationHtml: The Gallavardin effect refers to the phenomenon of the transmission of the mid-systolic murmur of aortic stenosis to the apex where it becomes higher pitched.

options.text: It is associated with a diastolic murmur
It is seen in aortic stenosis
It refers to the radiation of murmur to the carotids
The transmission makes the murmur low pitched

question: Which of the following is true about Gallavardin effect?

explanationHtml: A holosystolic murmur that is best heard over the lower left sternal border and radiating to the epigastrium most likely arises from tricuspid regurgitation.
question: A patient presents with easy fatiguability and shortness of breath on moderate physical activity. On auscultation, a holosystolic murmur is heard over the lower left sternal border and radiating to the epigastrium. Which of the following condition is most likely to be associated with this finding?

correctAnswer: C. It is a mid-systolic murmur
explanationHtml:
Still’s murmur is a mid-systolic murmur.

It is heard at the left sternal border in normal children and adolescents. It is a grade 2 murmur and is best heard in the supine position.

options.text: It is heard in mitral regurgitation
It is best heard in left lateral decubitus position

question: Which of the following is true about Still’s murmur?

explanationHtml:
Graham Steell murmur is the early to mid-diastolic murmur heard in pulmonary regurgitation.

It is best heard in 2nd left intercostal space and radiates along left sternal border. It can increase with inspiration.
question: Graham Steell murmur is heard in?

explanationHtml:
Carey Coombs murmur is heard in mitral valvulitis.

It is a mid-diastolic murmur heard during an episode of acute rheumatic fever causing mitral valvulitis.

It is produced due to the flow of blood through an edematous mitral valve and dissipates with the resolution of the acute attack.
question: Carey Coombs murmur is heard in?

explanationHtml:
Austin-Flint murmur is a low-pitched mid to late diastolic murmur of chronic severe AR.

It results from the turbulence at the mitral inflow area from the mixture of regurgitant and forward blood flow. It is best heard at the apex.

Austin-Flint murmur is often confused with the murmur of mitral stenosis. This can be differentiated based on the following:

Features Chronic AR MS
Opening snap Absent Present

Effect of vasodilator administration

Murmur becomes shorter and softer.

Mechanism- Fall in the diastolic pressure gradient between the aorta and left ventricle.

Murmur remains constant or increases in intensity.

Mechanism- Reflex increase in cardiac output and mitral valve flow.
question: Austin-Flint murmur is associated with which of the following conditions?

correctAnswer: A. ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario of transient loss of consciousness in this patient is suggestive of syncope. Hence, an ECG must be done to rule out cardiac causes for syncope like - arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, sinus node dysfunction, supra ventricular tachycardias) or a structural cardiac abnormality.

A CT would only be required if a seizure or transient ischemic attack (TIA) is suspected. However, in this case - the episode only lasted for a few seconds, the patient has no history of similar episodes in the past and there are no lasting neurological deficits after the episode. Therefore, option B is incorrect.

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness caused by global cerebral hypoperfusion. It can be due to multiple causes, but is broadly divided into - neurally mediated syncope, orthostatic hypotension and cardiac syncope.

The initial workup for a case of syncope includes:

  1. Detailed history of the episode and past history of similar episodes
  2. Physical examination mainly to check BP in standing and supine positions to
  3. rule out orthostatic hypotension.
  4. A resting ECG to look for cardiac arrhythmia
  5. Option B: If the ECG is normal, no further tests are needed. If the ECG is suggestive of cardiac arrhythmia, then further tests including continuous ECG monitoring and electrophysiological studies may be done.

Option C: Tilt-table testing is done in patients with recurrent syncopal attacks who are suspected to have vasovagal syncope. Psychiatric evaluation is done in patients with recurrent unexplained syncopal attacks.

Option D: Vestibular neuritis is associated with vertigo, where the patients typically complain of dizziness and a sense of spinning of the head.

options.text: ECG to rule out atrial fibrillation
If ECG is normal, CT scan should be done
Vestibular neuritis is a possible condition that can cause these symptoms

question: A 60-year-old man presented with an episode of acute onset dizziness and loss of consciousness which lasted for a few seconds followed by a regain of full consciousness. There were no similar episodes in the past. Which of the following is a true statement regarding this scenario?

explanationHtml: The T wave in ECG is due to ventricular repolarisation.
question: Which electrophysiological activity is responsible for the T wave in ECG?

explanationHtml:
The normal duration of the PR interval is 0.12-0.2 seconds (3 to 5 small boxes).

PR interval is said to be prolonged if it is > 0.2 seconds and short if it is < 0.12 seconds.

It is measured from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex. It represents the time from the start of atrial depolarization to the start of ventricular depolarization.

[[figure-1]]
question:
The PR intervals obtained from the ECG recording of 4 patients are given below. Which of the following patients has a normal PR interval?

Patient 1- 0.19s

Patient 2- 0.3s

Patient 3- 0.23s

Patient 4- 0.1s

explanationHtml:
The normal duration of the QRS interval is normally 0.1-0.11 seconds (less than 3 small boxes).

QRS interval represents the duration of ventricular depolarization. When the QRS complex is > 0.11 seconds, it is called a wide QRS complex. It can occur in:

  • Bundle branch blocks (RBBB or LBBB)
  • Depolarizations originating in the ventricles
  • Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
  • Hyperkalaemia
question: What is the normal QRS interval?

explanationHtml:
As all the waves (P, QRS, T) are negative in the given ECG, it should be lead aVR. All the depolarisations waves (P, QRS, T) move away from lead aVR in the normal sinus.

Depolarisation wave moving towards the positive pole of the lead (or active electrode) produces a positive deflection in the ECG and depolarization moving away from the positive pole of the lead produces a negative deflection in the ECG.

The lead aVR provides information from the right upper side of the heart.

[[figure-1]]

The given image shows a normal 12 lead ECG:

[[figure-2]]
question: Which lead does the given ECG tracing represent in a normal ECG?

explanationHtml:
In a normal ECG, a biphasic P wave is seen in lead V1 only.

Lead V1 is a chest lead. So, it records potentials in the horizontal plane. The P wave in lead V1 consists of:

  • Positive component corresponding to right atrial depolarization
  • Negative component corresponding to left atrial depolarization

[[figure-1]]
question: In a normal ECG obtained from a patient, a biphasic P wave may be seen in which of the following lead(s)?

explanationHtml:
Lead aVF would show the maximum R wave with the cardiac axis as +90 degrees.

The cardiac axis represents the mean QRS axis (direction of the mean depolarisation vector). The position of lead aVF is at +90 degrees. If the cardiac axis is also at +90 degrees, it would be in the same direction as lead aVF, and hence aVF would show maximum R wave amplitude.

The normal adult QRS axis is directed downward and to the left, which is between -30 degrees and +100 degrees. Axis deviation can be calculated as:

  • Left-axis deviation: Lies between -30 degrees and -90 degrees
  • Right-axis deviation: More positive than +90 to +100 degrees
  • Extreme axis deviation: Lies between -90 and +180 degrees

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following leads would show maximum R wave with the cardiac axis as +90 degrees?

explanationHtml:
Pseudo P pulmonale refers to tall peaked P waves seen in hypokalemia.
P-pulmonale refers to P waves taller than >2.5mm in an ECG lead.

[[figure-1]]

Hypocalcemia (Option C) prolongs the QT interval.

Hypercalcemia (Option D) shortens the QT interval.
question: Pseudo P pulmonale is seen in which electrolyte abnormality?

correctAnswer: D. Prolonged QT interval with flat T waves
explanationHtml:
Prolonged QT interval with flat T waves is seen in hypokalemia.

Hypokalemia prolongs ventricular repolarization. The ECG changes seen are as follows:

  • Flattening of T wave
  • ST-segment depression
  • Prolongation of QT interval
  • The appearance of U wave

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Prolonged PR interval with ST elevation
Decreased PR interval with ST depression
Decreased QT interval with tall T waves
Prolonged QT interval with flat T waves

question: Which of the following ECG findings are seen in a patient with hypokalemia?

explanationHtml:
The P waves in the given ECG are broad and notched. This is the P mitrale pattern which is seen in left atrial enlargement.

This patient has likely developed mitral stenosis (heard as a mid-diastolic murmur) secondary to his rheumatic heart disease. Mitral valve stenosis and atrial inflammation in rheumatic carditis lead to left atrial dilation.

The features of P mitrale are:

  • lead II: broad (>2.5mm) notched P waves
  • Lead V1: Biphasic wave with a prominent negative terminal component (representing delayed depolarization of the LA)

P pulmonale is seen in right atrial enlargement.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: The rabbit ear pattern is seen in the right bundle branch block. The ECG of RBBB below shows the rSR' pattern of the QRS complex (rabbit ear) in leads V1-V2 and slurred S wave in lead V6.

[[figure-2]]

Option D: Sawtooth pattern in ECG is seen in atrial flutter (shown below).

question: A 45-year-old male patient with a long-standing history of rheumatic heart disease comes to the clinic with complaints of dyspnea. Interpret the ECG finding.

explanationHtml:
In the given ECG, a peaked P wave can be seen. This is called P pulmonale and it is seen in cases of right atrial enlargement. The patient is showing features of heart failure possibly as a consequence of dysfunction caused by the overload.

Signs of heart failure in this patient:

  • Bilateral pitting edema in lower extremities (systemic congestion)
  • Worsening dyspnea due to increased PCWP causing pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary edema (pulmonary congestion)

The features of P pulmonale include:

  • The amplitude of the P wave is >2.5mm on Lead II
  • Prominent positive wave in the biphasic P wave of lead V1

[[figure-1]]
question: A 67-year-old man with a history of COPD presented with worsening dyspnea for 2 weeks. On examination, pedal edema was present. An ECG was done and lead II showed the following pattern. Which of the following is responsible for this ECG finding?

explanationHtml:
The given ECG shows deep S-waves in V6 and large R-waves in V1. This is suggestive of right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).

Diagnostic criteria for RVH:

  • Dominant R wave in V1 (R/S ratio > 1).
  • Dominant S wave in V5 or V6 (R/S ratio < 1).
  • Right ventricular strain pattern - ST depression/T wave inversion in the right precordial (V1-4) and inferior leads (II, III, aVF)
  • Right axis deviation of +110° or more.

For left ventricular hypertrophy, Sokolow Lyon criteria are commonly used.

It is based on the presence of tall left precordial R waves and deep right precordial S waves (S wave in V1 + [R wave in V5 or V6] >35 mm).

question: A patient was brought to the ER with complaints of multiple episodes of vomiting, increased frequency of urination, and constipation for the past 5 days. He also complained of lethargy and muscle pain. He is a known case of SCC of the lung. What is likely to be seen in the ECG of this patient?

QT interval of 0.55s suggests QT prolongation. It is not seen in digitalis toxicity. Rather, a QT shortening with characteristic “scooping” of the ST–T-wave complex, called a digitalis effect, is seen.

The ECG changes seen in digitalis toxicity are as follows:

  • Prolonged PR interval
  • ST-segment depression

QT interval represents the time taken for the ventricles to depolarize and repolarize. It is prolonged in the following:

  • Hypocalcemia
  • Hypokalemia

question: ECG of a patient revealed a QT interval of 0.55s. Which of the following will not be a differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Osborn waves are seen in hypothermia.

Osborn waves can also be seen in severe hypothyroidism (Option A), but even in those cases, hypothermia is the reason for the appearance of Osborn waves. Therefore, hypothermia is the better answer here.

It consists of an abrupt ascent right at the J point (the junctional point between the QRS complex and the ST segment) and then an equally sudden plunge back to the baseline. It is also called the J wave. This is because systemic hypothermia prolongs repolarisation.

[[figure-1]]

Osborn wave can also be seen in:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Brain injury
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Vasospastic angina
  • Cardiopulmonary arrest from oversedation
  • Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation

question: A 52-year-old man has come to the emergency complaining of a burning type of chest pain. Comment on his ECG recording shown below.

explanationHtml:
Premature ventricular beats are a type of ventricular tachycardias, not supraventricular tachycardias.

Tachycardia is defined as a heart rate of >100 beats/min. It can be classified based on the site of origin of the cardiac impulse as follows:

  1. Supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs) originate above the ventricles, that is, in the sinoatrial node, atria, or the atrioventricular node. Supraventricular tachycardias include:
    • Tachycardias originating from the atrium:
      • Sinus tachycardia- from the SA node
      • Focal atrial tachycardia
      • Multifocal atrial tachycardia
      • Atrial flutter
      • Atrial fibrillation
    • Tachycardias originating from the AV node:
      • Junctional tachycardia- automaticity within AV Node
      • AV nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT)
    • Tachycardia associated with accessory atrioventricular pathways: atrioventricular reentry tachycardia (AVRT)
  2. Ventricular tachycardias originate from the ectopic foci or the reentry pathways in the ventricles. Ventricular tachycardias include:
    • Premature ventricular beats
    • Ventricular tachycardia (VT)
      • Monomorphic VT- Very rapid monomorphic VT is also known as ventricular flutter
      • Polymorphic VT- associated with Torsades de pointes
    • Ventricular fibrillation

[[figure-1]]
question: All of the following are supraventricular tachycardias except:

explanationHtml:
The above ECG shows increased heart rate with wide QRS complexes (> 0.12s). This is suggestive of ventricular tachycardia (VT).

Types of ventricular tachycardia based on QRS morphology:

  • Monomorphic- a stable QRS morphology from beat to beat
  • Polymorphic- changing or multiform QRS variance from beat to beat. Torsades de pointes is an example of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
  • Bidirectional- has a beat-to-beat alternation in the QRS frontal plane axis. It is associated with digitalis toxicity or catecholaminergic polymorphic VT.

The most common cause of VT is ischemic heart disease.

Ventricular tachyarrhythmias occur due to impulses that originate within the ventricles. These impulses are conducted through the normal ventricular myocardial cells instead of the fast conducting Purkinje system. Hence, they present with wide QRS complexes ( >0.12 sec) on the ECG.

Supraventricular tachyarrhythmias occur due to impulses originating above the ventricles. These impulses reach the ventricles through the proper fast conduction pathway resulting in a narrow QRS complex. SVTs are associated with wide QRS in few exceptional conditions like:

  • Conduction block in the left or right bundle branch
  • Activation of ventricles from an accessory pathway- antidromic AVRT

The given ECG shows wide stable QRS complexes in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia:

[[figure-1]]

question: ECG of a patient who presented with palpitations to the ER is shown below. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common supraventricular arrhythmia is sinus tachycardia. It can either be physiological or pathological. Physiological sinus tachycardia is seen in exercise, fever, anemia, hyperthyroidism, etc.

Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias are those supraventricular tachycardias that occur with sudden onset and termination, they are non-sustained arrhythmias (lasts < 30 seconds). They include AVNRT, AVRT, and atrial tachycardias.

The most common sustained (lasts > 30 seconds) arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation.

Junctional tachycardia originates from ectopic foci in the AV node. It is an uncommon tachycardia.

question: A 49-year-old woman was brought to the emergency with complaints of dizziness, shortness of breath, and palpitations. ECG showed tachyarrhythmia with narrow QRS complex and irregular RR intervals. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The ECG shows narrow QRS complexes with irregular RR intervals and no distinct P waves. This is suggestive of atrial fibrillation.

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a supraventricular tachycardia caused by ectopic foci or small reentry circuits within the atria. It has an atrial rate of 400-600/min and a ventricular rate of 100-160/min.

Risk factors for developing AF include:

  • Age- usually above 60 years of age
  • Underlying heart disease
  • Hypertension
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Obesity
  • Sleep apnea
  • Post-cardiac surgery
  • Inflammatory pericarditis

Acute precipitating factors for AF include:

  • Hyperthyroidism
  • Acute alcohol intoxication
  • Acute illness like myocardial infarction and pulmonary embolism

question: A 65-year-old hypertensive patient presents with chest pain and dyspnea following an alcohol binge. His ECG is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above ECG shows narrow QRS complex, irregular RR intervals, and absent P waves which are suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Among the given options, amiodarone can be administered in patients having atrial fibrillation with coronary or structural heart disease.

Drugs for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation:

In patients without structural heart disease, class I agents are used. Class I agents act by blocking the Na+ channels leading to slower depolarization:

  • Flecainide
  • Propafenone
  • Disopyramide

In patients with coronary or structural heart disease, class III agents are used. Class III agents act by blocking the K+ channels leading to slower repolarization causing increased refractory period:

  • Amiodarone
  • Dofetilide
  • Sotalol
  • Ibutilide

question: A 50-year-old man was diagnosed with STEMI. He was admitted and given thrombolytic therapy. The next day he complained of palpitations and an ECG was taken. Which of the following drugs can be used to treat his condition?

explanationHtml:
A patient of atrial fibrillation usually has an irregular heart rate of >100/ min but this patient presents with a regular slow heart rate. The most likely cause of slow regular heart rate in chronic AF is digitalis toxicity. Symptoms such as nausea, anorexia are also suggestive of digitalis toxicity.

Digitalis lowers the AV nodal conduction by stimulating the vagal nerve endings leading to increased vagal tone. Hence digitalis toxicity can cause AV nodal block. This leads to a junctional escape rhythm taking over the ventricles causing slow and regular heart rate.

Digitalis toxicity can also lead to a variety of arrhythmias as it increases the intracellular calcium levels increasing the risk of tachyarrhythmias.
question: A 60-year-old man who is on treatment for chronic AF presents with nausea, dizziness, and anorexia. He has a regular heart rate of 50/min. The most likely cause is:

The given ECG shows narrow QRS complexes, hence it is supraventricular tachycardia. The RR intervals are regular and the normal P waves are replaced by sawtooth-shaped waves, known as flutter waves.

In atrial flutter, the ventricular rate is determined by the AV conduction ratio. The commonest AV ratio is 2:1. In the above ECG, the rhythm is atrial flutter 4:1 block with an atrial rate of about 270 and a ventricular rate of 68/min.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) occurs due to impulses arising from multiple abnormal foci in the atria. This leads to supraventricular tachycardia with p waves and QRS complexes of different morphologies. It is usually encountered in patients with chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness.

Therapy for MAT is directed at treating the underlying disease and correcting any metabolic abnormalities. Calcium-channel blockers and radiofrequency ablation of the AV node are the other treatment modalities.

The given ECG shows narrow QRS complexes with irregular RR intervals, hence it can be atrial fibrillation or multifocal atrial tachycardia. The next step is to look at the p waves. Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is characterized by at least 3 distinct P-wave morphologies (shown by arrows in the image). Whereas, in atrial fibrillation, there would be no distinct p waves seen.

  2. AVRT

Whereas, atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained arrhythmia among supraventricular tachycardias.

question: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias do not include:

explanationHtml:
The ECG is suggestive of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT) as it shows:

  • Narrow QRS complexes
  • No visible p waves
  • Pseudo R' waves in V1 lead

Adenosine is the preferred drug in stable paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT).

Treatment of PSVT:

In hemodynamically unstable patients, QRS-synchronous DC cardioversion should be done.

In hemodynamically stable patients,

1. Mechanical measures: These maneuvers result in an acute increase in the vagal tone which decreases AV conduction and terminates the arrhythmia. They include the following:

  • Valsalva maneuver
  • Lowering the head between the knees
  • Coughing
  • Splashing cold water on the face
  • Breath-holding
  • Carotid sinus massage

2. Pharmacologic therapy:

  • Adenosine- it is the first-line agent. It blocks conduction across the AV node and terminates the SVT. It is given as a 6-18 mg bolus
  • Calcium channel blockers- verapamil and diltiazem
  • Beta-blockers- esmolol, propranolol, and metoprolol
  • IV Procainamide- it is administered if the tachycardia is being mediated through an accessory pathway. It facilitates the AV conduction and therefore causes an initial increase in rate. Therefore, it is given after administering calcium channel blockers or beta-blockers.

question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the casualty after he developed sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, and palpitations at a party. His blood pressure is 100/62 mmHg. His ECG is shown below. What is the drug of choice to treat his condition?

explanationHtml:
The given ECG showing narrow QRS complex (<0.12 s) tachycardia with absent P wave is suggestive of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT). The next best step in the management of a patient with unstable vitals (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg) is synchronized cardioversion.

Synchronized cardioversion is the treatment of choice in unstable PSVT patients, in which shocks are delivered with the defibrillator/monitor in synchronized mode with an initial energy level of 100J. Synchronization times the delivery so that it is given at the peak of the QRS complex.

If the shock occurs in the ST segment or the T wave (unsynchronized), it can precipitate a more serious arrhythmia such as ventricular fibrillation.

Synchronized cardioversion Defibrillation

Used in unstable PSVT, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse

 Used in ventricular tachycardia without pulse and ventricular fibrillation.
Shock is delivered in sync with the R wave (in absolute refractory period) Shock is delivered at any time during the cardiac cycle.

Monophasic: 100-200 J

Biphasic: 50-100 J

Monophasic: 360 J

Biphasic:120-200 J

Other options:

Option A: In the absence of hemodynamic instability, a repeat dose of injection adenosine (maximum of 12mg) could be attempted.

Option B: IV Amiodarone is rarely used in the acute management of PSVT. Instead, it is used as an alternative to calcium channel blockers in chronic suppressive therapy.

Option D: Defibrillation is only done for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

question: The  ECG of a patient who presented to the ER is as given below. The patient was already given a carotid massage and IV Adenosine but the BP is currently 60/30 mm Hg. What is the next best step of management?

The next step in the management of PSVT in a hemodynamically stable (systolic blood pressure >90 mm Hg) patient is vagotonic maneuvres such as carotid sinus massage or Valsalva maneuver.

Carotid sinus massage can be considered in the absence of carotid bruits and no history of stroke. If vagal maneuvers fail or cannot be performed, intravenous adenosine can be used.

Non-DHP calcium channel blockers and beta blockers are second-line pharmacological agents in the management of PSVT. They can cause hypotension before and after terminating the arrhythmia.

If the patient is hemodynamically unstable (systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure <65 mm Hg), immediate QRS-synchronous direct current cardioversion is necessary.

question: A 65-year-old female patient is brought to the emergency department in a state of unconsciousness. Her BP is 70/50 mm of Hg. Her ECG is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of her condition?

explanationHtml:
Retrograde conduction via accessory pathways does not cause preexcitation.

Accessory pathways (APs) are abnormal conduction pathways connecting the atrium and ventricle. They can conduct impulses in the following ways:

Antegrade conduction:

  • Occurs from the atria to the ventricle
  • The impulses from atria reach the ventricles faster via the accessory pathway as compared to the normal AV nodal pathway as they bypass the AV nodal delay.
  • This leads to an earlier excitation of the ventricles known as the preexcitation of the ventricles and thus a wide QRS complex.
  • Example : antidromic AV reentry tachycardia (AVRT)

Retrograde conduction:

  • Occurs from the ventricle to the atria.
  • The impulses reach the ventricles via the normal AV nodal pathway but re-enter the atria through the accessory pathway.
  • Ventricular depolarization is normal, there is no preexcitation and thus a narrow QRS complex. It causes supraventricular tachycardia as the impulses re-enter the atria via the accessory pathway.
  • Examples : concealed accessory pathways (can cause SVTs) and orthodromic AVRT

    Note : Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome can be associated with sinus rhythm, orthodromic AVRT or antidromic AVRT.

options.text: Bundle of Kent has antegrade conduction

question: Which of the following is false about accessory pathways?

explanationHtml:
The most common reentrant tachycardia caused by an accessory pathway is orthodromic AV reentry.

Accessory pathways (APs) are abnormal conduction pathways connecting the atrium and ventricle. They can conduct impulses in the following ways:

Antegrade conduction:

  • Occurs from the atria to the ventricle
  • The impulses from atria reach the ventricles faster via the accessory pathway as compared to the normal AV nodal pathway as they bypass the AV nodal delay.
  • This leads to an earlier excitation of the ventricles known as the preexcitation of the ventricles and thus a wide QRS complex.
  • Examples- antidromic AVRT

Retrograde conduction:

  • Occurs from the ventricle to the atria.
  • The impulses reach the ventricles via the normal AV nodal pathway but re-enter the atria through the accessory pathway.
  • Ventricular depolarization is normal, there is no preexcitation and thus a narrow QRS complex. It causes supraventricular tachycardia as the impulses re-enter the atria via the accessory pathway.
  • Examples- concealed accessory pathways (can cause SVTs) and orthodromic AVRT.

AV nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT) is not caused by an accessory pathway. It involves tissues with different conduction speeds within the AV node or just adjacent to the AV node, known as the fast pathway and the slow pathway. This is known as dual AV nodal physiology.

Note : Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome can be associated with sinus rhythm, orthodromic AVRT or antidromic AVRT.

Rate-slowing drugs such as non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem), beta-blockers, and digoxin are contraindicated in these patients. They increase the refractoriness of the AV node with minimal or no effect on the accessory pathway. This can lead to faster ventricular rates, increasing the risk of ventricular fibrillation.

The classic ECG features in WPW are as follows:

  • A slurring and the slow rise of the initial upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave)

question: All are true about the condition that is diagnosed by the given ECG except:

explanationHtml:
The ECG shows the presence of delta waves (preexcitation wave), wide QRS, and short PR interval which are classically seen in Wolff Parkinson White (WPW) syndrome. In this patient, catheter ablation is the best for long-term management.

Patients with preexcitation who have symptoms of arrhythmia are at risk for developing AF and sudden death if they have an accessory pathway that allows rapid antegrade conduction (preexcitation & tachyarrhythmias are features of WPW syndrome due to the abnormal accessory pathway).

Complications of catheter ablation are rare but include AV block, cardiac tamponade, thromboembolic events, and hematoma at the access site.
question: A 30-year-old woman comes to the clinic with complaints of recurrent palpitation and lightheadedness. An ECG was taken and is as shown below. What is the best step in management?

correctAnswer: C. Frequently seen in patients with atrial fibrillation
explanationHtml:
Sick sinus syndrome is frequently seen in patients with concomitant atrial fibrillation.

Sick sinus syndrome (or sinus node dysfunction) is a group of abnormal heart rhythms. It is a disorder of the sinoatrial node caused by impaired pacemaker function and impulse transmission. This leads to a combination of abnormal rhythms, including atrial bradyarrhythmias, atrial tachyarrhythmias, and sometimes a pattern of alternating bradycardia and tachycardia, known as tachy-brady syndrome. These irregular rhythms can cause symptoms such as palpitations, decreased tissue perfusion, subsequent fatigue, lightheadedness, pre-syncope, and syncope.

The management of sick sinus syndrome includes identifying and correcting reversible factors, as an initial step.

Some examples of reversible causes of Sinus Node Dysfunction include,

  • Hypothyroidism
  • Sleep apnea
  • Anti-hypertensive medications eg. Beta-blockers
  • Anti-arrhythmic medications eg. Amiodarone, Procainamide

Ambulatory ECG monitoring is required to diagnose as the symptoms are nonspecific.

Treatment involves permanent pacing.

Other options:

Option A: The course of sinus node dysfunction is usually a slow progression over decades. In the early stages, most patients are asymptomatic.

Option B: It occurs most commonly in elderly patients due to the gradual loss of SA node function.

Option D: Beta-blockers are contraindicated in this condition.

options.text: Most patients are symptomatic in the early stages
