question: Which of the following is true regarding sick sinus syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The above ECG shows a pattern of premature ventricular contractions, one premature beat after one normal beat. This is seen in ventricular bigeminy.

Premature ventricular contractions/beats (PVC) are single ventricular beats that occur earlier than the next normal supraventricular beat. They originate from abnormal foci in the ventricular tissue:

  • Unifocal PVCs arise from a single focus and hence have the same QRS morphology
  • Multifocal PVCs arise from multiple foci and therefore have different QRS morphologies

They are not preceded by a P wave as they do not originate in the atria. They show wide QRS complexes (>120 ms) on the ECG because they are conducted via normal myocardial tissue instead of the Purkinje system.

Ventricular bigeminy refers to a pair of normal and premature ventricular contractions, whereas ventricular trigeminy refers to a premature beat that occurs after two normal beats. Quadrigeminy is when a premature beat follows three normal beats.

Few other terms associated with premature ventricular contractions:

  • Two successive PVCs are known as a couplet
  • Three successive PVCs are known as a triplet.

The given ECG shows ventricular bigeminy with premature beats circled in red and normal ventricular contractions circled in green.

question: A hypertensive patient was brought to the emergency due to complaints of palpitations and breathing difficulty. Comment on his ECG.

explanationHtml:
The ECG feature of ventricular tachycardia seen in the given image is a fusion beat. It occurs when a sinus and ventricular beat coincide to produce a hybrid complex.

Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is defined as ≥ 3 consecutive premature ventricular contractions at a rate of >100/min. It is characterized by:

  • Wide QRS complex
  • AV dissociation- Atrial activity independent of ventricular activity, seen on the ECG as every p wave not followed by QRS complex
  • Fusion beats- occur when a sinus and ventricular beat coincide to produce a hybrid complex
  • Capture beats occur when the SA node transiently ‘captures’ the ventricles, that is, ventricles are depolarized by the impulses from the SA node producing a QRS complex of normal duration.

The given ECG shows a fusion beat (red arrow), and a capture beat (green arrow) can also be seen:

[[figure-1]]

The given image shows capture beats in VT:

[[figure-2]]

Option C: Polymorphic QRS, that is, continuously changing QRS morphology is seen in polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Option D: Triphasic QRS (eg. RSR′ pattern on V1) is seen in supraventricular tachycardias with the wide QRS complex.
question: Identify the marked ECG feature in a patient diagnosed with ventricular tachycardia.

explanationHtml:
The rate of the given ECG is around 188 BPM ( >100 BPM) and it shows wide QRS complexes ( ≥ 0.12 s) with abnormal morphology (red arrows) and absence of P waves which suggests a diagnosis of ventricular tachycardia.

[[figure-1]]

Ventricular fibrillation (Option B) would not show discreet QRS complexes, and hence is not the answer in this case.

[[figure-2]]
question: What is the diagnosis of this patient from the ECG shown below?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario describes a man with history of coronary artery disease developing syncope. The ECG shows wide QRS complex (> 0.12 s) tachycardia with a single QRS morphology suggestive of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT). The most appropriate treatment of VT in a hemodynamically unstable (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg) patient is DC cardioversion.

VT can be casued by structural heart disease, scar-related reentry, cardiomyopathies, or abnormalities in the conduction pathways. VT is said to be sustained if it lasts for at least 30 seconds or requires intervention for termination.

Rapid VT can lead to hypotension and syncope, especially in patients with ventricular dysfunction. Patients with normal cardiac function may tolerate sustained VT, presenting with palpitations. Monomorphic VT associated with structural heart disease can progress to ventricular fibrillation (VF) and sudden cardiac arrest.

QRS synchronous electrical cardioversion is performed for unstable patients. Intravenous amiodarone is the preferred drug for stable VT associated with heart disease.

After restoring sinus rhythm, further evaluation is necessary to determine the underlying heart disease. Treatment options include antiarrhythmic medications, catheter ablation, or implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) for recurrent or high-risk VT. ICDs are commonly used for secondary prevention of sudden death in patients with sustained VT and structural heart disease.
question: A 50-year-old man is brought to the emergency following an episode of syncope during his morning walk. His blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. He has a history of myocardial infarction 5 yrs back. His present ECG is given below. Which is the most appropriate treatment for the patient?

explanationHtml:
Carotid sinus massage will be effective only in supraventricular tachycardias but not in ventricular tachycardias. This is because it acts by increasing the AV node block which does not play any role in the pathogenesis of ventricular tachycardia.

Hence, AV node blocking maneuvers (carotid sinus massage, valsalva) and drugs (adenosine) are not used in the management of VT.
question: All of the following are effective in the management of patients with ventricular tachycardia except:

explanationHtml:
Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is the most common arrhythmia associated with myocardial reperfusion, most commonly in the first 2 days after presentation.

Idioventricular rhythm is defined as ≥ 3 consecutive premature ventricular contractions with a heart rate of <50 bpm. If the heart rate is 60-100 bpm, it is known as accelerated idioventricular rhythm, and if it is more than 100 bpm it is known as ventricular tachycardia. It may be the result of an abnormal focus in the ventricle that generates an impulse faster than the sinus node and therefore assumes control.

Other causes of AIVR include:

  • Buerger disease
  • Congenital heart disease
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Myocarditis
  • Drugs: Digoxin toxicity, cocaine toxicity, and various anesthesia agents
  • Electrolyte abnormality
  • Postresuscitation

Episodes of AIVR have not been found to affect prognosis in acute MI and usually do not require intervention. If AIVR is accompanied by hemodynamic compromise, treatment with atropine or atrial pacing will often suppress the rhythm.
question: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm is the most common arrhythmia associated with:

explanationHtml:
An automated implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD) is a device placed in the chest or abdomen to detect arrhythmias and perform cardioversion, defibrillation, and pace the heart.

It is contraindicated in patients experiencing tachyarrhythmias with reversible or transient causes such as acute MI.

It is used in:

  • Brugada syndrome- refers to a sodium channelopathy with a high risk of arrhythmias that can lead to sudden cardiac death.
  • Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.
  • Cardiac resynchronization therapy for prevention of sudden cardiac death in heart failure.
  • High-risk situations of sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome with low ejection fraction

question: Automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (AICD) implantation is done for all of the following conditions except:

correctAnswer: A. 1 hour after onset of symptoms
explanationHtml:
Sudden cardiac death is defined as unexpected non-traumatic death in clinically well or stable patients who die within 1 hour after onset of symptoms.

The causative rhythm in most cases is ventricular fibrillation, which is usually preceded by ventricular tachycardia except in the setting of acute ischemia or infarction.
question: Sudden cardiac death is defined as unexpected nontraumatic death in stable patients within:

explanationHtml:
The given ECG is suggestive of ventricular fibrillation.

The characteristics observed in the above ECG that point towards ventricular fibrillation are:

  • Irregular waves with varying amplitude and no distinct QRS complexes
  • P waves not identifiable
  • PR interval not present

Possible mechanisms of ventricular fibrillation include spiral wave reentry and multiple circulating reentry wavefronts.

The ECG features suggestive of ventricular tachycardia are as follows:

  • Wide QRS complex with abnormal morphology (marked with red arrows in image below)
  • Absence of the P waves
  • Rate >100/min- in the ECG below, it is ~180 beats/min (1500/no. of small boxes between two R waves)

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of ischemic heart disease is brought to the emergency in an unconscious state. He has been neglecting symptoms of dizziness and palpitations for the past few days. His ECG is given below. The most possible diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
The given ECG finding shows torsades de pointes, which can occur due to hypomagnesemia (Crohn's disease causes chronic diarrhea which can cause excess GI loss of magnesium).

Torsades de pointes means twisting of points, it implies twisting of the QRS complexes around the isoelectric line of the ECG. It is a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that is seen in patients with a prolonged QT interval.

A prolonged QT interval usually results from prolonged ventricular repolarization (lengthening of T wave). A premature ventricular contraction falling in the elongated T wave can initiate torsades de pointes.

The features of torsades de pointes are:

  • Polymorphic QRS complexes that change in amplitude
  • Cycle length giving an appearance of oscillations around the baseline
  • QT prolongation

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient who is a known case of Crohn's disease was brought to the emergency. He complained of sudden onset cold sweats and palpitations. Which among the following is the likely cause of his ECG finding shown in the given image?

explanationHtml:
The given ECG showing a wide QRS complex tachycardia with waxing and waning QRS amplitude points to the diagnosis of torsades de pointes. As the patient is hemodynamically stable, intravenous MgSO4 is the treatment of choice.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) has a continually changing QRS morphology. Torsades de pointes is a type of polymorphic VT that occurs in people having a congenital or acquired prolongation of the QT interval. Patients present with near-syncope, syncope, or cardiac arrest.

IV MgSO4 is effective for both preventing and treating the long QT-related ventricular ectopic beat recurrences, which lead to torsades de pointes.

If magnesium alone is ineffective, isoproterenol infusion or pacing, to a rate of 100-120 depolarizations/minute, usually suppresses VT recurrences.

If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, then immediate defibrillation should be done.

question: The ECG of a pregnant lady having pre-eclampsia is shown below. Her vitals are stable. What is the best step in the management of the condition?

correctAnswer: B. It is slower than AV nodal pathway
explanationHtml: The bundle of Kent is the accessory pathway of conduction between the atria and ventricle in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. It conducts impulses faster than the AV nodal pathway and avoids AV nodal delay, leading to shortened PR interval. QRS is prolonged because of the AV nodal impulse reaching the ventricles after the aberrant impulse.

options.text: It is faster than AV nodal pathway
It is slower than AV nodal pathway

question: Identify the false statement about the bundle of Kent.

correctAnswer: A. ST segment elevation in V1-V3
explanationHtml:
The major feature of Brugada syndrome is transient or concealed ST-segment elevation in V1 to V3.

Brugada syndrome is a rare syndrome characterized by ST-segment elevation and negative T waves in more than 1 anterior precordial leads ( V1- V3 ). It is associated with mutations involving cardiac sodium channels. The patients have episodes of polymorphic VT which may lead to syncope or cardiac arrest.

It shows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and affects males more than females. The episodes of VT may occur either in sleep or maybe provoked by febrile illness or sodium channel-blocking drugs (Class I antiarrhythmics) like ajmaline, flecainide, and procainamide.

The episodes of VT can be suppressed using quinidine or catheter ablation. ICD can be used in individuals who have been resuscitated from cardiac arrest.

options.text: ST segment elevation in 1, V5, AvL
ST segment elevation in II , III AvF

question: Which of the following is seen in patients with Brugada syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Brugada syndrome is associated with right bundle branch block. It is an inherited disease that predisposes patients to potentially life threatening arrythmias.

The ECG below is depictive of Brugada syndrome with concave ST segments and negative T waves (to be seen in more than one anterior precordial leads, i.e., V1-V3)

[[figure-1]]
question: Brugada syndrome is associated with:

correctAnswer: B. Congenital long QT without deafness
explanationHtml:
Romano-Ward syndrome is a congenital long QT syndrome without deafness.

Romano-Ward syndrome is associated with specific genetic mutations affecting membrane potassium and sodium channels. The inheritance pattern may be autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant.

The preferred drugs for managing this condition are the beta-blockers. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation can also be done.

Jervell-Lange-Nielsen syndrome is congenital long QT with deafness.

question: Which of the following conditions is associated with AV block?

explanationHtml:
This patient has symptoms and ECG findings suggestive of Mobitz type I or Wenckebach block.

In the given ECG PR interval progressively increases in each successive cycle, until a P wave of the series fails to produce a QRS complex (dropped QRS). In this example, for every 5 'P' waves, there are only 4 'QRS' complexes; hence, this is a 5:4 Wenckebach block.
question: A concerned wife brought her 43-year-old husband to the clinic after an episode of light-headedness and palpitations. An ECG was taken. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The absence of a constant relationship between the P wave and the QRS complex (P-QRS dissociation) is a feature of complete heart block. It is not seen in Mobitz type II second-degree heart block.

The PR interval remains constant in Mobitz type II second-degree heart block but few p waves are not followed by QRS complex. It occurs due to a block in the bundle of His. The atrial rate is more than the ventricular rate.

options.text: Atrial rate more than the ventricular rate

question: All of the following may be seen in Mobitz type II heart block except:

explanationHtml:
The given ECG shows a constant PR interval in each successive cycle followed by a dropped QRS (P wave fails to produce a QRS complex). This pattern is suggestive of Mobitz type II block.

Mobitz type II block is characterized by an intermittent failure of conduction of the p wave without any change in the preceding impulses.

The dropped QRS is marked in the image below:

[[figure-1]]

Note: Bradyarrhythmias that cause syncope include those due to severe sinus node dysfunction and AV block( Mobitz type II block, complete AV block). Syncope due to bradycardia or asystole is referred to as Stokes-Adams attack.
question: A 56-year-old woman was brought to the emergency room after she lost consciousness briefly during a speech. An ECG was taken immediately. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above ECG shows a complete heart block.

Features in the ECG supporting the diagnosis of complete heart block:

  • PP interval is constant
  • RR interval is constant
  • P waves more in number than QRS complexes
  • There is no relation between P waves and the QRS complexes.

For a second-degree heart block, the QRS complex should be preceded by the P wave, whereas in a third-degree heart block, the QRS complex is independent of the P wave.

question: Interpret the given ECG:

explanationHtml:
QRS > 0.12s points towards a wide QRS complex. The left anterior fascicular block does not cause a wide QRS complex.

QRS interval is not usually prolonged by fascicular blocks. Such blocks are partial blocks and only cause axis deviation.

  • Left anterior fascicular block: left axis deviation
  • Left posterior fascicular block: right axis deviation

Wide QRS complexes (≥ 0.12 seconds) are seen in the following:

  • Ventricular tachycardias
  • Ventricular premature contractions
  • Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
  • Bundle branch blocks (complete blocks- QRS interval ≥ 0.12 seconds, incomplete blocks- QRS interval between 0.10–0.12 seconds)
  • Hyperkalemia
question: You observe that an ECG recording revealed a QRS complex > 0.12 seconds. Which of the following would you not include in the differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given ECG showing an inverted T wave and a prominent U wave in leads V2 to V5 is suggestive of hypokalemia.

Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of potassium less than 3.5mM. Hypokalemia delays ventricular repolarization and leads to broad flat or inverted T waves, a prominent U wave, prolongation of the QT interval, and ST depression.

[[figure-1]]

Hypokalemia leads to dynamic ECG changes. The image given shows the sequence of changes observed:

[[figure-2]]

Other options:

Option B- Hyperkalemia causes narrowing and peaking of the T wave, widening and flattening of the P wave, and QRS complex widening. Further increase in serum potassium concentration leads to the disappearance of the P wave and the formation of a sine wave as the QRS complex widens.

Option C- Hypocalcemia leads to prolongation of the QT interval, due to lengthening of the ST segment.

Option D- Hypercalcemia leads to shortening of the QT interval due to shortening of the ST segment

question: A 40-year-old male patient came to ED with complaints of weakness, paresthesia, and breathing difficulty. Relevant investigations were done. The ECG obtained is suggestive of :

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of valvular heart disease in developing countries is rheumatic fever. This is mainly due to the repeated infections with rheumatogenic streptococci and inadequate coverage of antibiotics. It mainly affects the mitral valve.

In developed countries, degenerative or inflammatory processes are the most common cause of valvular heart diseases.
question: What is the most common cause of valvular heart disease in developing countries?

explanationHtml:
The size of the mitral orifice in a normal adult is 4-6 sq cm.

Depending on the area of mitral valve opening (MVA), mitral stenosis can be classified as:

  • Progressive MS - MVA > 1.5 sq cm
  • Severe MS - MVA ≤ 1.5 sq cm
  • Very severe MS - ≤ 1 sq cm
question: What is the normal range for the mitral valve area in an adult?

explanationHtml:
Left ventricular hypertrophy is not seen in mitral stenosis. On the contrary, right ventricle hypertrophy is seen.

Mechanism of mitral stenosis (MS):

In a normal mitral valve, there is no obstruction to the flow of blood from the left atrium(LA) to the left ventricle. Therefore a small LA pressure is sufficient to empty the blood into the ventricle.

When the MVA is <~2 sq cm, blood flows from the left atrium to the left ventricle, propelled by a mildly elevated atrial pressure. Hence, patients are usually asymptomatic and may develop dyspnea only when the heart rate increases, as seen in exertion, excitement, fever, etc. All these conditions:

  • Increase the rate of blood flow across the mitral orifice, resulting in further elevation of the LA pressure
  • Decrease the diastolic filling time, resulting in a reduction in cardiac output

The image below explains the mechanism of mitral stenosis.

[[figure-1]]

question: A 45-year-old male patient comes to the clinic with 3 months history of breathlessness. After Evaluation, the patient is diagnosed with mitral stenosis. Which of the following is least likely to be heard on auscultation?

explanationHtml: The given image is of mitral stenosis showing fish mouth or buttonhole appearance.
question: A 48-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital in view of severe dyspnea. History revealed that the dyspnea was exertional initially and later worsened to breathlessness during normal daily activities. She died on the 3rd day following admission. The image of the autopsy of the heart is shown below. Identify the condition.

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of mitral stenosis. The more severe the thickening, the earlier the opening snap occurs in diastole. Hence, the decreased interval between A2 and opening snap (OS) indicates increased severity of the stenosis.

The auscultatory findings which are suggestive of increased severity of murmur are:

  • Decreased interval between A2 and OS
  • Increased duration of the diastolic murmur

Loud S1 is seen in the initial stages of MS when the mitral leaflets are flexible. When there is further thickening and calcification of the leaflets, they become immobile, and the amplitude of S1 decreases.

Increased severity of the stenosis increases the left atrial pressure. This increase in left atrial pressure can increase pulmonary artery pressure which leads to loud P2 on auscultation.
question: A 62-year-old woman presents with breathlessness for 5 months. She is unable to carry out her daily activities and has difficulty sleeping. On examination, she has a parasternal heave. On auscultation, opening snap (OS) is heard followed by a low pitched rumbling diastolic murmur. Which of the following findings is suggestive of increased severity of the given condition?

explanationHtml:
Left atrium (LA) is the first cardiac chamber to get enlarged in mitral stenosis (MS). It is due to the pressure overload of LA. It can be appreciated on the lateral and left anterior oblique views.

Other radiographic changes seen in MS are straightening of the upper left border of the cardiac silhouette, posterior displacement of the esophagus by an enlarged LA, and Kerley B lines due to distention of interlobular septae and lymphatics with edema.

Severe MS causing pulmonary hypertension leads to enlargement of the pulmonary artery, right ventricle, and right atrium. Left ventricle remains unaffected in isolated MS.
question: Which of the following cardiac chambers is enlarged in mitral stenosis on chest X-ray initially?

correctAnswer: C. Mitral orifice is < 1.5 sq cm
explanationHtml:
Mitral valvotomy is indicated in symptomatic (NYHA Functional Class II-IV) patients with mitral stenosis (MS) with orifice < 1.5 cm2 in normal-sized adults or <1 cm2/m2 body surface area.

Treatment of mitral stenosis:

  • Administration of warfarin in patients with MS who develop atrial fibrillation.
  • Surgical treatment includes:
    • Mitral valvotomy: It is done in symptomatic patients whose mitral orifice is less than 1.5 cm2. This can be either percutaneous mitral valvotomy or open surgical valvotomy.
    • Mitral valve replacement: This is done in patients whose mitral valve is severely distorted.

options.text: In all patients who are symptomatic

question: A patient with mitral stenosis presented with worsening dyspnea and fatigue which are now present at rest. He also complained of a feeling of heavy pounding in the chest with recurrent chest pain. You decided to evaluate the patient using echocardiography. When would you advise the patient to undergo a valvotomy?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario is suggestive of mitral valve prolapse.

It is caused due to the myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve. It may be associated with Marfan's syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. It is more common in females of the age group of 15- 30 years.

Most patients are usually asymptomatic. However, some patients may present with symptoms such as palpitations, syncope due to arrhythmias (premature ventricular contractions, ventricular tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation), non-specific chest pain, and dyspnea

Auscultation reveals mid-systolic clicks. If there is associated mitral regurgitation, a systolic murmur might also be heard. The duration of the murmur of MVP decreases on squatting and increases on standing. Whereas the duration of the murmur of MR increases on squatting and decreases on standing.
question: A 26-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for panic disorder was referred to the physician for complaints of palpitations and breathlessness. Detailed history revealed the presence of chest pain, which was substernal and not related to exercise. On auscultation, mid-systolic clicks were audible. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Carvallo’s sign refers to the increase in the intensity of systolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation with inspiration.

During inspiration, the venous return to the heart increases due to the negative intrathoracic pressure. This increases the leak from the right ventricle to the right atrium making the murmur louder.

In general, the right-sided heart murmurs increase in intensity with inspiration and decrease in intensity with expiration, while the opposite is true for left-sided heart murmurs. Pulmonic ejection sound is the only right-sided acoustic event that decreases in intensity with inspiration.
question: Carvallo’s sign is associated with the murmur of which valvulopathy?

explanationHtml:
The severity of mitral regurgitation (MR) can be assessed by the wide splitting of the S2. Due to severe regurgitation of blood, the pressure in the left ventricle falls rapidly, leading to the early closure of the aortic valve.

Clinical findings that indicate the severity of MR is:

  • Reduced cardiac output
  • Palpable systolic thrill
  • Palpable S3
  • Wide splitting of S2

Note: The intensity of murmur does not always correlate with the severity of the murmur. Intensity may be diminished in severe MR caused by LV dysfunction, acute MI and periprosthetic valve regugitation.
question: The severity of mitral regurgitation can be assessed by:

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is aortic stenosis.

Aortic stenosis is the narrowing of the aortic valve. It may be caused due to the calcification of the normal aortic valve, calcification of congenital bicuspid valve, and rheumatic heart disease.

Three cardinal clinical features of aortic stenosis are:

  1. Exertional dyspnea - this occurs due to the left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction. Raised end-diastolic LV volume and reduced LV compliance lead to increased LV pressure, leading to elevation of pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
  2. Angina pectoris - it occurs due to the combination of the increased O2 needs of hypertrophied myocardium and reduction of O2 delivery.
  3. Syncope - it occurs due to the combination of decreased cardiac output and systemic arterial dilation which lead to a reduction of cerebral perfusion.
question: A 65-year-old male patient presented with chest pain, exertional dyspnea and syncope. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The phonocardiogram given above is of an ejection systolic murmur, which is seen in aortic stenosis. It is also heard in pulmonary stenosis. They are differentiated based on the difference in symptoms, site of murmur, etc.

Clinical findings in aortic stenosis:

  • Pulse - slow rising and late peaking pulse which is known as pulsus parvus et tardus. A carotid thrill may also be palpated over these arteries.
  • Apical impulse - A double apical impulse may be recognized, and in the later stages, it may be displaced laterally.

Auscultation findings in aortic stenosis:

  • Early systolic ejection sound - heard in early stages, disappears when the valve becomes calcified and rigid
  • Paradoxical splitting of S2 - With worsening of stenosis, delayed closure of the aortic valve occurs. This leads to narrowing of S2 sound, and in severe cases, leads to paradoxical splitting of S2.
  • S4 and S3 - heard in severe cases
  • Ejection systolic murmur - starts after S1, increases in intensity to reach the peak, and ends before A2. It radiates to the neck and base of the heart. It is augmented by squatting and reduced by the strain of the Valsalva maneuver.

The image below shows phonocardiograms of normal and abnormal heart sounds.

[[figure-1]]
question: On auscultation of a patient, a murmur was heard which is depicted by the following phonocardiogram. Which of the given conditions is most likely to produce this murmur?

explanationHtml:
The above features point to a diagnosis of aortic stenosis. Wide splitting of S2 is not a feature of severe aortic stenosis. On the contrary, there might be single S2 or paradoxical splitting of S2.

Features of severe aortic stenosis are:

  • Pulsus parvus et tardus
  • Palpable carotid thrill
  • Louder and late peaking of systolic murmur
  • Single S2 or paradoxical splitting of S2
  • Presence of S3 and S4 heart sounds
  • Signs of right and left ventricular failure
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy
question: A patient presented with breathlessness on exertion and chest pain. Auscultation revealed an ejection systolic murmur heard best at the base of the heart. Echocardiography showed reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following features does not signify a severe form of this disease?

explanationHtml:
Acute myocardial infarction is not associated with aortic regurgitation.

Aortic regurgitation is the backflow of the blood from the aorta to the left ventricle.

It may be caused either due to the defect in the valve or defect in the aortic root (dilation of the aortic annulus).

Conditions that affect valves are:

  • Congenital
  • Endocarditis
  • Rheumatic fever
  • Myxomatous (prolapse)
  • Traumatic
  • Syphilis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis

Conditions that affect aortic root are:

  • Aortic dissection
  • Cystic medial degeneration
  • Marfan syndrome
  • Bicuspid aortic valve
  • Hypertension
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with aortic regurgitation?

explanationHtml:
The presence of a diastolic murmur along with the pistol shot sound over the femoral is most likely to be due to aortic regurgitation.

question: A 55-year-old male patient presents to the hospital with palpitations. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard in the left third intercostal space and pistol shot sound is heard over the femoral arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical features are suggestive of aortic regurgitation. An early diastolic murmur is a high-pitched decrescendo diastolic murmur.

Auscultatory findings in AR are:

  • Soft S1 - due to the early closure of the mitral valve
  • Diminished or absent A2
  • S3 - due to increased left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic volume. The presence of S3 may be a sign of impaired LV function.
  • Early diastolic murmur -
    • High-pitched, blowing, decrescendo, early diastolic murmur
    • Best heard in the left third intercostal space
    • Heard with the patient sitting up and leaning forward, with breath held in forced expiration
    • Duration of the murmur best correlates with the severity
  • Systolic ejection murmur - It is heard due to increased LV stroke volume and ejection rate.
  • Austin Flint murmur - a low-pitched, mid to late diastolic murmur. It is caused due to the large volume of regurgitant blood, hitting the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve or LV wall.

question: A 58-year-old man presented with exertional dyspnea and angina. On examination, the pulse was characterized by abrupt distention and quick collapse. Auscultation revealed an early diastolic murmur. Which of the following is a feature of this murmur with respect to the likely diagnosis in this case?

explanationHtml:
Volume of regurgitant blood - more than 60mL/ beat is the criterion for severe aortic regurgitation in transthoracic Doppler echocardiography (TTE).

Doppler echocardiography can be used to assess the severity of aortic regurgitation. According to this, AR is considered to be severe when:

  • Width of central jet/left ventricular outflow tract- more than 65%
  • Width of Vena contracta- more than 6mm
  • Regurgitant fraction of blood- more than 50%
  • Volume of regurgitant blood- more than 60mL/beat
  • Size of effective regurgitant orifice- more than 0.3cm2
question: Which of the following is the criteria for severe aortic regurgitation, in transthoracic doppler echocardiography?

explanationHtml:
The treatment of choice in symptomatic acute severe AR is aortic valve replacement (AVR).

Treatment of aortic regurgitation:

  • In non-severe AR, periodic monitoring can be done. The symptoms of dyspnea and decreased cardiac output can be managed by diuretics and vasodilators.
  • In severe AR, surgery (AVR) is indicated in the following conditions:
    • The patient is symptomatic.
    • The patient is asymptomatic, but the LV ejection fraction is less than 55% or LV end-diastolic diameter is more than 65mm.
    • The patient is asymptomatic and undergoing other cardiac surgeries.
question: What is the treatment of choice in symptomatic acute severe aortic regurgitation?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis in the above clinical scenario is tricuspid regurgitation.

Clinical features of tricuspid regurgitation are:

  • Distended neck veins with prominent c-v waves
  • Hepatomegaly with systolic pulsations
  • Positive hepatojugular reflex - the distension of the jugular vein when firm pressure is applied over the liver
  • Blowing holosystolic murmur along the lower left sternal margin

question:
On auscultation of a patient, a murmur was heard which is depicted by the following phonocardiogram. Which of the given conditions is most likely to produce this murmur?

  1. Mitral regurgitation
  2. Tricuspid stenosis
  3. Mitral stenosis
  4. Tricuspid regurgitation
  5. Atrial septal defect

explanationHtml:
A significant difference in blood pressure measured between two arms (>10 mm Hg) may be seen in Takayasu arteritis (subclavian artery disease), supravalvular aortic stenosis, aortic coarctation, and aortic dissection (all four options).

An early diastolic murmur in the right second intercostal space (aortic area) is suggestive of aortic regurgitation. Supravalvular aortic stenosis (Option A), which involves the part of the aorta distal to the aortic valve, is unlikely to cause aortic regurgitation and hence the best answer.

Features Supravalvular AS Takayasu arteritis Aortic dissection Coarctation of aorta
Aortic regurgitation Unlikely Present in 25% of cases Present in acute situations Present
BP difference between arms Present Present Present May be present

So the single best answer would be Supravalvular AS > Coarctation of the aorta.
question: A patient has a right upper limb BP of 180/95 mm Hg and a left upper limb BP of 130/90 mm Hg. He also has an early diastolic murmur in right 2nd intercostal space. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with these findings?

explanationHtml:
Barlow’s syndrome refers to mitral valve prolapse.

Mitral valve prolapse syndrome is also called as systolic click-murmur syndrome, Barlow’s syndrome or floppy valve syndrome. It is the most common abnormality leading to primary mitral regurgitation.

Note: Infantile scurvy is referred to as Barlow's disease.
question: Barlow’s syndrome refers to which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The mitral valve is the most common valve affected in infective endocarditis.

Infective endocarditis is the infection of the endocardial layer of the heart. It may involve the endocardial layer over the heart valves, mural endocardium, or septum. However, it can also affect intracardiac devices.

Note: Infection of the arteriovenous shunts and the arterio-arterial shunt is called infective endarteritis and not infective endocarditis.

question: In patients with infective endocarditis, the vegetations are most commonly present on:

explanationHtml:
Roth's spots are not the cardiac manifestation of infective endocarditis (IE). They are the immunological phenomenon seen in patients with infective endocarditis.

Symptoms of infective endocarditis can be broadly divided into cardiac and non-cardiac manifestations. Non-cardiac manifestations of infective endocarditis are further divided into immunologic and vascular phenomena.

  • Cardiac manifestations of IE:
    • Presence of new regurgitant murmurs
    • Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction
    • Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue
    • Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess.
    • Embolization of coronary arteries
  • Non-cardiac manifestations of IE:
    • Immunological phenomena (mnemonic ROGeR):
      • Osler's nodes- small, tender, red papules that are present on the distal finger and toe pads.
      • Roth's spots- white-centered retinal hemorrhages
      • Immune-complex mediated glomerulonephritis
      • Positivity for rheumatoid factor
    • Vascular phenomena:
      • Janeway lesions- these are faint, red, macular, painless lesions, commonly present on the thenar and hypothenar eminences.
      • Major arterial emboli
      • Septic pulmonary infarct
      • Mycotic aneurysm
      • Intracranial hemorrhages
      • Conjunctival hemorrhages
      • Splenic abscess
      • Cerebral abscess

The image below shows Roth spot on the retina.

[[figure-1]]

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of culture-negative infective endocarditis is the prior use of antibiotics.

Some proportion of patients with endocarditis have negative blood cultures. The important causes are:

  • Prior antibiotic use (most common cause)
  • IE due to fastidious organisms or unusual pathogens or fungi such as:

question:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of moderate aortic stenosis presented with fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats for 2 weeks. Blood tests showed the following. Echocardiography revealed an intracardiac mass on the mitral valve. Blood cultures showed growth of Streptococcus gallolyticus. What additional investigation should be performed?

correctAnswer: B. Patient with suspected IE presenting with fever
explanationHtml:
For a patient with low suspicion of IE, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) will be done as an initial investigation.

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is preferred as the initial investigation in all high-risk patients and/or in patients where a high clinical suspicion of infective endocarditis (IE) exists.

TEE is also preferred over TTE for evaluating:

  • Vegetations < 2mm in diameter
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE)
  • Detection of myocardial abscess
  • Detection of valve perforation
  • Detection of intracardiac fistulae
  • Detection of vegetations in a patient with a cardiovascular implantable electronic device (CIED)

question: Transesophageal echocardiography is preferred over transthoracic echocardiography as initial investigation in all of the following patients, except:

explanationHtml:
Atrial septal defect (ASD) is associated with a very low incidence of IE. In ASD, the velocity of the shunt blood is low due to the decreased pressure gradient between the two atria. This low velocity of the blood does not usually damage the lining endocardium.

Unrepaired VSD is the most frequent congenital heart disease lesion associated with IE, followed by ventricular outflow tract obstructive lesions, such as with tetralogy of Fallot.

correctAnswer: B. A patient with previous CABG surgery
explanationHtml:
Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis is not recommended for patients with previous coronary artery bypass graft surgery. They do not have a long-term risk of infection.

High-Risk Cardiac Conditions Requiring Endocarditis Prophylaxis Before Dental Procedures:

  • Prosthetic heart valves
  • Previous Endocarditis: Individuals with a history of endocarditis.
  • Congenital Heart Defects:
    • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease (including palliative shunts or conduits).
    • Completely repaired congenital heart defects within 6 months of repair.
    • Repaired congenital heart defects with residual lesions situated next to prosthetic material.
  • Pulmonary Artery Valve/Conduit Placement: After surgical or transcatheter placement of a pulmonary artery valve or conduit.
  • Post-Transplant Valvulopathy

Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended for patients with acquired valvular heart disease.

Standard regimen: Amoxicillin 2g orally is given 1 hour before surgery. In patients with penicillin allergy, clarithromycin and azithromycin 500mg orally can be given.

question: The blood culture of a patient with suspected infective endocarditis is positive for gram-positive cocci in chains. What is the treatment of choice?

explanationHtml:
The first-line agents used in the management of Burkholderia cepacia complex (BCC) infections are trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole), meropenem, minocycline, and ceftazidime (3rd generation cephalosporin).

Other options:

Option A: Burkholderia species are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides and polymyxins.

Option C: Tigecycline is less effective in the case of Burkholderia infections.

Option D: Carbapenems and 3rd generation cephalosporins have the same mechanism of action and compete for the same binding site. Hence, it is not a rational drug combination.

BCC is a group of bacteria known for causing severe respiratory distress and septicemia, particularly in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). BCC organisms are also found in ICU patients and individuals with chronic granulomatous disease, leading to lung disease. In the case of a lung transplant, if there's a pre-existing BCC infection present, it increases the risk of death following the transplant.

question: A 43-year-old patient presented with spikes of fever and difficulty in breathing. Transesophageal echo revealed vegetations in the heart. The culture was positive for Burkholderia cepacia. Which of the following is the first line of management?

explanationHtml:
Acute rheumatic fever is caused due to infection with group A streptococcus (GAS), which is Streptococcus pyogenes. It usually follows a streptococcal sore throat or scarlet fever. Other groups of streptococci do not cause acute rheumatic fever.

The pathogenesis of the development of ARF is based on the concept of molecular mimicry. The antibodies which are produced against M protein and N-acetyl glucosamine of group A streptococci, bind to and damage the human endothelial cells.

It mainly affects children between 5-14 years of age. Patients have various rheumatologic, cardiac, and neurological manifestations. Modified Jone's criteria is used for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

The main aim of treatment of rheumatic fever is to relieve symptoms, prevent inflammation and prevent further infections by group A streptoccus by the use of penicillins.

question: What is the causative organism of acute rheumatic fever?

explanationHtml:
The most common clinical feature of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is carditis, observed in up to 90% of cases when both clinical and subclinical forms are considered.

The second most common manifestation is polyarthritis. It classically presents as a migratory, asymmetrical arthritis affecting large joints such as the knees, ankles, elbows, and wrists. Arthritis is more common in adults than in children. ARF is mainly a disease seen in the 5 to 15-year age group.

There is a recognized discrepancy in different sources regarding what is considered the “most common clinical manifestation” of ARF. Western/foreign literature often mentions polyarthritis as the most common presenting feature, while Indian sources emphasize carditis (including both clinical and echocardiographically detected subclinical cases) as being more frequent.

question: What is the most common clinical feature seen in patients with acute rheumatic fever?

correctAnswer: B. Affects mainly the head and upper limbs
explanationHtml:
Choreiform movements in Sydenham’s chorea is mainly seen in the head & upper limbs.

Sydenham chorea is characterized by the presence of involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements of the hands, arms, shoulders, feet, legs, face, and trunk. The movements may be generalized or restricted to one side of the body.

It follows a long latent period (more than 6 months) and therefore can occur alone without any other clinical manifestations.

question: Evidence of preceding streptococcal infection is not essential for making a diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever in patients presenting with:

explanationHtml:
Characteristic initial valvular manifestation in acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is mitral regurgitation.

Damage of the valves leads to mitral regurgitation in the early stages. With repeated episodes of rheumatic fever, there is thickening, calcification, and stenosis of the affected valve.

Mitral regurgitation is the most common cardiac lesion in ARF, while mitral stenosis is the most common lesion in rheumatic heart disease.

Other cardiac manifestations of acute rheumatic fever include myocardial inflammation that can also affect electrical conduction pathways, leading to P-R interval prolongation (first-degree atrioventricular block or rarely higher-level block) and softening of the first heart sound.

Sydenham's chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements which mainly affect the head and upper limbs. In the tongue, it is visible as the characteristic darting movements.

Medications used to treat Sydenham chorea are:

  • Mild cases: managed by providing a calm environment
  • Severe cases: dopamine antagonists like haloperidol, pimozide, or antiepileptic medications like sodium valproate (preferred due to no extrapyramidal side effects) and carbamazepine

This patient has a rheumatic fever without carditis. He should be given prophylaxis till 21 years of age as the duration of secondary prophylaxis is 5 years or until 21 years of age (whichever is longer).

Secondary prophylaxis is given for patients with acute rheumatic fever (ARF). These patients are at a higher risk of developing a further episode of ARF after a group A streptococcal infection. Hence they should receive long-term penicillin prophylaxis to prevent recurrent infections.

The antibiotics that can be given for secondary prophylaxis are:

question: A 57-year-old male patient presented to the clinic for a routine clinical check-up. On examination, his BP was found to be 136/88 mmHg. During his subsequent visits, the systolic blood pressure recorded was found to be within the range of 130-138 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure was within the range of 86-88mmHg. explanationHtml:
SBP ≥140 mm Hg and DBP <90 mmHg is called isolated systolic hypertension.

White-coat hypertension is characterized by:

  • The office blood pressure is ≥140/90 mm Hg on ≥3 separate office visits
  • ≥2 blood pressure measurements taken outside the office are <140/90 mm Hg, frequently using home blood pressure monitoring; and
  • There is no evidence of hypertensive target organ damage.

Note: The ESC 2024 Guidelines for Hypertension reccommends that home BP measurements are more reliable to diagnose hypertension and if that is not feasible the diagnosis can be made on repeated BP measurements in the office on more than one visit, this method also helps to exclude white-coat hypertension as well.

Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV) is the gold standard for measuring large artery stiffness due to hypertension.

Long-standing hypertension can lead to structural and functional changes in arteries and target organs like the heart, brain, arteries, and kidneys. This is called hypertension mediated organ damage (HMOD).

question: Which of the following is the gold standard investigation to measure vessel wall stiffness in patients suspected to have hypertension mediated end-organ damage (HMOD)?

explanationHtml:
According to the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 2024 guidelines for the management of hypertension, for patients with hypertension and coexisting diabetes, the desired goals for systolic blood pressure are between 120-129 mmHg, and diastolic blood pressure is between 70-79 mmHg.

It is usually not possible to achieve a target blood pressure range of 120–129/70–79 mmHg in the following group of patients:

  • Patients >85 years of age who are frail with a limited life expectancy
  • Pre-treatment symptomatic orthostatic hypotension
  • Limited predicted lifespan, which is less than 3 year,s due to comorbidities or general frailty
  • High competing risk for non-cardiovascular death, such as advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) with eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m²

In such cases, personalized treatment goals are preferred because aggressive BP lowering may increase the risk of adverse effects, such as falls, syncope, or poor quality of life. If the hypertension management is not well-tolerated or the target of 120-129/70-79 is not achieved, ‘As low as reasonably achievable’ (ALARA) principle is recommended.
question: A 60-year-old male patient has grade 2 hypertension. He is also a known case of type 2 diabetes for 9 years. What is the desired goal for blood pressure range in this patient?

explanationHtml:
According to ESC 2024 guidelines, the target systolic blood pressure for hypertensive patients in the age group 18-85 years with coronary artery disease is between 120-129 mmHg.

If this target is not tolerated, the patient is more than 85 years of age, has significant frailty, or has a life expectancy of less than 3 years, the target blood pressure goals are personalized.

In a patient with coronary artery disease with blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and above, both lifestyle changes and pharmacological therapy are started as management.
question: While treating a 45 year old hypertensive patient with underlying coronary artery disease, what target systolic blood pressure should you titrate for, as per the  ESC 2024 guidelines?

explanationHtml:
In this patient with no markers of cardiovascular disease, no hypertension-mediated end-organ damage (HMOD), and normal renal function, immediate pharmacological treatment is recommended when the blood pressure (BP) is ≥140/90 mmHg according to the 2024 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of hypertension.

Guidelines for starting pharmacological therapy:

  • Adults 18–85 years with SBP ≥140 mm Hg or DBP ≥90 mm Hg without risk of ASCVD, target organ damage, comorbidites like diabetes.
  • Adults 18-85 years with SBP ≥130 mm Hg or DBP ≥80 mm Hg with risk of ASCVD, target organ damage, comorbidites like diabetes.
  • Adults ≥85 years, moderate-to-severe frailty, symptomatic OH, short life expectancy - personalised target blood pressure goals and treatment

In adults of 18-85 yrs, the recommended target BP is 120-129/70-79 mmHg, to reduce CVD risk.

ESC 2024 Hypertension grading:

BLOOD PRESSURE CATEGORY SYSTOLIC BP DIASTOLIC BP
Non-elevated <120 mmHg <70 mmHg
Elevated 120-139 mmHg 70-89 mmHg
Hypertension ≥140 mmHg ≥90 mmHg

Note: The latest guidelines for hypertension are the 2024 ESC guidelines. Major updates include new blood pressure categories - elevated, non-elevated and hypertension; new target for SBP (120-129 mmHg) and DBP (70-79 mmHg); pharmacological and lifestyle changes are started simultaneously for patients with hypertension ( BP > 140/90 mmHg).

Previously, ESH 2023 had the similar guidelines as ESC 2018 except ESH 2023 had updated SCORE2 and SCORE2-OP risk prediction models for cardiovascular risk assessment. The latest guidelines for hypertension from India was from 2016 NHM guidelines by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Hypertension grading according to NHM 2016 is - Grade 1 (140-159/90-99 mmHg) , Grade 2 (160-179/100-109 mmHg), Grade 3 (≥ 180 / ≥ 110 mmHg), Isolated systolic hypertension SBP ≥140 mmHg and DBP ≤ 90mmHg).They recommend monotherapy for Grade 1 and 2 hypertension.
question: A 58-year-old male patient has been diagnosed with hypertension.  On examination, there is no existing cardiovascular disease, no hypertension mediated organ damage (HMOD) and the renal function is normal. He should be immediately started with pharmacological management if his blood pressure is more than ______.

explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario, the patient is hypertensive along with chronic kidney disease. The preferred initial antihypertensive treatment is captopril with amlodipine.

The preferred treatment in hypertensive patients with chronic kidney disease is a combination of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) with calcium channel blockers (CCBs) or diuretics (ACEi/ARBs + CCBs/diuretics).
question: A 72-year-old man who is a known hypertensive for 12 years comes for a regular health check-up. On examination, his blood pressure is 172/100 mmHg. His serum creatinine is 1.5mg/dL, urinary albumin to creatinine ratio (UACR) is 40mg/g, and GFR is 49mL/min. What is the preferred antihypertensive treatment in this scenario?

explanationHtml:
Metoprolol, when added with verapamil, leads to bradycardia with AV block.

Verapamil and β blockers have additive effect on inhibiting SA node and AV conduction, and the combination should be avoided to prevent severe bradycardia and conduction block.

These agents can also have additive effect on decreasing left ventricular function which could seriously impair cardiac output in a patient with heart failure.

Other indications for beta-blockers are:

  • Congestive heart failure due to systolic dysfunction
  • Post myocardial infarction

question: A hypertensive patient underwent coronary angiography after he presented with chest pain. His angiographic image is as below. What is the preferred drug for the management of hypertension in this patient?

explanationHtml: The most likely etiology is pheochromocytoma. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache and profuse sweating. The presence of this triad in association with hypertension and elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrine makes pheochromocytoma a likely diagnosis.
question: A 30-year-old man presents with sudden onset of a headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. He had several such episodes in the past. During these episodes, his BP is found to be high. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely etiology?

explanationHtml:
Hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis is seen in Liddle's syndrome.

Liddle's syndrome (pseudo aldosteronism) is an autosomal dominant condition that is caused due to the increased activation of ENaC channels. This causes increased reabsorption of Na+ exchanged for K+ causing hypokalemia. Increased Na absorption leads to hypertension, and there is also a loss of H+ ion with K+, leading to metabolic alkalosis. It is associated with low renin and low aldosterone levels.
question: A 35-year-old female patient has hypokalemia, hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely etiology?

explanationHtml:
Hypertensive emergencies are situations in which grade 3 hypertension (BP>180/110 mmHg) is associated with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD).

Treatment of hypertensive emergency depends on the type of end-organ damage present (as shown in the table below). It is treated with rapidly acting intravenous antihypertensive agents.

The first step of management in hypertensive emergencies like hypertensive encephalopathy, is to immediately reduce mean arterial blood (MAP) pressure by only upto 25% in the first hour. Rapid reduction of blood pressure may lead to reduced cerebral blood flow and result in cerebral infarction.

The table below shows the treatment of various hypertensive emergencies with intravenous drug therapy.

question:
Which of the following statements are true with respect to hypertensive emergency as per ESC 2018 guidelines?

1) BP >180/110mm Hg
2) Acute end-organ damage is usually not present
3) The initial goal in hypertensive emergency presenting as encephalopathy is to bring down the SBP no more than 30% within 2 hours
4) Should be treated using parenteral drugs

explanationHtml:
Patient 3 suffers from hypertensive urgency as BP > 180/110 mmHg and end-organ damage is not seen.

Target organ damage is absent in hypertensive urgency but is present in a hypertensive emergency.

Severe hypertension (grade 3) is generally defined as blood pressure ≥180/110 mmHg. Hypertensive emergency, hypertensive urgency, and malignant hypertension are all forms of severe hypertension.

Option A: Patient 1 suffers from hypertension. Since BP <180/110 mmHg it is not a hypertensive crisis (urgency or emergency).

Option B: Patient 2 has a BP > 180/110 mmHg along with symptoms of hypertensive encephalopathy. This is an example of a hypertensive emergency as there is severe hypertension with signs or symptoms of hypertensive-mediated organ damage (HMOD).

Option D: Patient 4 has a BP > 180/110 mm Hg along with papilledema. This is a case of severe hypertension associated with fundoscopic changes (flame hemorrhages, papilloedema) which is suggestive of malignant hypertension. Microangiopathy, DIC, and encephalopathy may also be present. Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and small arteries is seen. The prognosis is very poor if untreated.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) or acute hypertensive encephalopathy is a rare complication in patients with an acute rise in blood pressure. Due to the acute rise, there is increased cerebral perfusion and edema of the brain. Clinically it is recognized by alteration in mental status, nausea, headache, visual disturbance, seizure, or development of focal neurological deficits.
question:
Which of the following patients would you diagnose as having hypertensive urgency?

  1. A 50-year-old man with a BP of 162/104 mm Hg with no other complaints
  2. A 47-year-old woman with alteration in mental status, nausea, headache, and a BP of 190/120 mm
  3. A 60-year-old man with a BP of 188/120 mm Hg without any target organ damage
  4. A 55-year-old woman with a BP of 200/140 mm Hg along with papilloedema

explanationHtml:
The above scenario points towards the diagnosis of malignant hypertension. The drug which is least useful in the management is furosemide(diuretic).

Volume depletion is common in patients with malignant hypertension, and the administration of a diuretic together with a hypertensive agent can lead to an extreme drop in blood pressure.

Diuretics are generally not recommended for the rapid reduction of blood pressure in patients with hypertensive crises. They are used only in conditions of volume overload such as acute pulmonary edema.
question: A 55-year-old female patient who is a known case of hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with a severe headache and vomiting. The patient is agitated and her blood pressure is 220/120 mmHg. Ophthalmoscopy reveals the presence of papilledema. Which of the following antihypertensive is least useful in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
A strong modifiable risk factor for the development of hypertension is obesity.

Hypertension is defined as repeated office systolic blood pressure of ≥ 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure of ≥ 90 mm Hg (ESC 2024).

Primary/essential hypertension is the leading cause of hypertension in adults. It is caused due to the interaction of genetic factors with various other factors such as diet, sedentary lifestyle, etc. In some people, hypertension may result from renal, endocrine, or adrenal disorders (secondary hypertension).

Risk factors of hypertension can be divided into modifiable and non-modifiable:

Non-modifiable risk factors are:

  1. Age- risk increases with age
  2. Sex- in young and middle-aged adults, the risk is higher in males
  3. Genetic factors- mutation in the genes which encode the components of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, atrial natriuretic peptide, and alpha adducin
  4. Ethnicity

Modifiable risk factors are:

  1. Obesity
  2. High alcohol intake
  3. High salt intake
  4. Sedentary lifestyle
  5. Stress
  6. Dyslipidemia
  7. Diet low in potassium and calcium
question: Which of the following is a strong modifiable risk factor for the development of hypertension?

correctAnswer: B. Left anterior descending coronary artery
explanationHtml:
The left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) coronary artery is most commonly involved in coronary artery disease (CAD) or coronary heart disease or ischemic heart disease.

The regions affected are the anterior wall of the left ventricle near the apex and the anterior portion of the ventricular septum.

CAD is caused by plaque buildup in the walls of the coronary arteries that narrow over time and can partially or totally block the blood flow causing myocardial ischemia and subsequently infarction.

question: Which of the following arteries is most commonly involved in patients with coronary artery disease?

explanationHtml:
Subendocardium is the region of the myocardium most vulnerable to ischemic damage.

The myocardium is perfused from the epicardium to the endocardium. This results in the subendocardium being the least perfused region making it most vulnerable to ischemic damage.

A narrow zone of the myocardium immediately beneath the endocardium is spared from necrosis because it can be oxygenated by diffusion from the ventricle.

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of Wellens syndrome. It is alternatively known as anterior, descending, T-wave syndrome. The ECG pattern of Wellens syndrome is relatively common in patients who exhibit symptoms consistent with unstable angina.

ECG in the pain-free interval is characterized by deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in precordial leads and with minimal or no ST elevations. Cardiac enzymes are normal or mildly elevated.

These patients are at high risk for impending large anterior wall acute myocardial infarction.

The ECG below shows biphasic T waves in leads V2 and V3 and inverted T waves in leads V4 and V5 in Wellens syndrome.

question: A patient presented to the emergency with symptoms of unstable angina. ECG done in pain-free interval showed biphasic T waves in precordial leads without ST changes. Cardiac troponins were normal. Coronary angiography revealed stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Troponin I is normal ; CK-MB is normal
explanationHtml:
The levels of cardiac markers remain unchanged in stable and unstable angina as there is no necrosis of cardiac myocytes.

The clinical presentations of ischemic heart disease can be broadly classified into:

  • Chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) - this includes
    • Stable angina - this is an episodic angina that occurs with predictable severity, frequency, and threshold of precipitation by stressors, and is relieved by rest and nitrates
  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) - this includes
    • Unstable angina - this is diagnosed in patients with symptoms suggestive of an ACS with no elevation of biomarkers
    • Myocardial infarction - it is the necrosis and death of a portion of the myocardium due to prolonged ischemia. The cardiac biomarkers are elevated in this condition

question: In a patient with suspected stable angina, which of the following findings are likely to be present?

explanationHtml:
When a patient with angina is asked to localize the sensation, he or she typically places a hand over the sternum, sometimes with a clenched fist, to indicate a squeezing, central, substernal discomfort. This is called Levine’s sign.

Option A: Mayne's sign- Drop of at least 15 mmHg in the diastolic blood pressure on raising the arm. It occurs in patients with aortic regurgitation (not reliable).

Option C: Frank’s sign- Diagonal crease in the ear lobe indicative of cardiovascular diseases and/or diabetes.

Option D: Friedreich's sign- Exaggerated drop in JVP seen in constrictive pericarditis.

question: While evaluating a patient with chest pain in the emergency, you ask him to localize the sensation. He places a hand over the sternum with a clenched fist. What is this sign called?

correctAnswer: D. Crescendo decrescendo nature of pain
explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of stable angina in which the pain is usually crescendo-decrescendo in nature.

Characteristic features of pain in stable angina:

  • Squeezing, central, substernal discomfort
  • Crescendo-decrescendo in nature
  • Typically lasts 2 to 5 min
  • Can radiate occasionally to neck, jaw, epigastrium, shoulders, left arm.

Angina is rarely localized below the umbilicus or above the mandible. Myocardial ischemic discomfort does not radiate to the trapezius muscles, that radiation pattern is more typical of pericarditis.

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with chest discomfort, associated with a squeezing sensation in the substernal area. She added that it was precipitated by physical activity and relieved on taking rest. Which of the following is a feature of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario is suggestive of STEMI with bradycardia which is a feature of inferior wall myocardial infarction. Up to one-half with inferior infarction show evidence of parasympathetic hyperactivity (bradycardia and/or hypotension).

Many patients have a normal pulse rate and blood pressure within the first hour of STEMI.

About one-fourth of patients with anterior infarction have manifestations of sympathetic nervous system hyperactivity (tachycardia and/or hypertension).

question: A patient presented with angina and ECG showed ST-segment elevation. The pulse rate was found to be 54 beats/min and blood pressure was 98/56 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml: A transient midsystolic or late systolic apical murmur due to mitral regurgitation secondary to dysfunction of the mitral valve apparatus (papillary muscle dysfunction, LV dilation) may be present in STEMI.

question: A patient was admitted with acute MI. During a daily examination, a transient murmur was heard. What is the most likely cause for this finding?

explanationHtml:
Myoglobin is the earliest to rise in acute MI followed by troponin, CK-MB and then LDH.

Serum myoglobin and heart-type fatty acid-binding protein are smaller molecules that diffuse through interstitial ﬂuids more rapidly after cell death than the larger CK and troponin molecules. They become abnormal as early as 30 minutes after myocardial injury. Neither molecule is specific to myocardial tissue. Myoglobin levels are not tested in routine practice.
lessonTitle: Ischemic Heart Disease   Presentation And Diagnosis
question: Which of the following cardiac biomarkers is the earliest to rise after acute myocardial infarction?

explanationHtml:
The most preferred cardiac biomarker for myocardial injury/acute MI amongst the given options is cardiac troponin-I.

Cardiac troponin-I, CK-MB, and myoglobin are significantly more specific for acute-MI than cardiac troponin-T.

The cardiac troponins are particularly valuable when there is clinical suspicion of a small MI that may be below the detection limit for CK-MB measurement. They have replaced CK-MB as the biomarker of choice for diagnosing myocardial infarction.

Cardiac troponins:

  • Most specific cardiac biomarker for myocardial injury/acute MI
  • Elevations are useful for short & long-term prognoses in MI
  • Elevations correlate with the estimation of infarct size and risk of death
  • Newer highly sensitive assays for troponins become positive within the first 3 hours after onset of chest pain in MI

question: A patient is under evaluation for acute MI. Which of the following biomarkers would you prefer to test for?

correctAnswer: D. A 48-year-old man diagnosed with angina
explanationHtml:
Troponins are not elevated in patients suffering from angina. Troponins are elevated in the case of myocardial necrosis (seen in MI) whereas angina is associated with myocardial insufficiency/ischemia.

Conditions associated with an elevation in cardiac troponins:

  • MI
  • Myocarditis
  • Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
  • Myocardial contusion
  • Cardioversion/defibrillation
  • LV strain from CHF
  • Hypertensive crisis
  • RV strain from PE
  • Renal disease
  • Sepsis

question: Elevated cardiac troponins may not be seen in which of the following patients?

explanationHtml:
Troponin (serial) is the preferred biomarker for diagnosing a reinfarction, which usually occurs within 28 days of an MI.

Reinfarction is indicated when a ≥20 percent rise in troponin is seen on measuring the levels at an interval of 3-6 hours.

question: Which of the following biomarkers is preferred for diagnosing reinfarction in a patient post-NSTEMI?

correctAnswer: B. Ratio of LDH 1 / LDH 2 > 1 in plasma
explanationHtml:
In myocardial injury, the LDH-1 fraction increases, and the ratio of LDH-1 to LDH-2 becomes >1 in the plasma. This is called flipped LDH pattern.

Normally, the LDH-2 fraction is greater than the LDH-1 fraction in the plasma, and therefore, the ratio of LDH-1 to LDH-2 is normally <1.

question: What is the maximum predicted heart rate in a 50-year-old gentleman on exercise tolerance test?

correctAnswer: D. AAA with transverse diameter of 5.5 cm
explanationHtml:
Treadmill exercise testing (treadmill test) may be safely performed in patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

Absolute contraindications to exercise testing:

  • Acute myocardial infarction (within 2 days)
  • High-risk unstable angina
  • Uncontrolled cardiac arrhythmia with hemodynamic compromise
  • Active endocarditis
  • Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis
  • Decompensated heart failure
  • Acute pulmonary embolism or pulmonary infarction
  • Acute myocarditis or pericarditis
  • Severe pulmonary hypertension
  • Aortic dissection

Relative Contraindications to exercise testing:

  • Known left main coronary artery stenosis
  • Moderate aortic stenosis with uncertain relation to symptoms
  • Tachyarrhythmias with uncontrolled ventricular rates
  • Acquired complete heart block
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with severe resting gradient
  • Mental impairment with limited ability to cooperate

question:
Which of the following is not a contraindication for performing an exercise tolerance test?

AAA : abdominal aortic aneurysm

explanationHtml:
Phenylephrine, an alpha-receptor agonist, cannot be used for a patient undergoing stress echocardiography as it causes vasoconstriction.

Dobutamine (preferred agent) and vasodilators (dipyridamole, adenosine, regadenoson) are used for pharmacological stress echocardiography.

Pharmacologic stress testing is used in those who cannot exercise because of pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, musculoskeletal disease, or exertional dyspnea.

Stress echocardiography can be done using either exercise (e.g.: treadmill test or bicycle test) or pharmacologic agents.

question: Which of the following drugs cannot be used for a patient undergoing stress echocardiography?

correctAnswer: C. Failure to increase systolic BP by at least 20mmHg
explanationHtml:
A failure to increase systolic blood pressure by 10 mm Hg, or a sustained decrease in systolic blood pressure of 10 mm Hg or more, is suggestive of multivessel (or left main) CAD.

Other abnormalities on exercise testing that are suggestive of multivessel CAD include:

  • Early-onset of ischemic ST-segment depression
  • ST-segment depression of ≥2 mm (0.2mV) involving 5 or more leads, or persisting ≥5 minutes into recovery
  • Exercise-induced ST-segment elevation is also consistent with multivessel CAD
  • Recent evidence suggests that ST-segment elevation of ≥1 mm in lead aVR may be a significant predictor of left main coronary artery disease, proximal left anterior descending (LAD) artery disease, or at least multivessel CAD

An exercise tolerance/treadmill test involves walking in place on a treadmill while monitoring the electrical activity of your heart. Throughout the test, the speed and incline of the treadmill increase. The results show how well your heart responds to the stress of different levels of exercise.

question: Which questionnaire is used for the assessment of a patient who presented with symptoms of angina?

explanationHtml:
During acute myocardial infarction, the ECG evolves through 3 stages:

  1. T-wave peaking and T-wave inversion:
    • Peaked T-wave aka hyperacute T-wave- first ECG change (occurs within minutes)
    • If the blood flow is restored or the oxygen demands of the heart are met, the T waves will revert to normal
    • If myocardial cell death has occurred, T wave inversions appear (over days) and persist for months to years.
    • A nonspecific finding and is indicative only of ischemia and not diagnostic of infarction
  2. ST-segment elevation occurs over minutes to hours (after T-wave peaking)
  3. The appearance of new pathologic Q-waves:
    • Occurs over hours to days (after ST-segment elevation) and is indicative of an evolving MI
    • The persistence of pathological Q-waves indicates irreversible myocardial cell death

[[figure-1]]

question: Which of the following ECG findings is first to appear in a patient suspected of acute myocardial infarction?

explanationHtml:
Measurement of troponin is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours.

[[figure-1]]

Troponin T/I:

  • Highly specific for MI
  • Troponin I is more important than troponin T.
  • Troponins will remain elevated longer than creatine kinase (CK), for up to 14 days.
  • This makes troponins a superior marker for diagnosing MI in the recent past (late diagnosis).
  • Reinfarction: It is now clear that cardiac troponin (cTn) increases rapidly, even if it is from an abnormal baseline in patients with reinfarction.
  • Sometimes, cTn concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. In this case, the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement

Creatine kinase (CK):

  • Less sensitive and specific than troponins
  • When cTn is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH):

  • Normally, LDH2>LDH1, but in MI, LDH1>LDH2. This is called the flipping of the LDH ratio
  • Not preferred for diagnosis

Myoglobin:

  • The earliest enzyme to increase after MI.
  • Not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle

Heart-type fatty acid-binding protein (H-FABP), which mainly exists in cardiomyocytes, has recently emerged as a potential biomarker that was found to be sensitive for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. H-FABP as an early marker and cTnI as a late marker would be the ideal combination to cover the complete diagnostic window for AMI

question: A patient presented with the complaints of chest pain. Which among the following is the best investigation to diagnose MI within 2-4 hours?

explanationHtml:
There is no ST-segment elevation in unstable angina.

Differential diagnosis of ST-segment elevation (Mnemonic-ELEVATION):

  • Electrolytes(Hypercalcemia, Hyperkalemia)
  • Left bundle branch block
  • Early(Benign) repolarization, Embolism(Acute pulmonary)
  • Ventricular hypertrophy
  • Arrhythmia(Brugada syndrome), Aneurysm of LV, Aortic dissection, Antiarrhythmic drugs(Class 1c)
  • Tako-tsubo syndrome, Tumor invading left ventricle, Trauma to ventricles
  • Infarction(MI), Inflammation(Myocarditis, Pericarditis)
  • Osborn J waves (Hypothermia or hypercalcemia)
  • Non-atherosclerotic vasospasm(Prinzmetal's angina)

question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with an ST-segment elevation?

explanationHtml:
The above scenario in which rest pain is associated with ST-segment elevation and transient coronary vasospasm is suggestive of Prinzmetal's angina. The drug of choice is a calcium channel blocker.

Prinzmetal variant angina (PVA) is a clinical syndrome in which chest pain occurs without the usual precipitating factors. It usually results from coronary vasoconstriction (vasospasm) and tends to involve the right coronary artery.

It is a supply ischemia and usually causes transmural ischemia (subendocardial in classic angina pectoris).

It often affects women under 50 years of age. It characteristically occurs in the early morning, awakening patients from sleep, and may be associated with arrhythmias or conduction defects.

The clinical diagnosis of PVA is made by the detection of transient ST-segment elevation with rest pain. Coronary angiography demonstrates transient coronary spasm which is the diagnostic hallmark of PVA.

Nitrates and calcium channel blockers both can be used in alleviating symptoms in Prinzmetal's angina. However due to the development of nitrate tolerance in some individuals, they are less preferred and calcium channel blockers such as verapamil, diltiazem are used as first-line agents.

question: A 38-year-old woman presented with chest pain that was unrelated to physical exertion. ECG showed ST-segment elevation. Intracoronary acetylcholine provocation testing revealed a transient spasm of the right coronary artery. What is the drug of choice in this condition?

correctAnswer: B. 1.5 million units IV over 1 hour
explanationHtml:
In patients with STEMI, streptokinase is administered as an intravenous infusion, with a dose of 1.5 million units over the course of 1 hour.

Fibrinolytic therapy should ideally be initiated within 30 minutes of presentation. The fibrinolytic agents that have been approved for IV use in patients with STEMI are:

  • Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)
  • Streptokinase
  • Tenecteplase (TNK)
  • Reteplase (rPA)

Adverse effects of streptokinase:

  • Transient hypotension
  • Allergic reactions
  • Hemorrhage

Fibrinolytic agent with:

question: Which of the given fibrinolytic agents is least preferred for thrombolysis in a patient with MI?

Tenecteplase and reteplase are referred to as bolus fibrinolytics as their administration does not require prolonged intravenous infusion.

question: While planning thrombolysis for a patient with MI, use of which of the following agents will reduce the chances of a dosing error?

Contraindications for the use of fibrinolytic agents

Absolute contraindications

Relative contraindications

History of hemorrhagic stroke at any time

Current use of anticoagulants (INR ≥2)

Non-hemorrhagic stroke or other cerebrovascular events within last three months

Recent (<2 weeks) invasive or surgical procedure

Severe uncontrolled hypertension unresponsive to emergency treatment

Prolonged (>10 min) cardiopulmonary resuscitation

Suspicion of aortic dissection

Known bleeding diathesis

Active internal bleeding (excluding menses)

Pregnancy

Hemorrhagic ophthalmic condition (e.g., hemorrhagic diabetic retinopathy)

Active peptic ulcer disease
