question: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with violent shaking of arms and legs for the past 15 minutes. He is a chronic alcoholic whose last intake was 2 days ago. IV lorazepam is administered to this patient. After 5 minutes, the seizures have not stopped. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Continue treatment for another 18 months
explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario of a girl on antiepileptics for 6 months with no further seizures, no family history, normal EEG, neurological examination, and intelligence, antiepileptics should be continued for another 18 months since she’s already taken for 6 months (minimum 2 years) to prevent seizure recurrence.

Anti-epileptic drugs withdrawal is considered only when an adult patient has been seizure-free for ≥2 years along with the following criteria:

  • Normal CNS examination including intelligence
  • Normal EEG and normal MRI
  • Single seizure type
  • No family history of epilepsy.

It is preferable to reduce the dose of the drug gradually over 2–3 months.

Other options:

Option A: Sudden cessation of drug therapy may cause recurrence of seizure hence not advised.

Option B: The patient has a seizure-free interval of only 6 months and therefore, is not yet eligible for considering medication withdrawal.

Option D: Life-long treatment is not necessary in this case as the patient meets all the above-mentioned criteria for drug withdrawal after 2 years.

Note: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), the most common idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndrome is known to have a high risk of seizure recurrence, and hence antiepileptics are continued lifelong in a majority of patients.

options.text: Stop the treatment and follow up
Gradually taper the drug and stop treatment

question: A 16-year-old girl, who is taking antiepileptics, has had a seizure-free period of 6 months. She has no family history of epilepsy. Her EEG is now normal and she has a normal neurological exam and intelligence. What would your advice be?

explanationHtml:
Weight gain, alopecia, and thrombocytopenia are the side effects of valproate use.

Adverse effects of Sodium Valproate (mnemonic: VALPROATE)

  • Vomiting
  • Alopecia
  • Liver toxicity
  • Pancreatitis
  • Rash
  • Obesity
  • Anorexia
  • Teratogenicity (most common: spina bifida), thrombocytopenia, tremors
  • Edema

The first-line agents for treating GTCS are valproate, leviteracetam, and lamotrigine.
question: A 30-year-old man on antiepileptic therapy for GTCS presents with weight gain, alopecia and thrombocytopenia. Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is the most likely cause for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Café au lait is a neurocutaneous marker seen in neurofibromatosis, not a component of West syndrome.

The triad of West syndrome is:

  • Infantile spasms (also called Salaam spells)
  • Developmental regression
  • Hypsarrhythmia (abnormal EEG)

West syndrome is treated with:

  • ACTH injections
  • Vigabatrin if associated with tuberous sclerosis
question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with West syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is of infantile spasms, developmental regression and the EEG showing hypsarrhythmia is suggestive of West syndrome. The drug of choice for this condition is ACTH.

West syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in infancy. It is characterized by a triad of

  • Infantile spasm (also called salaam spells) is a convulsive disease characterized by brief, symmetric axial muscle contraction (neck, trunk, and/or extremities).
  • Developmental regression
  • Hypsarrhythmia (Himalayan wave pattern) on EEG: Characterized by a high-voltage, slow, chaotic background with multifocal spikes

Treatment of West syndrome includes:

  • ACTH
  • Vigabatrin if associated with tuberous sclerosis
question: A 4-month-old child was brought with repeated epileptic spasms. The child had reached his normal milestone at the age of 2 months. But the parents noticed that he lost the ability to hold his head steadily and he recently couldn't track light or sound. The EEG findings are shown below. What is the drug of choice for the treatment of this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows a Shagreen patch, which is a typical feature of tuberous sclerosis. Vigabatrin is effective in the control of seizures in patients with tuberous sclerosis.

Tuberous sclerosis (Bourneville disease) is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in either the TSC1 or the TSC2 gene. The clinical features seen are as follows:

  • Seizures
  • Intellectual disability
  • Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas)
  • Shagreen patch
  • Hypomelanotic macules
  • Periungual fibromas
  • Renal angiomyolipomas
  • Cardiac rhabdomyomas.

A Shagreen patch is an irregularly thickened, slightly elevated, soft, skin-colored plaque, usually in the lumbosacral region.
question: Which of the following drugs is effective in controlling infantile spasms in a patient who has the neurocutaneous marker as shown in image?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario of focal seizure with impaired consciousness which along with hippocampal sclerosis is suggestive of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.

The following image shows left hippocampal sclerosis:

question: A 14-year-old boy develops an episode of involuntary jerky movements of the left hand accompanied by a repetitive chewing movement. He had a blank look on his face and was unresponsive during this episode. He also has no memory of the episode. EEG was normal and MRI showed hippocampal sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Seizures can be controlled with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine
explanationHtml: Seizures of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy are not controlled with carbamazepine. The condition is refractory to anticonvulsant therapy but responds well to surgical intervention.

options.text: It results in focal seizures with dyscognitive features
The person experiences an aura before the seizure
It is associated with a family history of epilepsy
Seizures can be controlled with anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding mesial temporal lobe epilepsy ?

explanationHtml:
Oxcarbazepine is known to worsen myoclonic seizures and is therefore contraindicated in it.

Drugs like carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin can worsen the myoclonic, absence, tonic and atonic seizures and are therefore avoided.
question: Which of the following drugs must be avoided in myoclonic seizures?

correctAnswer: C. EEG showing less than 3Hz Spike and wave discharge
explanationHtml:
EEG showing <3Hz spike and wave discharge is a characteristic feature of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in childhood. It may occur due to various reasons such as developmental anomalies, mutations, trauma, infections, etc. It is characterized by a typical triad of

  • Multiple seizure types
  • Intellectual disability
  • Typical <3 Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG

Treatment includes administration of anti-epileptic drugs such as lamotrigine and sodium valproate. It is frequently refractory to medical therapy and usually has a poor prognosis.

Note: EEG with symmetric 3 Hz spike and wave pattern is seen in typical absence seizure.

options.text: EEG showing less than 3Hz Spike and wave discharge

question: Which of the following is seen in patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Glucocerebrosidase infusions are not the treatment for Lafora's disease. There is no approved treatment for Lafora body disease.

The mainstay of management is anti-epileptic drugs, valproate in particular; however, other AEDs such as topiramate, ethosuximide, and phenobarbital can be used to control seizures. Most recently, perampanel, a new AMPA receptor antagonist AED, is shown to be effective.

Lafora body disease is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease and has an adolescent onset. It is associated with polyglucosan intracellular inclusion bodies. It is characterized by:

  • Progressive myoclonus
  • Epileptic seizures
  • Dementia
  • Ataxia.

Diagnosis is by DNA sequencing. Death usually occurs within 10 years of the onset of the disease.
question: Which of the following is false regarding Lafora’s disease?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of a gelastic seizure.

This condition is also known as gelastic epilepsy, and is a rare type of seizure that involves a sudden burst of energy, usually in the form of laughing or crying. It is seen when the seizure focus is within the left prefrontal cortex. Gelastic seizures have been associated classically with hypothalamic hamartomas.

Option A: Kluver Bucy syndrome is characterized by hypersexuality, placidity, a tendency to explore the environment with the mouth, inability to recognize the emotional significance of visual stimuli, and constantly shifting attention, called hypermetamorphosis.

Option B: Witzelsucht is a tendency to joke and make puns.

Option C: Pseudobulbar affect is defined by involuntary, sudden, and frequent episodes of laughing or crying that are generally out of proportion or inappropriate to the situation.
question: You are at a criminal court to provide medical testimony. The trial ends with the accused being sentenced to life imprisonment. Abruptly, the convict breaks into uncontrollable laughter. Within minutes, he collapses and starts to have a seizure. His lawyer reports that he has a childhood seizure disorder. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario reveals multiple types of seizures such as atonic seizures (sudden falls), absence seizures (blank stares and unresponsive), and generalized tonic-clonic seizures in this patient. This is a characteristic feature of Lenox-Gastaut syndrome.

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is a rare type of epilepsy syndrome that begins in childhood. It may occur due to various reasons such as developmental anomalies, mutations, trauma, infections, etc. It is characterized by a typical triad of

  • Multiple seizure types
  • Intellectual disability
  • Typical <3 Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG

Treatment includes administration of anti-epileptic drugs such as lamotrigine and sodium valproate. It is frequently refractory to medical therapy and usually has a poor prognosis.

options.text: Focal seizures progressing to generalized seizures
Myoclonic epilepsy progressing to generalized seizures

question: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the OPD following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She had previous episodes of sudden falls at school and also sometimes stares with a blank face. She is also found to be having poor scholastic performance. Her EEG reveals a slow spike and wave pattern.  What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
A decrease in the cerebral blood flow below 20 mL/100 g/min causes reversible ischemia.

If this state is prolonged for several hours to days, it can lead to infarction. A decrease in CBF to 0 causes the death of the brain tissue within 4–10 min.

Normal cerebral blood flow (CBF) in an adult brain at rest is 50–55 mL/100 g/min.
question: Ischemia occurs in the brain when the cerebral blood flow falls below _____.

explanationHtml:
This patient with mitral stenosis and acute onset weakness of the left arm is most likely to have had an embolic stroke, which is a type of ischemic stroke. Embolic strokes tend to occur suddenly with maximum neurologic deficit present at onset.

Mitral stenosis is known to cause atrial fibrillation and is a common cause of cardioembolic stroke.

Transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a temporary, focal neurological deficit of sudden onset (stroke-like symptoms) lasting for less than 24 hours. This occurs due to focal ischemia of the brain, retina or cochlea. Most TIAs last for less than 1 hour to a few minutes.

There is a high risk of developing an ischemic stroke after a TIA, especially for the first 3 months following a TIA.
question: A patient presented with acute onset of weakness of the left arm which resolved completely in 10 days. He is known to have mitral stenosis, hypertension and dyslipidemia.  What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This patient's clinical features are suggestive of a transient ischemic attack. The risk of stroke following TIAs is determined by the ABCD2 score.

CHADS2-VASc score is used to determine the risk of stroke in a patient with atrial fibrillation.

CURB-65 is a scoring system used to predict mortality in patients with community-acquired pneumonia.

APACHE II is a scoring system used to predict ICU mortality.
question: A patient presented with right-sided hemiparesis that completely resolved in 4-6 hours. What score will you use to determine the risk of a future stroke in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario along with the ECG findings are suggestive of atrial fibrillation. The risk of stroke in this condition is determined by CHA2DS2-VASC score.

The ECG show irregular QRS complexes of normal morphology and absent P waves.
question: A 67-year-old patient with hypertension, diabetes, and asthma is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse during a routine physical examination. ECG findings are shown below. How is the risk of stroke determined in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Lacunar infarcts, also called small vessel stroke, refer to infarction following atherothrombotic or lipohyalinotic occlusion of small penetrating arteries in the brain. These penetrating arteries arise from the stem of the middle cerebral artery, circle of Willis, and basilar and vertebral arteries.

The principal risk factors are hypertension and old age.

The image below shows two lacunar infarctions on a CT.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 73-year-old woman who was brought to the ER with hemiparesis was found to have a lacunar infarction. What causes this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Crural monoplegia with urinary incontinence
explanationHtml:
Crural monoplegia with urinary incontinence is not caused by a lacunar stroke. It is caused by the occlusion of A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery. Crural monoplegia refers to a monoplegia of the lower limbs.

The types of lacunar syndromes are as follows:

  1. Pure motor hemiparesis - infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule
  2. Pure sensory stroke - infarct in the thalamus
  3. Ataxic hemiparesis - infarct in the pons or internal capsule
  4. Dysarthria and clumsy hand syndrome - infarction in the pons or internal capsule.

[[figure-1]]

The ACA is divided into two segments:

  • The pre-communal (A1) circle of Willis, or stem, which connects the internal carotid artery to the anterior communicating artery
  • The post-communal (A2) segment distal to the anterior communicating artery

[[figure-2]]
question: Which of the following is not caused by a lacunar stroke?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario where the patient is unable to perform learned skilled movements is suggestive of apraxia. The lesion is likely to be in the dominant parietal lobe as apraxia is a feature of a lesion in this area.

The features of dominant parietal lobe lesions are as follows:

  • Apraxia - inability to perform learned skilled movements
  • Acalculia - difficulty performing simple mathematical tasks
  • Alexia - inability to recognize or read written words or letters
  • Agnosia - inability to recognize and identify objects, persons, or sounds
  • Dysphasia - language disorder marked by deficiency in the generation of speech and its comprehension
  • Contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia
  • Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, dysgraphia, finger agnosia, right-left confusion)

Features of non-dominant parietal lobe lesions include:

  • Spatial disorientation
  • Constructional apraxia
  • Contralateral inferior homonymous quadrantanopia
  • Contralateral hemineglect.
question: A patient is diagnosed with an ischaemic stroke. His son says that he holds the comb incorrectly while combing his hair. During the evaluation, he was unable to button his shirt when requested. The lesion is most likely to be in which lobe?

explanationHtml:
Neglect is not a feature of temporal lobe lesion. It is a feature of a non-dominant parietal lobe lesion.

Features of dominant temporal lobe lesions:

  • Complex hallucinations - visual, auditory or olfactory
  • Memory impairment
  • Complex partial seizures
  • Wernicke’s aphasia
  • Contralateral superior quadrantanopia

Features of non-dominant temporal lobe lesions:

  • Poor non-verbal memory
  • Loss of musical skills
  • Complex hallucinations
  • Contralateral superior quadrantanopia.
question: Which of the following features is not likely to be seen in a patient with a temporal lobe lesion?

explanationHtml:
Antisocial behavior, urinary incontinence, and impaired memory in this patient are suggestive of frontal lobe involvement.

Features of frontal lobe lesions:

  • Disinhibition
  • Lack of initiative
  • Antisocial behavior
  • Impaired memory
  • Incontinence
  • Grasp reflexes
  • Anosmia.
question: A 43-year-old man is brought to the hospital due to extremely aggressive behaviour towards his family. His family members also say that he has become forgetful and has developed urinary incontinence. Which of the following lobes is likely to be involved in his disease process?

explanationHtml:
Paracentral lobule (PCL) is the continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri of the superolateral surface into the medial surface of cerebral hemisphere. It controls the motor and sensory innervations of the contralateral lower extremity. It is also responsible for cortical control of micturition and defecation.

The anterior two-thirds of PCL belong to Brodmann area 4, it reflects the primary motor cortex for the muscles of contralateral leg, foot, and perineum,it is functionally important in control of bladder and anal sphincters. Therefore, it's called the cortical center of defecation and micturition.

The posterior third of the PCL contains 3,2 and 1, it reflects the primary somatosensory representation of the leg and foot.

The A2 segment of the anterior cerebral artery supplies the paracentral lobule. Lesions in the paracentral lobule lead to:

  • Weakness and loss of sensation in contralateral lower limb
  • Urinary incontinence
  • Fecal incontinence.
question: In the sagittal section of the brain given below if the coloured area is affected, which of the following is not seen?

explanationHtml:
Lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus cause Wernicke’s or Fluent aphasia due to the involvement of the Wernicke's area. The speech is full of jargon and neologisms that make little sense (area no 22).

Broca's (Option B) or motor/non-fluent aphasia is seen in lesions of the inferior frontal gyrus which contains the motor speech area. Speech is non-fluent and interrupted, with a paucity of functional words.

The ability to name objects is compromised in anomic aphasia (Option C). This aphasia is caused by damage to the angular gyrus that disrupts visual information processing and transmission to the Wernicke area.

Conduction aphasia (Option D) is seen in lesions of the arcuate fasciculus, the bundle of nerve fibers connecting the Wernicke and Broca's areas. Repetition of words is impaired and paraphasias are observed, though not as much as in Wernicke aphasia.
question: Which type of aphasia is seen in the lesions of the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus?

explanationHtml:
Prosopagnosia, also called face blindness, is the inability to recognize faces including one's own image. This occurs due to occipitotemporal lobe damage, seen in posterior cerebral artery (PCA) strokes involving cortical branch occlusion.
It is not seen in anterior cerebral artery strokes.

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies parts of the frontal lobe, corpus callosum, paracentral lobule, and other deeper structures.

Signs and symptoms of ACA occlusion and structures involved:

  • Urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence
  • Paratonic rigidity
  • Abulia (Akinetic mutism), lack of spontaneity, slowness
  • Gait impairment
  • Paralysis of contralateral foot and leg
  • Paresis of the contralateral arm
  • Cortical sensory loss over the contralateral lower limb
  • Dyspraxia of left limbs, tactile aphasia in left limbs.
question: A 60-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation complains of sudden onset weakness of the right lower limb, with urinary and faecal incontinence. MRI shows an ischaemic stroke involving the left anterior cerebral artery. Which of the following features would you not expect to see in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Hemiplegia is most commonly associated with infarction of the area of distribution of middle cerebral artery.

Middle cerebral artery supplies the motor cortex responsible for sending the output to the motor neurons. Infarction in this territory leads to hemiplegia.

Infarction of area of distribution of vertebral, anterior spinal and posterior cerebral arteries can also lead to hemiplegia.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]
question: Infarction of area of distribution of which of the following arteries is most likely to be seen in a patient with hemiplegia?

explanationHtml:
Aphasia is not a feature of right middle cerebral artery infarct (MCA).

Aphasia occurs when there is damage to the dominant hemisphere, i.e., left hemisphere. The dominant hemisphere contains the language network which includes Broca’s area, Wernicke’s area, their interconnections and connections with frontal, parietal and temporal areas.

The MCA originates from the internal carotid artery. The stem of the MCA is referred to as the M1 segment. It gives rise to cortical and penetrating/lenticulostriate branches.

MCA stem occlusion leads to :

  • Contralateral hemiplegia
  • Hemianesthesia
  • Homonymous hemianopia
  • Global aphasia (dominant hemisphere)
  • Anosognosia, constructional apraxia, neglect (non-dominant hemisphere)

Occlusion of the lenticulostriate branches of MCA (lacunar stroke) may affect the genu of the internal capsule. This can lead to dysarthria with contralateral clumsy hand (fine motor weakness).
question: Which of the following features is not expected to be seen in a patient with a right middle cerebral artery infarct?

correctAnswer: C. Left M2 segment of MCA – inferior division
explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of homonymous right superior quadrantanopia (pie in the sky appearance) and sensory aphasia. These are seen in occlusion of the inferior division of the opposite side middle cerebral artery (MCA).

Parts of the middle cerebral artery:

  • The MCA originates from the internal carotid artery. The stem of the MCA is referred to as the M1 segment.
  • In the Sylvian fissure, the MCA divides into superior and inferior divisions. These branches are referred to as the M2 segments of the MCA.

Occlusion of the following sites and their effects are given below:

  • MCA stem (M1) - leads to contralateral hemiplegia, hemianesthesia and homonymous hemianopia amongst other features
  • Superior division of MCA (M2) on the dominant side - leads to motor aphasia (Broca's) and facio-brachial weakness
  • Inferior division of MCA (M2) on the dominant side - leads to sensory aphasia (Wernicke's) and contralateral superior quadrantanopia

The following image of coronal section of cerebral hemisphere shows the segments of MCA:

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Left M2 segment of MCA – inferior division
Right M2 segment of MCA – superior division

question: Visual field examination of a 52-year-old stroke patient reveals the finding shown in the image. During examination, you notice that he is not able to comprehend your instructions and sometimes gives irrelevant replies. What is the likely site of arterial occlusion?

correctAnswer: D. MCA territory of the left hemisphere
explanationHtml:
The presence of Wernicke’s aphasia without motor involvement suggests an infarct in the MCA territory of the left (dominant) hemisphere.

Wernicke’s area is located in the superior temporal gyrus in the dominant hemisphere (mostly the left side). This area is supplied by the inferior division of MCA.

MCA divides into superior and inferior divisions in the Sylvian fissure. These branches are referred to as the M2 segments of MCA.

  • The superior division - supplies the frontal and the superior parietal cortex.
  • The inferior division - supplies the inferior parietal and temporal cortex.

An infarct in the territory of the inferior division of MCA in the dominant hemisphere causes Wernicke’s aphasia without weakness. As the frontal cortex (containing the motor area) is supplied by the superior division and is not affected, weakness is not observed.

An infarct in the inferior division of MCA of the non-dominant hemisphere (mostly the right side) causes hemineglect without weakness.

options.text: ACA territory of the right hemisphere
ACA territory of the left hemisphere
MCA territory of the right hemisphere
MCA territory of the left hemisphere

question: A patient is found to have Wernicke’s aphasia without motor involvement. Where is the infarct likely to be?

explanationHtml:
Aphasia (dominant hemisphere), constructional apraxia and neglect (non-dominant hemisphere) are seen in MCA stem occlusion. These features are absent in anterior choroidal artery occlusion.

Features common to both MCA and anterior choroidal artery occlusion include:

  • Contralateral hemiplegia
  • Hemianaesthesia
  • Homonymous hemianopia.
question: Which of the following is not a feature of an anterior choroidal artery lesion?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of pontine haemorrhage. Clinical features of pontine haemorrhage are:

  • Deep coma
  • Quadriparesis and multiple cranial nerve dysfunction
  • Decerebrate rigidity
  • Pin-point pupils
  • Hyperpnea, hyperpyrexia, severe hypertension, and hyperhidrosis

Option A: The presence of hyperpyrexia and pin-point pupils rule out the possibility of spinal cord trauma.

Option B: Morphine poisoning is a differential diagnosis for pin-point pupils. But it leads to slower respiratory rate, not tachypnea.

Option D: In ponto-medullary laceration, medullary involvement would cause respiratory depression, leading to apnea. But here tachypnea is noted.
question:
A man is rushed to the ER after losing control of his car and crashing into a tree. Examination findings are given below. What is the most likely cause for his presentation?

BP - 190/100 mmHg

Respiratory rate - 22/minute

GCS - 9/15

Temperature - 106.8 °F

Head and neck examination - Minor abrasions over the face

CNS - Quadriparesis. Pupils are 2 mm and unreactive.

explanationHtml:
A patient presenting within 4.5 hours of the onset of focal neurological deficit, like sudden onset hemiparesis in this case with a normal non-contrast CT brain is most likely experiencing an ischemic stroke. The next step in management is to administer Intravenous thrombolysis.

Intravenous thrombolysis using a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator - rtPA Alteplase (0.9 mg/kg) or Tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg) should be immediately administered to patients with ischemic stroke who arrive in the window period (within 4.5 hours of symptom onset) with disabling symptoms.

As soon as the diagnosis of stroke is made clinically, a non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the brain is done to differentiate between hemorrhagic and ischemic stroke, because the management of the two is entirely different. Once an ischemic stroke is confirmed, the goal is to limit the size of the infarct by optimizing perfusion to the penumbra. Since the blood flow in the ischemic areas of the brain is dependent on high blood pressure, the target blood pressure is higher than normal in ischemic stroke.

Antihypertensives should only be administered if: (Option D)

  • BP is > 220/120 mmHg
  • BP is > 185/110 mmHg when the patient is planned for thrombolytic therapy.

Systolic blood pressure should not be lowered below 140 mmHg.

Other options:

Option A: If CT is normal it only rules out hemorrhagic stroke and changes of ischemic stroke usually take time to appear on NCCT.

Option B: Aspirin + clopidogrel is used in secondary prevention of stroke and also to prevent stroke following transient ischemic attacks. It is also used as a first line treatment for minor non-disabling strokes.
question: A patient presents with left-sided facial paralysis and left-sided limb weakness for the past 1 hour. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and her non-contrast CT brain appears normal. What would be the next step of management?

explanationHtml: A sustained blood pressure > 185/110 mmHg and recent myocardial infarction are contraindications for initiating thrombolysis in ischemic stroke.
question:
Thrombolysis is contraindicated in which of the following patients with ischaemic stroke?

1. A patient brought to the ER within half an hour of onset of symptoms

2. A 57-year-old man brought to the ER within 3 hours of onset of symptoms and having platelet count of 180,000 / µL

3. A patient with a sustained BP of 190/120 mm of Hg

4. A patient with a history of gastrointestinal bleeding about a month ago

5. A patient who has recent history of myocardial infarction

explanationHtml:

question: A patient with acute ischemic stroke requires IV thrombolysis. His symptoms had begun at 6:30 PM and he was brought to the hospital by 7:00 PM. For this treatment to be beneficial for the patient, it should be administered within what time?

explanationHtml:
Neglect is a feature of stroke that need not be treated. Although neglect indicates a poor prognosis, most patients recover without any treatment in 1-6 months.

Dysphagia(Option A) poses a high risk of aspiration and hence can't be left untreated. Spasticity(Option B) can be treated with baclofen, tizanidine. Untreated, it creates a psychosocial impact on the patient. Fever(Option C) is deleterious in stroke patients and must be treated.

Neglect can arise from injury to cortical-limbic-reticular network, that directs attention and integrates the localization and identification of a stimulus. Neglect is associated with poor scores and slower recovery, but severe neglect is rare beyond 6 months. Recovery is rapid in the first 2 weeks, regardless of the side of stroke. By 3 months, patients might have some residual visual neglect. The choice of an intervention depends on the mechanism of neglect, the patient can be treated for an underaroused right hemisphere which has difficulty processing sensory inputs.

Neurogenic dysphagia is an important cause of pulmonary infection in any patient with stroke, motor neuron disease, even transient dysphagia can lead to malnutrition, dehydration, aspiration pneumonia, and airway obstruction with asphyxia, it increases the risk of death and institutionalization. Early placement of nasogastric tube to feed patients after stroke has improved nutrition and reduced deaths.

Spasticity is seen in less than 20% of stroke patients. Patients with bilateral weakness from hypoxic injury are likely to have signs of spasticity. Exaggerated cutaneous and autonomic reflexes and involuntary spasms are disabling problems associated with spasticity. Physical modalities like slow stretching movements and daily passive exercises will reduce symptoms of spasticity and risk of contractures. Baclofen, tizanidine, and clonidine are used in reducing clonus and extensor spasms.

The most likely diagnosis for this patient is Gerstmann syndrome. It is commonly associated with damage to the left (dominant) inferior parietal lobule.

Gerstmann syndrome consists of:

Option B: Anton syndrome also known as visual anosognosia occurs due to bilateral infarction in the distal PCAs. It produces cortical blindness and the patients are unaware of the blindness or may even deny it.

Option C: Millard-Gubler syndrome occurs due to ventral pontine injury. It causes functional loss of the 6th and 7th cranial nerves and corticospinal tract. This presents as diplopia, ipsilateral facial palsy, ipsilateral loss of corneal reflex, contralateral hemiparesis.

question: A patient has developed confusion and keeps bumping into objects. He can speak fluently. But on examination, he cannot differentiate between fingers and cannot write. He also gets confused with the examiner's right and left sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Hemisensory loss and severe burning pain in the affected regions is classically seen in Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, also known as thalamic pain syndrome.

Dejerine- Roussy syndrome occurs due to occlusion of the thalamic and thalamogeniculate branches arising from the P1 segment resulting in contralateral hemisensory loss and severe burning pain in the affected regions.

The P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery extends from the basilar bifurcation to the junction with the posterior communicating artery.

This pain responds poorly to analgesics. Anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine or gabapentin or tricyclic antidepressants may be beneficial.
question: A 78-year-old woman presents with right hemisensory loss followed by agonizing, burning pain in the affected regions. The pain responds poorly to analgesics. These features are classically seen in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Anton's syndrome. It occurs due to bilateral infarction in the distal posterior cerebral artery (P2 segment) and is associated with the following features:

  • Cortical blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction
  • Denial of vision loss due to being unaware of being blind, also known as visual anosognosia
  • Confabulation- Making up stories to fill memory gaps in the setting of obvious cortical blindness

Option D: Riddoch phenomenon is a condition where cortical blindness is associated with the perception of only moving targets.
question: A 73-year-old woman was brought to the OPD since she has been tripping over things at home. explanationHtml:
The persistence of visual image even after shifting gaze is called palinopsia. It is seen in Balint’s syndrome.

Balint’s syndrome results due to low flow in the watershed areas between distal PCA and MCA territories. It is characterized by the following:

  • Palinopsia - persistence of a visual image despite gazing at another scene
  • Asimultagnosia - difficulty to focus on more than one item in the visual field
  • Optic ataxia - Inability to reach accurately under visual guidance
  • Ocular apraxia - Inability to direct gaze accurately to a new target

Claude's syndrome is a distinctive brainstem syndrome characterized by ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiataxia. It is due to an intrinsic or extrinsic lesion in the midbrain.

Note: While some authors use the term simultanagnosia, others use asimultanagnosia instead. A few authors also use these two terminologies interchangeably.
question: A patient with a history of ischemic heart disease now comes to the hospital due to problems with vision. She complains that while turning her head, the image of the previous target still persists for a few seconds before she can see the new target. explanationHtml:
Opsoclonus is not seen in Balint's syndrome.

The features of Balint’s syndrome are:

  • Optic ataxia - the inability to guide the arm to reach a certain object in the visual field
  • Simultanagnosia - the inability to perceive more than one object at a time. In other words, it is the inability to recognize multiple elements in a visual presentation, one object or some elements of a scene can be appreciated but not the display as a whole.
  • Ocular apraxia - the inability to control voluntary purposeful eye movements
  • Palinopsia - the persistence of a visual image even after the stimulus has been removed

Note: While some authors use the term simultanagnosia, others use asimultanagnosia instead. A few authors also use these two terminologies interchangeably.

Weber’s syndrome occurs due to infarction in the distribution of the penetrating branches of the PCA. It affects the cerebral peduncle, especially medially, and damages III cranial nerve and the pyramidal fibers. It results in contralateral hemiplegia and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy.

Claude's syndrome is a distinctive brainstem syndrome characterized by ipsilateral third cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiataxia. This is due to an intrinsic or extrinsic lesion in the midbrain.
question: A patient presents with ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral hemiplegia. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Ipsilateral paralysis of the lower face is not seen in Weber's syndrome. However, there is contralateral paralysis of the lower face.

Weber syndrome is caused by infarction in the distribution of the penetrating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). It affects the cerebral peduncle, especially medially, with damage to the fascicle of cranial nerve III and the pyramidal fibers.

The resultant clinical findings are contralateral hemiplegia of the face, arm, and leg secondary to corticospinal and corticobulbar tract involvement, and ipsilateral oculomotor paresis including a dilated pupil.

Convergence‐retraction nystagmus is irregular, jerky nystagmus in which both eyeballs rhythmically converge and retract into the orbit, particularly on attempting an upward gaze.

Wallenberg syndrome, also called lateral medullary syndrome, is due to occlusion of the ipsilateral vertebral artery in most cases. In the remainder, posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion is responsible.

Wallenberg / lateral medullary syndrome affects the following structures:

  • Descending tract and nucleus of cranial nerve V - Ipsilateral impaired sensation over half of the face
  • IX and X cranial nerves - Ipsilateral paralysis of palate, vocal cord, diminished gag reflex

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage. The most common cause for this condition is the rupture of a berry aneurysm, also known as a saccular aneurysm.

CT shows hyperattenuating material filling the subarachnoid space, which is suggestive of SAH. Most commonly, it occurs around the circle of Willis due to the rupture of a berry aneurysm at this location.

Most unruptured intracranial aneurysms are completely asymptomatic. Prodromal symptoms occasionally suggest the site of the enlarging unruptured aneurysm. For example, cranial nerve III palsy with loss of ipsilateral light reflex and focal pain above or behind the eye suggests an expanding aneurysm at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and internal carotid artery.

Ruptured aneurysms cause an excruciating thunderclap headache followed by a transient loss of consciousness.

Non-contrast CT scan is the investigation of choice for SAH. LP shows xanthochromatic CSF.

Treatment involves clipping or coiling the aneurysm to eliminate the risk of rebleeding.
question: A 62-year-old man presents to the casualty with a severe headache, fever, and vomiting for the past 5 hours. There is no history of trauma. CT head is shown below. What is the most common cause for his presentation?

explanationHtml:
Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery will most likely compress the oculomotor nerve. This is because the posterior communicating artery is anatomically located very close to the oculomotor nerve.

Patients with an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery can present with symptoms of oculomotor nerve palsy such as:

  • Unilateral ptosis (LPS)
  • Outward eye deviation (MR)
  • Dilated pupil.

The nerves controlling the pupils are located very superficially and these are always affected due to the mass effect of the aneurysm. Therefore the pupil sparing third nerve palsies are unlikely to be due to an aneurysm.

Pupil-sparing oculomotor nerve palsy is often assumed to be caused by ischemic injuries such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus.

Expanding unruptured aneurysms can occasionally lead to prodromal symptoms which suggest the location of the aneurysm.
question: Which of the following structures is most likely to be compressed by an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery?

correctAnswer: A. Origin of posterior communicating artery
explanationHtml:
The size and site of aneurysm are important in predicting the risk of rupture. Aneurysms with the following features have a greater risk of rupture:

  • Size >7 mm in diameter
  • Located at the top of the basilar artery (i.e origin of the posterior cerebral artery)
  • Located near the origin of the posterior communicating artery.

The most common location of Berry aneurysm is the anterior communicating artery.
question: At which of the following locations does a Berry aneurysm have the highest risk of rupture?

explanationHtml:

Subdural hematoma refers to the haemorrhage between the dura and arachnoid mater. The image of the CT scan reveals a hyperdense crescentic lesion. Mass effect with midline displacement can also be seen.

Causes of SDH are:

  • Trauma
  • Anticoagulants
  • Antiplatelets
  • Alcohol abuse
  • Shaken baby syndrome.

Non-contrast CT is the investigation of choice. Radiographic features of subdural hemorrhage are:

  • Typically unilateral
  • Crescent-like distribution (concavo-convex) around the periphery of the brain
  • Not limited by sutures and can fill dural reflections

  • Acute subdural hemorrhage: Hyperdense collections on CT

The typical presentation is an initial loss of consciousness following trauma, a complete transient recovery (lucid interval), and a rapid progression of neurological deterioration.

This condition is treated by rapid surgical evacuation and ligation or cautery of the damaged vessel.

question: A 50-year-old hypertensive man presented with an acute-onset headache for the past 2 hours, neck stiffness, nausea, and vomiting. He claims it is the worst headache of his life. The clinical scenario describes a 53 year old patient admitted in view of a cerebrovascular accident developing neurologic deterioration (drowsy with minimal response) on the second day, and CT brain showing significant edema of MCA territory with midline shift. The next line of management is decompressive surgery.

Cerebral edema is a potential complication in 5-10% of patients with strokes, leading to obtundation and brain herniation. The severity of edema is highest on the second or third day after the stroke and can last for around 10 days.

Medical management may not be successful in case of significant edema or infarcts involving the cerebellum.

Decompressive surgery is recommended for patients who are less than 60 years old and experience deterioration ≤ 48 hours, despite receiving medical therapy. Hypodensity on head CT within the first 6 hours of stroke onset, involving ≥ one-third of the MCA territory, early midline shift, and a diffusion-weighted imaging volume on MRI within 6 hours ≥ 80 mL are predictors of severe cerebral edema.
question: A 53-year-old man was admitted with a history of a cerebrovascular accident. On the second day, he becomes drowsy with minimal response. CT finding is shown in the image below. What will be your next line of management?

SAH can present with fever, positive Kernig’s sign, and Brudzinski’s sign, as well as mimic meningitis or encephalitis.

Treatment with the calcium channel antagonist nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 h) improves outcome, by preventing ischemic injury.

question: A 50-year-old woman complains of numbness of her hands, generalized weakness, and easy fatiguability. She is a vegetarian. She looks very pale and her peripheral smear reveals macrocytic hypochromic anemia. If untreated, she is at risk of developing which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Sjogren's syndrome causes large fiber sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy, making it the least likely among the listed options to present as a small fiber neuropathy.

It primarily involves the dorsal root ganglia, producing a sensory ganglionopathy characterized by:

  • Progressive sensory ataxia with positive Romberg's sign
  • Loss of vibration sense and proprioception
  • Non-length-dependent distribution — asymmetrically involving the face, trunk, and limbs
  • Abnormal nerve conduction study (NCS) with reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs)

A pure small fiber neuropathy or cranial neuropathy (particularly trigeminal) can also be seen in sjögren's, but this is not the characteristic presentation. The dominant neurological manifestation remains the large fiber ataxic sensory ganglionopathy.
question: Which of the following conditions is not a likely cause of small fiber neuropathy?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss. This pattern is characteristic of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathies.

It consists of:

  • Acute form - Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy [AIDP] also known as Guillain-Barré syndrome [GBS]
  • Chronic form - Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy [CIDP]

Option B: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a multiple degenerative motor neuron disease. It leads to muscle weakness and disability in the absence of sensory symptoms and signs.

Option C: Mononeuropathy multiplex refers to multiple compressive mononeuropathies. It presents as asymmetric subacute or acute sensory and motor symptoms and signs.

Option D: Polyradiculopathy or plexopathy due to diabetes mellitus presents with asymmetric weakness.
question: A 30-year-old man presents with weakness of both the lower limbs. On examination, there is a sensory loss in the lower limbs and both the proximal and distal leg muscles have reduced power. This presentation is characteristic of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml: Hereditary motor neuropathy does not present with asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss. It presents with symmetric distal weakness without sensory loss.
question: A patient presented with peripheral neuropathy with asymmetric distal weakness without sensory loss. The differential diagnosis for this condition would include all except:

explanationHtml:
Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy.

Other examples of rare hereditary neuropathies are Friedreich’s ataxia, familial amyloid polyneuropathy and Tangier disease.
question: What is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy?

explanationHtml:
In hyperthyroidism, excessive thyroxine causes sympathetic autonomic overactivity, not neuropathy.

Hypothyroidism can be associated with peripheral neuropathy, most typically carpal tunnel syndrome. Treatment is the correction of hypothyroidism.
question: All of the following are associated with autonomic neuropathies, except:

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of burning feet syndrome, seen in HSAN 1.

There are five types of hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies (HSAN I–V), of which the most important are HSAN I and HSAN III.

HSAN I has an autosomal dominant inheritance. It presents in adolescence or adulthood as a distal small-fiber neuropathy. It causes burning feet syndrome in which patients present with:

  • Burning sensation of feet, especially at night
  • Sensory loss
  • Foot ulcers.

Option B: Dejerine Roussy syndrome, also known as thalamic pain syndrome usually occurs after a stroke. The patient experiences burning pain over affected areas of the body.

Option C: HSAN III or Riley Day syndrome presents in childhood. It presents with labile BP, decreased tearing, hyperhidrosis, reduced sensitivity to pain, and areflexia.

Option D: Charcot Marie Tooth disease is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy. It is a hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN) which presents with motor weakness and skeletal deformities.
question: A young woman presents with complaints of insomnia due to her feet becoming very hot and painful at night. On examination, she has multiple superficial foot ulcers, and she is unable to feel light touch and crude touch. What is your diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Distal Symmetric Sensory and Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy
explanationHtml:
Distal symmetric sensory and sensorimotor polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy and is seen in approximately one-third of patients with DM.

Other neuropathies seen in diabetes mellitus are:

  • The most common mononeuropathies are median neuropathy at the wrist and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
  • Diabetic autonomic neuropathy is typically seen in combination with DSPN
  • Cranial neuropathy (third nerve palsy is the most common) and diabetic neuropathic cachexia

The Michigan diabetic neuropathy score is a screening tool used to assess diabetic neuropathy.

options.text: Distal Symmetric Sensory and Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy

question: Which of the following is the most common type of neuropathy seen in diabetes?

explanationHtml:
Duloxetine is a selective serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SSNRI) and is one of the first-line drugs used in the treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy.

Treatment of painful sensory neuropathies:

  • First-line:
    • Lidoderm 5% patch
    • Tricyclic antidepressants (e.g., amitriptyline, nortriptyline)
    • Gabapentin, Pregabalin
    • Duloxetine
  • Second-line:
    • Carbamazepine
    • Phenytoin
    • Venlafaxine
    • Tramadol
  • Third-line:
    • Mexiletine

Optimal glucose control is considered the cornerstone for the treatment of diabetes and its complications. Intensive glucose control has been shown to prevent the development of peripheral neuropathy.
question: Which of the following can be prescribed as a first-line drug for a patient with painful diabetic neuropathy?

explanationHtml:
Lead poisoning does not cause sensorimotor neuropathy. It causes symptoms and signs of primarily motor neuropathy. The most common presentation of lead poisoning is encephalopathy.

The sensation is generally preserved but the autonomic nervous system can be affected in lead poisoning.
question: Sensorimotor neuropathy may be caused by all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
Isoniazid (INH), which is a first-line anti-tuberculosis drug, inhibits pyridoxal phosphokinase, resulting in pyridoxine deficiency and neuropathy. Prophylactic administration of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10 mg/day can prevent neuropathy from developing.

10 mg daily suffices for prophylaxis but patients with evidence of vitamin B6 deficiency may require up to 50 mg daily.

Current WHO guidelines recommend routine substitution of pyridoxine to patients who are at risk of peripheral neuropathy, e.g., malnutrition, chronic alcohol dependence, diabetics, HIV.

However, pyridoxine excess (acute intoxication or long-term use of large doses) is also found to cause peripheral neuropathy.
question: Which of the following vitamins will you prescribe for a patient on antitubercular therapy?

explanationHtml:
The image shows Mee’s lines, transverse white striae of the fingernails. This along with history is suggestive of chronic arsenic poisoning probably due to a contaminated water source. Arsenic poisoning causes toxic sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

The neuropathy manifests 5–10 days after ingestion of arsenic and progresses for several weeks, mimicking Guillain–Barre's Syndrome.
question: During a regular health checkup, you notice the following nail finding in a 64-year-old man. He lives near a smelting industry on the banks of a river. Which of the following conditions can be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given image showing thickening of tissues in the temporal and orbital regions with coarse overlying skin suggests a diagnosis of plexiform neurofibroma.

Plexiform neurofibroma represents an uncommon variant (30%) of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1). Plexiform neurofibromas are usually evident at birth and result from a diffuse thickening of nerve trunks and surrounding tissues that are usually located in the orbital or temporal region of the face. The skin overlying it may be coarse and associated with hyperpigmentation.

Plexiform neurofibromas may produce an overgrowth of an extremity and a deformity of the corresponding bone.

NF1 is clinically diagnosed when any 2 of the following 7 features are present:

  • ≥ 6 Café-au-lait macules
  • Axillary or inguinal freckling
  • Two or more iris lisch nodules
  • ≥ 2 neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma
  • A distinctive osseous lesion, such as sphenoid dysplasia or cortical thinning of long bones with or without pseudoarthrosis.
  • Optic gliomas
  • A first-degree relative with NF-1
question: Identify the diagnosis.

explanationHtml:
Campylobacter jejuni is one of the most common risk factors for GBS.

Infections that may trigger GBS are:

  • Campylobacter jejuni
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
  • Epstein Barr virus
  • Mycoplasma
  • Varicella zoster virus
  • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), dengue, or influenza, Zika, hepatitis

Less commonly vaccinations, surgical procedures, and trauma have been reported to trigger the development of GBS.

question: Which of the following is the most common antecedent infectious cause of Guillain-Barre syndrome?

explanationHtml:
IgG isotype of autoantibody is involved in the pathogenesis of GBS.

IgM isotype autoantibodies are known to play a role in some types of chronic immune neuropathies.

question: Which of the following autoantibody isotype is involved in the pathogenesis of Guillian-Barre syndrome?

explanationHtml: Autoantibodies in GBS due to Campylobacter jejuni infection are directed most commonly against GM1 gangliosidase.

question: In Guillain-Barre syndrome due to antecedent infection with Campylobacter jejuni, the autoantibodies are most commonly directed against which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) is the most common type of GBS.

There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome, which are recognized by electrodiagnostic studies and pathological distinctions. These include:

A. Demyelinating

  • Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common

B. Axonal

  • Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)
  • Acute motor–sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)

C. Regional GBS syndromes

  • Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS)
  • Pure sensory forms
  • Ophthalmoplegia with anti-GQ1b antibodies as part of severe motor-sensory GBS
  • GBS with severe bulbar and facial paralysis
  • Acute pandysautonomia

question: Which type of Guillain-Barre syndrome most commonly affects patients in the pediatric age group?

explanationHtml:
In AMAN, the complement along with IgG is deposited at the nodes of Ranvier of large motor axons.

In AIDP, complement deposits along the outer surface of the Schwann cell.

question: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy differs from acute motor axonal neuropathy, in that, in the latter, the complement deposition along with IgG antibodies occurs at:

explanationHtml:
Bladder dysfunction is not usually severe and does not appear early in the course of Guillain-Barre Syndrome(GBS). If bladder dysfunction is a prominent feature and comes early in the course, diagnostic possibilities other than GBS should be considered.

GBS is an acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. It is an autoimmune disorder triggered by infections like:

  • Campylobacter jejuni
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
  • Epstein Barr virus
  • Mycoplasma
  • Varicella zoster virus
  • Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), dengue, or influenza

It manifests as a rapidly evolving areflexic motor paralysis, with or without sensory disturbance. The usual pattern is ascending paralysis. Proximal and distal muscles are equally involved. The lower cranial nerves are frequently affected, causing bulbar weakness.
lessonTitle: Guillain Barre Syndrome And Other Immune Mediated Neuropathies
question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with Guillian-Barre syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Loss of proprioception is severe in Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS).

GBS affects the large sensory fibers, leading to attenuation or loss of deep tendon reflexes and loss of proprioception.

Cutaneous sensory deficits (e.g., loss of pain and temperature sensation) are usually relatively mild.
lessonTitle: Guillain Barre Syndrome And Other Immune Mediated Neuropathies
question: Which of the following sensory deficits is severely affected in a patient with Guillain-Barre syndrome?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS). Protein levels are elevated (100-1000mg/dl) in the CSF of a patient with this condition.

The CSF cell counts are usually normal. Albuminocytologic dissociation, which is an elevation in CSF protein without an elevation in white blood cells, is characteristic in GBS.

Causes of albuminocytologic dissociation are:

  • Guillain-Barre Syndrome
  • Spinal cord tumours

question: A patient presents with complaints of lower extremity weakness. He initially noticed difficulty climbing the stairs and now he is unable to stand. He gives a history of bloody diarrhea a few weeks ago. Which of the following parameters are expected to be elevated in the CSF of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Subclavian steal syndrome does not present with autonomic dysfunction.

Option A: Polyneuropathy is seen in sporadic and familial amyloidosis. In some cases, autonomic insufficiency presents before distal painful polyneuropathy accompanied by sensory loss

Option B: Guillain-Barré syndrome is associated with autonomic instability. This can present with BP fluctuations, arrhythmias, and GI disturbances.

Option C: Botulinum toxin binds presynaptically to cholinergic nerve terminals. After uptake into the cytoplasm, it blocks ACh release. Thus, patients with botulism present with motor paralysis and autonomic disturbances.

question: Which of the following conditions does not present with autonomic dysfunction?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Guillian-Barre syndrome (GBS). Postural hypotension is a common autonomic disturbance seen in this condition.

Autonomic involvement is common and may occur even in patients whose GBS is otherwise mild.

The usual autonomic manifestations are:

  • Loss of vasomotor control with wide fluctuation in blood pressure, postural hypotension
  • Cardiac dysrhythmias

question: A 23-year-old patient presents with rapidly progressing symmetric ascending paralysis since 2 days. Nerve conduction studies are consistent with demyelination. He is found to have an elevated protein level in his CSF. Which of the following autonomic disturbance is likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Weakness is not seen in the triad of Miller-Fisher syndrome (MFS).

Miller Fisher syndrome is a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome(GBS). Like Guillain-Barré syndrome, symptoms may be preceded by a viral illness. It classically presents as a triad of:

  • Ataxia
  • Areflexia
  • Ophthalmoplegia

The condition is usually not associated with weakness, and even if present, is very mild. It is strongly associated with antibodies to the ganglioside GQ1b.

The prognosis in Miller Fisher syndrome is usually good with recovery beginning within 2 to 4 weeks of the symptom onset, and completing by 6 months. Some individuals are left with residual deficits. Relapses are rare.

Treatment for Miller Fisher syndrome is identical to treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome: intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) or plasmapheresis and supportive care.
lessonTitle: Guillain Barre Syndrome And Other Immune Mediated Neuropathies
question: The triad of Miller-Fisher syndrome includes all of the following, except:

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome(GBS) probably as a result of COVID-19. IV Immunoglobulin is the recommended initial therapy for patients with GBS.

High-dose intravenous immune globulin (IVIg) and plasmapheresis are both equally effective in GBS and can be used as the initial therapy. However, IVIg is often the initial therapy chosen because of its ease of administration and good safety record. It is administered as five daily infusions for a total dose of 2 g/kg body weight. Glucocorticoids have not been found to be effective in GBS.
lessonTitle: Guillain Barre Syndrome And Other Immune Mediated Neuropathies
question: A patient presented to the ER with tingling, numbness, and weakness in all four limbs.  She says that the weakness started in the lower limbs and progressed to the upper limbs within a day. History is significant for a recent COVID-19 infection and surgery for cervical spondylosis and disc herniation 3 years ago. CT brain was normal and an MRI of the lumbar spine showed foraminal narrowing at L2-L3. CSF analysis showed increased protein levels. Which of the following is recommended for the initial therapy of this patient?

correctAnswer: C. GBS deteriorates >9 weeks after onset or relapses at least three times
explanationHtml:
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) should be suspected when GBS deteriorates >9 weeks after onset or relapses at least three times.

Onset is usually gradual over a few months or longer, but in a few cases, the initial attack is indistinguishable from that of GBS.

CIDP is distinguished from GBS by its chronic course. In other respects, this neuropathy shares many features with the common demyelinating form of GBS, including elevated CSF protein levels and the electrodiagnostic studies findings of acquired demyelination.

Diseases associated with CIDP are:

  • Pregnancy

question: A patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is undergoing nerve conduction study. Which of the following findings is least likely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
'No electrophysiological evidence of nerve functionality' is not an indication of nerve biopsy in CIDP patients.

In CIDP, nerve biopsy is indicated when:

  • Other causes of polyneuropathy cannot be ruled out
  • Electromyography (EMG) shows axonal involvement

explanationHtml:
NSAIDs are not used in the treatment of CIDP.

The treatment of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) includes high-dose IV immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, and glucocorticoids.

Initial therapy is usually with IV immunoglobulin. If all the first-line agents fail, immunosuppressants are attempted either alone or as an adjunctive treatment.

question: All of the following can be used for the treatment of a patient with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, except:

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of multiple myeloma and the pattern of polyneuropathy seen in this condition is sensorimotor type.

Multiple myeloma-associated polyneuropathies occur in ~5% of patients with the commonly encountered type of multiple myeloma.

Myeloma with osteosclerotic features, although representing only 3% of all myelomas, is associated with polyneuropathy in one-half of cases.

Polyneuropathy generally does not reverse even with successful suppression of the myeloma.

question: A 63-year-old man presented with complaints of fatiguability and chronic back pain. On evaluation, he was found to have anemia and hypercalcemia. The X-ray of his skull is given below. Which of the following statements is true with regard to neuropathy seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Most common pattern of peripheral neuropathy in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is mononeuritis multiplex (multifocal motor-sensory neuropathy). It is asymmetric, due to ischemic lesions of nerve trunks and roots.

Some cases present as a distal, symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Small- to medium-sized arteries of the vasa nervorum, particularly the epineural vessels, are affected in PAN, resulting in a widespread ischemic neuropathy.

Combination therapy with glucocorticoids and rituximab is increasingly recommended as the standard initial treatment, particularly for ANCA-associated vasculitis.

question: What is the most common pattern of peripheral neuropathy in patients with polyarteritis nodosa?

explanationHtml:
The sensory loss just below the circumferential level of the umbilicus corresponds to the lesion at the T10 spinal cord segment. It indicates the involvement of the cord adjacent to T7-T8 vertebral bodies.

The spinal cord has 31 segments, but they do not always correspond to the same vertebral body.

The first seven pairs of cervical spinal nerves exit above the same-numbered vertebral bodies. All the subsequent nerves exit below the same-numbered vertebral bodies. This is because of the presence of eight cervical spinal cord segments but only seven cervical vertebrae.

The lower spinal nerves take an increasingly downward course to exit via intervertebral foramina.

question: A patient has sensory loss just below the circumferential level of the umbilicus. This corresponds to a lesion at which spinal cord segment?

explanationHtml:
Quadriplegia and weakness of the diaphragm (manifesting as difficulty in breathing) are associated with spinal cord lesion at the level of C1-C4 spinal segments.

Diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve arising from C3 - C5.

The uppermost level of weakness and reflex loss with lesions:

  • At C5-C6 : Biceps
  • At C7: Finger, wrist extensors, and triceps
  • At C8 : Finger and wrist flexion

Note: Horner’s syndrome (characterized by miosis, ptosis, and facial hypohidrosis) may accompany a cervical cord lesion at any level.
question: A patient presents with quadriplegia and difficulty in breathing. This presentation can be seen in spinal cord lesions at what level?

explanationHtml:
The Beevor’s sign localizes the spinal cord injury at T10-T12.

Beevor’s sign is the abnormal upward movement of the umbilicus on abdominal wall contraction in the supine position. This is because a lesion in the T10-T12 level of the spinal cord paralyzes the lower abdominal muscles but the upper abdominal muscles are normally resulting in the upward movement of the umbilicus.

[[figure-1]]
question: Beevor’s sign is noted in a patient who has spinal cord injury. At what level is the injury likely to be?

explanationHtml:
Lesions at L2 – L4 spinal nerve roots do not cause paralysis of the knee flexors.

The paralysis of the flexion at the knee occurs due to the lesion at L5 – S1.

options.text: Paralysis of hip flexion and adduction

question: A patient has a spinal cord lesion at the level of L2 – L4 spinal nerve roots. All of the following may be seen in this patient, except:

explanationHtml:
The clinical features of the conus medullaris syndrome include:

  • Bilateral saddle anesthesia
  • Bladder and bowel dysfunction
  • Impotence
  • Absence of bulbocavernosus (S2-S4) and anal reflexes (S4-S5)

The conus medullaris is the tapered caudal termination of the spinal cord, comprising all the sacral and single coccygeal segments. Damage at this level of the cord, often occurs due to injuries to the lumbar vertebra, result in conus medullaris syndrome. Muscle strength is largely preserved in this condition.
question:
Which of the following features would you expect to see in a patient with conus medullaris syndrome?

  1. Bilateral saddle anesthesia
  2. Bladder and bowel dysfunction
  3. Normal sexual function
  4. Absence of anal reflex
  5. Absence of patellar reflex

explanationHtml:
Early loss of bladder control is a feature of the conus medullaris syndrome.

It is characterized by urinary retention and atonic anal sphincter, which cause overflow urinary incontinence and fecal incontinence, respectively.

Option A: In the cauda equina syndrome, there is relative sparing of bladder control.

Options C and D: Bladder dysfunction is uncommon in Guillian–Barre syndrome and ALS.
question: Which of the following conditions will you suspect in a patient who has bladder dysfunction early in the progression of the disease?

explanationHtml:
This is a case of cauda equina syndrome (CES).

CES signifies an injury of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots within the spinal canal distal to the termination of the spinal cord at L1-L2. It is commonly due to a ruptured lumbosacral intervertebral disk, lumbosacral spine fracture, hematoma within the spinal canal, compressive tumor, or other mass lesions.

Low back pain, weakness, and areflexia in the legs, saddle anesthesia, or loss of bladder function may occur.

Treatment options include surgical decompression, sometimes urgently in an attempt to restore or preserve motor or sphincter function, or radiotherapy for metastatic tumors.
question: A patient with a history of a backache for 10 days, has now presented with sudden onset difficulty in micturition and defaecation. There was no history of a cough or fever previously. What is the diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Symmetric weakness of lower limbs
explanationHtml:
Symmetric weakness of lower limbs helps in a diagnosis of conus medullaris syndrome.

There is an asymmetric motor loss in cauda equina syndrome.

Mass lesions in the lower spinal canal often produce a mixed clinical picture with elements of both cauda equina and conus medullaris syndromes.
question: Which of the following features will help you differentiate conus medullaris syndrome from cauda equina syndrome?

correctAnswer: B. Contralateral loss of pain sensation
explanationHtml:
The Brown–Sequard syndrome presents with contralateral loss of pain sensation.

Lateral hemisection of the spinal cord produces the Brown–Séquard syndrome (also known as the hemicord syndrome). Knife or bullet injuries and demyelination are the most common causes of this condition.

Clinical features include:

  • Ipsilateral weakness (corticospinal tract involvement)
  • Ipsilateral loss of joint position and vibratory sense (posterior column involvement)
  • Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sense (spinothalamic tract involvement) one or two levels below the lesion
  • Ipsilateral segmental signs like radicular pain, muscle atrophy, or loss of a deep tendon reflex

options.text: Contralateral loss of joint sense and position
Ipsilateral loss of complete sensory functions

question: Which is the characteristic pattern seen in Brown-Sequard syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Proprioception is the type of sensation lost on the same side (ipsilateral) in Brown–Sequard syndrome. This is due to a lesion of the posterior column.

The sensations of crude touch, pain and temperature are lost on the opposite side, due to the lesions of anterior column or spinothalamic tract.
question: A patient is diagnosed with Brown–Sequard syndrome with a lesion on the right side. Which of the following sensations on the right side will be affected?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of cape distribution of sensory deficit is seen in central cord syndrome.

This condition affects the cervical cord producing arm weakness > leg weakness. A dissociated sensory loss i.e. loss of pain and temperature with preservation of light touch, joint position, and vibration sensations is seen over the shoulders, lower neck, and upper trunk (cape distribution).

It results from selective damage to the gray matter nerve cells and the decussating spinothalamic tracts surrounding the central canal. These decussating fibers carry crude touch, pain, and temperature sensations.

Spinal trauma, syringomyelia, and intrinsic cord tumors are the main causes.

[[figure-1]]

Option A: In Brown–Sequard Syndrome, ipsilateral weakness and loss of joint position and vibratory sense, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sense, one or two levels below the lesion is seen.

Option C: Anterior spinal artery syndrome is caused due to an ASA infarct. It typically presents as loss of motor function and pain/temperature sensation, with relative sparing of proprioception and vibratory sense below the level of the lesion.

Option D: In foramen magnum syndrome, compressive lesions near the foramen magnum may produce weakness of the ipsilateral shoulder and arm followed by weakness of the ipsilateral leg, then the contralateral leg, and finally the contralateral arm. This is referred to as 'around the clock' pattern.
question: A patient was brought to the casualty after he was hit by a plastic pipe on the back by a bully. On examination, the patient was found to have marked upper extremity weakness compared to the lower extremities. He also had a loss of pain and temperature sensations over the shoulders, lower neck, and upper trunk. Other sensations were intact in this region. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Suspended distribution of sensory deficit
explanationHtml:
The MRI shows a syrinx located at C6–C7 in the cervical spine which is suggestive of syringomyelia. Suspended distribution of sensory deficit is a feature of this condition.

Syringomyelia is a developmental cavity of the cervical cord that may enlarge and produce progressive myelopathy or may remain asymptomatic.

It presents as a central cord syndrome with unilateral sensory loss in the hands initially. There is a loss of pain and temperature sensation with the sparing of touch and vibration. The sensory deficit has a distribution that is 'suspended' over the nape of the neck, shoulders, and upper arms (cape distribution) or in the hands. Areflexic weakness is seen in the upper limbs.

Extension of the syrinx into the grey matter of the cord causes muscle wasting in the lower neck, shoulders, arms, and hands with asymmetric or absent reflexes in the arms. Extension of the syrinx into the medulla (syringobulbia) causes palatal or vocal cord paralysis, dysarthria, horizontal or vertical nystagmus, episodic dizziness or vertigo, and tongue weakness with atrophy.

options.text: Around the clock pattern of weakness

question: The MRI spine of a patient is shown below. What is the characteristic deficit seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of an 'around-the-clock' pattern of weakness, which is seen in foramen magnum syndrome.

Around the clock pattern of weakness is described as a sequential weakness of the ipsilateral shoulder and arm followed by weakness of the ipsilateral leg, then the contralateral leg, and finally the contralateral arm. The weakness may begin in any of the limbs.

The lesions in the foramen magnum area interrupt decussating pyramidal tract fibers destined for the legs, resulting in weakness of the legs. There is typically suboccipital pain spreading to the neck and shoulders in foramen magnum syndrome.
question: A patient presents with quadriparesis. He says that it started in his left arm, then progressed to the left leg, and then later to the right leg and arm. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Anterior spinal artery thrombosis does not lead to loss of vibration sense. Vibration sense is carried by the posterior column.

Anterior spinal artery syndrome or anterior cord syndrome is the result of occlusion or diminished flow in the anterior spinal artery. There is bilateral tissue destruction at several contiguous levels that spares the posterior columns.

All spinal cord functions (motor, sensory, and autonomic) are lost below the level of the lesion, except vibration and position sensation.

options.text: Loss of power in the lower limbs

question: Anterior spinal artery thrombosis is characterized by all of the following, except:

explanationHtml:
The early feature of dysautonomia that can occur in this patient is spastic bladder.

Dysautonomia due to brain and spinal cord disease above the level of the lumbar spine results first in increased urinary frequency and small bladder volume. Eventually, incontinence occurs. These features are suggestive of an upper motor neuron lesion, i.e., spastic bladder.

On the other hand, dysautonomia due to peripheral nervous system (PNS) disease of autonomic nerve fibers results in large bladder volumes, increased urinary frequency, and overflow incontinence. These are features suggestive of a lower motor neuron lesion, i.e., flaccid bladder.

Postvoidal residual volume helps to distinguish between upper and lower motor neuron bladder dysfunction in the early stages of dysautonomia.
question: A patient with neurofibromatosis 1 is found to have multiple tumors above the level of the lumbar spine. Which of the following is an early feature of dysautonomia in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Syringobulbia is a condition that affects the brainstem, not the spinal cord. It is a neurological disorder characterized by a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) which affects the brainstem (medulla).

The following autonomic disorders are associated with spinal cord involvement:

  • Syringomyelia
  • Multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica
  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
  • Traumatic quadriplegia
  • Subacute combined degeneration
  • Tetanus
  • Stiff-person syndrome
  • Spinal cord tumors
question: Which of the following autonomic disorders do not involve the spinal cord?

explanationHtml:
Sacral sparing is not a feature of extramedullary tumors, it is seen in intramedullary tumors. Differences between extramedullary and intramedullary syndromes are:

Extramedullary Intramedullary
Radicular pain Poorly localized burning pain
Early sacral sensory loss Sacral sparing
Incontinence due to the superficial location of the corresponding sensory and motor fibers in the spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts Corticospinal tract signs appear later

Extramedullary tumors lie outside the cord and compress the spinal cord or its vascular supply. Intramedullary tumors arise within the substance of the cord.

The spinothalamic tract has a laminated configuration with the sacral fibers outermost, and hence, there is an early sacral sensory loss in extramedullary tumors.
question: Which of the following features would you not expect to see in a patient with an extramedullary tumor in the spinal cord?

correctAnswer: C. High consumption of refined rice
explanationHtml:
Subacute combined degeneration (SACD) is due to the deficiency of vitamin B12. Pernicious anemia, partial gastrectomy, and Diphyllobothrium latum infestation can lead to this condition. High consumption of refined rice leads to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.

The most severely affected regions in SACD are the posterior columns at the cervical and upper thoracic levels.

Clinical features include:

  • Signs of both peripheral nerve and spinal cord involvement
  • Paresthesias in the hands or feet > Weakness and unsteadiness of gait
  • Loss of vibration or joint position sense in the legs
  • Mental slowing, depression, confusion, delusions, and hallucinations

SACD is treated by a replacement regimen of intramuscular daily injections of 1000 μg of vitamin B12 for the first week, followed by weekly 1000 μg injections for 1 month, and monthly injections thereafter.
question: Which of the following is not a cause of subacute combined degeneration?

correctAnswer: D. Decreased synaptic transmission at the myoneural junction
explanationHtml:
Myasthenia gravis is associated with a decrease in synaptic transmission at the myoneural junction.

Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular (myoneural) junction.
