options.text: Decreased acetylcholine release at the nerve endings
Increased acetylcholine release at the nerve endings
Increased synaptic transmission at the myoneural junction
Decreased synaptic transmission at the myoneural junction

question: Myasthenia gravis is associated with which of the following?

correctAnswer: C. Damage to muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase
explanationHtml:
In myasthenia gravis, damage to muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase is not a mechanism by which anti-AChR antibodies reduce the number of available AChRs at the neuromuscular junction.

The anti-AChR antibodies reduce the number of available AChRs at the neuromuscular junction using three distinct mechanisms:

  • Accelerated turnover of AChRs
  • Damage to the postsynaptic muscle membrane mediated by antibodies and complement
  • Blockade of the active site of the AChR

Patients whose sera test negative for both AChR and MuSK antibodies possess antibodies specific to another protein at the neuromuscular junction called low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4). LRP4 plays a functional role in the clustering of AChRs.

Anti-MuSK antibodies are directed against muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase (MuSK), a protein involved in AChR clustering at the neuromuscular junction.

Damage to muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase
Blockade of the active site of the AChR

question: In myasthenia gravis, the anti-AChR antibodies reduce the number of available AChRs at the neuromuscular junction by all of the following mechanisms except:

explanationHtml:
Remissions may occur spontaneously but are usually not complete or permanent.

The cardinal clinical features of myasthenia gravis include:

  • Women are affected by myasthenia gravis more frequently than men, in a ratio of ~3:2.
  • Weakness and fatigability of muscles - Weakness may increase upon repeated use or later in the day. It may improve with rest or sleep.
  • Diplopia and ptosis - They are common initial clinical complaints. The cranial muscles, particularly the eyelids and the extraocular muscles, are typically involved early in the course of myasthenia gravis.
  • Limb weakness - It is often proximal and may be asymmetric.
  • Deep tendon reflexes - They are preserved despite muscle weakness.
lessonTitle: Myasthenia Gravis And Other Neuromuscular Junction Disorders

options.text: Weakness and fatigability of muscles is present
Lids and extraocular muscles are involved

question: Which of the following statements about myasthenia gravis is false?

correctAnswer: C. Myoid cells in thymus serve as the source of autoantigens
explanationHtml:
The presented features—fatigable weakness, diplopia, worsening toward the evening, and nasal speech—are characteristic of myasthenia gravis (MG). In this condition, myoid cells in the thymus serve as the source of autoantigens.

In the thymus, certain specialized cells known as myoid cells mimic skeletal muscle and display acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on their surface. These receptors can become targets for an aberrant immune attack, causing the generation of AChR-directed antibodies and leading to defective neuromuscular junction function in myasthenia gravis.

The thymus is abnormal in approximately 75% of patients with AChR antibody-positive MG, most commonly showing hyperplasia. Only about 10% of patients have an associated thymoma.
lessonTitle: Myasthenia Gravis And Other Neuromuscular Junction Disorders

options.text: Thymoma is present in more than 75% of the patients with this condition
In most of the cases the thymus is hypoplastic
Myoid cells in thymus serve as the source of autoantigens
Thymus is abnormal in 20% of patients with AChR antibody–positive status

question: A school teacher presents to the OPD with excessive fatigability and double vision. She says that her symptoms are aggravated towards the end of the day. Her colleagues told her that, lately, she has developed a nasal twang in her voice. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Thymoma is associated with hypogammaglobulinemia, not hypergammaglobulinemia. Thymoma with hypogammaglobulinemia is also called Good’s syndrome.

The following conditions are associated with thymomas:

  • Myasthenia gravis (30%)
  • Pure red cell aplasia (5-8%)
  • Hypogammaglobulinemia (~5%)
  • Polymyositis
  • SLE
  • Thyroiditis
  • Sjogren's syndrome
  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Addison's disease
  • Pernicious anemia
  • Scleroderma
  • Panhypopituitarism
  • Aplastic anemia
  • Limbic encephalitis

question: A 55-year old woman presented with shortness of breath, cough with expectoration and fever for ten days. Chest x-ray revealed mediastinal widening. CECT chest showed a well-circumscribed heterogeneous solid enhancing mass lesion. FNAC showed features in favor of thymoma. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Absent deep tendon reflex is not a feature of myasthenia gravis (MG).

MG usually occurs in young females. Patients usually present with weakness and fatiguability of the muscles, which worsens on repeated use or late in the day and improves on rest. The cranial muscles, particularly the eyelids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course of MG. Diplopia and ptosis are common initial complaints. When MG becomes generalized, the proximal muscles of the limbs are affected first. Despite the muscle weakness, the deep tendon reflexes remain normal. Snarling expression on smiling (facial weakness), nasal timbre of speech (weakness of palate and tongue), and difficulty swallowing may be seen. Bulbar weakness and respiratory depression are seen more frequently in MuSK antibody–positive MG.

MG is an autoimmune disorder most commonly caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR). These antibodies cause damage to the postsynaptic muscle membrane and increased endocytosis of the AChR. This autoimmune response against the AChR seems to be mediated by the thymus. The myoid (muscle-like) cells present in the thymus express AChRs on their surface and are postulated to provide the autoantigen which triggers this autoimmune reaction. Around 75% of MG patients show thymus disorders, distribution of which is as follows:

  • Thymic hyperplasia (majority)- 65% of the patients
  • Thymomas- 10% of the patients.

The tests which are used to confirm the diagnosis of MG include:

  • Anti-AChR antibody immunoassay: 85% of myasthenic patients have detectable anti-AChR antibodies, but only 50% of patients with weakness limited to ocular muscles. The presence of anti-AChR antibodies is highly suggestive of MG, but a negative test does not exclude the disease. Antibodies to MuSK and LRP4 are found in some patients
  • Recurrent nerve stimulation test: At low frequency (3 Hz) testing, MG shows a decremental response > 10%, while Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) shows a variable response. While at higher frequencies, MG shows normal or decremental response and LEMS shows an incremental response.
  • Block and jitter response on single-fiber electromyography
  • Positive edrophonium test: improvement of ptosis on the administration of anticholinesterase such as edrophonium
  • Positive ice-pack test: improvement of ptosis on the application of ice-pack on the affected eye

The first line of medical management in MG is anticholinesterase drugs. Pyridostigmine 30–60 mg three to four times daily is the most commonly used drug.

Patients are evaluated for associated thymic abnormalities using a CT chest. Thymectomy is considered in patients with thymoma and in generalized MG patients with anti-AChR antibodies.

Immunotherapy therapy can be initiated in patients with poor control on pyridostigmine after thymectomy. Glucocorticoids, cyclosporine, or tacrolimus are generally effective within 1-3 months. Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil may take several months to show beneficial effects and are used for the long-term management of MG. Rituximab has shown effectiveness in patients with MuSK antibodies. Intravenous eculizumab, which binds to terminal complement component 5, is also effective.

Myasthenic crisis is the life-threatening exacerbation of MG leading to respiratory failure. Treatment for myasthenic crisis should take place in intensive care units. It is important to rule out excessive anticholinesterase medication as a cause of deterioration by temporarily discontinuing these drugs. Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) are beneficial in hastening recovery.
lessonTitle: Myasthenia Gravis And Other Neuromuscular Junction Disorders
question: What is not a feature of myasthenia gravis among the following?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis and ptosis is the most common ocular feature of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction most commonly caused by anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The disorder is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles where the weakness increases during repeated use and may improve following rest.

Ptosis and diplopia are common initial complaints due to early involvement of the lids and extraocular muscles (EOMs). Of them, Ptosis is a more common manifestation than diplopia. Ptosis in myasthenia gravis is insidious, bilateral, and frequently asymmetrical.

Investigations of myasthenia gravis include:

  1. Ice pack test -This tests for a transient improvement of the ptotic eyelid on placing an ice pack for 2 minutes, as the cold inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by acetylcholinesterase.
  2. Tensilon (Edrophonium) test - This tests for a transient improvement in the weakness on administration of a short-acting anticholinesterase such as edrophonium.
  3. Antibody testing - for Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies, MuSK protein antibodies helps support a diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.
lessonTitle: Myasthenia Gravis And Other Neuromuscular Junction Disorders
question: A 45-year-old patient comes with complaints of progressive weakness as the day progresses. He is found to have antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which is the most common ocular finding in this disease?

correctAnswer: D. Pupils are affected in 50% of the cases
explanationHtml:
The pupils are always spared in myasthenia gravis (MG), differentiating it from other disorders marked by similar ocular symptoms (e.g. botulism)

If weakness remains restricted to the extraocular muscles for 3 years, it is likely that it will not become generalized. These patients are said to have ocular MG.

Ptosis and/or diplopia are the initial symptoms of MG in up to 85% of patients. The ptosis may increase with sustained upward gaze or by holding up the opposite eyelid with the examiner's finger (curtain sign).

Cogan lid twitch is characteristic of MG. It refers to a brief overshoot twitch of the lid when the patient is made to gaze upwards after a period of downgaze.

RNS studies (repetitive nerve stimulation) and anti-AChR antibodies are often negative. Single-fiber EMG (SFEMG) testing may be required for confirming the diagnosis in seronegative patients.
lessonTitle: Myasthenia Gravis And Other Neuromuscular Junction Disorders

Manually raising the more ptotic lid causes increased ptosis on the opposite side
Extraocular muscle involvement produces binocular diplopia
Pupils are affected in 50% of the cases

explanationHtml:
Dysferlin deficiency is not associated with congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS). CMS is an uncommon cause of neuromuscular junction failure in newborns. In CMS, the immune system is unaffected.

The common syndromes associated with CMS are as follows:

  • Slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome (SCCMS)
  • Fast-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome (FCCMS)
  • Primary acetylcholine receptor deficiency

question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with congenital myasthenic syndrome?

correctAnswer: D. Incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation
explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). Incremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation is a feature of this condition.

LEMS is a neuromuscular junction disorder associated with the reduced acetylcholine (Ach) release from the presynaptic nerve terminals, despite normal ACh vesicle numbers.

LEMS occurs due to a hamper in the normal calcium flux (essential for acetylcholine release) caused due to autoantibodies acting against the P/Q voltage-gated calcium channel (VGCC).

An association of malignancy, mainly small cell lung cancer (SCLC) accounts for about half of all the LEMS cases.

Most patients with LEMS present with symptoms as slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness. In LEMS, the weakness improves for a while after exertion. Diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes help differentiate between LEMS and myasthenia gravis.

Diagnosis of LEMS can be made when there is a 100% increase in amplitude of action potential in a compound muscle after exercise or by repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS).

options.text: Paraneoplastic syndrome seen in lung adenocarcinoma
Incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation

question: A 65-year-old man who is a laborer presents with progressive weakness of the legs. He says that the weakness is more in the morning and as the day progresses, it improves for a while usually. He is a known smoker. Examination reveals diminished deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) is the most sensitive test to diagnose myasthenia gravis. The occurrence of jitter in the presence of a normal fibre density confirms the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis.

Other laboratory tests for the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis (MG) are:

  • Anti-AChR radioimmunoassay: positive results confirm diagnosis, but negative results do not rule out the condition
  • Anti-MuSK antibodies: Done in patients who tested negative for AChR antibody
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation: a decrease of >10% in the amplitude of evoked potentials indicates a high probability of MG
  • Endrophonium chloride: Improvement of symptoms on administration of edrophonium indicates MG. However, this test is not routinely done now.

explanationHtml:
Pyridostigmine is the first-line drug of choice in the treatment of symptomatic myasthenia gravis.

Treatment for myasthenia gravis involves:

  • Symptomatic treatment: Anticholinesterase agents – Pyridostigmine is the initial therapy of choice.
  • Immunotherapy: glucocorticoids, azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, rituximab
  • Plasmapheresis and IVIG: These can be used in cases where immediate management is required.
  • Thymectomy

    Complement Inhibitors: Eculizumab, Ravulizumab, Zilucoplan.

explanationHtml:

question: A female patient with myasthenia gravis was admitted with complaints of sore throat, fever, cough, and weakness. She had a history of repeated hospital admissions due to exacerbation of myasthenia gravis. During some of the episodes, she even required intubation. Blood culture on admission revealed MRSA infection. Which of the following drugs can be safely administered to this patient for treating the infection?

explanationHtml:
Myasthenia gravis patients are resistant to depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, e.g., succinylcholine. The primary pathology of myasthenia gravis is a decreased number of acetylcholine receptors. Therefore, these patients have a scarcity of receptors on which depolarising NMBA's act.

Local anesthetics and inhalation anesthetics are usually well-tolerated in myasthenia gravis with occasional exacerbations.

question: Patients with myasthenia gravis are resistant to anesthesia with which of the following drugs?

explanationHtml:
Pyridostigmine is an anticholinesterase inhibitor that does not alter the disease process of myasthenia gravis.

Anticholinesterase inhibitors improve muscle contractions by allowing released acetylcholine to accumulate and act on the receptors over a large area and also have the additional direct depolarizing effect on the motor endplate.

They do not alter the disease process but provide symptomatic relief. The underlying disease process continues and ultimately it may not be possible to restore muscle strength with anticholinesterase inhibitors alone. It is due to the reduction of the receptors by the antibodies.

Drugs like prednisone, mycophenolate mofetil, and azathioprine are immunosuppressive agents that reduce the antibody titers and can modify the disease process.

question: All of the following are the drugs that are used for the treatment of patients with myasthenia gravis. Which of the following does not alter the disease process?

correctAnswer: D. It is caused by biochemical abnormality of myelin
explanationHtml:
Demyelinating disorders do not include biochemical abnormalities of myelin. Disorders occuring due to biochemical abnormalities of myelin are called dysmyelinating disorders.

Multiple sclerosis is the most common immune-mediated, inflammatory demyelinating disorder. It commonly presents in adulthood.

options.text: Multiple sclerosis is the most common type
It is caused by biochemical abnormality of myelin

question: Which of the following statements is false regarding demyelinating disorders?

correctAnswer: B. It is an autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system
explanationHtml:
Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system. It is characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (scarring), and neuronal loss.

The peripheral nervous system is spared in MS.

The course of the disease may be relapsing-remitting or progressive. The clinical course of manifestation can be variable ranging from a benign condition to a rapidly evolving and incapacitating disease.

options.text: It is an acute inflammatory condition of neurons
It is an autoimmune disease affecting the central nervous system
It may also involve the peripheral nervous system
The condition is always benign and resolves spontaneously

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding multiple sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
HLA-DRB1 is a risk factor for the development of multiple sclerosis, not HLA-B27.

Risk factors supporting the course of development of multiple sclerosis include:

  • Cigarette smoking
  • Vitamin D deficiency
  • Family history, HLA-DRB1
  • Exposure to Epstein-Barr virus (Human Herpesvirus 4) after early childhood
question: A patient with weakness of the limbs and reduced vision, after evaluation, was diagnosed to be a case of multiple sclerosis. Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of this condition?

explanationHtml:
In multiple sclerosis, the slowing of conduction is due to the loss of the myelin sheath.

Under normal circumstances, nerve conduction in myelinated axons occurs in a saltatory manner i.e from one node of Ranvier to another. But, when demyelination sets in, the nerve impulse are unable to travel as fast due to not being saltatory. This produces either a conduction block or delay.

Lesions due to multiple sclerosis begin with perivenular cuffing by inflammatory mononuclear cells. Myelin-specific autoantibodies cause degeneration of myelin sheaths. As lesions evolve, prominent astrocytic proliferation (gliosis) is observed.

Demyelination is the hallmark in the pathology of multiple sclerosis. But, it is not solely a disease affecting the myelin sheath. Partial or total axonal destruction (neuronal loss) can also occur.
question: The slowing of conduction in multiple sclerosis is due to which of the following?

correctAnswer: B. Both Myelin basic protein & Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein
explanationHtml: The autoantibodies in multiple sclerosis are directed against both myelin basic protein (MBP) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG).

options.text: Both Myelin basic protein &amp; Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein

question: Autoantibodies in multiple sclerosis are directed against which of the following?

correctAnswer: C. Remyelination of axons in the central nervous system
explanationHtml:
Remyelination of axons in the central nervous system leads to the formation of shadow plaques.

Shadow plaques develop due to the partial remyelination of the naked axons by surviving oligodendrocytes or those that differentiate from precursor cells.

options.text: Demyelination of axons in the central nervous system
Demyelination of axons in the peripheral nervous system
Remyelination of axons in the central nervous system
Remyelination of axons in the peripheral nervous system

question: Which of the following processes lead to the formation of shadow plaques in patients with multiple sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
An electric shock-like sensation radiating down the back into the legs is called Lhermitte's sign. It is associated with multiple sclerosis.

It is induced typically by flexion or other movements of the neck. Lhermitte’s sign can also occur simultaneously with other disorders of the cervical spinal cord like cervical spondylosis.

Option A: Uhthoff ’s phenomenon refers to the unilateral visual blurring that may occur during a hot shower or with physical exercise. It is an exacerbation of the symptoms of multiple sclerosis due to heat.

Option C: Stransky's sign is a clinical sign in which vigorous abduction followed by the sudden release of the little toe causes an extensor plantar reflex. It is seen in pyramidal tract lesions.

Option D: Cornell's sign is a clinical sign in which scratching along the inner side of the extensor hallucis longus tendon elicits an extensor plantar reflex. It is seen in pyramidal tract lesions.
question: A 40-year-old woman with a history of multiple sclerosis comes to the hospital. She describes an electric shock–like sensation radiating down the back into the legs. What is the name of this sign?

explanationHtml:
The MRI image shows Dawson's fingers.

Dawson's fingers are demyelinating plaques through the corpus callosum, arranged at right angles along medullary veins (callososeptal location). They are a characteristic feature of multiple sclerosis and presents as T2 hyperintensities.

MRI is the imaging of choice in a patient with multiple sclerosis due to its high sensitivity.

Option A: Black hole lesions are multiple sclerosis plaques indicative of the chronic stage when they display T1 hypointense signals. They signify axonal destruction and irreversible damage.

Option B: The molar tooth sign refers to the appearance of the midbrain in an axial section in which the elongated superior cerebellar peduncles gives the midbrain the appearance of a molar or wisdom tooth. It is seen in Joubert syndrome.

Option C: Tram-track sign in the brain refers to the parallel calcification of the cortex in patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome.
question: An MRI image of a patient with multiple sclerosis is shown below. What is this sign called?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and the MRI finding of Dawson's fingers are suggestive of multiple sclerosis. Revised McDonald’s criteria is used in the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis. It takes into consideration the clinical attacks and objective lesions. In addition, it also involves the assessment of the lesions based on MRI and other imaging techniques.

The Kurtzke expanded disability status scale (EDSS) and functional status (FS) score are widely used measures of neurologic impairment, which are performed following the confirmed diagnosis of multiple sclerosis.
question: A woman presents with recurrent episodes of blurry vision, tingling and numbness in the legs, and falls. She says that during hot weather, she finds it difficult to walk and often falls. Recently she had flu, due to which the symptoms aggravated. MRI brain was done which showed Dawson's fingers. What is the criteria used for the clinical diagnosis of her condition?

correctAnswer: C. Kurtzke expanded disability status scale
explanationHtml:
The Expanded disability status scale (EDSS) gives a measure of neurological impairment in multiple sclerosis.

EDSS scores <3.5: The patient walks normally, shows no disability

EDSS scores >5.5: Progressive disease, gait impairment, and occupational disability

EDSS scores =10.0: Death due to multiple sclerosis
question: In patients with multiple sclerosis, which of the following is used to determine neurological impairment?

explanationHtml:
Glucocorticoids are used in the clinical management of either first attacks or acute exacerbations.

Intravenous methylprednisolone administration at a dose of 500–1000 mg/day for 3-5 days, followed by a course of oral prednisolone beginning at a dose of 60–80 mg/day and gradually tapered over 2 weeks is given.

These medications reduce the severity and shorten the duration of attacks.

Disease-modifying therapies for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis are:

  • IFN-β-1a
  • IFN-β-1b
  • Glatiramer acetate
  • Natalizumab
  • Fingolimod
  • Dimethyl fumarate
  • Teriflunomide
  • Mitoxantrone
  • Alemtuzumab
question: A 45-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents with an exacerbation of her symptoms. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed to her for initial management?

correctAnswer: C. A patient with acute form of multiple sclerosis with no remissions
explanationHtml:
Marburg’s variant is an acute form of multiple sclerosis, typically with no remissions.

It is a fulminant demyelinating process that in some cases progresses, leading to death within 1–2 years. Marburg’s variant does not seem to be associated with infection or vaccination.

Clinical management by high-dose glucocorticoids, plasma exchange, and cyclophosphamide have been tried, with uncertain benefit.

options.text: A patient with chronic form of multiple sclerosis with no remissions
A patient with acute form of multiple sclerosis with remissions
A patient with acute form of multiple sclerosis with no remissions
A patient with chronic form of multiple sclerosis with remissions

question: Which of the following patients have Marburg’s variant of multiple sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of neuromyelitis optica, which is also known as Devic's disease.

It is an aggressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis. Attacks of Optic neuritis can be bilateral or unilateral and myelitis can be severe and involve three or more contiguous vertebral segments.

Core clinical characteristics are:

  • Optic neuritis
  • Acute myelitis
  • Area postrema syndrome: episodes of otherwise unexplained hiccups or nausea or vomiting
  • Acute brainstem syndrome
  • Symptomatic narcolepsy or acute diencephalic clinical syndrome with NMOSD*-typical diencephalic MRI lesions
  • Symptomatic cerebral syndrome with NMOSD*-typical brain lesions

Option A: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a demyelinating condition most frequently associated with an antecedent infection

Option C: Riddoch syndrome is the ability to consciously perceive the stimulus in a blind field. It is seen when there is a lesion in the occipital lobe.

explanationHtml:

question: A 40-year-old male is diagnosed to have SUNCT. It can be distinguished from trigeminal neuralgia by the presence of all except:

explanationHtml:

This most commonly involves the second and/or third divisions (Option B) of the trigeminal nerve territory. Bilateral or early-onset pain is associated with multiple sclerosis. Unilateral trigeminal nerve compression can be due to the superior cerebellar artery.

Pain is repetitive, severe, and brief and can be triggered by touch, cold, wind, or eating. Physical signs are usually absent, although the spasms may make the patient wince and sit silently (tic douloureux). No signs of sensory loss are present (Option D)

The drug of choice is carbamazepine.

It helps improve tremors and reduce both 'off' time and dyskinesia. It does not improve features that fail to respond to levodopa. It does not prevent the development or progression of non-dopaminergic features such as freezing, falling, and dementia.

Progressive supranuclear palsy is an example of Parkinson's plus syndrome.

Parkinson's plus syndrome or atypical parkinsonism refers to a group of conditions that present with parkinsonism (rigidity and bradykinesia) but are different from PD due to underlying differences in clinical manifestations and pathology. They may have degeneration of the striatum, globus pallidus, cerebellum, and brainstem as well as the SNc. These include multiple system atrophy (MSA), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), and corticobasal syndrome (CBS).

PSP is often misdiagnosed as Parkinson’s disease (PD). The substantia nigra is damaged in both diseases and this accounts for the overlapping symptoms which are observed. In PSP, impairment of cognitive functions occurs before the motor or ocular signs and this serves as an important distinguishing feature.

Immunohistochemistry broadly classifies them into two subtypes: synucleopathies and tauopathies.

question: A 60-year-old man presented with Parkinsonism and cerebellar features. MRI showed the finding as shown in the image. What is the likely diagnosis?

Orthostatic hypotension is not a core clinical feature of Lewy body dementia (LBD) as per DSM-5.

LBD also known as dementia with Lewy bodies is the second most common type of progressive dementia after Alzheimer’s disease. Protein deposits, called Lewy bodies, deposit in nerve cells in the brain region involved in thinking, memory, and movement (motor control)

Core features of LBD as per DSM-5 are fluctuating cognition, attention, alertness, recurrent visual hallucination, and Parkinsonian symptoms. Suggestive features are REM sleep behavior disorder and severe neuroleptic sensitivity.
Orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, and constipation are other features of LBD.

Treatment of LBD includes rivastigmine and donepezil which may improve cognition, and reduce hallucinosis and delusion. Pimavanserin may be used to treat psychosis.

explanationHtml:
An elderly male with a history of features of Parkinsonism nonresponsive to levodopa should raise suspicion for Parkinson plus syndromes which include progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP).

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), also known as the Steele-Richardson-Olszewski syndrome, is a tauopathy and is considered a neurodegenerative disease with no current efficacious treatment. It is characterized by decreased cognition, abnormal eye movements (supranuclear vertical gaze palsy), postural instability and falls, as well as parkinsonian features and speech disturbances.

The atrophy of the midbrain results in hummingbird sign of the brainstem (in the sagittal plane). The preserved pons form the body of the bird, and the atrophic midbrain, the head, with beak extending anteriorly towards the optic chiasm. Midbrain atrophy is best confirmed with the reduction in the midbrain to pons ratio.

Mickey mouse appearance, which is the reduction of anteroposterior midline midbrain diameter, at the level of the superior colliculi is seen on axial imaging.

Rapid, semi-purposeful, graceful, dance-like, involuntary movements are seen in chorea.

Hyperkinetic movement disorders:

Tremor

Rhythmic oscillation of a body part due to intermittent muscle contractions

Dystonia

Involuntary, sustained or repeated muscle contractions often associated with twisting movements and abnormal posture

Athetosis

Slow, distal, writhing, involuntary movements with a propensity to affect arms and hands

Chorea

Rapid, semi-purposeful, graceful, dance-like, non patterned, involuntary movements involving distal or proximal muscle groups

Myoclonus

Sudden, brief (<100ms), jerk-like arrhythmic muscle twitches

Tics

Brief, repeated, stereotyped muscle contractions that can often be suppressed for a short time

Sydenham's chorea (also called St. Vitus's dance) is a type of chorea that is typically seen in childhood (5-15 years) with prior exposure to group A streptococcal infection and is thought to be autoimmune in nature. It is characterized by the acute onset of choreiform movements and behavioral disturbances and is self-limiting.
question: An 8-year-old girl exhibits rapid, semi-purposeful, graceful, dance-like, involuntary movements. What is this finding?

question: During rounds, you see that a patient diagnosed with stroke exhibits wild, flinging movements on his right side. Where is the lesion likely to be?

explanationHtml:
The most common acute drug-induced movement disorder is dystonia.

Drug-induced movement disorders are primarily associated with drugs that block dopamine receptors(neuroleptics) or central dopaminergic transmission. Neuroleptics are the commonest cause of this condition. Drug-induced movement disorders are classified as:

  • Acute: Dystonia is the most common acute hyperkinetic drug reaction; generalized in children, focal in adults.
  • Subacute: Akathisia is the commonest reaction in this category
  • Tardive syndromes: Develop after months to years of initiation of the drug.
    • Tardive dyskinesia is the most common. Choreiform movements affecting the mouth, lips, and tongue are seen. In severe cases, trunks, limbs, and respiratory muscles may also be affected.
    • In one third, TD remits within 3 months of stopping the drug and improvement occur over several years.

explanationHtml:
The most common movement disorder is essential tremor.

It can present in childhood but dramatically increases in prevalence over the age of 70 years. Essential tremor is characterized by a high-frequency tremor 6-10 Hz that predominantly affects the upper extremities.

The tremor is characteristically improved by alcohol and worsened by stress.

explanationHtml:
Westphal akinetic variant has the worst prognosis.

Huntington's disease shows an autosomal dominant inheritance. It is a trinucleotide repeat expansion disease with multiple CAG repeats (>40 repeats) in the coding region of the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p. It demonstrates genetic anticipation with earlier onset if inherited from the father.

It presents in the second to third decade of life with cognitive impairment as an early feature. The dominant cognitive feature of HD is executive dysfunction. Additionally, dementia is seen later as the disease progresses.

Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia. Decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea. Treatment consists of haloperidol, tetrabenazine (Dopamine depletor).

St. Vitus's dance is another name for Sydenham's chorea.

Sydenham's chorea is more common in females. It is typically seen in childhood (5-1 5 years) with prior exposure to group A streptococcal infection and is thought to be autoimmune in nature.

It is self limited.Treatment is generally restricted to those with severe chorea.The chorea generally responds to dopamine-blocking agents, valproic acid, and carbamazepine.

correctAnswer: C. Symptoms that begin or worsen with activity
explanationHtml:
In restless leg syndrome (RLS), symptoms begin or worsen with rest. It is also called as Willis-Ekbom disease.

The four core symptoms required for the diagnosis of RLS are:

  • An urge to move the legs
  • Usually caused or accompanied by an unpleasant sensation in the legs (creepy-crawly feeling, paresthesia, or burning)
  • Symptoms that begin or worsen with rest and partial or complete relief by movement
  • Worsening during the evening or night

Restless leg syndrome is a typical sensory-motor disorder that generally affects the legs during rest periods, especially sleep. There is an irresistible urge to shake the legs associated with burning sensation, itching, and cramps of the legs. In idiopathic cases, dopaminergic hypofunction is postulated.

In patients with restless legs syndrome, iron stores are initially repleted, and the aggravating factors are eliminated. If RLS still persists, initial therapy with a gabapentinoid (pregabalin, gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil) is preferred, rather than a dopamine agonist (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine). This is due to the high frequency of intermediate and long-term augmentation with dopamine agonists, as well as their risk of impulse control disorders.

FDA-approved drugs for the treatment of restless leg syndrome:

  • Gabapentin
  • Ropinirole
  • Pramipexole
  • Rotigotine

A dopamine agonist is used as an alternative in patients with increased risk for side effects from gabapentinoids, such as those with obesity and its complications, a past or present history of moderate to severe depression, a disorder causing gait instability or respiratory failure, and a history of substance use disorder.

Non-pharmacological treatments that can be used in restless leg syndrome are:

  • Avoiding alcohol at bedtime
  • Massaging affected legs
  • Hot baths
  • Applying hot or cold to the affected area
  • Engaging in moderate exercises

explanationHtml:
Bulbar paralysis refers to LMN palsy of cranial nerves 9 to 12. It is seen due to disease processes affecting primarily the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves.

The manifestations of bulbar palsy include paralysis of tongue, muscles of swallowing, and facial muscles. There is difficulty handling secretions and maintaining an airway.

Causes of bulbar palsy include:

question: Which of the following is referred to as bulbar paralysis?

explanationHtml:
Primary lateral sclerosis is a progressive isolated upper motor neuron disorder.

The spectrum of motor neuron disease includes:

  • Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS):
    • It is the most common form of motor neuron disease
    • Includes upper and lower motor neuron pathology (UMN +LMN)
  • Primary lateral sclerosis:
    • It is a progressive isolated upper motor neuron disorder (UMN)
    • Some patients develop lower motor neuron signs later in their clinical course, at which point the disease is called upper motor neuron-onset ALS
  • Progressive muscular atrophy:
    • It is a progressive isolated lower motor neuron disorder (LMN)
    • Some patients develop upper motor neuron signs later in their clinical course, at which point the disease is called lower motor neuron-onset ALS
  • Progressive bulbar palsy:
    • It is a progressive upper and lower motor neuron (UMN +LMN) disorder of cranial muscles
    • This condition may occasionally stay isolated to the bulbar segment, but more commonly, upper and lower motor neuron signs and symptoms spread to involve other segments. This is then referred to as bulbar-onset ALS

question: Which type of disorder is primary lateral sclerosis?

correctAnswer: A. Anterior horn cell + corticospinal tract
explanationHtml:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) involves the anterior horn cells and corticospinal tract.

ALS is the most common form of progressive motor neuron disease.

The pathologic hallmark of motor neuron degenerative disorders is the death of lower motor neurons and upper, or corticospinal, motor neurons. LMN consist of anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and their brainstem homologs innervating bulbar muscles. UMN originate in layer five of the motor cortex and descend via the pyramidal tract to synapse with lower motor neurons, either directly or indirectly via interneurons.

Although at its onset, ALS may cause selective loss of function of only upper or lower motor neurons, it ultimately causes progressive loss of both categories of motor neurons.
lessonTitle: Als And Other Motor Neuron Diseases
question: Which of the following is involved in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

ALS is characterised by both upper and lower motor neuron (UMN + LMN) dysfunction. The signs of UMN dysfunction include spasticity and brisk jaw jerk, while the signs of LMN dysfunction include atrophy and weakness of limbs.

Usually, an MRI is normal in ALS; however, a T2-weighted MRI can sometimes show increased signal in the corticospinal tract

question: A middle-aged man presents with progressive atrophy and weakness of his hands and forearms. On examination, he is found to have spasticity of the legs and brisk jaw jerk. Neuroimaging revealed increased signal in the corticospinal tracts on T2 weighted MRI. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario with both UMN (positive Babinski sign) and LMN (absent reflexes and wasting of muscles) signs are suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). It is also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, after the famous New York Yankee baseball player who was affected with the disorder.

ALS was first described by Charcot in the 19th century and is also referred to as Charcot's disease.

Option A: Kennedy disease is a gradually progressive neuromuscular disorder characterised by wasting of proximal and bulbar muscles. It is caused by a mutation in the androgen receptor gene.

Option C: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease is an inherited leukodystrophy characterized by problems with coordination, motor skills, and learning.

Option D: Charcot-Marie-tooth disease encompasses a group of hereditary sensory and motor neuropathies.

question: A young college student presents with multiple episodes of falls while climbing stairs. He stated he had been feeling clumsy and weak for the past few months. On examination, he was found to have bilateral positive Babinski's sign and atrophy of muscles of lower limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were absent. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is suggestive of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This condition is linked to mutations of the gene encoding copper-zinc (Cu, Zn) superoxide dismutase type 1 (SOD1). Familial ALS accounts for about 10% of all ALS cases.

Option B: Mutations in the NADPH oxidase genes cause chronic granulomatous disease (CGD).

Option C: Hereditary deficiency of myeloperoxidase (MPO) predisposes to immune deficiency.

Option D: Glutathione peroxidase deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia.

question: A 42-year-old man who presented with progressive weakness was found to have a mix of upper and lower motor neuron findings on examination. His father and his cousin had passed away in their 40s due to similar symptoms. A mutation of the gene encoding which of the following enzymes is likely implicated here?

explanationHtml:
Orthostatic hypotension is not a feature seen in classical ALS. Autonomic symptoms are not classically seen in ALS, although a few cases with autonomic insufficiency have been reported and these are classified separately as ALS-plus syndromes.

Other options:

Option A: Split-hand syndrome in ALS refers to a pattern of muscle wasting where muscles of the thumb (thenar) side are affected more than those on the medial (hypothenar) side, producing a “split” appearance.

Option C: There is a well-established link between ALS and frontotemporal executive dysfunction (dementia) that may precede or follow the onset of upper and/or lower motor neuron dysfunction

Option D: Dropped head syndrome is an important clinical sign in ALS caused by severe neck extensor weakness (LMN), which leads to an inability to maintain level head position.

question: All of the following features can be seen in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, except:

correctAnswer: D. A patient with bowel and bladder dysfunction
explanationHtml:
The patient with bowel and bladder dysfunction is unlikely to have ALS, as these findings are not seen in ALS. Even in the late stages of ALS, sensory & bowel & bladder functions are preserved.

Fasciculations, muscle cramps, weakness, atrophy, and bulbar palsy are LMN features seen in ALS.

Spasticity, increased reflexes, flexor spasms, and pseudobulbar palsy are UMN features in ALS.

A frequent bulbar UMN symptom seen in ALS is the pseudobulbar affect. This is manifested as episodes of uncontrolled crying or laughing, often inappropriate to the mood or provoked by trivial stimuli.

question: Which of the following patients is unlikely to have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The diagnosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is predominantly based on clinical criteria.

The diagnostic clinical criteria for ALS include the presence of :

  • upper motor neuron signs
  • lower motor neuron signs
  • progressive weakness

Major symptoms of ALS include muscle wasting, fasciculations, spasticity, and hyperreflexia.

Other diagnostic modalities like MRI and CSF examination can also help in diagnosis, although they are not used as the sole criterion. MRI is done to exclude any structural pathology, and CSF analysis helps eliminate infections or inflammation.

EMG findings can confirm lower motor neuron damage and help distinguish ALS from similar disorders. Blood parameters can be checked to rule out metabolic or nutritional deficiencies (like vitamin B12 or E).

A muscle biopsy can be performed if there is a clinical suspicion of inflammatory myopathy.

Riluzole improves survival in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. It reduces the release of glutamate, thereby preventing excessive stimulation by the neurotransmitter.

A newer drug, edaravone, was found to slow the progression of ALS-related disability, probably due to antioxidant action.

Posterior column carries proprioception which is essential for coordination of motor movements. Loss of this leads to the development of a stomping gait. This is seen in cases of vitamin B12 deficiency leading to subacute combined degeneration, tabes dorsalis or diabetic neuropathy.
question: A patient walks with a stomping gait. When asked to close his eyes and walk, he is unable to do so. Which of the following tracts is probably affected?

explanationHtml:
Intention tremor is a feature of cerebellar ataxia, not resting tremor.

Cerebellar ataxia is characterized by the following symptoms:

  • Gait impairment
  • Unclear speech or scanning speech
  • Blurred vision due to nystagmus
  • Dysdiadochokinesis
  • Intention tremors - tremor on goal-oriented movements

Bilateral and symmetric involvement suggests the following etiologies:

  • Genetic - SCA gene mutations
  • Metabolic - Vitamin B1 or B12 deficiency
  • Immune - Antigliadin antibody syndrome
  • Toxic - Phenytoin, amiodarone, alcohol

Focal, unilateral symptoms with headache, impaired level of consciousness, ipsilateral cranial nerve palsies and contralateral weakness suggest a space-occupying cerebellar lesion.
question: Which of the following features would you not expect to find in a patient with cerebellar ataxia?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia, which is most likely to be caused by small cell lung cancer here.

Paraneoplastic syndromes causing cerebellar ataxia are associated with various antibodies:

Cancer Antibody seen
Breast and ovarian cancers Anti-Yo antibody

Sometimes, paraneoplastic ataxias may be the only presenting symptom of the underlying cancer. In paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxias, serum anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies may be elevated, affecting speech and gait.
question: A 70-year-old man presented with gait instability, slurring of speech, and intention tremors, for a few months. He was a former smoker who quit 10 years back. After extensive workup, a paraneoplastic cause was suspected, and chest CT was ordered. It showed a 3cm wide mass near the right hilum. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Friedreich's ataxia is the most common form of inherited ataxia (autosomal recessive), comprising one-half of all hereditary ataxias.

Friedrich's ataxia has autosomal recessive inheritance and presents before 25 years of age. The median age of death is 35 years. Women have a significantly better prognosis than men.

Friedrich's ataxia presents with clinical features such as dysarthria, progressive staggering gait, frequent falls and titubation. Other neurological symptoms include nystagmus, loss of fast saccadic movements, loss of vibratory and proprioceptive sensation, and ataxia or trunk and limb movements. The lower extremities are more severely involved than the upper ones.

Cardiac involvement occurs in 90% of patients. It presents with cardiomegaly, symmetric hypertrophy, and conduction defects. Musculoskeletal deformities are common and include progressive scoliosis, pes cavus, and pes equinovarus.
question: What is the most common inherited ataxia?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of Friedrich's ataxia, in which the dorsal root ganglion cells are involved first.

The primary sites of pathology are the spinal cord, dorsal root ganglion cells, and the peripheral nerves.

Spinal cord tracts are involved, and degeneration occurs predominantly in the spinocerebellar tracts, lateral corticospinal tracts, and posterior columns. Degeneration of cranial nerves (glossopharyngeal, vagus, hypoglossal) and deep cerebellar nuclei can occur. Peripheral nerves are also involved, and there's a loss of large myelinated fibers. Cerebellar atrophy is also seen.

Cardiac changes occur due to myocyte hypertrophy, fibrosis, and degeneration of cardiac ganglia.

Note: Friedrich's ataxia may also be associated with vitamin E deficiency.
question:
A 24-year-old man presents with complaints of swaying while walking, frequent falls and slurring of speech. He also gives a history of involuntary nodding movements of the head. On examination, you note the following findings. Which of the following regions of the spinal cord is involved first in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario and smear showing macroovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, is suggestive of megaloblastic anemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency. Myopathy is not a feature of vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 deficiency may produce the following neurological manifestations:

  • Loss of vibration sense and proprioception
  • Paresthesia - upper limb paresthesias occur before lower limbs are affected.
  • Unsteady gait - due to sensory ataxia
  • Peripheral neuropathy

question: A middle-aged vegan woman presented with tingling and numbness over the limbs and progressive fatigue. Her peripheral smear is given below. Which of the following neurological manifestation would you not expect to see in this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of subacute combined degeneration (SACD) due to vitamin B12 deficiency.

SACD presents with the following features:

  • Loss of vibration sense and proprioception
  • Paresthesia - upper limb paresthesias occur before lower limbs are affected.
  • Unsteady gait - due to sensory ataxia
  • Loss of deep tendon reflexes
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Optic neuropathy - can present as blurring of vision
  • Psychiatric manifestations such as:
    • Irritated behavior
    • Severe dementia
    • Frank psychosis

MRI spine shows myelopathy and areas of demyelination. Myelopathy of SACD tends to be diffuse rather than focal.

Treatment is replacement therapy is with 1000 μg of intramuscular vitamin B12 repeated at regular intervals or by oral vitamin B12.
question: A 30-year-old man presented with swaying while walking, tingling in palms and feet, and blurring of vision. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent, proprioception and vibration sense are absent over the lower limbs. MRI spine reveals diffuse demyelination. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario is suggestive of tabes dorsalis. It presents with loss of reflexes in lower limbs, not hyperreflexia.

Tabes dorsalis (also known as syphilitic myelopathy), seen in tertiary syphilis, is a chronic degeneration and demyelination of the dorsal column tracts of the spinal cord and dorsal roots.

It presents with the following clinical features:

  • Loss of reflexes in lower limbs
  • Romberg's sign
  • Bilateral Argyll Robertson pupils - accommodation reflex present, pupillary reflex absent
  • Loss of position sense and vibration
  • Stabbing/pricking pain in the legs - this is fleeting or repetitive
  • Ataxia of the legs and gait disturbances
  • Paresthesias
  • Bladder disturbances
  • Acute abdominal pain with vomiting - visceral crisis

Note: Diabetic polyradiculopathy may simulate tabes.

explanationHtml:
Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive condition presenting in the first decade of life.

It is associated with a high incidence of recurrent pulmonary infections, lymphomas, Hodgkin's disease, breast cancer, and acute T cell leukemias.

Histology shows loss of Purkinje cells, granules, and basket cells in the cerebellar cortex. There is a loss of neurons in the deep cerebellar nuclei, inferior olives of the medulla, and anterior horn and dorsal root of the spinal cord.

Clinical features of ataxia-telangiectasia include:

  • Progressive telangiectatic lesions
  • Oculomotor apraxia
  • Truncal and limb ataxia
  • Dysarthria
  • Extensor plantar reflexes
  • Myoclonic jerks
  • Areflexia
  • Distal sensory deficits
  • Nystagmus
  • Cellular and humoral immunodeficiency (absent/ill-developed thymus)

question: Which of the following is false regarding ataxia telangiectasia?

explanationHtml:
The given case scenario describes an elderly woman with urinary incontinence, dementia (cognitive decline), and a history of multiple falls (suggestive of a gait abnormality or ataxia). These form the classical triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH).

Both frontotemporal dementia (Option B) and Parkinson’s disease (Option C) are common causes of dementia associated with falls, but urinary incontinence is not commonly appreciated. NPH is, therefore, the most likely diagnosis.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus refers to a disproportionate enlargement of the ventricles compared to the degree of cortical atrophy. It is a communicating hydrocephalus caused by delayed resorption of cerebrospinal fluid. Out of the classical triad of symptoms, most patients present with one or two. Hence, neuroimaging showing dilated ventricles is essential, as well as an L- dopa challenge test to rule out parkinson’s disease is recommended.

A characteristic MRI of NPH is given below, showing dilated lateral ventricles which are out of proportion to sulcal deepening:

question: An elderly woman is brought to the OPD with complaints of behavioral change, a history of multiple falls, urinary incontinence, and dementia. What is your diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. III, IV, V and VI
explanationHtml:
The cranial nerves III, IV, V, and VI are affected by cavernous sinus syndrome.

The cavernous sinus syndrome is a condition caused by any pathology involving the cavernous sinus. The oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV) and trigeminal (V) nerves pass in relation to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. The abducent (VI) nerve passes through the cavernous sinus.

Patients with this condition usually present with the following features:

  • Orbital or facial pain
  • Orbital swelling and chemosis due to occlusion of the ophthalmic veins
  • Fever
  • Oculomotor neuropathy (III, IV, and VI)
  • Trigeminal neuropathy (V)

Causes of cavernous sinus syndrome include:

  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis - most common
  • Carotid artery aneurysm
  • Carotid-cavernous fistula
  • Tumors such as meningioma.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following cranial nerves are affected in cavernous sinus syndrome?

correctAnswer: C. The condition is also known as tic douloureux
explanationHtml:
Tic douloureux is another term for trigeminal neuralgia.

Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by frequent paroxysms of severe pain in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin. It is sometimes seen in the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

Middle-aged and elderly females are primarily affected. The pain usually lasts for a short time (seconds to minutes), but it may be intense enough that the patient winces, hence the term 'tic'.

A characteristic feature is the presence of trigger zones, typically on the face, lips, or tongue. Patients usually report excruciating pain during activities such as washing the face or brushing the teeth. However, no signs of sensory loss can be demonstrated.

options.text: The region of ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve is always spared
The pain usually last for a few hours
The condition is also known as tic douloureux
It is more common in men

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding trigeminal neuralgia?

correctAnswer: A. Oligodendrocyte-derived myelin covering the beginning of the nerve
explanationHtml:
The high frequency of trigeminal neuralgia in patients with multiple sclerosis occurs due to the involvement of oligodendrocyte-derived myelin covering the beginning of the nerve.

Multiple sclerosis is a disorder of oligodendrocyte myelin. It should be ruled out when trigeminal neuralgia is bilateral or develops in a young adult. In such cases, the cause is a demyelinating plaque near the root entry zone of the fifth cranial nerve in the pons. In these patients, a facial sensory loss is also often found in association.

options.text: Oligodendrocyte-derived myelin covering the beginning of the nerve
Oligodendrocyte-derived myelin covering the terminal part of the nerve
Schwann cell–derived myelin sheath covering the beginning of the nerve
Schwann cell–derived myelin sheath covering the terminal part of the nerve

question: The high frequency of trigeminal neuralgia in patients with multiple sclerosis is mainly attributed to the involvement of ______.

explanationHtml:
The superior cerebellar artery most often compresses the trigeminal nerve as it emerges from the brainstem. This causes lancinating pain in the distribution of the nerve which is known as trigeminal neuralgia.

Though trigeminal neuralgia can be diagnosed by the clinical features, MRI is recommended to define the underlying cause. In cases refractory to medical management, it also helps to plan for surgical decompression.
question: In patients with trigeminal neuralgia, the nerve is most commonly compressed by ______.

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia and the drug of choice is carbamazepine.

Oxcarbazepine is an alternative to carbamazepine that has less bone marrow toxicity and is equally efficacious.

Other drugs used are lamotrigine, gabapentin and baclofen.
question: A food vlogger presents with complaints of episodes of piercing electric-shock like pain on the left side of her face. The episodes are triggered by chewing food and last for a few minutes. She is further distressed as it interferes with her work. She has tried over the counter analgesics to no avail. What is the drug of choice for her?

explanationHtml:
Maximal weakness occurs within 48 hours as a rule in Bells' palsy.

Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, peripheral facial paralysis or paresis of acute onset due to a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve.

Clinical presentation of Bell’s palsy:

  • Pain behind the ear (may precede paralysis and last for 1-2 days)
  • Bell's phenomenon
  • Asymmetrical face
  • Hyperacusis (due to stapedial paralysis)
  • Loss of taste (involvement of chorda tympani).

MRI may reveal swelling and uniform enhancement of the geniculate ganglion and facial nerve.

Approximately 80% of patients recover within a few weeks or months. The presence of incomplete paralysis in the first week is the most favorable prognostic sign. Recurrence may be seen in some cases.

options.text: MRI shows enhancement of geniculate ganglion

question: Which of the following is false about Bell's palsy?

explanationHtml:
Herpes simplex virus is most commonly implicated in causing Bell’s palsy.

Varicella-zoster virus is the second most common cause.
question: Which of the following viruses is most commonly implicated in Bell’s palsy?

correctAnswer: C. It is a normal phenomenon evident in facial paralysis
explanationHtml:
Bell’s phenomenon refers to a normal phenomenon that becomes evident in facial paralysis. The eyeballs roll up and outwards on attempting to close the eyes.

It is also known as the palpebral oculogyric reflex. It is a normal protective reflex resulting in the elevation of globes while blinking to protect the eyes from injury. It also serves to provide a wiper blade-like cleansing function of the cornea by the eyelid.

However, it occurs behind the closed eyelids in healthy individuals. It becomes noticeable in Bell's palsy as the eyelids fail to close completely.

The image below shows a patient with evident Bell’s phenomenon.

[[figure-1]]

options.text: Eyeballs roll upwards on attempting to open the eyes
Eyeballs roll downwards on attempting to close the eyes
It is a normal phenomenon evident in facial paralysis
It is an abnormal phenomenon evident in facial paralysis

question: Which of the following is true about Bell’s phenomenon?

correctAnswer: D. Acyclovir 1g twice daily for 10 days
explanationHtml:
Acyclovir may be considered as add-on therapy for patients with severe Bell's palsy as 400mg five times daily for 10 days. Monotherapy is not recommended.

Treatment of Bell's palsy involves prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days and then tapered over the next 5 days. Randomized trials found no added benefit of the antiviral agents valacyclovir and acyclovir when compared to glucocorticoids alone.

The use of paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep prevents corneal drying.

For patients with permanent paralysis, cosmetic surgical procedures have been used to restore a relatively symmetric appearance to the face.

options.text: Paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep
Prednisone 60-80 mg daily during the first 5 days

question: On returning from work, a man noticed that his mother had developed mild right-sided facial drooping. Believing it to be due to a stroke, he immediately took her to the hospital. After extensive evaluation, the doctor ruled out stroke and diagnosed her with Bell's palsy. Which of the following would not be a part of the management of her condition?

explanationHtml:
The features are suggestive of lower motor neuron (LMN) type of facial palsy.

In the image, the absence of wrinkling over the right side of the forehead and incomplete closure of the right eyelid is characteristic of LMN type of facial palsy.

In upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, the upper part of the face is spared due to bilateral UMN innervation.

Features of facial nerve palsy:

Feature UMN LMN

Facial muscles involved Lower Both upper and lower

Note: Deviation of the angle of mouth should not be confused with drooping of the angle of mouth. Deviation of the angle of the mouth occurs on the normal side due to the action of unaffected facial muscles, while drooping occurs on the affected side.
question: A 35-year-old patient presents with facial weakness and pain for the past 2 days. The following signs are seen on examination. What is the cause?

explanationHtml:
Patient 1 has left UMN facial nerve palsy and patient 2 has right LMN facial nerve palsy.

In an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, wrinkling on the forehead and eyelid closure remains intact. In this lesion, the contralateral side of the face is affected. The first-order neurons from the left cerebral hemisphere cross over (left to right) at the cortical level and relay in the right facial nerve nucleus in the pons. From here the second-order neurons (right facial nerve) descend and supply the right side of the face.

Hence, a left UMN lesion causes paralysis of the lower half of the face on the right side. In facial palsy, the angle of the mouth deviates towards the normal side. In this patient, since the mouth deviates towards the left, the right facial nerve is affected.

In lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions, there is an absence of wrinkling on the forehead and incomplete closure of the eyelid on the ipsilateral side of the face.

Feature UMN LMN
Side affected Contralateral Ipsilateral
Facial muscles involved Lower Both upper and lower
Forehead wrinkling Present Absent
Emotional incontinence Present Absent
Corneal reflex Normal Absent

Atrophy Absent Present

question: During the neurological examination of a patient, you note that he has bilateral lower motor neuron palsy of the facial nerve. Which of the following is least likely to cause this?

explanationHtml:
The given features are suggestive of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion of the facial nerve in which the emotional response is affected. Patients with UMN lesions of the facial nerve have emotional incontinence i.e. involuntary, uncontrollable laughter, or crying with a paradoxical deficit of facial expression.

Normally cerebellum modulates motor outputs in response to sensory inputs. UMN facial palsy (type of pseudobulbar palsy) is associated with disruption of cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathways leading to loss of cerebellar modulation resulting in:

  • Emotional dysmetria (difficulty in fine-tuning emotional responses)
  • Emotional disinhibition (excessive emotional output)

Difference between UMN and LMN facial palsy:

question: You are evaluating a woman with unilateral facial weakness. However, you notice forehead wrinkling is intact. On examination, which of the following findings would you not expect?

correctAnswer: C. Occurs due to anomalous regeneration of the facial nerve fibers
explanationHtml:
Facial synkinesis occurs due to anomalous regeneration of facial nerve fibers.

Following facial nerve injury , the recovering nerve fibers may aberrantly regenerate and supply other muscles. This results in involuntary muscular movements in the face during voluntary facial movements.

Some examples include:

  • Retraction of the mouth on closure of the eyelids:
    • Seen when fibers originally connected with the orbicularis oculi aberrantly innervate the orbicularis oris
  • 'Crocodile tears' also known as Bogorad syndrome:
    • It refers to anomalous tearing occurring with activity of the facial muscles, such as eating.
    • Due to aberrant innervation of the lacrimal gland.

Note: Frey's syndrome is an aberrant connection between the auriculotemporal nerve and the great auricular nerve, resulting in gustatory sweating.

options.text: Refers to simultaneous bilateral facial nerve palsy
Refers to facial nerve palsy associated with trigeminal neuralgia
Occurs due to anomalous regeneration of the facial nerve fibers
Loss of emotional response is seen in this condition

question: Which of the following statements is true about facial synkinesis?

correctAnswer: A. The contractions are painful and irregular
explanationHtml:
Hemifacial spasms are painless irregular contractions occurring on one side of the face.

They commonly occur as sequelae to Bell's palsy. It can also be seen in irritative lesions of the facial nerve such as acoustic neuroma and basilar aneurysm.

Treatment is with carbamazepine or gabapentin. In resistant cases, baclofen may be tried. Local injection of botulinum toxin and surgical decompression are alternative options.

options.text: The contractions are painful and irregular
It is a complication of Bell's palsy
Local injection of botulinum toxin is effective

Ramsay-Hunt syndrome occurs as a complication following reactivation of a previous herpes zoster infection. It is characterized by facial paralysis along with vesicular rash in the external auditory canal and pinna.

Congenital facial weakness along with abnormal occular abduction, signifies Moebius syndrome. Patients may present with bilateral concurrent facial nerve paralysis.

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of glossopharyngeal neuralgia which is associated with cardiac symptoms such as bradycardia, asystole, hypotension, and fainting.

It involves the glossopharyngeal (IX) and sometimes portions of the vagus (X) nerve. The condition resembles trigeminal neuralgia but is less common. There is no demonstrable sensory or motor deficit.

It can result from vascular compression, multiple sclerosis or tumors.

The drug of choice is carbamazepine. If unsuccessful, surgical procedures are indicated:

  • Microvascular decompression (if vascular compression is evident)
  • Rhizotomy of glossopharyngeal and vagal fibers in the jugular bulb
question: A 70-year-old man presented with complaints of sudden stabs of pain in the throat on yawning. Each episode only lasted for a few seconds and was exacerbated on trying to clear the throat. Which of the following findings can you see on examination?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of neonatal meningitis and Escherichia coli is the most common cause of this condition.

The causes of neonatal meningitis in decreasing order of frequency are:

  • Escherichia coli
  • Group B Streptococci
  • Listeria monocytogenes

Empirical treatment of neonatal meningitis is with ampicillin + 3rd generation cephalosporins.
question: A 25-day-old baby is brought to the hospital with complaints of poor feeding and lethargy. On examination, he is found to have bulging fontanelles and hypothermia.  Which of the following is the most common cause of his condition?

explanationHtml:
The most common cause of meningitis in patients aged 2-50 years is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The common causes of meningitis in this age group include:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Group B streptococci
  • Hemophilus influenzae
  • Listeria monocytogenes
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of meningitis in a 30-year-old patient?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of acute bacterial meningitis. This condition is most likely caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) like Staphylococcus epidermidis in a patient with an Ommaya reservoir.

An Ommaya reservoir is an intraventricular catheter system used for the delivery of drugs into the cerebrospinal fluid. CoNS and S. aureus are important causes of meningitis that occurs following invasive neuro-surgical procedures, or as a complication of the use of Ommaya reservoirs. CoNS are the most common organisms associated with neurological infections after use of Ommaya reservoirs.
question: A 66-year-old patient presents with fever, neck rigidity, and headache for the past 3 days. He has a history of metastatic non-small cell lung cancer for which he had received intrathecal chemotherapy via an Ommaya reservoir 10 days ago. On examination, Kernig and Brudzinski's signs are positive. Which organism is most likely implicated here?

explanationHtml:
The sign being elicited here is Kernig's sign and this along with the given clinical features are suggestive of acute bacterial meningitis. Empirical treatment with cefepime, vancomycin and ampicillin is recommended for patients on immunomodulatory drugs as they are at risk for Listeria infection.

Risk factors for Listeria meningitis include:

  • Age>50
  • Diabetes
  • Chronic illness
  • Malignancy
  • Immunosuppressive therapy
question: A 45-year-old man presents with fever, headache, photophobia and neck rigidity since the last 2 days. He had undergone a heart transplant one year back and is on immunomodulatory drugs. During examination, the following sign is elicited. What is the therapy of choice for this patient?

correctAnswer: D. Metronidazole is the drug of choice
explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of meningococcal meningitis and the drug of choice is a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone. Chloramphenicol is used in patients with penicillin allergy.

It is caused by Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative, oxidase-positive, catalase-positive diplococci. Outbreaks usually occur in mass gatherings such as in army camps or hostel dorms.

The risk of infection is increased in patients with terminal complement deficiency, hypogammaglobulinemia and hyposplenism. This is because opsonization by complement is a major mechanism by which the bacteria is cleared from the blood.

Characteristic clinical findings include:

  • Maculopapular or purpuric rash
  • Shock due to capillary leak
  • Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome)

Rifampicin, ciprofloxacin and cephalosporins can be used to treat carriers.

options.text: Carriers of this disease can be treated with Rifampicin
It can lead to adrenal hemorrhage
Terminal complement deficiency increases the risk of this disease
Metronidazole is the drug of choice

question: A 21-year-old female complains of fever, headache and vomiting from the past 3 days. She has been living in the army recruitment camp for the last three weeks. On examination, she has neck stiffness and a maculopapular rash was noted over the trunk and extremities. Which of the following is false about the disease she's likely suffering from?

explanationHtml:
Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime is the drug of choice for empirical treatment of meningococcal meningitis. However, Penicillin G remains the antibiotic of choice for susceptible strains.

Empirical antimicrobial therapy is initiated in patients with suspected bacterial meningitis before the results of CSF Gram stain and culture are known.

S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis are the most common etiologic organisms of community-acquired bacterial meningitis. Due to the emergence of penicillin-resistant and cephalosporin-resistant S. pneumoniae, empirical therapy of community-acquired suspected bacterial meningitis should include a combination of:

  • Dexamethasone
  • Third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefepime)
  • Vancomycin
  • Acyclovir - HSV encephalitis is the main differential
  • Doxycycline - during tick season.

Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime provides better coverage for susceptible S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and group B streptococci and good coverage for N. meningitidis. Cefepime is a broad-spectrum fourth-generation cephalosporin with activity similar to that of cefotaxime or ceftriaxone against S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis with additional greater activity against Enterobacter species and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
question: A patient came with complaints of high-grade fever and altered sensorium. He was diagnosed to be suffering from meningococcal meningitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical treatment option?

explanationHtml:
Ciprofloxacin is used for chemoprophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis for close contacts. Ceftriaxone and rifampicin are also used.

Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis among close contacts of a patient with invasive meningococcal disease is recommended to prevent secondary cases.

  • Rifampin - was earlier used widely, but is not optimal due to the high risk of adverse events, emerging resistance, and the need for compliance for four doses.
  • Ciprofloxacin - widely used as a single oral dose, but it cannot be given in pregnancy and those below 18 years of age.
  • Ceftriaxone - can be given in pregnancy and all ages as a single IM or IV dose. However, reduced susceptibility of isolates to ceftriaxone has occasionally been reported.

Recommended chemoprophylaxis for high-risk close contacts for meningococcal meningitis:

Patient group Drug Age Dose Route and duration

Non-pregnant individuals

Rifampicin

 <1 month 5 mg/kg Oral every 12 hrs for 2 days
>1 month 10 mg/kg Oral every 12 hrs for 2 days

Ciprofloxacin

>18 years 500 mg Oral single dose

Children and pregnant women

Ceftriaxone

 <15 years 125mg IM single dose
> 15 years 250 mg IM single dose
question: Which drug is used for mass chemoprophylaxis for meningococcal meningitis?

correctAnswer: A. Lymphocytosis, low glucose, high protein
explanationHtml:
The features and imaging findings are suggestive of tuberculous meningitis. CSF analysis would likely show lymphocytosis, low glucose and high protein.

If the CSF is allowed to stand, a 'spider’s web clot' or 'cobweb' coagulam may form due to the high level of protein.
question: A 45-year-old patient with a history of fever for 1 month presents with headache and ataxia. Imaging reveals dilated ventricles and significant basal exudates. Which of the following would most likely be seen in the CSF?

explanationHtml:
The given symptoms cluster of fever, vomiting, and neck stiffness is suggestive of meningitis. A CSF analysis showing increased opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly increased protein, and normal glucose is suggestive of viral meningitis. Among the given options, Coxsackie (Option D) is the only viral cause of meningitis.

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option B: Bacterial meningitis shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.

Option C: Fungal meningitis shows lymphocytic/neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose.
