question: A college student presents with fever, headache, and confusion. Lumbar puncture was positive for HSV DNA, detected by PCR. An MRI brain is done to localize the lesions. Which area on the brain is most likely to show lesions?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of herpes simplex encephalitis and the CSF analysis would likely show 100 RBC/microliter. HSV encephalitis is associated with hemorrhagic necrosis of inferomedial temporal and frontal lobe resulting in significant number of RBCs in the CSF.

It is caused by both HSV 1 and HSV 2. Patients present with fever, headache, seizures, personality, and behavioral changes.

CSF analysis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, moderately elevated protein levels and normal glucose concentration. EEG shows periodic lateralized spike-wave discharges.

The drug of choice for the condition is acyclovir.
question: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, headache, seizures and aphasia. MRI shows hyperintensity in the left frontotemporal region. Which of the following would likely be seen in the CSF analysis?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features and EEG point towards a diagnosis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). The EEG shows periodic biphasic or triphasic sharp-wave complexes seen as spikes.

CJD is a spongiform encephalopathy caused by a prion. It presents as rapidly progressive dementia and is fatal within 1 year of onset of symptoms.

Patients present with myoclonus, akinetic mutism, cerebellar or visual disturbances and pyramidal/extrapyramidal dysfunction (hypokinesia). Insomnia, apathy and other behavioral abnormalities may be seen.

Four types of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease have been described:

  1. Sporadic (sCJD): Accounts for 85-90% of cases
    • MRI shows cortical ribbon sign
  2. Variant (vCJD): mad cow disease, Kuru
    • MRI shows hockey stick sign
  3. Familial (fCJD): 10% of cases (these individuals carry a PRPc mutation)
  4. Iatrogenic

CSF analysis shows a positive assay for 14-3-3 protein. Management is mainly supportive.

Note: Hepatic encephalopathy will show a triphasic wave pattern (negative-positive-negative wave). They are also seen in Hashimoto encephalopathy and CO2 narcosis.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 60-year-old man with progressive dementia of recent onset presents with intermittent irregular jerky movements. The EEG is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Hemolytic anemia is not a hypoproliferative anemia.

Anemia can be defined as hemoglobin of < 13 g/dl in men and < 12 g/dl in women. Based on the mechanism of reduction of hemoglobin, anemia can be classified as:

  • Hypoproliferative anemias - due to impaired production of RBCs
  • Hemolytic anemias and hemoglobinopathies - due to increased destruction of RBCs
  • Anemia due to blood loss

Hypoproliferative anemias are characterized by an abnormally low reticulocyte response (reticulocyte index <2–2.5) to reduced RBC production. They include:

  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Anemia of chronic disease (inflammation, renal disease, or malignancies)
  • Thalassemia
  • Sideroblastic anemia
  • Aplastic anemia
  • Megaloblastic macrocytic anemias (folate and vitamin B12 deficiency)
  • Non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemias (alcohol use)
question: Which of the following is not a hypoproliferative anemia?

explanationHtml:
The corrected reticulocyte count (CRC) of this patient is 3.

CRC = Reticulocyte % x (Actual Hb / Normal Hb)

Plugging in the values given in the question,
CRC = 9% x 5/15 = 3%
Alternatively, CRC can be calculated using hematocrit (PCV) as follows:
CRC = Reticulocyte % x (Actual PCV / Normal PCV)

For these calculations, take normal Hb as 15g/dL and normal PCV as 45%.

The patient's hemoglobin level (5 g/dL) is significantly lower than the normal hemoglobin level (15 g/dL). To obtain an accurate assessment of reticulocyte production relative to the reduced number of circulating red blood cells, a correction factor has to be applied. CRC accounts for the anemia and provides a more precise estimate of the reticulocyte count.

When polychromatophilic macrocytes (prematurely released reticulocytes/shift cells) are observed in the peripheral blood smear, a second correction is applied to account for the longer life of reticulocytes to yield reticulocyte production index (RPI).

In the classification of anemia, the patient's reticulocyte count is compared to the expected reticulocyte response. Reticulocytes can be identified by staining their ribosomal RNA with a supravital dye, resulting in the formation of blue or black punctate spots. They can be quantified manually or by using fluorescent dyes. The presence of reticulocytes indicates active red cell production.

The premature release of reticulocytes is typically associated with increased EPO stimulation. In hemolytic anemia, red cell production can increase six to seven times. If the RPI < 2 in a patient with anemia, a defect in erythroid marrow proliferation or maturation has to be suspected.
question: A 25-year-old woman came to the OPD one year after the birth of her last child. She had been treated for iron deficiency anemia while pregnant. On examination, she is pale and investigations show a Hb of 5g/dl and a reticulocyte count of 9%. What is her corrected reticulocyte count? (Take normal Hb as 15g/dl)

explanationHtml:
Red cell distribution width (RDW) measures the range of red blood cell volumes and provides an assessment of their variability (anisocytosis).

The normal range of RDW is 11-14%. In the presence of uneven cell size (anisocytosis), the RDW increases to 15-18%.

RDW has clinical utility in two main scenarios:

  • In cases of microcytic anemia (low MCV), it helps differentiate between iron deficiency and thalassemia. Thalassemia is characterized by uniformly small red blood cells with a normal RDW, while iron deficiency leads to greater size variability and an increased RDW.
  • A high RDW can indicate dimorphic anemia caused by chronic atrophic gastritis. Vitamin B12 malabsorption results in macrocytic anemia and blood loss leads to iron deficiency (microcytic anemia).
question: What does the red cell distribution width deal with?

correctAnswer: D. A 70-year-old woman undergoing dialysis for the past 3 years
explanationHtml:
The black arrows in the given image denote target cells or codocytes. RBCs which contain a hyperchromic dense center (known as 'bull's eye') surrounded by pale ring and then a dark outer ring, are called target cells. They are not a feature of renal disease (Patient D).

Target cells are seen in the following conditions:

  • Thalassemia
  • Iron deficiency anemia
  • Liver disease
  • Post-splenectomy
  • Hemoglobin C disease
  • As artifacts in improperly prepared slides

A 19-year-old girl who underwent emergency splenectomy after a road accident
A 25-year-old man with hemoglobin C disease

question: Which of the following patients is unlikely to have the following finding on a peripheral smear study?

explanationHtml:
The small, dense RBCs with absent central pallor seen in the given peripheral smear are called spherocytes. They appear due to decreased membrane surface area and are seen in the following conditions:

  • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  • Hereditary spherocytosis
  • Clostridial sepsis
  • Snake bites
question: A first-year pathology resident prepares the following smear from a patient's blood sample. Which of the following is it suggestive of?

explanationHtml:
The given peripheral smear shows teardrop cells or dacrocytes. These are classically seen in marrow infiltration or fibrosis and are not typically seen in sideroblastic anemia.

Teardrop cells are seen in the following conditions:

  • Myelofibrosis
  • Myelodysplastic syndromes
  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Thalassemia
  • Severe iron deficiency
question: The following finding is not typically seen in which of the following conditions?

  • Sickle cell disease (postsplenectomy)
  • Hyposplenism
  • Megaloblastic anemia
  • Dyshematopoesis
  • Hemolytic anemia

Thalassemia presents with microcytic, hypochromic RBCs, and target cells.

Lead poisoning presents with basophilic stippling or punctate basophilia on peripheral smears. These are RNA fragments seen as numerous basophilic granules dispersed in the cytoplasm of RBCs, as shown below.

Iron absorption takes place in the duodenum. In sleeve gastrectomy, a portion of the stomach is resected but the duodenum remains intact. Hence, the surface area of iron absorption is not affected.

[[figure-1]]

Dietary iron is efficiently absorbed in its heme form. Non-heme iron is less efficiently absorbed mainly because of interference by phosphates, tannins, oxalates, and other food constituents. Acidic pH enhances iron absorption by promoting the conversion of ferric to ferrous iron by the enzyme ferrireductase.

[[figure-2]]

The following are malabsorptive procedures that reduce the duodenal surface area and hence, reduce iron absorption:

  • Biliopancreatic diversion
  • Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
  • Duodenal switch
question: A 30-year-old man with a BMI of 41 kg/m2 is being evaluated for bariatric surgery. Which of the following procedures does not reduce the surface area for iron absorption?

explanationHtml:
Tea contains tannins, which inhibit iron absorption. Hence, it should not be taken with iron supplements. Iron absorption is also reduced by:

  • Calcium supplements and antacids
  • Milk and dairy products
  • Proton pump inhibitors

Grapefruit and kiwi are acid-containing citrus fruits that create an acidic pH and hence, increase iron absorption.

Broccoli contains ascorbic acid that also enhances iron absorption.
question: You have prescribed oral iron supplements for an anemic young woman. Which of the following foods should she avoid taking along with these supplements?

The earliest sign of iron deficiency is a decrease in serum ferritin levels. This is called the state of negative iron balance.

Iron deficiency anemia develops in 3 stages:

  • Stage of negative iron balance - decrease in iron stores with normal serum iron and RBC morphology
  • Stage of iron-deficient erythropoiesis - decrease in serum iron levels with normal RBC morphology
  • Stage of iron deficiency anemia - fall in hemoglobin with microcytic hypochromic RBCs
question: The levels of which of the following will be detected first in a patient with iron deficiency?

explanationHtml:
TIBC (total iron-binding capacity) does not decrease during the stage of a negative iron balance of iron deficiency anemia.

The progression to iron deficiency develops in 3 stages:

  • Stage of negative iron balance - Decrease in iron stores with normal serum iron and RBC morphology
  • Stage of iron-deficient erythropoiesis - Decrease in serum iron levels with normal RBC morphology

question: Which of the following is not seen in the stage of negative iron balance in iron-deficiency anemia?

correctAnswer: D. Tingling and numbness of lower extremities
explanationHtml:
Tingling and numbness of the lower extremities are suggestive of peripheral neuropathy. It is a feature of vitamin B12 deficiency, not iron deficiency.

Iron-deficiency anemia is associated with the following findings:

  • Smooth tongue - due to loss of papillae
  • Cheilosis - fissuring at corners of mouth
  • Brittle nails
  • Koilonychia - spooning of nails
  • Pica - craving for non-edible foods like ice chips, hair, paper, clay
  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome - dysphagia due to the formation of esophageal webs

question: Patients with which of the following do not need to be evaluated for iron deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Image 4 shows dense RBCs with loss of central pallor or spherocytes. They are seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and hereditary spherocytosis, not iron deficiency anemia.

[[figure-1]]

The peripheral blood smear in iron deficiency anemia shows:

  • Microcytic hypochromic cells
  • Target cells
  • Pencil-shaped or cigar-shaped cells
  • Poikilocytosis- variations in the shape of RBCs
  • Anisocytosis- variations in the size of RBCs.
question: Which of the following PBF findings is least likely to be seen in patients with iron deficiency anemia?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of iron deficiency anemia due to the following findings:

  • Low MCV (N: 87-96 fL)
  • Low MCH (N: 27-33 pg)
  • Elevated RDW
  • High TIBC

Option A: Anemia of chronic disease is associated with low TIBC.

Options B and D: Anemia due to B12 and folate deficiency presents with a high MCV (macrocytosis).
question:
A 28-year-old woman is brought to the ER after she faints at home. Her husband says that she is very body-conscious and does intermittent fasting. She has been on a vegan diet for the past 2 months. Lab values are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hb - 6 g/dL

MCV - 67 fL

MCH - 24 pg

RDW - elevated

TIBC - high

Peripheral smear - target cells noted

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of anemia of chronic disease. The chief mediator of this condition is hepcidin.

Anemia of chronic disease is associated with chronic inflammatory states such as inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic infections, and malignancies.

Hepcidin is a positive acute-phase reactant (ARP) that increases in chronic inflammatory states. It binds with ferroportin which results in both reduced iron intake in the gut and reduced iron transfer from macrophages to erythroid progenitor cells in the bone marrow. Hence, hepcidin is a negative regulator of iron balance.
question: A 62-year-old woman is found to have a Hb of 7.2 g/dl and high ferritin levels. She has been undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer since last year. Which of the following is responsible for this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Normocytic normochromic anemia is seen in chronic kidney disease (CKD).

It is also seen in the following conditions:

  • RBC membrane disorders - hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis
  • RBC enzyme disorders - G6PD deficiency, Pyruvate kinase deficiency
  • Parvovirus B19 infection
  • Anemia of chronic disease - can also present as microcytic anemia
question: Normocytic normochromic anemia is seen in patients with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of anemia of chronic disease due to the following findings:

  • Low MCV (N: 87-96 fl)
  • Low TIBC (N: 300-360μg/dL)
  • Elevated ferritin level (N: 50-200 μg/L)
  • Decreased transferrin saturation (N: 25-50%)
question:
A 38-year-old woman presented to the OPD with progressive tiredness over the last 2 months. She also reported having heavy menstrual bleeding during her previous 2 cycles. She is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis. Lab investigations are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

Hb - 7 gm/dL

MCV - 55 fL

TIBC - 290 μg/dL

S. Ferritin - 250 μg/L

Transferrin saturation - 20%

explanationHtml:
Anemia of CKD is a form of hypoproliferative anemia presenting with decreased reticulocytes.

It mainly occurs due to a failure of erythropoietin production by the diseased kidney and a reduction in the survival of RBCs. Also, patients with CKD maintained on chronic hemodialysis may develop iron deficiency from blood loss through the dialysis procedure.

The following features are seen:

  • Normocytic and normochromic RBCs
  • Decreased reticulocytes
  • Serum iron, transferrin saturation, TIBC are usually normal or low
  • Decreased serum ferritin

The degree of anemia usually correlates with the severity of the renal failure.

Note: Anaemia in CKD is not the same as anaemia of chronic disease.
question: A 60-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis  is found to have a hemoglobin of 6.3 mg/dl. Which of the following will be additionally seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Inherited forms of sideroblastic anemia are usually X-linked. Rarely, autosomal recessive forms may also occur.

X-linked sideroblastic anemia results from the deficient activity of the erythroid form of ALA-synthase (ALA-synthase 2) and is associated with ineffective erythropoiesis
question: What is the predominant inheritance pattern of sideroblastic anemia?

explanationHtml:
High serum iron levels are seen in patients with sideroblastic anemia.

Sideroblastic anemia presents with the following features:

  • Serum iron level - high/normal
  • Transferrin saturation - high
  • Serum ferritin levels - high
  • TIBC - low/normal
  • Peripheral smear - dimorphic population (both microcytes and macrocytes).
  • Bone marrow study - marked erythroid hyperplasia.

The iron profile of sideroblastic anemia is opposite to that of iron deficiency anemia.
question: Which of the following would not be seen in patients with sideroblastic anemia?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows ringed sideroblasts, which are erythroid precursors in the marrow. In these cells, iron deposits in the mitochondria form a ring around the nucleus and are stained by Prussian blue.

Siderocytes are the mature equivalents of ringed sideroblasts found in circulation. These cells have iron-containing basophilic granules called Pappenheimer bodies, as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

Ringed sideroblasts and Pappenheimer bodies are pathognomonic of sideroblastic anemia.
question: The bone marrow biopsy sample of a patient with chronic anemia is stained with Prussian blue, as shown below. The stained deposits are present in which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Chloramphenicol is known to cause sideroblastic anemia.

The agents known to cause sideroblastic anemia are:

  • Isoniazid
  • Chloramphenicol
  • Linezolid
  • Excessive alcohol
question: Which of the following drugs is known to cause sideroblastic anemia?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows hypersegmented neutrophils (> 5 nuclear lobes), which are seen in megaloblastic anemia. Chronic alcoholism causes non-megaloblastic macrocytic anemia.

Megaloblastic anemia is a form of macrocytic anemia with impaired nucleic acid metabolism and defective erythropoiesis. The causes include vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, and orotic aciduria. Nuclear maturation lags behind cytoplasmic maturation giving the appearance of hypersegmented neutrophils. Peripheral smear findings include:

  • Oval macrocytes
  • Anisocytosis
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils

Other features of ineffective erythropoiesis seen in megaloblastic anemias include:

  • Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants in red cells. They are usually single, round, dark purple-red in color and peripheral in location, as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

  • Basophilic stippling is due to the ribosomal aggregates in the RBC, which appear as blue granules of varying sizes.
  • Cabot rings are red cell inclusions appearing as fine, purple filamentous loops or figure-of-eight forms, as shown below. They are presumed to be remnants of mitotic spindles.

[[figure-2]]
question: The peripheral blood smear of a patient is given below. All of the following can cause this except:

explanationHtml:
Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworm) infection does not affect the absorption of cobalamin or vitamin B12. Small amounts of blood loss during the attachment of hookworms to the intestinal mucosa can cause iron-deficiency anemia.

Vitamin B12-intrinsic factor (IF) complex is absorbed in the ileum. Tropical sprue, Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) infection and Crohn's disease affect the ileum leading to defective absorption of vitamin B12.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions are unlikely to develop cobalamin deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia is seen in cyanocobalamin or vitamin B12 deficiency, not conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia due to ineffective erythropoiesis. This leads to the formation of nucleated RBCs in the marrow, which undergo early lysis. This leads to increased unconjugated bilirubin in the plasma.

The clinical features of cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency include:

Glossitis

Angular cheilosis
Gastrointestinal

Anorexia

Weight loss

Diarrhea

Constipation

Thrombocytopenia

Leucopenia

Ineffective erythropoiesis and unconjugated jaundice

Atherosclerosis leading to PVD, CAD (due to elevated homocysteine)
Neurological (only B12)

Peripheral neuropathy

Subacute combined degeneration (degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the spinal cord)

Others

question: Which of the following would not be seen in a patient with cyanocobalamin deficiency?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of folate deficiency.

It is associated with the following clinical and laboratory findings:

  • Raised MCV (normal: 80-100 fL) - macrocytosis
  • Normal MCHC (normal: 33-36 g/dl)
  • Increased MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin)
  • Elevated RDW (red cell distribution width)
  • Decreased reticulocyte count - due to destruction of abnormal erythroid precursors
  • Elevated homocysteine
  • Normal MMA (methyl malonic acid)

In vitamin B12 deficiency, elevated homocysteine and elevated MMA levels are seen.
question:
A 56-year-old male patient is being evaluated for peripheral neuropathy and excessive tiredness. He has uncontrolled diabetes and consumes alcohol nearly every day. Lab investigations reveal the following findings. What is the likely diagnosis?

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) - 112 fL

Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) = 34 g/dl

Temafloxacin is not associated with megaloblastic anemia.

Megaloblastic anemia is associated with the following drugs:

  • Anticonvulsant drugs - phenytoin, primidone, barbiturates
  • Sulfasalazine
  • Nitrofurantoin
  • Tetracycline
  • Folate antagonists - trimethoprim, methotrexate, pyrimethamine, pentamidine, cotrimoxazole

Temafloxacin is a fluoroquinolone with severe adverse effects like hemolytic anemia and allergic reactions. It was withdrawn from the market and is no longer used.
question: Which of the following drugs is not associated with megaloblastic anemia?

explanationHtml:
This patient likely has folate deficiency secondary to the use of an anti-folate anti-convulsant drug. Lamotrigine has no effect on folate metabolism and does not cause its deficiency.

The following anticonvulsants have anti-folate properties:

  • Phenytoin
  • Barbiturates (amobarbital)
  • Primidone

Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic macrocytic anemia which results in the following findings in RBCs:

  • Anemia (low Hb = 10g/dl)
  • Macrocytic (high MCV = 110 fl)
  • Hyperchromic (high MCH = 40 pg)

question: A dose of oral 58-Co-labeled cobalamin was administered to a 65-year-old woman. The 24-hour urinary excretion of radiolabeled cobalamin was found to be < 10%. The test was repeated after a 5-day course of antibiotics and showed urinary excretion > 10%. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Megaloblastic anemia that is responsive to treatment with uridine is suggestive of orotic aciduria.

Orotic aciduria is a rare inborn error of metabolism in children. It occurs due to a defect in the pyrimidine synthesis pathway causing a failure of conversion of orotic acid to uridine. It manifests in early childhood with anemia and failure to thrive.
question: A child diagnosed with megaloblastic anemia failed to respond to treatment with vitamin C, vitamin B12, and folic acid. He was started on uridine monophosphate which improved his symptoms. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario in a patient with a history of autoimmune thyroiditis is suspicious for pernicious anemia. It is an autoimmune cause of B12 deficiency. Antibodies against gastrin are not seen in these patients. The following autoantibodies are seen:

  • Type I or blocking antibodies - prevent the combination of IF and cobalamin
  • Type II or binding antibodies - prevent attachment of IF to the ileal mucosa
  • Anti-parietal cell antibodies - target the gastric proton pump located in these cells

This leads to the deficiency of the intrinsic factor of Castle (IF) and hydrochloric acid produced by the parietal cells. The resulting atrophic gastritis causes high gastrin and low pepsinogen levels. Lack of IF further causes vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue and a red, painful tongue. On examination, there is reduced vibration sense and proprioception in the feet. She is under treatment for Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Peripheral smear reveals macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Gastric biopsy in pernicious anemia shows loss of glandular elements, not hypertrophy.

This is an autoimmune condition that occurs in genetically susceptible individuals. One of the common triggers of the disease process is Helicobacter pylori infection. Gastric biopsy findings in pernicious anemia include the following:

  • Atrophy of all layers of the body and fundus
    • Loss of glandular elements
    • Absence of parietal and chief cells and replacement by mucus cells
    • Mixed inflammatory cell infiltrate (excess of CD4 cells against gastric H+/K+-ATPase)
    • Intestinal metaplasia
  • Antral mucosa is usually well preserved.
question: A pathologist receives a gastric biopsy sample of a patient with pernicious anemia. Which of the following findings is he unlikely to find?

explanationHtml:
Patients with pernicious anemia have an increased risk of intestinal-type of gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric carcinoid tumors. These patients must undergo regular endoscopic screening for these conditions.

The presumed mechanism is prolonged achlorhydria due to parietal cell loss. This leads to hypergastrinemia and cellular hyperplasia.
question: Patients with pernicious anemia are at a higher risk of which of the following?

explanationHtml: Reduced nutritional intake is the most common cause of folate deficiency.
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of folate deficiency?

explanationHtml:
Dietary folates are absorbed from the duodenum and jejunum in the form of monoglutamates.

Vitamin B12 absorption takes place in the terminal ileum.
question: Dietary folates are absorbed from which of the following sites?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of dorsal column involvement of the spinal cord due to underlying vitamin B12 deficiency.

Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (SACD). It affects the following structures:

  • Dorsal column - sensory loss, paresthesias, incontinence, sensory ataxia (positive Romberg sign with eyes closed)
  • Lateral column - spasticity and paraplegias in later stages

Folate deficiency is typically not associated with neurological manifestations. In patients with combined deficiency of B12 and folate, B12 deficiency must always be corrected first. This is because the administration of folate supplements may improve hematologic abnormalities but worsens neurological manifestations.

Treatment of cobalamin deficiency is as follows:

  • Replenishment of body stores: Six 1000-μg IM injections of hydroxocobalamin given at 3- to 7-day intervals.
  • Maintenance therapy: 1000 μg hydroxocobalamin IM once every 3 months

Treatment of folate deficiency is as follows:

  • 5–15 mg oral folic acid daily for a minimum of 4 months.

Option C: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke's syndrome with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and nystagmus. As this is due to cerebellar damage, Romberg's sign would be positive even with eyes open.

Option D: Pyridoxine deficiency causes pellagra like syndrome with features of dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia.
question: A 49-year-old woman is brought with increased forgetfulness and clumsiness for the past 1 month. Since the death of her husband 3 months ago, she has been tired and eating poorly. She began taking over-the-counter iron and folic acid tablets 2 months ago. Examination reveals positive Romberg's sign with eyes closed and loss of vibration in lower extremities. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml: Usage of phenytoin leads to folate deficiency and megaloblastic anemia. Hence, folic acid must be supplemented.
question: A 19-year-old girl with a seizure disorder is started on phenytoin therapy. Which of the following must be supplemented in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. 4-5 mg pre-conceptionally and in first trimester
explanationHtml:
The recommended prophylactic dose of folic acid in women who have had a previous fetus with a neural tube defect is 4-5 mg daily, pre-conceptionally, and during the first trimester of pregnancy. Following the first trimester, these patients are then switched to 400 μg of folic acid for the remainder of the pregnancy.

This high dose of folic acid (4-5 mg) should be initiated at least one to three months before pregnancy and should be continued for 12 weeks after pregnancy. The patient can be prescribed 1 mg tablet of folic acid and advised to take them 4- 5 times a day or they can be recommended 5mg tablets/capsules once daily.

Prophylactic folic acid with 400 μg daily, pre-conceptionally, and throughout pregnancy is indicated in all pregnant women to prevent megaloblastic anemia and reduce the incidence of neural tube defects.

options.text: 400 μg pre-conceptionally and in first trimester
4-5 mg pre-conceptionally and in first trimester

question: A 23-year-old woman comes to you for pre-conceptional counseling. Her previous pregnancy resulted in fetal death due to a neural tube defect. What dose of folic acid would you recommend?

explanationHtml:
Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome (IGS) is an autosomal recessive disorder.

IGS occurs due to mutations in either the cubulin (CUBN) or amnionless (AMN) genes. They form the cubam receptor responsible for the absorption of the Cbl-IF complex. Hence, this condition leads to congenital cobalamin malabsorption. It is the most common cause of megaloblastic anemia due to B12 deficiency in infancy in Western countries.

Affected children present with lethargy, failure to thrive, and neurological symptoms like hypotonia, developmental delay, and movement disorders. Non-specific proteinuria with normal renal function is seen in 90% of patients.
question: Which of the following would not be seen in a patient with Imerslund-Grasbeck syndrome?

explanationHtml:
In intravascular hemolysis, there is elevated MCV, LDH, and urinary urobilinogen, with low haptoglobin.

Laboratory abnormalities seen in intravascular hemolysis:

Lab parameters Derangement Mechanism
MCV High Compensatory reticulocytosis
S. LDH High Released from RBCs
S. Unconjugated bilirubin High Hemoglobin from RBCs is converted to bilirubin
Urinary urobilinogen High Unconjugated bilirubin is excreted as urobilinogen in urine
S. Haptoglobin Low Free hemoglobin in circulation binds to haptoglobin causing reduced haptoglobin levels

Additionally, hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinemia may be seen on urine examination.

explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a hemolytic anemia due to an intracorpuscular defect.

It is caused due to an acquired somatic mutation leading to deficiency of membrane protective factors CD59 and CD55. This makes the RBC extremely sensitive to complement activation and causes intravascular hemolysis.

The other conditions occur due to extracorpuscular defects.

Option A: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia, RBCs are coated with autoantibodies. This triggers phagocytosis in the reticuloendothelial system leading to extravascular hemolysis.

Option C: Familial hemolytic uremic syndrome (atypical HUS) is an inherited abnormality with excessive complement activation leading to episodic and excessive production of membrane attack complex destroying normal RBCs.

Option D: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is non-immune hemolysis resulting from intravascular red blood cell fragmentation due to abnormalities in the microvasculature.
question: Which of the following is not due to an extracorpuscular defect in RBCs?

correctAnswer: C. Deficiency of CD 55 and CD 59
explanationHtml:
Deficiency of CD55 and CD59 is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

It is due to an acquired mutation in the X-linked phosphatidylinositol class A PIG-A gene (Option A) causing a deficiency of GPI anchor proteins. GPI is a glycolipid that anchors membrane protective factors such as CD59 and CD55 to the membrane. The deficiency of CD55 and CD59 makes the RBC sensitive to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis(Option B). The anemia is usually normo-macrocytic (Option D).

Hemolysis tends to occur at night due to a slight decrease in blood pH during sleep, which triggers complement activity (nocturnal hemoglobinuria). PNH is characterized by hemolytic anemia, pancytopenia, and venous thrombosis.

PNH is diagnosed using flow cytometry. The drugs of choice for treatment are Eculizumab or Ravulizumab which work against complement C5. Supportive management of PNH includes folic acid and iron supplementation. Bone marrow transplantation is another option for the treatment of this condition.
question: Which of the following is true about paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?

explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a type of hemolytic anemia associated with pancytopenia and venous thrombosis.

In PNH, there is complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis. Bone marrow dysfunction also occurs, resulting in pancytopenia. Transformation to aplastic anemia or acute myeloid leukemia (AML) may rarely occur.

PNH is also associated with venous thrombosis (cerebral, renal, hepatic). This is the most common cause of death in PNH.

Option A: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is inherited aplastic anemia with neutropenia with pancreatic insufficiency and malabsorption.

Options B and C: Pyruvate kinase and G6PD deficiency are inherited RBC enzyme disorders causing extravascular hemolytic anemias. They do not affect other cell lines and are not associated with venous thrombosis.
question: A patient with hemolytic anemia develops features of pancytopenia and venous thrombosis. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of intravascular hemolysis due to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). The gold standard for diagnosis is flow cytometry.

Flow cytometry is performed with fluorescently labeled monoclonal antibodies that bind to GPI-anchored proteins (CD59, CD55). Most tests also use FLuorescent AERolysin (FLAER), a reagent that directly binds the GPI anchor. Absence of CD59 and CD55 are diagnostic of PNH.

Other investigations in PNH include:

  • Ham test (acidified serum lysis) - lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH due to complement fixation.
  • Bone marrow biopsy:
    • Hypercellularity with erythroid hyperplasia is seen in classical presentations.
    • Patients who develop pancytopenia will have hypocellular bone marrow.
  • Imaging - to evaluate venous thrombosis.

Option B and D: Eosin-5′-maleimide-binding and acidified glycerol lysis tests are done in hereditary spherocytosis.
question:
A 31-year-old woman presents with a fever and cough. She also reports excessive tiredness and occasional dark-colored urine for the past 6 months. Chest X-ray reveals lower lobe pneumonia. Labs reveal the following. What is the investigation of choice for this condition?

Hb - 7.6 g/dL

RBC - 2 million/mm3

WBC - 5,000/mm3

Platelets - 100,000/mm3

Reticulocyte count - 3.2%

S. LDH - High

S. Haptoglobin - Low

Coombs test - negative

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). C5 complement inhibitors like eculizumab and ravalizumab are the drugs of choice in PNH.

Management of PNH involves the following:

  • C5 complement inhibitors prevent the formation of membrane attack complex and complement-mediated lysis.
  • Bone marrow transplant is useful for patients with severe pancytopenia
  • Supportive measures:
    • Transfusion of filtered RBCs
    • Folic acid, and iron supplementation
    • Anticoagulants in case of venous thrombosis
question: A 46-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain and yellowish discoloration of her skin. She gives a history of dark-colored urine which is more pronounced in the early mornings. Imaging reveals hepatic venous thrombosis. Flow cytometry reveals the absence of GPI-anchored proteins. What is the drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
The peripheral smear shows hyperchromic RBCs with loss of central pallor or spherocytes. These findings are suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis. The eosin-5-maleimide test is the most specific investigation for this condition.

It is a flow cytometric test based on the interaction between the dye eosin-5-maleimide and band 3 protein.

Other investigations that can be performed in this condition are:

Acidified glycerol lysis test: Spherocytes from patients with hereditary spherocytosis lyse more quickly than normal red blood cells when incubated in a phosphate buffered hypotonic solution with added glycerol. It has greater sensitivity and specificity than the osmotic fragility test.

Osmotic fragility test: Detects hemolysis by measuring the fraction of total hemoglobin released from red cells when suspended in progressively more dilute salt concentrations.

Note: NESTROFT (Naked eye single tube red-cell osmotic fragility test) is a highly sensitive test used as a screening test for thalassemia.
question: A 10-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of fatigue. On examination, he is jaundiced and mild splenomegaly is noted. He was adopted and his family history is unknown. Peripheral smear findings are shown below. What is the most specific investigation for this condition?

correctAnswer: A. Cholecystectomy is only indicated for patients with clinical cholelithiasis at the time of splenectomy
explanationHtml:
Cholecystectomy at the time of splenectomy is indicated in patients with hereditary spherocytosis (HS) only if they have symptomatic cholelithiasis at the time of surgery. It is usually carried out via a laparoscopic approach.

Penicillin prophylaxis after splenectomy is controversial. Routine penicillin prophylaxis is not mandatory for adults. It is recommended up to age of five and for at least one year following splenectomy.

Guidelines for the timing of splenectomy in HS:

  • Mild cases - avoid splenectomy.
  • Moderate cases - delay until puberty
  • Severe cases - at 4–6 years of age

options.text: Cholecystectomy is only indicated for patients with clinical cholelithiasis at the time of splenectomy
Cholecystectomy cannot be performed via laparoscopic route for patients with HS and pigment gall stones
Splenectomy is indicated in patients with mild and asymptomatic disease only after puberty
Lifelong penicillin prophylaxis after splenectomy is mandatory for all adult patients

question: Which of the following is true regarding the treatment of hereditary spherocytosis?

explanationHtml:
The given peripheral smear shows oval, elongated, rod, or cigar-shaped RBCs suggestive of elliptocytosis. The hereditary form is most commonly associated with the spectrin genes.

The following proteins are implicated in hereditary elliptocytosis (HE):

  • α-Spectrin (SPTA1 gene) - 65%
  • β-Spectrin (SPTB gene) - 30%
  • Band 4.1

The treatment of choice is splenectomy, preferably after 5 years of age.
question: The peripheral smear of a patient is given below. What is the most common mutation associated with the hereditary form of this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Females can inherit the mutation
explanationHtml:
G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder. Male children of an affected man are not affected as they receive only the paternal Y chromosome. However, the mutation can be passed on to female children, who are typically carriers of the disease.

G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymatic disorder of RBCs. G6PD enzyme is involved in the generation of NADPH and protects RBCs from oxidative injury. Hence, patients with G6PD deficiency can have acute exacerbation by oxidative injury caused by drugs, fava beans, acute infection, etc. This acute exacerbation is characterised by exaggerated hemolysis.

options.text: Only male children will be affected

question: A young couple comes to you for genetic counseling. The husband is a known case of G6PD deficiency and is concerned about passing it on to his future children. What is the chance that his children will inherit the disease?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical features are suggestive of an acute hemolytic reaction following the administration of cotrimoxazole. This is suggestive of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

In G6PD deficiency uncontrolled oxidative stress causes hemoglobin to denature and form Heinz bodies. Removal of Heinz bodies by macrophages in the spleen results in the formation of characteristic bite cells or degmacytes or blister cells (as shown in the image).

A hemolytic attack starts with abrupt onset of malaise, weakness, and abdominal or lumbar pain. After an interval of several hours to 2–3 days, the patient develops jaundice and often dark urine, due to hemoglobinuria.

Drugs that carry the risk of clinical hemolysis in persons with G6PD deficiency:

Drug groups

Primaquine

Chloroquine

Dapsone/chlorproguanil

sulphones

Sulfisoxazole

antibiotics

Cotrimoxazole

Nalidixic acid

Others

question: A 35-year-old male with chronic bacterial prostatitis was treated with cotrimoxazole.  Within a few days, he developed malaise, jaundice, abdominal pain, and dark urine. The blood picture is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The above peripheral smear shows basophilic stippling. It is characteristic of 5' nucleotidase deficiency.

Pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase (P5'N-1) deficiency is the third most common enzyme abnormality causing hereditary hemolytic anemia. It is an autosomal recessive trait.

The hallmark of this enzyme deficiency is the presence of pronounced basophilic stippling and accumulation of pyrimidine nucleotides (RNA remnants) within erythrocytes.

Cabot rings may also be seen. They are thin, threadlike, red to violet rings or figure-of-8 shaped inclusions in red blood cells. They are remnants of the mitotic spindle and are seen in conditions causing dyserythropoiesis.

Basophilic stippling is also seen in the following conditions:

  • Lead toxicity
  • Sideroblastic anemia
  • Severe thalassemia
  • Conditions with impaired cell division
question: The peripheral smear of a patient is given below. It is characteristic of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The antibody involved in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is IgG, which causes extravascular hemolysis.

IgG is called a warm antibody, as it binds to target proteins at 37 oC. On the other hand, cold antibodies or IgM are reactive at 4 to 30oC.

In AIHA, autoantibodies against RBC antigens are produced which coat the RBC membrane. The Fc portion of the antibody is recognized by the Fc receptor on macrophages causing phagocytosis. RBC destruction takes place in extravascular sites where macrophages are abundant.
question: A patient with SLE is found to have warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Name the antibody and the site of hemolysis in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is commonly associated with CLL (chronic lymphocytic leukemia). It is not a typical feature of CML (chronic myeloid leukemia).

AIHA can develop secondary to several autoimmune and infectious causes, as well as drugs. Drug-induced hemolytic anemia can occur by the following mechanisms:

Mechanism Drugs

Adsorption:

Drugs coat the RBC membrane. Antibodies are directed against the membrane–drug complex

Cefotetan

Ceftriaxone

Piperacillin

Innocent bystander:

Drugs bind to antibodies in the plasma. This immune complex activates the complement system and destroys nearby RBCs (innocent bystanders)

Sulfonamides

Quinine

Quinidine

Phenothiazines

Some drugs trigger the production of autoantibodies Methyldopa
question: Patients with which of the following are least likely to develop autoimmune hemolytic anemia?

explanationHtml:
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and hereditary spherocytosis are not Coomb's positive conditions. The following are Coombs-positive hemolytic anemias:

  • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA)
    • Warm AIHA
    • Cold agglutinin disease
  • Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH)
  • Drug-induced hemolytic anemia

[[figure-1]]

In PCH, the direct Coomb's test will be positive for complement only. This condition is characterized by the presence of the Donath-Landsteiner antibody. It is a unique antibody with anti-P specificity at 4°C. Hence, it binds to the RBC at 4°C. However, it causes complement-mediated lysis at 37°C.

Interpretation of direct Coomb's test results:

Condition Agglutination with
anti- IgG anti- C3
Warm AIHA + +
Drug-induced + +
PCH - +
Cold agglutinin disease (IgM) - +
PNH - -
question:
Which of the following are associated with a positive Coombs test?

  1. Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria
  2. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  3. Cold agglutinin disease
  4. Drug-induced hemolytic anemia
  5. Hereditary spherocytosis

explanationHtml:
Donath Landsteiner antibody is specific for paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH). PCH is a rare form of autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

The mechanism of this antibody includes:

  • Binding to RBCs at 4°C
  • Complement-mediated lysis at 37°C

This condition presents with intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Blood transfusion is required in severe anemia. It is a self-limiting condition.

The differences between PCH and PNH are given below:

Condition Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH)
Onset Chronic with acute exacerbations Acute
Pathogenesis Complement-mediated destruction of CD59/55(–) RBCs Immune lysis of normal red cells
Diagnosis Flow cytometry to display a CD55/CD59(–) red cell population Test for Donath-Landsteiner antibody
Triggers Infections, alcohol, exercise, stress, or medications Triggered by viral infection
question: A 20-year-old woman presented with fatigue and intermittent dark-colored urine. Further evaluation revealed positive Donath  Landsteiner antibodies. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) is not seen in prosthetic heart valves. It is associated with macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

MAHA refers to cell fragmentation that occurs in microcirculation. Microvascular lesions lead to luminal narrowing due to the deposition of fibrin and platelets. These produce shear stress that mechanically injures passing red cells. Hence, it is a type of non-immune hemolysis (Coombs-negative). On peripheral blood smear, schistocytes are seen.

Common causes of MAHA include:

  • Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
  • Hemolytic uremic syndrome
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Vasculitis
  • Malignant hypertension
  • APLA syndrome
  • Drug-induced hemolysis
  • Eclampsia
question: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is seen in all of the following except:

explanationHtml:
The best prognosis in atypical HUS is seen in membrane cofactor protein (MCP) gene mutation.

Familial HUS or atypical HUS (aHUS) is the only inherited cause of extracorpuscular hemolytic anemia. It can occur due to mutations in any one of several genes encoding complement regulatory proteins. Mutations in the following genes are seen:

  • Membrane cofactor protein - best prognosis
  • Complement factor B - worst prognosis
  • Complement factor H - most common
  • Complement factor I - least common

In these patients, infection or other triggers cause complement activation through the alternative pathway. This causes hemolysis and damage to endothelial cells in the kidney. It is usually self-limited.

The standard treatment is plasma exchange. Eculizumab has recently been shown to be beneficial in atypical HUS.
question: In patients with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, which of the following mutations is associated with the best prognosis?

explanationHtml:
Deferoxamine has poor oral bioavailability and is administered parenterally (SC/IV).

Oral formulations of both deferiprone and deferasirox are available.

The adverse effects of iron chelators include:

  • Deferiprone - neutropenia, and agranulocytosis.
  • Deferasirox - transaminitis and mild, asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine
  • Deferoxamine - occasional cataracts, deafness, and local skin reactions, but is usually well-tolerated
question: You have decided to prescribe an oral iron chelator for a 10-year-old girl with thalassemia. Which of the following will you not prefer?

correctAnswer: B. Naked eye single tube red-cell osmotic fragility test
explanationHtml:
Naked eye single tube red-cell osmotic fragility test (NESTROFT) is the most sensitive test to detect thalassemia in the population. Hence, it is an effective screening test.

The principle is based on the decreased osmotic fragility of red cells in thalassemia. It is performed as follows:

  1. Mix EDTA blood and 0.36% buffered saline solution.
  2. Shake the tube and leave it at room temperature for 30 minutes.
  3. Shake the tube again and immediately hold the tube in front of a piece of paper with text.
NESTROFT Inference Reason
Lines visible (negative) Normal Hemolysis has occurred
Lines not seen (positive) Thalassemia Stable RBC, unable to lyse

The image below shows a positive NESTROF test (test tube marked as T1) as the line is not visible through the test tube. The test tube marked as C shows the control (Please note that a negative NESTROF test would show visible lines similar to the appearance of the control).

[[figure-1]]

The following tests are specific and used to confirm the diagnosis of thalassemia:

  • Hemoglobin electrophoresis
  • High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)
  • Genetic testing

Note: Eosin 5' maleimide (EMA) flow cytometry is the most specific test for the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis.

options.text: Naked eye single tube red-cell osmotic fragility test

question: Which of the following is the best test to screen patients for thalassemia?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is consistent with β-thalassemia minor. The diagnosis can be established by hemoglobin electrophoresis.

This condition presents with the following features:

  • Microcytes (N: 80-96 fL)
  • Hypochromic (N: 27-33 pg)
  • Mild anemia
  • Target cells
  • Normal iron profile

Hemoglobin electrophoresis findings are as follows:

  • ≥4% of HbA2
  • ≤5% of HbF
question:
During a master health check-up, a 25-year-old woman was found to have the following lab values. Which of the following will help in establishing a diagnosis in this patient?

Hemoglobin - 10g/dl

MCV - 75 fL

MCH - 25 pg

Peripheral smear - Microcytes with target cells

Iron profile - Normal

explanationHtml:
Acute pain crisis is not associated with sickle cell trait. Acute pain crisis is classicaly seen in sickle cell disease.

Manifestations of sickle cell trait include:

  • Often asymptomatic.
  • Hyposthenuria
  • Painless hematuria - due to papillary necrosis
  • Recurrent UTIs
  • Risk of renal medullary carcinoma - rare
  • Increased risk of CKD
  • Sloughing of papillae with urethral obstruction is very rare
  • Anemia and painful crises are rare.
question: Which of the following clinical manifestations is not associated with sickle cell trait?

explanationHtml:
Acute pain crisis is the most common clinical presentation of sickle cell anemia.

These are intermittent episodes of vaso-occlusion in connective and musculoskeletal structures. This results in ischemia resulting in acute pain and tenderness, fever, tachycardia, and anxiety. The management includes vigorous hydration, evaluation for underlying causes, and aggressive analgesia.

Other manifestations of sickle cell anemia include:

  • Hand-foot syndrome - painful infarcts of the digits and dactylitis
  • Priapism - infarction of the penile venous outflow tracts
  • Chronic lower leg ulcers - ischemia and superinfection in the distal circulation
  • Splenic sequestration crisis - life-threatening complication due to acute venous obstruction that requires emergency transfusion and/or splenectomy
  • Aplastic crisis - commonly secondary to parvovirus B19 infection
  • Acute chest syndrome - sickling within the lung, producing pain and temporary pulmonary dysfunction. Treatment may include lifelong transfusion support, using partial exchange transfusion
  • Stroke - common in children
question: Patients with sickle cell anemia most commonly present with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is a lymphoid neoplasm. It is not a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) are a group of disorders that cause an increased number of red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. According to 5th edition WHO classification (2022), myeloproliferative neoplasms consist of the following:

  • Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)
  • Polycythemia vera (PV)
  • Primary myelofibrosis (PMF)
  • Essential thrombocythemia
  • Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML)
  • Chronic neutrophilic leukemia (CNL)
  • Chronic eosinophilic leukemia
  • Myeloproliferative neoplasm, not otherwise specified
question: According to WHO 2022 classification, which of the following is not a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm?

explanationHtml:
The most common myeloproliferative neoplasm is polycythemia vera.

It is a hematopoietic stem cell neoplasm with extensive uncontrolled proliferation of morphologically normal red blood cells in the body, and is also frequently associated with an increase in white blood cells and platelets.
question: What is the most common myeloproliferative neoplasm?

explanationHtml:
This patient has increased Hb and normal WBCs and platelets. The next step is to measure RBC mass to evaluate for polycythemia.

A person has to be evaluated for polycythemia if there is:

Men Women
Raised Hb (or) >16.5 g/dL >16.0 g/dL
Raised PCV >49 % >48 %

This condition is due to either a true increase in the number of RBCs (absolute polycythemia) or an apparent increase due to a decrease in the plasma volume (relative polycythemia). Both of these conditions can be differentiated by measuring RBC mass (the amount of total blood volume that is occupied by RBCs).

In patients with absolute polycythemia, erythropoietin (EPO) levels must be measured.

  • Primary polycythemia - low or normal EPO levels
  • Secondary polycythemia - elevated EPO levels
question:
During a routine health checkup, the following lab reports were obtained for a young male patient. What will be your next step in the evaluation?

Hb: 17 g/dl

TLC: 5500 /μL

Platelets: 1,69,000 /μL

explanationHtml:
Polycythemia vera is associated with low or normal erythropoietin (EPO) levels.

Polycythemia refers to an increase in the number of red blood cells (RBC) in the body. It is classified as:

Primary polycythemia (polycythemia vera) Secondary polycythemia
Pathophysiology Caused by mutations in the hematopoietic stem cells

Hypoxia (COPD, carbon monoxide poisoning)

Autonomous EPO production

Erythropoietin (EPO) Normal or low High
WBCs, and platelet count High (due to increased production of all cell lines) Normal

Autonomous production of erythropoietin occurs in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

Relative (spurious) polycythemia refers to an apparent increase in RBC or hemoglobin count due to a decrease in the plasma volume. It is commonly seen in dehydration.
question: A 45-year-old man is found to have a hemoglobin level of 18 g/dl, a hematocrit of 54%, and an elevated erythropoietin level. Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common cytogenetic abnormality in polycythemia vera is the JAK2 mutation.

JAK2 mutations can be found in the following neoplasms:

  • Polycythemia vera
  • Essential thrombocythemia
  • Primary myelofibrosis
question: What is the most common cytogenetic abnormality in patients with polycythemia vera?

correctAnswer: B. Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation
explanationHtml:
Generalized pruritus seen in polycythemia vera (PV) is a consequence of the activation of mast cells by JAK 2 mutation.

Other options:

Option A: The risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with erythrocytosis, not the degree of thrombocytosis.

Option C: In polycythemia vera, there is an increased risk of H.pylori infection.

Option D: Thrombosis is the major cause of mortality in polycythemia vera. The incidence of acute leukemia in patients not exposed to chemotherapy or radiation therapy is low.

PV is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder in which red cells, granulocytes & platelets accumulate in the absence of a physiological stimulus. The most common mutation seen in PV is the JAK2 mutation.

Clinical features of polycythemia vera are:

  • Thrombosis is the most common manifestation and is the major cause of mortality. Uncontrolled erythrocytosis causes increased viscosity of the blood causing thrombosis of the vessels. Patients may present with stroke, transient ischemic attacks, myocardial infarction, and Budd-Chiari syndrome.
  • Aquagenic pruritis is generalized itching following a warm bath or a shower due to increased mast cells and histamine.
  • Erythromelalgia is erythema and pain in the fingers, hands, and feet due to increased platelet stickiness.
  • Splenomegaly due to increased destruction of RBCs in the spleen
  • Gout is due to the excessive proliferation of the marrow cells leading to elevated uric acid levels.

options.text: Risk of thrombosis strongly correlates with the degree of thrombocytosis
Generalized pruritus is a consequence of mast cell activation by JAK 2 mutation
It is protective against H.pylori infection
Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common cause of mortality

question: Which of the following statements about polycythemia vera is true?

explanationHtml:
Low WBC count is not a feature of polycythemia vera. It is associated with an elevated WBC count.

Common laboratory findings of polycythemia vera are:

  • Elevated hemoglobin concentration, hematocrit levels, and RBC count
  • Elevated WBCs and platelet counts
  • Low to normal erythropoietin levels
  • Elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase
question: Which of the following would not be seen in patients with polycythemia vera?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia vera. In these patients, ruxolitinib, a Janus-kinase inhibitor is used to provide symptomatic relief.

The treatment of polycythemia vera is as follows:

  • Therapeutic phlebotomy - definitive treatment
  • Anticoagulants - in patients with thrombosis
  • Symptomatic relief:
    • Ruxolitinib
    • Hydroxyurea
    • Interferon-alpha
    • PUVA therapy
question: A 40-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of severe itching every time he takes a hot shower. He also reports a burning sensation in his fingers and frequent headaches. His hemoglobin is 18 g/dL and his EPO levels are low. Which of the following can provide symptomatic relief in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Enlargement of the spleen > 8 cm below the costal margin or weight > 1000 g is called massive splenomegaly. It is not a feature of essential thrombocythemia (ET), as it causes only mild splenomegaly.

The causes of massive splenomegaly include:

  • CML
  • Primary myelofibrosis
  • CLL
  • Lymphoma
  • Hairy cell leukemia
  • AIHA
  • Gaucher's disease
  • Sarcoidosis

ET is a neoplasm in which the body produces too many platelets, resulting in a platelet count > 4.5 lakhs/μL. It occurs due to the mutations in the JAK2, CALR, or MPL genes.

The majority of the patients are asymptomatic and are diagnosed incidentally. Some patients may present with thrombotic events or, rarely, hemorrhages. The following findings are seen:

  • Peripheral smear - abnormally large platelets
  • Bone marrow biopsy - megakaryocytosis showing hyperlobulated nuclei
question: You are a first-year medicine resident. While examining a patient, you note that his spleen is enlarged 8.5 cm below his costal margin. You would include all of the following in your differential diagnosis except:

explanationHtml:
The first-line drug for cytoreductive therapy in patients with essential thrombocythemia is hydroxyurea.

Treatment of essential thrombocythemia is as follows:

  • No symptoms or risk of thrombosis:
    • Observation alone
    • Low dose aspirin may be considered
  • High risk of thrombosis (cardiovascular risk factors, prior history of thrombosis)
    • Low dose aspirin
    • Cytoreduction with hydroxyurea, busulfan, or interferon-alpha
question: A 24-year-old woman, who was diagnosed with essential thrombocythemia, is being planned for cytoreductive therapy. What first-line drug should she be started on?

explanationHtml:
The image shows the deposition of numerous collagen fibers in the bone marrow, which indicates marrow fibrosis. These clinical findings and history of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration are diagnostic of primary myelofibrosis.

In this condition, the neoplastic proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells results in increased and abnormal proliferation of the megakaryocytes. These megakaryocytes release excessive amounts of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and TGF-β. Increased growth factors lead to the deposition of collagen in the bone marrow which eventually leads to fibrosis.

The clinical features include:

  • Early phase:
    • Thrombocytosis (large, abnormal platelets) and leukocytosis
    • Hypercellularity of bone marrow
  • Late phase:
    • Pancytopenia
    • Hypocellularity and fibrosis of bone marrow (dry tap)
    • Teardrop-shaped RBCs and leukoerythroblastosis (premature release of nucleated erythroid and early granulocytes into blood)
  • Hepatosplenomegaly - due to extramedullary hematopoiesis.
question: A 60-year-old man was referred with severe anemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral smear showed teardrop cells, nucleated RBCs, and giant abnormal platelets. Bone marrow aspirate could not be obtained despite multiple attempts, hence a bone marrow biopsy was done. The findings are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Fanconi anemia results in pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow. Hence, it is not likely in this patient.

Causes of pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow include:

  • Inherited aplastic anemia
    • Fanconi anemia
    • Dyskeratosis congenita
    • Shwachman-Diamond syndrome
  • Acquired aplastic anemia

Causes of pancytopenia with hypercellular bone marrow include:

  • Primary bone marrow disorders
    • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
    • Myelodysplastic syndrome
    • Myelofibrosis
  • Systemic diseases
    • Megaloblastic anemia
    • Alcoholism
    • Sarcoidosis
    • Tuberculosis
    • Brucellosis
question: Bone marrow aspirate of a patient with pancytopenia revealed a hypercellular marrow. Which of the following conditions is unlikely?

explanationHtml:
The most likely diagnosis is dyskeratosis congenita. This condition is characterized by pancytopenia along with the clinical triad of:

  1. Reticular skin pigmentation
  2. Nail dystrophy
  3. Oral leukoplakia

[[figure-1]]

Option A: Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by pancytopenia, congenital anomalies, and an increased risk of malignancies.

Option B: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome presents with bone marrow failure and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

Option C: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome presents with low RBC counts due to congenital erythroid aplasia.

Note: Fanconi anemia is different from Fanconi syndrome. Fanconi syndrome is a disorder of renal tubular function (type 2 RTA) that results in increased excretion of glucose, amino acids, bicarbonates, and phosphates.
question: A 20-year-old male patient with the following exam findings is found to have pancytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Herpes simplex infection is not a cause of acquired aplastic anemia.

Secondary causes of acquired aplastic anemia include:

  • Radiation
  • Toxins - Benzene
  • Drugs
    • Chemotherapy drugs (including cyclophosphamide)
    • Sulfonamides
    • Chloramphenicol
  • Infections:
    • 1-2 months after an attack of seronegative viral hepatitis
    • HIV, EBV, CMV
    • Parvovirus B19
  • Eosinophilic fasciitis
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  • Graft vs host disease
question: All of the following can cause acquired aplastic anemia except:

explanationHtml:
The clinical and laboratory findings, as well as bone marrow hypocellularity are diagnostic of aplastic anemia. In this young patient, the best method of management is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia and resulting bleeding manifestations, anemia, and frequent infections. Bone marrow biopsy reveals hypocellularity with fatty infiltration of the bone marrow. The management is as follows:

  • Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation - best method of management in young patients
  • Antithymocyte globulin with cyclosporine - elderly patients and patients without HLA-matched donors
  • Eltrombopag - a thrombopoietin analog used as add-on therapy
question: A 25-year-old lady is being evaluated for recurrent epistaxis. On examination, the spleen is not palpable. Investigations reveal Hb of 6 g/dL, platelet count of 18,000/μL, and WBC count of 3000/μL. The results of a bone marrow biopsy are given below. What is the best method of management in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The most common cytogenetic abnormality seen in myelodysplastic neoplasm is the 5q deletion.

Myelodysplastic syndromes/neoplasm (MDS) are a group of disorders in which abnormal stem cells produce increased numbers of immature blood cells. These immature cells are defective and die prematurely resulting in lower numbers of mature blood cells. It is characterized by pancytopenia and a high risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The cytogenetic abnormalities identified in this condition include:

  • 5q deletion
  • 3q deletion
  • 7q deletion
  • Monosomy 7
  • Monosomy 5

5th edition WHO Classification of MDS (2022):

1. MDS with defining genetic abnormalities:

  • MDS with a low blast and isolated 5q deletion (MDS-5q): <5% blasts in the bone marrow or <2% blasts in the peripheral blood.
  • MDS with a low blast and SF3B1 mutation (MDS-SF3B1): Detection of ≥15% ring sideroblasts may substitute for SF3B1 mutation.
  • MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation (MDS-biTP53): <20% blasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

2. MDS, morphologically defined:

  • MDS with low blasts: <5% blasts in the bone marrow or <2% blasts in the peripheral blood.
  • MDS-hypoplastic: ≤25% bone marrow cellularity
  • MDS with increased blasts (IB)
  • MDS-fibrosis: 5-19% of blasts in bone marrow or 2–19% in peripheral blood

3. Childhood myelodysplastic neoplasm:

Type Blasts in
bone marrow		 Blasts in peripheral blood
Childhood MDS with low blasts <5% <2%
Childhood MDS with increased blasts 5-19% 2-19%
question: What is the most common cytogenetic abnormality seen in patients with myelodysplastic neoplasm?

explanationHtml:
Lenalidomide is the drug of choice in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) associated with 5q deletion.

It is a thalidomide derivative with the following benefits in these patients:

  • Patients achieve transfusion independence
  • Normal or near-normal hemoglobin levels
  • Normalization of cytogenetics

Adverse effects include:

  • Myelosuppression (worsening thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, necessitating blood count monitoring)
  • Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism

However, hematopoietic stem cell transplant remains the definitive treatment.
question: A patient with myelodysplastic syndrome was found to have 5q deletion. What is the drug of choice for this patient?

explanationHtml:
The average lifespan of platelets in circulation is 7–10 days.

Thrombopoietin (TPO) is the regulator of platelet production. A reduction in platelet and megakaryocyte mass increases the level of TPO, which then stimulates platelet production.

The shelf life of donor platelets is 5 days. It is stored on a special agitator at 20-24 °C. The half-life of transfused platelets is 3-5 days.
question: What is the lifespan of a platelet?

explanationHtml:
Hemarthrosis is highly suggestive of a coagulation disorder, not a platelet disorder.

Bleeding diathesis can occur due to:

  • Platelet disorders - mucocutaneous bleeding like petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, epistaxis, menorrhagia, gastrointestinal (GI) bleeds
  • Coagulation disorders - hemarthrosis, muscle hematomas, and bleeding into soft tissues
  • Disorders of the vessel wall (Henoch-Schönlein purpura, scurvy) - purpura and ecchymosis

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following would you not expect to see in patients with a platelet disorder?

explanationHtml:
Bernard Soulier syndrome is a disorder of platelet adhesion. It occurs due to an inherited defect in the GPIb-IX complex.

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following is a disorder of platelet adhesion?

explanationHtml:
Thrombocytopenia is a feature of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

It is an X-linked recessive condition caused by mutations in the WASP gene. It affects T-cells and platelets and presents with the following features:

  • Eczema
  • Thrombocytopenia - along with decreased platelet size, impaired platelet aggregation response
  • Immunodeficiency - low IgM, high IgE, defective regulatory T cells causing recurrent bacterial infections.

Option A: Platelet storage pool disorder is a disorder of defective platelet granule formation.

Option C: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a type of small vessel vasculitis in children and young adults.

Option D: Hemophilia is a coagulation disorder, hence the platelet count is not affected.
question: Patients with which of the following conditions would have a low platelet count?

explanationHtml:
Immune-mediated destruction of platelets is seen in drug-induced thrombocytopenia. Common drugs that cause this are quinidine, heparin, sulfa compounds.

Drug-dependent antibody binding can only be demonstrated in the presence of the drug in the laboratory assays. The thrombocytopenia normally occurs within 21 days of initial exposure and usually gets resolved after 7-10 days once the drug is stopped.

Immune-mediated destruction of platelets is seen in:

  • Drug-induced thrombocytopenia
  • Infection-induced thrombocytopenia
  • Idiopathic/ immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)

Option A: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a disorder of platelet adhesion. There are no autoantibodies against platelets.

Option B: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is an inherited disorder with defective granule formation in platelets. It affects platelet activation and aggregation.

Option C: Thrombotic microangiopathies like thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) lead to thrombocytopenia due to increased platelet consumption.
question: Immune-mediated destruction of platelets is seen in patients with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario and image showing petechiae are suggestive of immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder with autoantibodies against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX. It can either be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to autoimmune conditions like SLE or infections like HIV and hepatitis C.

It presents with features of mucocutaneous bleeding. CBC shows isolated thrombocytopenia and peripheral smear does not reveal any hemolysis.

Acute ITP Chronic ITP
Common in children Common in adults (females > males)
Associated with an antecedent viral infection Not associated with antecedent infection
Spontaneous remission in 80% cases Spontaneous remission is not usually seen

Options A and B: HUS and TTP are microangiopathies. They are associated with hemolysis and schistocytes on peripheral smear.

Option D: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia typically presents within 5-10 days of treatment. Hence, it is not the likely diagnosis in this patient.
