question: A young man comes to you with complaints of bleeding gums and the following skin rash. He reports that he had diarrhea last week after eating at a roadside eatery. History is significant for deep vein thrombosis 6 months ago that was treated with heparin. His CBC report revealed a platelet count of 15,000/µL, normal RBC and WBC count. His peripheral smear was normal. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Bleeding into the joints is a common manifestation
explanationHtml:
This scenario is suggestive of acute immune thrombocytopenic purpura. Bleeding into the joints is seen in coagulation disorders and is not a manifestation of this condition.

Immune thrombocytopenic purpura or idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an acquired disorder in which there is an immune-mediated destruction of platelets. It can be acute or chronic.

Acute ITP is common in children and is usually preceded by viral infection. It presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, petechiae, ecchymosis). Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, fever and jaundice are absent. The following laboratory features are seen:

  • Thrombocytopenia (commonly <20,000 / μL)
  • Bleeding time - prolonged
  • PT/aPTT/INR - normal
  • Bone marrow - normal/increased megakaryocytes
  • Peripheral smear - normal

This condition resolves spontaneously in 80% of the cases. Treatment is as follows:

  • Oral glucocorticoids or IVIG (if glucocorticoids are contraindicated) - If platelet count < 30,000/ μL and patient is asymptomatic or has minor bleeding or risk factors for bleeding (antiplatelet drugs/anticoagulants or concomitant bleeding disorders)
  • IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG : If severe bleeding symptoms
  • Platelet transfusion + IV methylprednisolone + IVIG: In life-threatening bleeding (like intracranial hemorrhage)

options.text: Bone marrow biopsy shows increased megakaryocytes
Bleeding into the joints is a common manifestation
The condition resolves spontaneously in 80% patients

question: Two weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection, a 5-year-old presents with ecchymosis and petechiae all over the body. Abdominal examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly. The platelet count is 15,000/µL and the coagulation profile is normal. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

correctAnswer: A. She requires regular platelet transfusions until platelet count is normalized
explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario in an adult patient is suggestive of chronic ITP (idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura). She does not require platelet transfusion. It is recommended only for patients with severe bleeding manifestations (intracranial/ gastrointestinal) or platelet count < 5000 μL.

Chronic ITP can either be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to autoimmune conditions like SLE or infections like HIV and hepatitis C. Depending on the clinical features, the management is as follows:

Clinical features Management

1.

Minor bleeding manifestations (and/or)

Platelet count > 5000/ μL

Prednisone (OR)

Anti-D immunoglobulin therapy - effective only in Rh-positive patients (OR)

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

2.

Severe ITP (any of the following):

  • Significant GI / intracranial bleeding
  • Platelet count < 5000/μL
  • Signs of impending bleeding (retinal or large oral mucosal bleeds)

Platelet transfusion (AND)

High-dose glucocorticoids (AND)

IVIG / Anti-D immunoglobulins + Rituximab
3. Relapse after first-line therapy Splenectomy
4. Unresponsive to all other therapy or relapse after splenectomy Thrombopoietin receptor agonists - romiplostim (subcutaneous), eltrombopag (oral)

options.text: She requires regular platelet transfusions until platelet count is normalized
Prednisone or anti-D immunoglobulins can be used as the first-line treatment
Splenectomy may be done if she relapses after medical management
Romiplostim and eltrombopag can be used if there is no response to splenectomy

question: A 50-year-old woman comes to the ER after developing a spontaneous nosebleed. Over the past 1 week, she has noticed blood on her toothbrush while brushing her teeth. She was diagnosed with hepatitis C three months ago. Investigations reveal a platelet count of 32,000/ µL and a bleeding time of 9 minutes . Which of the following is false regarding the treatment of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Splenectomy is the treatment of choice in a case of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) relapse after first line therapy with glucocorticoids. The relapse usually occurs once they are tapered. Vaccination against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae) is advised before splenectomy is performed.

It is important to note that in some patients ITP resolves by itself, and observation along with intermittent IV immunoglobulins and anti - Rh(D) administration or administration of a thrombopoietin receptor agonist (eltrombopag, romiplostim) can be a viable option before splenectomy is considered.

The treatment of ITP is as follows:

Clinical features Management

1.

Minor bleeding manifestations (and/or)

Platelet count > 5000/ μL

Prednisone (OR)

Anti-D immunoglobulin therapy - effective only in Rh-positive patients (OR)

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG)

2.

Severe ITP (any of the following):

  • Significant GI / intracranial bleeding
  • Platelet count < 5000/μL
  • Signs of impending bleeding (retinal or large oral mucosal bleeds)

Platelet transfusion (AND)

High-dose glucocorticoids (AND)

IVIG / Anti-D immunoglobulins + Rituximab
3. Relapse after first-line therapy Splenectomy
4. Unresponsive to all other therapy or relapse after splenectomy Thrombopoietin receptor agonists - romiplostim (subcutaneous), eltrombopag (oral)

ITP is an acquired disorder characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of platelets and possibly inhibition of platelet release from the megakaryocyte. Secondary causes of ITP include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), HIV-AIDS, and Hepatitis C.

ITP usually presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, very low platelet count, and normal peripheral blood cells. Patients typically exhibit ecchymoses and petechiae or they may incidentally discover thrombocytopenia during a routine complete blood count. Rarely, life-threatening bleeding may occur. The presence of wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages can serve as warning signs of potentially life-threatening bleeding.
question: Which of the following is the best treatment for the relapse of immune thrombocytopenic purpura?

explanationHtml:
Abciximab can cause a drop in platelet count within 24 hours of initial exposure. Hence, these patients must be monitored for thrombocytopenia. This is due to naturally-occurring antibodies that cross-react with the drug bound to the platelets.

Thrombocytopenia due to other drugs typically occurs several days after exposure (average 21 days) and resolves in 7-10 days after drug withdrawal. Drug-induced thrombocytopenia can occur due to the following mechanisms:

  • Bone marrow suppression - chemotherapeutic drugs
  • Drug dependent antibodies that react with platelet surface antigens - quinine and sulfonamides
  • Naturally occurring antibodies that cross-react with drugs bound to the platelets - platelet Gp IIb/IIIa inhibitors

Some of the drugs that cause thrombocytopenia are:

  • Antibiotics - ampicillin, cephalosporins, piperacillin, vancomycine
  • Analgesics - ibuprofen, acetaminophen
  • Anti-epileptics - phenytoin, carbamazepine
  • Heparin
  • Amiodarone
question: It is your first day as an intern in the medicine ward. The senior resident tells you to check the platelet count of a patient who is being monitored for thrombocytopenia. He was started on a new medication the previous night. What drug was most likely prescribed?

explanationHtml:
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is not associated with bleeding. On the contrary, it is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis.

This condition occurs due to the production of antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex (platelet factor 4, a platelet-specific protein). These antibodies can activate platelets and result in thrombosis. It is seen 5-14 days after exposure to heparin.

These antibodies can be detected using ELISA or serotonin release assay. This condition is managed by discontinuing heparin and using alternative anticoagulants.
question: Patients with all of the following usually present with bleeding except:

explanationHtml:
Enoxaparin is a low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and LMWH are contraindicated in the treatment of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) as they may interact with HIT antibodies which are antibodies against the complex of protein platelet factor 4 (PF4) and heparin.

HIT can occur following exposure to unfractionated heparin and less commonly with LMWH.

The treatment of HIT is as follows:

  • Discontinue heparin
  • Anticoagulation with non-heparin anticoagulants even in the absence of thrombosis, since there is a high risk of thrombosis.
    • Direct thrombin inhibitors: Argatroban, lepirudin, bivalirudin
    • Danaparoid (heparinoid)
question: Which of the following cannot be used in the treatment of patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?

explanationHtml:
This scenario is suggestive of pseudothrombocytopenia. It is seen in blood samples collected with EDTA as the anticoagulant.

EDTA causes a reduction in the calcium content of the collected blood sample. This triggers in vitro platelet clumping and agglutination by antibodies (usually IgG), as shown below:

[[figure-1]]

When a low platelet count is obtained with an EDTA sample, the peripheral blood smear should be evaluated. The platelet count must also be determined in blood collected in sodium citrate or heparin collection tubes or fresh fingerstick blood sample.
question: The CBC of a 33-year-old woman revealed a low platelet count. However, further evaluation revealed this to be an in vitro sampling error. Which of the following is the likely cause of this finding?

correctAnswer: B. Ristocetin aggregation test is normal
explanationHtml:
The ristocetin aggregation test is abnormal (no aggregation) in patients with Bernard-Soulier (BS) syndrome.

It is an inherited disorder of platelet function or qualitative platelet disorder due to deficiency of the Gp Ib-IX receptor. This is the platelet membrane receptor for the von Willebrand factor (vWF). The binding of the vWF to the GpIb-IX-V complex on the platelet membrane is essential for platelet adhesion to the vessel wall.

This condition presents with mild thrombocytopenia and peripheral smear shows large platelets.

Platelet aggregation tests are performed to measure platelet activation and aggregation in vitro. Various platelet agonists like ADP, epinephrine, collagen, and ristocetin can be used to perform these tests. In Bernard-Soulier syndrome, the following responses are seen:

  • With ristocetin - No response/no aggregation, as ristocetin specifically binds to the platelet membrane via the Gp Ib-IXa receptor
  • With ADP or epinephrine - Normal response, as Gp IIb-IIIa receptor is not involved in this process

options.text: Platelet aggregation tests with epinephrine and ADP are normal

question: Which of the following is false regarding patients with Bernard-Soulier syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

vWD occurs due to deficient or abnormal von Willebrand factor (vWF). vWF is synthesized by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes (gene located on chromosome 12p). It is then stored in endothelial storage vesicles, Weibel-Palade bodies. Metalloprotease ADAMTS13 cleaves ultra-large multimers of VWF which are responsible for platelet adhesion.

The functions of vWF and the corresponding symptoms include:

  • Adhesion of the platelets to the exposed subendothelium - symptoms of both platelet and bleeding disorders
  • Prolongs the half-life of factor VIII by binding to it in circulation - hemophilia A like symptoms (rare)
question: Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?

explanationHtml:
Autosomal hemophilia is also called type 2N von Willebrand disease (vWD), as the clinical presentation is similar to hemophilia.

The types of vWD are:

Type Inheritance Mechanism Important characteristics
1 AD Partial quantitative deficiency of VWF Most common type
3 AR Complete quantitative deficiency Most severe VWD
2A AD Loss of VWF multimers (increased cleavage by ADAMS13) Platelet adhesion defect
2B AD Increased binding of VWF to platelets causing VWF-platelet complex destruction Thrombocytopenia
2M AD Decreased affinity of VWF to platelets Platelet adhesion defect, very rare
2N AR Decreased affinity of VWF to Factor VIII Autosomal hemophilia

In pseudo vWD, the vWF is normal. However, platelets have an increased affinity for vWF. It presents similar to vWD 2B with thrombocytopenia.
question: Which of the following is called autosomal hemophilia?

correctAnswer: A. A man with aortic stenosis with gastrointestinal bleeding
explanationHtml:
Heyde’s syndrome is aortic stenosis with gastrointestinal bleeding, due to angiodysplasia of the gastrointestinal tract.

The shear stress on blood passing through the stenotic aortic valve produces a change in the von Willebrand factor making it susceptible to serum proteases. Hence, large multimer forms are lost, leading to an acquired type 2 von Willebrand disease (vWD). The condition is reversed with the replacement of the aortic valve.

Other causes of acquired vWD include:

  • Multiple myeloma
  • Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma
  • Polycythemia vera
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus

options.text: A man with aortic stenosis with gastrointestinal bleeding
A woman with aortic stenosis with intracranial bleed
A man with aortic regurgitation with gastrointestinal bleeding
A woman with aortic regurgitation with intracranial bleed

question: Which of the following patients has Heyde's syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Bleeding time is increased in von Willebrand disease (vWD). It is a combination of a platelet adhesion defect with factor VIII deficiency.

The laboratory findings in vWD include:

  • Platelet count is normal (except type 2B)
  • Bleeding time is prolonged
  • Ristocetin aggregation is abnormal
  • Other platelet aggregation tests are normal
  • Prothrombin time (PT) is normal
  • aPTT is prolonged
  • VWF activity is decreased
  • Factor VIII activity is decreased
question: Which of the following laboratory findings is seen in a patient with von Willebrand's disease?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand's disease. The preferred first-line treatment is desmopressin (DDAVP).

This drug acts on endothelial V2 receptors causing the release of VWF and factor VIII from endothelial stores. DDAVP can be given intravenously or by an intranasal spray. The side effects include tachyphylaxis and hyponatremia.

VWF concentrate and factor VIII concentrate are reserved for patients with severe disease or prior to major procedures. Antifibrinolytic therapy (tranexamic acid or ε-aminocaproic acid) may be used for the prevention and treatment of mucosal bleeding.
question: A 28-year-old woman is being evaluated for prolonged bleeding following a tooth extraction. She also reports heavy bleeding during menses and recurrent gum bleeds. Labs show increased aPTT, normal PT, and increased bleeding time. Which of the following is the first-line treatment for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Thrombocytopenia is not seen in Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia.

Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia is a disorder of platelet aggregation caused due to a congenital defect or deficiency of the GpIIb/IIIa receptor. However, the platelet count is normal and single isolated platelets are seen without clumping on peripheral smear. Patients presents with superficial mucocutaneous bleeding in this condition. The levels of vWF are normal.

Normally, release of ADP causes platelets to change shape and bind to fibrinogen through the GpIIb/IIIa receptor. In Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia, absence of the receptor causes abnormal aggregation (absent or reduced) on adding ADP. However, aggregation in response to ristocetin is normal, as it is dependent on GpIb and vWF.

Secondary platelet dysfunction can be seen in the following conditions:

  • Uremia
  • Paraproteinemia
  • Myeloproliferative disorders

options.text: Abnormal platelet aggregation on adding ADP

question: Which of the following features is not seen in patients with Glanzmann’s thrombasthenia?

explanationHtml:
Pagoclone is an anxiolytic medication. It is not an antiplatelet drug.

The thienopyridine drugs are ADP receptor or P2Y12 antagonists that inhibit ADP mediated platelet aggregation. They include the following drugs:

  • Clopidogrel - commonly used
  • Ticagrelor - reversible drug with a shorter t1/2, does not require activation, may cause mild, self-limited dyspnea
  • Prasugrel - 10 times more potent than clopidogrel, rapid onset of action, better absorption, more predictable
  • Ticlopidine

Clopidogrel and prasugrel are prodrugs that require activation by cytochrome P450 enzymes. CYP2C19 polymorphisms can cause reduced platelet inhibition with clopidogrel and increased risk of cardiovascular events.
question: A physician decides to start a patient with stroke on antiplatelet medication. All of the following drugs would be effective except:

explanationHtml:
Combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is called Evans syndrome.

Options B and C: May-Hegglin anomaly and Fechtner syndrome are autosomal dominant hereditary conditions presenting with bleeding, sensorineural hearing loss, glomerulonephritis, and/or eye abnormalities. The severity of the bleeding symptoms is out of proportion to the moderately decreased platelet count.

Option D: Rosenthal syndrome or hemophilia C refers to factor XI deficiency.
question: A 24-year-old woman underwent evaluation for bleeding manifestations and severe anemia. Investigations revealed combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The most common side effect of aspirin is gastrointestinal symptoms. The use of enteric-coated aspirin does not reduce these side effects.

Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase (COX)-1, which causes reduced synthesis of thromboxane A2. At high doses, it also inhibits COX-2, which results in the anti-inflammatory effects of aspirin.

The major GI side effects include dyspepsia, erosive gastritis, peptic ulcers with bleeding and perforation. The overall risk of major bleeding with aspirin is 1–3% per year, which increases 2-3 fold if there is concurrent use of other antiplatelet drugs or anticoagulants. The risk of bleeding can be reduced by eradication of Helicobacter pylori infection and giving proton pump inhibitors (PPIs).

Aspirin sensitivity refers to bronchospasm or urticaria/angioedema seen immediately after administration of aspirin. It is also called Samter's triad (asthma, recurrent nasal polyps, aspirin sensitivity). In patients with aspirin resistance, there is failure of aspirin to produce its normal platelet inhibitory functions.
question: What is the most common side effect experienced by patients taking enteric-coated aspirin?

explanationHtml:
Dipyridamole increases extracellular adenosine levels.

It is an antiplatelet drug that increases levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP) in platelets by:

  • Blocking the reuptake of adenosine and increasing extracellular adenosine levels
  • Inhibiting phosphodiesterase-mediated cAMP degradation

This increase in cyclic AMP reduces intracellular levels of calcium. This inhibits platelet activation and aggregation.

[[figure-1]]

Dipyridamole is a weak antiplatelet used in combination with aspirin for the prevention of stroke in patients with TIA.

Side effects include gastrointestinal and vasodilatory complaints (headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension). Due to it's vasodilatory effects, it is contraindicated in patients with symptomatic coronary artery disease.

options.text: Increases levels of cyclic AMP in platelets

question: Which of the following is incorrect about the mechanism of action of dipyridamole?

explanationHtml:
Abciximab is safe in patients with renal impairment. It belongs to the group of GpIIb-IIIa receptor antagonists. These are parenteral drugs that are used in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome.

There are three important drugs in this group:

Feature Abciximab Eptifibatide Tirofiban
Gp IIb/IIIa antagonist Non-specific Specific Specific
Plasma half-life Short (min) Long (2.5 h) Long (2.0 h)
Platelet-bound half-life Long (days) Short (s) Short (s)
Renal clearance No Yes Yes

Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia and bleeding are the most common side effects. Thrombocytopenia can occur within 24 hours of initiation.
question: A 62-year-old man diagnosed with myocardial infarction is planned for percutaneous intervention. He was diagnosed with diabetic nephropathy 2 months ago. The cardiologist decides to start him on aspirin and an additional antiplatelet drug. Which of the following can be used for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Plasmapheresis is the mainstay of the treatment of patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

The best response to this therapy is seen in patients with ADAMTS13 autoantibodies. Plasmapheresis is continued until the resolution of platelet count and signs of hemolysis for at least 2 days.

Option A: The first line of treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia is glucocorticoids. The second line includes rituximab and splenectomy.

Option B: Treatment of disseminated intravascular coagulation is primarily supportive with measures to treat the underlying cause.

Option D: Treatment of HUS is primarily supportive. Dialysis is usually required. In some varients of HUS plasma infusion/exchange can be effective by replacing the complement-regulatory proteins.
question: Plasmapheresis is the mainstay of treatment in patients with which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Large vessel arterial or venous thromboemboli are not seen in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). This condition is associated with microvascular thrombosis.

TTP occurs due to deficiency or autoantibodies against the metalloprotease ADAMTS13, which normally cleaves multimers of vWF. In this condition, the vWF molecules persist causing pathogenic platelet adhesion and aggregation. This causes localized platelet thrombi and fibrin deposits at various sites.

It presents with the following pentad of clinical features:

  1. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia - mechanical shearing of RBCs as they pass through platelet rich-microthrombi
  2. Thrombocytopenia - deposition of platelets in microthrombi
  3. Renal failure - microthrombi in the renal vasculature
  4. Neurologic findings - headache, confusion, transient focal neurologic deficits
  5. Fever
question: Which of the following is not seen in patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

correctAnswer: B. PT and aPTT are prolonged
explanationHtml:
In patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), the PT and aPTT are normal, as consumptive coagulopathy is not seen.

TTP and HUS are thrombotic microangiopathies with overlapping clinical features. TTP can be primary (ADAMTS13 deficiency) or secondary (associated with infections like HIV and drugs like quinine).

Note: In disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), thrombocytopenia and microangiopathy are seen. It is associated with consumption of clotting factors and fibrinogen resulting in prolonged PT and aPTT.

options.text: Clinical features overlap with hemolytic uremic syndrome
It is common in patients with HIV infection
It can be associated with use of quinine

question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding patients with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

explanationHtml:
Factor V Leiden mutation is the most common inherited cause of venous thrombosis. Venous thrombosis typically manifests as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary thromboembolism.

Hypercoagulable states or thrombophilias can be inherited or acquired:

  • Inherited causes in decreasing order of prevalence are as follows:
    • Factor V Leiden mutation
    • Prothrombin mutation
    • Protein C deficiency
    • Protein S deficiency
    • Antithrombin III deficiency
  • Acquired causes include:
    • Surgery
    • Malignancy
    • Antiphospholipid syndrome
    • Trauma
    • Pregnancy
    • Long-haul travel
    • Obesity
    • Oral contraceptives/hormone replacement
    • Myeloproliferative disorders
    • Polycythemia vera
question: What is the most common genetic abnormality seen in patients with recurrent history of venous thrombosis?

explanationHtml:
Platelet storage pool disease (SPD) is an example of an autosomal dominant qualitative platelet disorder. It refers to a group of disorders characterized by a deficiency of platelet granules causing secretion defects.

[[figure-1]]

Bernard Soulier syndrome, Glanzman thrombasthenia, and Chediak-Higashi syndrome are inherited as autosomal recessive traits.
question: Which of the following qualitative platelet disorders are inherited as autosomal dominant?

Chronic lymphoid leukemia (CLL) is the most common type of leukemia in adults.

The common types of leukemia in various age groups is as follows:

  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) - most common acute leukemia in adults
  • Acute lymphoid leukemia (ALL) - most common cancer in childhood. The most common subtype of ALL is B-cell ALL
  • Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL) - most common lymphoid malignancy in adults
question: What is the most common type of leukemia in adults?

explanationHtml:
Evan's syndrome does not predispose to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

The following conditions predispose to AML:

Genetic conditions:

  • Down's syndrome:
    • Young children <4 years
    • Typically of the acute megakaryocytic subtype and associated with GATA1 mutations
    • Excellent clinical outcomes
  • Defective DNA repair in conditions like ataxia telangiectasia, Fanconi anemia, and Bloom syndrome

Environmental factors:

  • Drugs:
    • Alkylating agents - cyclophosphamide, melphalan, dacarbazine, platinum compounds, after 4-6 years of exposure
    • Topoisomerase II inhibitors - etoposide, after 1-3 years of exposure.
  • Radiation - high dose radiation, therapeutic radiation in patients exposed to alkylating agents
  • Chemicals - benzene, petroleum products, pesticide

Hematological disorders with increased risk of AML:

  • Myeloproliferative disorders
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  • Aplastic anemia
  • Myelodysplastic syndrome
  • Multiple myeloma
question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for acute myeloid leukemia?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario of congenital neutropenia is suggestive of Kostmann syndrome. It is associated with an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Kostmann syndrome occurs due to mutations in the G-CSF receptor and neutrophil elastase. This causes bone marrow failure specifically in the myeloid lineage. It presents in young children as recurrent bacterial infections (such as otitis media, cellulitis) and oral ulcers.

Option A: Bloom syndrome occurs due to defects in DNA repair. It is not associated with neutropenia but has a higher risk of AML.

Option C: Diamond-Blackfan syndrome refers to congenital erythroid aplasia. It is also associated with a higher risk of AML.

Option D: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is due to defective phagolysosome formation. It is not associated with neutropenia.
question: A 2-year-old girl was referred with recurrent bacterial infections. Parents report that their first child also had similar features and died at the age of 18 months from myeloid leukemia. Investigations revealed markedly reduced absolute neutrophil count. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a chloroma. It is commonly associated with the M2 subtype of acute myeloid leukemia, also called AML with maturation according to the FAB classification.

Chloroma is also called myeloid sarcoma, extramedullary myeloid tumor, or granulocytic sarcoma. It is an extramedullary tumor mass consisting of myeloid blasts, with or without maturation. It is called chloroma due to the peculiar green color, caused by myeloperoxidase. The sites affected include orbit (most common), skull, oral cavity including gingiva, paranasal sinuses, sternum, ribs, vertebrae, and pelvis.

In contrast, AML M5 (acute monocytic leukemia) often presents with diffuse gingival infiltration or hypertrophy owing to the widespread infiltration of monocytic cells rather than discrete tumor masses.

Note: The FAB classification is an older classification and does not give an idea about the prognosis of the disease. Now WHO classification has been predominantly used. WHO-5 2023 is the latest classification for hematolymphoid and leukemia disorders. According to this, ‘Myeloid Sarcoma’ has been made into a separate classification. Hence, the given clinical scenario with the history of greenish gingival mass will be classified as a Myeloid Sarcoma based on the WHO-5 2023 classification. Since MPO positivity is characteristic of a myeloid cells, this case would be a myelocytic lineage AML.
question: A 60-year-old man is being evaluated for suspected acute myeloid leukemia. He reports a fast-growing swelling in his mouth for the past 1 week. On examination, there is a greenish gingival mass with a necrotic surface. As per the FAB classification, this presentation is likely associated with which of the following?

explanationHtml: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is commonly seen in patients with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).
question: Patients suffering from which type of AML are more prone to develop disseminated intravascular coagulation?

explanationHtml:
The given image shows swollen and spongy gums, indicating gum infiltration. This is a characteristic feature of acute monocytic leukemia (AML-M5).

Infiltration of the gingivae, skin, soft tissues or meninges with leukemic blasts is characteristic of the monocytic subtypes and those with 11q23 chromosomal abnormalities.

Less commonly, infiltration is also seen in acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML-M4).
question: Oral cavity examination of a 56-year-old man with suspected leukemia revealed the following. What subtype of AML is he likely to be suffering from?

explanationHtml:
On flow cytometry, the immunophenotype of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is CD41 and/or CD61 positive (platelet-specific antigens).

Flow cytometry is useful in establishing the different subtypes of AML:

Phenotype CD markers
Myeloblastic CD11b,13,33,117
Promyelocytic(M3) CD13,33
Myelomonocytic(M4) CD11b,13,14,33

question: Which of the following would be seen on flow cytometry of a patient with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia?

correctAnswer: B. A blast count of ≥20% is required for the diagnosis of AML with BCR-ABL1 fusion
explanationHtml:
A blast count of ≥20% is required for the diagnosis of AML with BCR-ABL1 fusion.

The WHO classification of AML incorporates morphology, immunophenotype, genetic abnormalities and clinical features. This is in contrast to the previously used French-American-British (FAB) classification which was based on only morphology of myeloid precursors.

In the 2022 WHO classification, several AML subtypes with defining genetic abnormalities (e.g; RUNX1-RUNX1TI fusion, CBFB-MYH11 fusion, PML-RARA fusion) can be diagnosed irrespective of blast percentage. However, AML with BCR-ABL1 fusion remains an exception and requires >/= 20% blasts for diagnosis.

options.text: The clinical features are not considered to define the subtype
A blast count of ≥20% is required for the diagnosis of AML with BCR-ABL1 fusion
It is only based on morphological features of myeloid precursors
The cut off value of blast cells for diagnosis is 20 %

question: Which of the following is true about the WHO classification of acute myeloid leukemia?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myeloblastic leukemia (AML).

According to the WHO criteria, the diagnosis of AML requires any one of the following:

  • Blast cell count ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
  • Presence of any one of the following cytogenetic abnormalities:

AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities includes the following chromosomal aberrations:

Two gene mutations have been added to the criteria of AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities in addition to chromosomal aberrations. Both gene mutations are associated with a good prognosis.

question: A 65-year-old woman presented with fatigue and fever for the past 2 months. Investigations revealed pancytopenia and the following peripheral smear findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. A 48-year-old man newly diagnosed with AML with a family history of lymphoma
explanationHtml:
Young age of onset is associated with a good prognosis in patients with AML. Family history does not affect the prognosis.

Poor prognosis is seen in the following cases:

  • Advancing age (usually defined as > 60 years)
  • Previous hematologic disorders - myeloproliferative neoplasms and myelodysplastic syndrome
  • Longstanding cytopenias >3 months before diagnosis
  • Therapy-related AML (chemotherapy for other cancers)
  • Chromosomal aberrations with poor outcomes

explanationHtml:
Pelger-Huet anomaly is not a feature of myeloblasts. Auer rods and Phi bodies are considered pathognomonic of AML.

Myeloblasts have the following characteristics as shown in the following image:

  • Large, uniform population of cells
  • Prominent nucleoli (yellow arrow in the image)
  • Primary cytoplasmic granules
  • Auer rods - needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by fusion of lysosomes (black arrow)
  • Phi-bodies - fusiform or spindle-shaped rods similar to Auer rods that require special stains for hydroperoxidases
  • Pseudo-Chediak-Higashi syndrome - Giant lysosomes forming intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies

[[figure-1]]

Pelger-Huet anomaly refers to neutrophils with bilobed nuclei that occur as a benign, inherited condition. Pseudo-Pelger-Huet anomaly refers to an acquired defect seen in CML, myelodysplastic syndrome.

Note: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder with abnormal lysosomal trafficking (LYST gene). Presents with oculocutaneous albinism and immunodeficiency.
question: A pathologist is examining the peripheral smear of a patient with suspected leukemia. All of the following features are suggestive of a myeloblast except:

  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) - most common
  • Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
  • Solid malignancies of the genitourinary tract
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
  • Drugs - all-trans-retinoic acid, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)
  • Idiopathic Sweet syndrome - common in women following respiratory tract infection

This condition presents with the following triad:

  • Fever
  • Neutrophilia
  • Dense dermal infiltrate of neutrophils:
    • Pinkish-red to reddish-brown edematous painful plaques
    • Occur over the head, neck, extremities
question: A patient presents to the ER with a sudden-onset fever and the following painful rash over her face and upper limbs. CBC reveals neutrophilia. This presentation is associated with all of the following conditions except:

explanationHtml:
The most commonly used complete remission induction regimen in patients with AML is cytarabine and an anthracycline (e.g., daunorubicin, idarubicin).

The treatment of AML is as follows:

  • Induction chemotherapy with a 7+3 regimen:
    • Cytarabine - continuous intravenous infusion for 7 days
    • IV daunorubicin on days 1,2,3
    • Side effects include neutropenia, sepsis
  • Post-remission therapy:
    • High dose cytarabine
    • Allogenic hematopoeitic stem cell transplant

Novel agents include gemtuzumab ozogamicin, a CD33 monoclonal antibody.
question: What is the most commonly used complete remission induction regimen in patients with AML?

correctAnswer: D. Arsenic trioxide and all transretinoic acid
explanationHtml:
The presence of blast cells with numerous Auer rods, MPO (myeloperoxidase) positive cells, and t(15:17) is diagnostic of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). The preferred treatment regimen is arsenic trioxide and all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA).

[[figure-1]]

APL is characterized by t(15; 17) translocation resulting in the PML-RAR-alpha fusion gene (promyelocyte-retinoic acid receptor alpha). It is a highly curable subtype of leukemia. The treatment is as follows:

  • Induction therapy:
    • ATRA + anthracycline (daunorubicin or idarubicin) or cytarabine (OR)
    • ATRA + arsenic trioxide
  • Consolidation therapy:
    • Post remission anthracycline-based chemotherapy

options.text: Arsenic trioxide and all transretinoic acid

question: A 60-year-old man came with generalized bone pain, and easy bruisability for the past 6 months. His WBC count was 60,000 cu. mm and bone marrow aspiration revealed the following. Immunohistochemistry was positive for MPO and cytogenetic studies showed presence of t(15:17). What is the preferred treatment regimen?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario describes a patient of APL (acute promyelocytic leukemia) developing fever, tachypnea, and pulmonary infiltrates while on medical treatment. This is suggestive of APL differentiation syndrome, an adverse effect of all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA). The management involves glucocorticoids like dexamethasone.

Along with glucocorticoids, the other management of APL differentiation syndrome includes chemotherapy for cytoreduction and supportive measures. In severe cases, temporary discontinuation of ATRA is necessary.

ATRA is an oral drug that induces the differentiation of leukemic cells bearing the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation. While ATRA reduces the incidence of DIC associated with cytarabine and daunorubicin used earlier in APL, it can cause APL differentiation syndrome due to the adhesion of differentiated neoplastic cells to the pulmonary vasculature endothelium.

In low-risk APL patients with a low leukocyte count at presentation, a combination of ATRA and arsenic trioxide (ATO) has been found to be superior and is the current standard of care.
question: An 18-year-old girl with the diagnosis of acute promyelocytic leukemia was treated medically. She developed fever and tachypnea and a chest X-ray showed pulmonary infiltrates. What drug should she be given next?

correctAnswer: C. His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is otherwise healthy and is blood type O+
explanationHtml:
In the case of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), allogeneic stem cell transplants are the treatment of choice. His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is blood type O positive would be the best choice.

Other options:

Option A: An identical twin brother would not be the donor of choice. The therapeutic benefit of stem cell transplant in hematological malignancies is due to the graft-versus-leukemia (GvL). Donor T lymphocytes attack malignant hematopoietic stem cells of the recipient that remain after high-dose chemotherapy. Despite having a low rate of graft versus host disease (GvHD), stem cells from an identical twin do not have a desirable degree of GvL effect, leading to higher rates of recurrence post-transplant.

Option B: Autologous (umbilical cord transplant) is not recommended as higher rates of relapse have been reported.

Option D: An HLA identical sibling is preferred over an unrelated HLA identical donor because there is a greater chance of matching for minor histocompatibility complex (mHC). This reduces the risk of GvHD. ABO compatibility is also important to consider, but a minor ABO mismatch (Rh mismatch) doesn't have any impact on hemolysis, graft-versus-host disease, or survival.

options.text: His HLA identical 50-year-old brother who is otherwise healthy and is blood type O+
An HLA identical matched unrelated donor who is blood type O–

question: A 47-year-old man with a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia with a blood type O negative blood group presents to the transplant clinic to discuss proceeding with an allogeneic stem cell transplant. Which of the following would be an optimal donor?

explanationHtml:
The highest incidence of T-ALL (T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma) is at 10-19 years (adolescence) when the thymus reaches the maximum size.

On the other hand, B-ALL which is more common has a peak incidence at 3 years (1-10 years). At this age, the number of normal bone marrow pre-B cells (the cell of origin) is at its greatest.
question: Individuals in which age group have the highest incidence of T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma?

  • Transient myeloproliferative disorder:
    • Associated with GATA1 mutations.

    • Require close follow-up as 20-30% may develop AML by 3 years of life
question: Children with Down's syndrome are at an increased risk of developing all of the following except:

CD10 is also called the common ALL antigen (CALLA). It is the specific immunohistochemical marker for pre-B cell ALL. This is the most common type of ALL and is associated with a good prognosis. However, CD10 is negative in infantile leukemia, which is associated with translocation (4;11).

Intrathecal methotrexate is used for CNS prophylaxis in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It is essential in this condition as nearly 1/3 of patients develop CNS involvement at relapse without prophylactic therapy.

question: A 3-year-old boy with Down's syndrome was brought with recurrent infections and bruising over his legs. Further workup was diagnostic of acute lymphoblastic leukemia and he was started on chemotherapy. Which of the following must be added on to prevent metastases to the central nervous system?

explanationHtml:
Bone pain is the most common symptom in multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy in which there is an increased proliferation of monoclonal plasma cells. There is an increased production of monoclonal paraprotein (M protein).

Clinical features of multiple myeloma:

  1. Bone pain (most common):
    • Due to proliferation of tumor cells, activation of osteoclasts that destroy bone, and suppression of osteoblasts that form new bone.
    • Persistent localized pain in a patient with myeloma usually signifies a pathological fracture.
  2. Fever due to recurrent bacterial infections (second most common)
  3. Acute kidney injury due to:
    • Hypercalcemia (most common)
    • Amyloid deposits
    • Hyperuricemia
    • Recurrent infections
    • Infiltration of the kidney by myeloma cells
  4. Normocytic-normochromic anemia due to:
    • Replacement of normal marrow by expanding tumor cells
    • Inhibition of hematopoiesis by factors made by the tumor
    • Reduced production of erythropoietin by the kidney

Myeloma defining events (MDE) include the presence of one or more features such as hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia and lytic bone lesions.
question: What is the most common symptom seen in patients with multiple myeloma?

correctAnswer: C. There is decreased anion gap
explanationHtml:
There is decreased anion gap in multiple myeloma due to the M protein.

Anion gap in the serum is calculated as Na⁺ – (Cl– +HCO3–).

The M protein is cationic, resulting in the retention of chloride causing decreased anion gap.

Only 1% of patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) go on to develop multiple myeloma. Hyperviscosity symptoms in multiple myeloma occurs due to excessive production of M proteins, usually of IgG3 or IgA subtype. Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (IgM myeloma) is the most common cause for hyperviscosity syndrome due to excess IgM paraprotein in these cases.

Radioisotopic bone scanning is less useful in diagnosis because the bone lesions are lytic in nature and are rarely associated with osteoblastic new bone formation.

options.text: Increased monoclonal IgG1 causes hyperviscosity syndrome
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance mostly progresses to multiple myeloma
Radioisotope bone scanning can be used for diagnosis

question: Which of the following is true about multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
In this scenario, the patient has increased M protein (>30g/l), bone marrow clonal plasma cells >10%, and evidence of end-organ damage (fatiguability and back pain). The most likely diagnosis is multiple myeloma.

Diagnostic criteria for plasma cell disorders:

Criteria Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) Smoldering multiple myeloma (asymptomatic myeloma) Multiple myeloma Non-secretory myeloma
M protein (>30g/l) No Yes Yes No
Bone marrow plasma cells (>10%) No Yes Yes Yes

End organ damage (CRAB)

S. Calcium >11 mg/dl

Renal, S. Creatinine >2 mg/dl

Anemia, Hemoglobin <10g/dl

Lytic bone lesions

 No No Yes Yes

Note: Solitary plasmacytoma of bone has only a single area of bone destruction due to clonal plasma cells, no M protein, bone marrow appears normal, and no end-organ damage.

Plasma cell leukemia is an aggressive plasma cell proliferative disorder with >20% abnormal plasma cells in the peripheral blood.
question:
A 72-year-old man presented with complaints of fatiguability and chronic lower back pain. Laboratory findings are as follows. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hemoglobin - 9 g/dl

Serum calcium - 11.5 mg/dl

Serum M protein - 50 g/l

Bone marrow biopsy showed 15 % clonal plasma cells

explanationHtml:
Light Chain Cast Nephropathy is the most common cause of renal failure in multiple myeloma.

It results from excessive production of monoclonal light chains (Bence Jones proteins), which bind to Tamm-Horsfall protein and precipitate within renal tubules, forming obstructive casts and cause tubular injury.

Other mechanisms involved in acute kidney injury in multiple myeloma are:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Amyloid deposits
  • Hyperuricemia
  • Recurrent infections
  • Infiltration of the kidney by myeloma cells
  • Tubular damage by excretion of light chains (Fanconi's syndrome)
question: What is the most common cause of renal failure in patients with multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
In this patient with hypokalemia and urine pH of 5.1, type 2 renal tubular acidosis (adult Fanconi’s syndrome) is the likely diagnosis. It is commonly associated with multiple myeloma.

Normally, light chains are filtered, reabsorbed in the proximal tubules, and catabolized. In multiple myeloma, there is an increased amount of light chains and the tubular cells are overloaded.

This leads to proximal tubular damage either directly from light chain toxic effects or indirectly from the release of intracellular lysosomal enzymes.

Clinical features of renal tubular acidosis type 2:

  • Metabolic acidosis
  • Urine pH <5.3
  • Proteinuria (only light chains)
  • Glycosuria
  • Aminoaciduria

Alport's syndrome is characterised by hematuria, hearing loss and eye abnormalities.
question: A patient was brought to the hospital with dehydration and generalised weakness. He was diagnosed with multiple myeloma 2 years ago. Investigations revealed metabolic acidosis and hypokalemia. Urine analysis showed a pH of 5.1, glycosuria, and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The immunophenotype of tumor cells in multiple myeloma is CD38 and CD138.

Multiple myeloma is derived from plasma cells in which B cell markers (CD19, CD20) are lost.

Immunophenotype of tumor cells in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma / Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia is CD19, CD20, surface IgM+, CD38. A lymphoplasmacytic cell retains B cell markers and carries plasma cell markers.
question: What is the immunophenotype of tumor cells in multiple myeloma?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, the patient most likely has multiple myeloma as there are pathological fractures and elevated M protein. Serum M protein is likely to constitute IgG.

The serum M component is IgG in 53% of patients, IgA in 25%, and IgD in 1%.

Serum IgM is elevated in Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma).
question: A 45-year-old patient presented with multiple fractures and bone pain. Serum electrophoresis revealed elevated serum M protein. What does it most likely to constitute?

explanationHtml:
In the given clinical scenario, the patient has normal SPEP and clonal plasmacytosis. The most likely diagnosis is non-secretory myeloma.

Non-secretory myeloma is characterised by the absence of M protein in the serum or urine. Bone marrow clonal plasmacytosis > 10% and myeloma defining symptoms.

Option A: In multiple myeloma, SPEP demonstrates a sharp peak (church spire or M band) in the gamma globulin region, as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

Option B: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia) also demonstrates a localized peak (M band) in the gamma globulin region. Immunofixation is required to identify the type of immunoglobulin.

Option C: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) does not present with myeloma-defining symptoms. Clonal bone marrow cells will be less than 10%
question:
A 60-year-old man presented with fatigue and back pain since 3 months. Investigations were done and are as follows. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hemoglobin=7 g/dl

Total leukocyte count =9000/cu.mm

Serum protein = 6 gm%

Serum albumin = 3.5 g/dl

Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) shows the given pattern

Bone marrow clonal plasmacytosis = 15%

explanationHtml:
Serum β2-microglobulin levels are the best modality to predict the median survival period.

Albumin levels alone cannot be used to predict the median survival period. It is used in combination with β2-microglobulin for risk stratification.

Patients with β2-microglobulin levels <3.5 mg/L and albumin levels > 3.5 g/dl have a median survival period of 5 years. Those with levels >3.5 mg/L and albumin < 3.5 g/dl have a survival period of fewer than 2 years.

Durie-Salmon staging is unable to predict outcomes with newer agents. Hence it is no longer used.

Factors associated with poor prognosis:

  • Plasma cell labeling index
  • Chromosomal aberrations
  • Circulating plasma cells
  • Performance status
  • Highly elevated LDH
  • Extramedullary disease
  • De novo plasma cell leukemia
question: A 69-year-old business tycoon is diagnosed with multiple myeloma. He is worried about his business empire and asks you how long he will survive. Which of the following is the best predictor for this?

explanationHtml:
17p deletion is associated with a poor prognosis in multiple myeloma.

Chromosomal abnormalities in multiple myeloma are classified as follows:

Standard risk (6-7 years survival):

  • t(11;14) (most common)
  • t(6;14)
  • 13q deletion

High risk (2-3 years survival):

  • 17p deletion
  • t(4;14)
  • t(14;16)
  • t(14;20)
question: In patients with multiple myeloma, the presence of which of the following is associated with a poor prognosis?

correctAnswer: D. Normal alkaline phosphatase and elevated ESR
explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, hypercalcemia along with the skull demonstrating typical 'punched out' lesions is characteristic of multiple myeloma. Normal alkaline phosphatase and elevated ESR are consistent with multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell dyscrasia with the proliferation of plasma cells derived from a single clone. It is associated with an increased osteoclast activity with suppression of osteoblast activity, causing punched-out lytic lesions in the bone and hypercalcemia.

Signs and symptoms:

  • Bone pain is the most common symptom
  • Pathologic fractures
  • Recurrent bacterial infections
  • Renal failure
  • Normocytic normochromic anemia, elevated ESR, hypercalcemia, normal ALP (ALP is a marker of bone growth and hence is not increased in multiple myeloma)
  • Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray. The lesions are purely osteolytic with little or no osteoblastic activity. Hence alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is normal. The most common site of lytic lesion in multiple myeloma is the vertebral column.
  • Electrophoresis: M spikes
  • Urinalysis: Bence Jones proteinuria
  • Bone marrow biopsy: Plasma cells

options.text: High alkaline phosphatase and normal ESR
High alkaline phosphatase and elevated ESR
Normal alkaline phosphatase and normal ESR
Normal alkaline phosphatase and elevated ESR

question: An X-ray skull of a patient with marked hypercalcemia is shown below. Which of the following laboratory parameters is consistent with his diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, the symptoms and bone marrow biopsy are characteristic of multiple myeloma. Lenalidomide + bortezomib + dexamethasone is the treatment of choice in this condition.

This combination achieves close to a 100% response. Hence it is one of the preferred induction regimens in transplant-eligible multiple myeloma patients.

Other pharmacological agents are used as second-line and have a 90% response rate. Chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation prolongs overall survival.

The image below shows a bone marrow biopsy with an increased number of plasma cells.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 68-year-old male patient presented with multiple fractures. He has been suffering from recurrent infections for the past 6 months. Bone marrow biopsy showed the following. What is the treatment of choice in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor.

It has a rapid response and is effective in poor-prognosis myeloma. Side effects include neuropathy (both peripheral and autonomic). Subcutaneous and weekly administration can reduce neuropathic side effects.

Other proteasome inhibitors include carfilzomib (second-generation) and ixazomib, an oral proteasome inhibitor, used in relapsed disease.

Option A: Lenalidomide is an immunomodulatory analogue of thalidomide.

Option B: Rituximab is an anti-CD-20 monoclonal antibody.

Option C: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent.
question: Which of the following is a proteasome inhibitor?

explanationHtml:
In the above clinical scenario, the hyperviscosity symptoms and rouleaux formation on peripherals smear point to a diagnosis of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia. It does not cause lytic bone lesions.

Waldenstrom's macroglöbulinemia is a B-cell malignancy affecting lymphoplasmacytoid and plasma cells. It is characterized by high levels of circulating IgM antibodies.

Clinical features include:

  • Hyperviscosity symptoms
    • Recurrent infections
    • Epistaxis
    • Visual disturbances
  • Peripheral neuropathy - due to myelin-associated glycoprotein causing demyelination.
  • Lymphadenopathy
  • Hepatosplenomegaly
  • Ophthalmoscopic examination may reveal vascular segmentation and dilation of the retinal veins.

Investigations:

  • Bone marrow shows >10% infiltration with lymphoplasmacytic cells
  • Serum M component is >30 g/L (3 g/dL). The size of the IgM paraprotein results in little renal excretion, and only 20% of patients excrete light chains.

The image below shows rouleaux formation.

[[figure-1]]
question: A 64-year-old male patient is admitted with complaints of weakness of the extremities, blurry vision, and nose-bleeds. On examination, there is lymphadenopathy and dilatation of the retinal veins. Peripheral smear is given below. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
The biopsy showing amyloid deposits stained by congo red, along with family history points to a diagnosis of familial amyloidosis (AF). It is most commonly due to the mutation of the transthyretin gene (TTR).

Amyloidosis is a group of protein misfolding disorders characterized by the accumulation of abnormal proteins called amyloid fibrils in various organs.
question: A 19-year-old boy presented with progressive shortness of breath, and easy fatiguability for 3 years. His older brother died of cardiac arrest during a football match a few years ago. Further evaluation revealed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Biopsy and staining of subcutaneous fat showed the following. What mutation is likely in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The patient has non-specific symptoms, which along with macroglossia and raccoon eyes are suggestive of amyloidosis.

Clinical features include:

  • Fatigue
  • Weight loss
  • Nephrotic range proteinuria due to renal amyloidosis and is associated with hypoalbuminemia
  • Cutaneous ecchymoses around the eyes are called the 'raccoon-eye' sign. Due to easy bruising as a result of amyloid deposits or deficiency of clotting factor X.
question: A 60-year-old man presented with progressive weight loss, generalized edema. On evaluation, he had nephrotic range proteinuria, macroglossia, and raccoon eyes. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
The kidneys are the most frequently involved organ in amyloidosis and are affected in 70–80% of patients.

The heart is the second most commonly affected organ (50–60% of patients).

The spleen is frequently involved, and there may be functional hyposplenism in the absence of significant splenomegaly.

Liver involvement causes cholestasis.

Macroglossia, a pathognomonic sign of AL amyloidosis is seen in only 10% of patients.
question: Which of the following is the most commonly involved organ in amyloidosis?

explanationHtml: Cardiac disease is the leading cause of death from primary amyloidosis.
question: What is the leading cause of death in patients with primary amyloidosis?

correctAnswer: C. A woman who underwent radiotherapy for carcinoma cervix
explanationHtml:
The only well-established risk factor for developing chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is exposure to significant levels of ionizing radiation.

This may be in the form of radiation therapy for malignancy or other conditions and nuclear accidents. It is dose-dependent, and low-dose radiation exposure is not a risk factor.

There are no familial associations, infections, or toxins associated with the development of CML.

question: Which of the following patients are at risk of developing chronic myeloid leukemia?

correctAnswer: D. Balanced translocation between long arm of chromosomes 9 and 22
explanationHtml:
Philadelphia chromosome is a balanced translocation between the long arm of chromosomes 9 and 22. It is present in the majority of patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

In a balanced translocation, a part of one chromosome is shifted to another chromosome and vice versa. In this case, the ABL gene present in chromosome 9 is translocated next to the BCR gene (breakpoint cluster region) on chromosome 22. It leads to the formation of shortened chromosome 22, which has been named the Philadelphia chromosome after the place of discovery.

[[figure-1]]

Myelocytes will be predominantly elevated in the peripheral smear of the patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

The clinical hallmark of CML is the uncontrolled production of mature and maturing granulocytes. All of the stages of development of granulocytes can be noted on the peripheral smear in varying numbers:

  • Myeloblast - large cells with a round or oval nucleus, cytoplasm is dark and has no granules
  • Myelocyte - nucleus is oval and is eccentrically placed.
  • Metamyelocyte - nucleus is like a kidney bean-shaped
  • Band forms - nucleus is in the shape of C or U.
  • Segmented neutrophils- nucleus has 2-5 lobes.

All the cells except the myeloblast have a granular cytoplasm. Due to the varied appearance of the cells, it is called garden party appearance or college girl's appearance.

question: In patients with chronic myeloid leukemia, which of the following are predominantly elevated in the peripheral smear?

explanationHtml:

[[figure-1]]

In CML, the following bone marrow findings are noted:

  • Markedly hypercellularity - due to increased granulocytic precursors

    • Megakaryocytes - normal or increased
    • Erythroid precursors - usually decreased
  • Sea blue histiocytes - macrophages with abundant wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm.
  • Bone marrow fibrosis may occur due to the deposition of reticulin.
  • Pseudo-Gaucher cells - macrophages with wrinkled tissue paper appearance, as shown below. Due to the increased turnover of the cells, there is an increased accumulation of glucocerebroside within the macrophages.

explanationHtml:
A blast count ≥ 20% in peripheral blood is indicative of a blast crisis, not the accelerated phase of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

CML can be divided into three phases:

  • Chronic stable phase - Blasts < 10% in peripheral blood and bone marrow
  • Accelerated phase - any of the following:
    • Blasts comprising 10-19% of white blood cells (WBCs) in peripheral blood and/or bone marrow
    • Peripheral blood basophils ≥20%
    • Thrombocytopenia or thrombocytosis not responsive to therapy
    • Additional cytogenetic abnormalities in Philadelphia chromosome cells
  • Blast crisis:
    • Blasts ≥ 20% of peripheral blood WBCs or bone marrow
    • Extramedullary blast proliferation

Majority of the patients present in the chronic stable phase. Without effective treatment, CML in the chronic phase will eventually move into an accelerated phase at first and then into the blast phase.

explanationHtml:
The smear shows small round lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm and the presence of a smudge cell. The most probable diagnosis is chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). Patients with CLL may have autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA).

[[figure-1]]

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia, also known as small lymphocytic lymphoma is a lymphoproliferative disorder that occurs due to the monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes. It is more common in men than women. Increasing age and family history are important risk factors. CLL is one of the few leukemias not linked to radiation exposure.

The majority of the patients are asymptomatic and are diagnosed during routine blood tests. Some patients may have painless lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Increased B cells may produce autoantibodies leading to autoimmune complications like autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia (ITP).

explanationHtml:
Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). This is because there is no clear survival benefit with chemotherapy in asymptomatic patients.

Chemotherapy and monoclonal antibodies are used in the presence of the following features:

  • Progressive marrow failure - worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia
  • Progressive splenomegaly
  • Progressive lymphadenopathy
  • Presence of constitutional symptoms like weight loss, fever, night sweats

Important drugs used in the management of CLL are fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, bendamustine, and rituximab.

Lymphoid malignancies associated with Epstein-Barr virus include:

  • Burkitt's lymphoma
  • Post-organ transplant lymphoma
  • Primary diffuse large B cell lymphoma of the CNS
  • Hodgkin's disease
  • Extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma, nasal type

Primary effusion lymphoma is a variant of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that presents with pleural effusions, usually without apparent tumor mass lesions. It is most common in the setting of immune deficiency disease, especially AIDS.

explanationHtml:
Burkitt lymphoma is a fast-growing, high-grade type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

NHL was earlier classified on the basis of its morphology and clinical behaviour. However, this classification is not currently used. Based on the clinical behavior, NHL is classified as:

  • Low grade - CLL/SLL (small lymphocytic lymphoma), follicular lymphoma
  • Intermediate grade - mantle cell and marginal cell lymphoma
  • High grade - diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), Burkitt's lymphoma

The most aggressive NHL is DLBCL, whereas the most rapidly progressive tumor is Burkitt's lymphoma. Most pediatric NHLs are high-grade and aggressive.

question: Which of the following types of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and its corresponding grade are correctly matched?

explanationHtml:
The gastrointestinal tract is the most common extranodal site in patients with non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL). The stomach is most commonly involved, followed by the small intestine. The skin is the second-most common site.

Mycosis fungoides is a mature T-cell NHL that is (CD4+), which primarily involves the skin. However, extracutaneous spread to bone, viscera and lymph nodes can also be seen. When malignant T-cells in the skin enter circulation, it is called Sezary syndrome. It presents as erythroderma (diffuse erythema and scaling). Histologically, there are Sézary-Lutzner cells (with cerebriform nuclei) and Pautrier microabscesses in epidermis.

CNS is the most common extranodal site in patients with HIV infection. Primary CNS lymphoma (histologically, DLBCL) is one of the AIDS-defining malignancies.

  • Performance status ≥ 2 (ECOG) or ≤70 (Karnofsky)
  • Ann Arbor stage III or IV
  • >1 site of extranodal involvement

question: A physician is in Africa, working with the Doctors Without Borders group. He encounters a 7-year-old boy with the following finding. His parents say that he had a jaw swelling for 2 months that failed to resolve with antibiotics. A biopsy of the swelling reveals a starry sky appearance. correctAnswer: D. Cells labelled B represent the stars in starry sky appearance
explanationHtml:
The given image shows the characteristic starry sky appearance of Burkitt's lymphoma. The reactive macrophages (labelled as A) represent the stars in starry sky appearance. On the other hand, the homogenous tumour cells (labelled as B) represent the sky.

The neoplastic cells are homogeneous, medium-sized B cells with a high growth fraction. These cells are positive for CD19, CD10, BCL-6 & CD43.

On histopathological examination, the tissue shows an infiltration of medium sized tumor cells with basophilic cytoplasm. These cells are interspersed with reactive macrophages which have a pale cytoplasm. The arrangement of these two types of cells gives an appearance of a 'starry sky'. Reactive leukocytes and macrophages are not stained by special stains. They are positive for CD14, CD40, CD11b & CD64.

The growth fraction of these lymphomas is very high, with frequent mitotic figures. The fraction of Ki-67+ (MIB-1+) stained cells is nearly 100%.

explanationHtml:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of hairy cell leukemia (HCL).

In this condition, most patients present with symptoms related to cytopenias or splenomegaly. On bone marrow aspiration, a dry tap is obtained due to HCL-induced marrow fibrosis and the interlocking cell borders of hairy cells (distinct from myelofibrosis).

Tumor cells share certain characteristics of memory B cells. CD11c, CD25, CD103, CD123 is the characteristic immunophenotype diagnostic of this condition. Pan-B markers such as CD19, CD20, and CD22 may also be positive.

Note: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma involves both white and red pulp of the spleen, whereas hairy cell leukemia is limited to the red pulp. All non-Hodgkin's lymphomas involve white pulp of spleen except:

  • Hairy cell leukemia
  • Hepatosplenic lymphoma
question: A 55-year-old man presented with fatigue and dragging sensation in the left upper abdomen. Physical examination revealed massive splenomegaly and no lymphadenopathy. CBC revealed pancytopenia. Bone marrow aspirate yielded a dry tap. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor cells tested positive for CD19, CD22, CD11c, CD25, CD103 and CD123. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Annexin A1 on bone marrow specimens
explanationHtml:
Annexin A1 on immunophenotyping of bone marrow specimens is the best method to differentiate hairy cell leukemia from other B-cell malignancies. It has 100% sensitivity and specificity.

Hairy cells on Wright-stained peripheral blood smear are an important diagnostic finding. Typical hairy cells are mononuclear cells with abundant pale blue-grey agranular cytoplasm with elongated (hairy) projections. Intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called ribosome-lamellar complexes can also be seen in 50% of cases. However, these can be seen in other B-cell disorders also.

Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) stain is an important tool and is positive in 95% of cases of hairy cell leukemia. However, it is not pathognomonic.

The following pattern of bone marrow involvement is near to pathognomonic for hairy cell leukemia (>99%):

  • Diffuse infiltration of tumor cells with honeycomb appearance.
  • Individual cells have a fried egg appearance such that the nucleus of each hairy cell is surrounded by a halo of cytoplasm, as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

The selection of initial treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma is usually based on presenting stage and prognostic factors.

Recurrent hemarthrosis is the most common bleeding manifestation of severe hemophilia. Hemophilia is said to be severe when the residual activity of factor VIII is <1%.

Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive hemorrhagic disorder and is caused by mutations in either the F8 gene (hemophilia A or classic hemophilia) or the F9 gene (hemophilia B). Clinically, it is impossible to distinguish between hemophilia A and hemophilia B as they present with similar symptoms. It can be classified based on residual activity of FVIII or FIX as severe (<1%), moderate (1–5%), or mild (6–30% )

Hemophilia presents early in life- bleeding after circumcision or when beginning to walk or crawl.

Clinical features:

  • Acute hemarthrosis:
    • Local pain, swelling
    • Erythema
    • Muscle contractures due to fixed positioning.
  • Chronic hemarthrosis:
    • Synovial thickening
    • Synovitis (due to intraarticular blood)

The most common joint affected is the knee. One joint is affected more than the other. This is called the target joint. Muscle hematomas can lead to compartment syndromes.

Hematuria is common but self-limited. Life-threatening bleeds such as bleeding into oropharyngeal spaces, CNS, and retroperitoneum can occur.

Treatment: Without treatment, severe hemophilia may limit life expectancy. Factor replacement for hemophilia has been the mainstay of therapy.

  • FVIII dose (IU) = Target FVIII levels – FVIII baseline levels × body weight (kg) × 0.5 unit/kg .
  • FIX dose (IU) = Target FIX levels – FIX baseline levels × body weight (kg) × 1 unit/kg

The FVIII half-life of 8–12 h requires injections twice a day to maintain therapeutic levels, whereas the FIX half-life is longer, ~24 h so that once-a-day injection is sufficient.

explanationHtml:
In disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC), fibrinogen levels are decreased due to increased bleeding.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acquired syndrome characterized by the widespread activation of blood clotting factors within blood vessels, resulting in a loss of clotting control. The primary mechanism of DIC involves the uncontrolled generation of thrombin through multiple pathways which leads to sustained coagulation activation, the formation of fibrin, and the consumption of clotting factors and platelets.

Infections are the most frequent cause of DIC.

Laboratory investigations in DIC:

  • Decreased platelet count
  • Prolonged PT/TT
  • Prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
  • Decreased fibrinogen
  • Elevated fibrin degradation products (D-dimers)
  • Peripheral smear: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia in DIC with schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells)

The treatment involves platelet transfusion when platelet counts are below 10,000-20,000/μL. Replacement of fibrinogen and coagulation factors is with fresh frozen plasma (FFP) along with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.

In cases of low-grade DIC associated with solid tumors or acute promyelocytic leukemia low doses of continuous-infusion heparin has been effective.

This patient presents with petechiae, and abdominal distension with schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. This child most likely has Kasabach-Merritt syndrome (secondary DIC). His abdominal mass is likely to be a hepatic hemangioma.

Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a life-threatening complication that occurs in patients with giant hemangiomas. It is most commonly seen in infants.

Clinical features:

  • Enlarged abdomen
  • Hepatomegaly or jaundice
  • Petechiae, bruising, and frank bleeding
  • Painful lesions
  • Anemia

It is characterized by profound thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy leading to a DIC-like picture.

Other options:

Option A: Neuroblastomas are tumors of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla that are derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and the most frequently diagnosed tumor in infancy. Brain tumors are the most common solid tumors in childhood. They present as a flank mass that crosses the midline.

Option B: Hepatoblastoma is the most common childhood liver tumor. Histologically it is composed of small polygonal embryonal cells forming trabeculae, acini, or papillary structures in the developing liver.

Option C: Wilms tumor is the most common primary malignant renal tumor in children and is the second most common malignant abdominal tumor in children. The clinical presentation usually involves an asymptomatic unilateral abdominal mass, hypertension, abdominal pain, and gross painless hematuria. Constitutional symptoms of fever, anorexia, and weight loss can also be present at the time of diagnosis.

Genomic Convention (as stated in Harrison 21E) includes the initiating methionine (AUG) from the translation start site, even though it is cleaved off in the mature protein. The features of multiple episodes of acute severe pain in fingers and toes with spontaneous resolution are suggestive of dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), which usually occurs in sickle cell anemia.

The sickled RBCs have a sticking tendency towards the endothelium of the small venules. These abnormalities provoke unpredictable episodes of vaso-occlusion. Dactylitis is characterized by severe pain affecting the bones of the hands, feet, or both. It is often the first symptom of sickle cell anemia in children.

Infectious complications of blood transfusion include:

question: A 40-year-old man is being evaluated in the ward for fatigue and pallor. One week ago, he had undergone a blood transfusion following a road accident. Further evaluation reveals Hb of 8.1 g/dl and positive direct Coomb's test and history of previous blood transfusion. What is the likely mechanism of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is the most common cause of transfusion-related fatalities.

TRALI is due to the presence of anti-HLA class II antibodies in the donor plasma. These antibodies bind recipient leukocytes, which aggregate in the pulmonary vasculature and release mediators that increase capillary permeability. Multiparous women are frequently implicated donors. Recipients with a history of liver disease, smoking, alcohol use are at a higher risk.

It occurs within 6 hours of transfusion and results in hypoxia and signs of non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema with bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray. It is managed with supportive care.

Note: According to the latest edition of Harrison's, transfusion associated circulatory overload (TACO) is the leading cause of death followed by TRALI.

The metabolic complication of massive blood transfusion is hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.

Massive blood transfusion is defined as the transfusion of 50% of a patient’s total blood volume over 3 hours or more than 10 units within 24 hours. The anticoagulant citrate used in the storage of blood components binds to calcium and results in hypocalcemia.

The complications of massive transfusion are:

  • Hypocalcemia
  • Hyperkalemia (Option C)
  • Hypokalemia
  • Hypothermia (Option D)
  • Citate toxicity
  • Metabolic alkalosis (Option A)

question: Following a normal vaginal delivery, a 30-year-old woman develops severe postpartum hemorrhage. Over the next 24 hours, she undergoes transfusion of 11 units of pRBCs. She is at risk for all of the following complications except:

explanationHtml:
The patient is being transfused blood and has complaints of backache, this is suggestive of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

The first step is to stop transfusion immediately and then collect blood samples for testing.

Acute hemolytic transfusion reactions typically occur within the first 24 hours following a blood transfusion, primarily due to ABO incompatibility.

It presents with symptoms such as hypotension, tachypnea, tachycardia, fever (1-2°C increase in temperature), chills, chest and back pain, hemoglobinuria, and hemoglobinemia. In severe cases, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), acute renal failure, shock, and death can occur.

Management of immune-mediated acute hemolytic transfusion reactions is to provide supportive care, administer vigorous hydration with isotonic saline and use diuretics to maintain urine output.

This is because the excess sodium citrate (anticoagulant) in the transfused blood gets converted to bicarbonate (23 mEq from each unit of blood), leading to metabolic alkalosis.

Metabolic acidosis can also be seen in multiple blood transfusions, as citrate is acidic, but metabolic alkalosis is more common.

The time interval between primary HIV infection and the manifestation of AIDS is 10 years.

[[figure-1]]

After exposure to the HIV virus, there occurs primary infection following an incubation period of 2-4 weeks, which is usually symptomatic in more than 50% of cases, following 3-6 weeks there is acute HIV syndrome due to wide dissemination of the virus, characterized by fever, sore throat, diarrhea, lymphadenopathy, and rash.

This peak viremia drops as the immune response develops, to reach a plateau about 3 months later. Following this there is a prolonged period of clinical latency, during which infected individuals are asymptomatic, lasting for a median of 10 years.

Following this period, chronic persistent infection develops which is the hallmark of HIV disease called Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Long-term non-progressors: a small part of untreated HIV-infected people with CD4 counts within the reference range for >10 years.

Elite controllers: Some long-term non-progressors have undetectable viral loads.

Salient features of transmission of HIV:

  • Male to female transmission > female to male transmission.

DC-SIGN is a type of cell surface lectin receptor to which the HIV virus has the affinity to bind. The expression of this type of receptor on dendritic cells (antigen-presenting cells) enhances the infectivity of HIV.

It is characterized by acute burst of viremia and wide virus dissemination and seeding of lymphoid organs (e.g., gut-associated lymphoid tissue), culminating in the destruction of CD4+ cells.

The p24 antigen capture assay is used as a screening test for HIV infection in patients suspected of having the acute HIV syndrome.

Option B: The acute HIV syndrome is typical of an acute viral syndrome and is very similar to acute infectious mononucleosis. The clinical findings include fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. Rash, headache, arthralgia, and anorexia/weight loss can also be seen.
