In patients with relatively high CD4+ T cell counts, the typical pattern of pulmonary reactivation occurs (60–80%). In patients with lower CD4+ T cell counts, disseminated disease is seen.

question: What is the most common opportunistic infection in HIV-infected individuals?

correctAnswer: B. Concurrent treatment with anti-retroviral therapy
explanationHtml:
Concurrent treatment with anti-retroviral therapy is the most likely explanation in this case resulting in Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). Its characteristics are:

  • Temporary paradoxical exacerbation of symptoms (lymphadenopathy, fever or worsening of pulmonary infiltrations, pleural effusion) and radiographic manifestations of TB after starting ART. This occurs as a result of immune reconstitution due to simultaneous administration of ART and ATT.
  • It is seen weeks to months following the initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy (cART).
  • It is most common in previously untreated patients starting therapy with a CD4+ T cell count <50/μL who experience a sudden drop in viral load.
  • The earlier ART is started and the lower the baseline CD4+ T-cell count, the greater the risk of IRIS.
  • In severe cases, the use of immunosuppressive drugs such as glucocorticoids may be required to blunt the inflammatory component of IRIS while specific antimicrobial therapy takes effect.

Note: Hypersensitivity to isoniazid is extremely rare and the presentation includes maculopapular rash.

question: A previously untreated HIV-positive patient is diagnosed with tuberculosis and treatment is initiated for both the diseases. Two weeks into treatment, he suddenly complains of high fever, severe malaise and worsening cough. What is the likely explanation?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with a positive Kernig's sign, is suggestive of meningitis. Cryptococcus is the leading infectious cause of meningitis in patients with AIDS. It generally occurs in untreated patients, with CD4+ T cell counts <100/μL.

Most patients present with a picture of subacute meningoencephalitis. The CSF profile may show modest elevations in WBC or protein levels and decrease in glucose. The CSF opening pressure is usually elevated (yeast colonies obstruct the free flow of CSF causing increased CSF pressure).

The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made by identification of Cryptococcus neoformans yeast cells in CSF with india ink stain or by the detection of cryptococcal antigen using latex agglutination (CrAg).

Prophylaxis: Oral fluconazole when CD4+ T cell count is <100/μL.

Treatment:

  • Induction - IV or liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, continuing with amphotericin alone ideally until the CSF culture turns negative.
  • Maintenance - Oral fluconazole until the CD4+ T cell count has increased to >200 cells/μL for 6 months in response to cART.

AIDS-defining malignancies are those cancers that a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected person is at a high risk of developing. When a HIV-infected person develops one of the AIDS-defining malignancies it suggests that he has AIDS.

AIDS-defining malignancies include the following:

  • Kaposi sarcoma - It is a multicentric neoplasm of vascular origin and has a strong association with HHV - 8.
  • Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma

question: A 45-year-old HIV-positive woman presented with fever and malaise. She gives a history of bleeding from the following lesions. Warthin-Starry staining of a biopsy sample taken from the lesion showed which organism?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cerebral toxoplasmosis. MRI scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis is one of the most common AIDS-defining opportunistic CNS infections and usually occurs in patients with CD4+ T cell counts <200/μL. It is usually a reactivation of latent tissue cysts.

It usually has multiple lesions in multiple locations which are associated with inflammation and central necrosis, and hence show ring enhancement on contrast MRI. Sometimes an eccentric nodular area of enhancement is seen within the ring; this so-called eccentric target sign is typical of cerebral toxoplasmosis. Surrounding edema is also present.

Treatment includes sulfadiazine/pyrimethamine and leucovorin for a minimum of 4–6 weeks.

Primary prophylaxis: It is given to patients with IgG antibody to toxoplasma and CD4+ T cell count <100/μL. A single double strength tablet of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) is given.

Secondary prophyaxis/maintanace therapy: It is given when CD4+ T cell counts <200 cells/μL. Sulfadiazine/pyrimethamine and leucovorin is given. It is discontinued if the CD4+ T cell counts are maintained >200/μL for 6 months.

Option A: Cryptococcal meningitis presents with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs. Seizures and focal neurologic deficits are rarely seen. On MRI imaging the common findings are :

  • Dilated perivascular spaces
  • Leptomeningeal enhancement
  • Basal ganglia pseudocysts

Option B: Primary CNS lymphoma also presents with seizures and focal neurological deficit. Symptoms of fever, night sweats and weight loss are present in 80% of the patients. On imaging, it is identified as a CT hyperdense enhancing supratentorial mass, with MRI T1 hypointense, T2 iso- to hypointense, vivid homogeneous enhancement as well as restricted diffusion.

Option C: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, caused by JC virus, is characterized by demyelination in subcortical white matter reflected on MRI as multiple, non-enhancing white matter lesions.

CMV retinitis is a necrotic retinal infection that results in a painless irreversible vision loss. Patients may complain of blurred vision, floaters (described by patient as flies or spiders in the field of vision), and scintillations. It is usually bilateral and is characterized by perivascular hemorrhage and exudates in the retina (pizza pie appearance or scrambled eggs and ketchup appearance).

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection. It is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection, occurring predominantly at CD4+ T cell counts of <50/μL.

The most common presentation is disseminated disease with fever, weight loss, and night sweats. The diagnosis is made by culture of blood or involved tissue.

CT scan shows peribronchial inflammation of the infected lung giving rise to a tree in a bud appearance (small round structures attached to linear structures) indicated by the arrowhead. In severe cases, there might be bronchiectasis and cavity formation.

Treatment consists of clarithromycin or azithromycin with ethambutol. Rifabutin or ciprofloxacin or amikacin may be added in patients with extensive disease. Primary prophylaxis with azithromycin is indicated in patients with CD4+ T cell counts <50/μL.

question: A 50-year-old man with HIV presents with lab reports showing: Low albumin, massive proteinuria. Renal ultrasound shows large, echogenic kidneys. Blood pressure is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml:
The most common form of heart disease associated with HIV infection is coronary heart disease.

In patients with HIV infection, cardiovascular disease may be a direct consequence of HIV infection, a complication of anti-retroviral therapy or due to classical risk factors like smoking.

Exposure to HIV protease inhibitors and reverse transcriptase inhibitors have been associated with an increase in total cholesterol and/or risk of MI (Myocardial infarction).

Dilated cardiomyopathy associated with congestive heart failure (CHF) is referred to as HIV-associated cardiomyopathy. This generally occurs as a late complication of HIV infection and, histologically, displays elements of myocarditis.

explanationHtml:
Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended for all HIV patients, regardless of CD4 T lymphocyte cell count or clinical stage.

This is done to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV infection. A secondary goal of ART is to reduce the risk of HIV transmission.

question: Anti-retroviral therapy in HIV-infected individuals should be initiated at _______

correctAnswer: B. It detects HIV antibodies and antigen
explanationHtml:
The 4th generation HIV test combines the detection of antibodies against HIV-1 & HIV-2 with detection of the core p24 antigen of HIV-1. Inclusion of p24 antigen capture allows detection of HIV-1 infection even before seroconversion i.e., presence of antibodies in the blood.

The approximate time to positivity following infection is 15 to 20 days. Consequently, the window period between infection and detection of the infection is shortened.

Fourth-generation HIV testing is highly sensitive (99.9%) and is the CDC-recommended initial screening test for HIV. No further testing is required for specimens that are non-reactive on ELISA screening.

Generation Serological test
First generation IgG antibody
Second generation IgG antibody
Third generation IgM and IgG antibody
Fourth generation IgM and IgG antibody and p24 antigen

Didanosine is the most likely causative drug. The clinical scenario, suggestive of pancreatitis, is a dose-limiting side effect of didanosine and occurs more frequently in alcoholic patients and those with hypertriglyceridemia.

Option A: Nevirapine side-effects include severe liver problems, skin rash, and skin reactions.

question: A 46-year-old man, who is a chronic alcoholic, presented with acute dull and boring abdominal pain. His history is significant for ongoing treatment with ART. Serum lipase levels were noted to be grossly elevated. What is the most likely causative drug?

explanationHtml:
Enfuvirtide is the antiretroviral drug administered parenterally, used only in the treatment of those who have evidence of HIV replication i.e., high viral load, despite ongoing antiretroviral therapy.

Enfuvirtide prevents viral fusion and entry by binding to the gp41 subunit of the HIV-1 envelope. It is not active against HIV-2. It is administered as a twice-a-day subcutaneous injection.

Note: Zidovudine is also available as a parenteral formulation.
question: An HIV-positive patient is upset because he has a high viral load despite good compliance with ART. The physician decides to start him on a parenteral drug. Which of the following drugs will be helpful for this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an acute infection with hepatitis B virus. The preferred regimen in the management of HIV-1 and hepatitis B co-infection is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir.

This regimen is also the first-line management in adults, adolescents, pregnant women, and HIV-TB co-infection.

Antivirals that are effective against hepatitis C infection are sofosbuvir, grazoprevir and glecaprevir.

Abacavir is not used in HIV and hepatitis-B co-infection. It is used in the first-line ART regimen for patients with abnormal serum creatinine values.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) drugs like lamivudine, its closely related drug emtricitabine, and the nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) tenofovir have activity against hepatitis B virus. question: Which of the following antiretroviral drugs is not used in HIV & hepatitis B co-infection?

explanationHtml:
Screening of patients for HLA-B5701 is recommended before initiation of abacavir since it is associated with hypersensitivity.

The hypersensitivity syndrome includes fever, maculopapular rash, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal problems, malaise and fatigue. Hence, abacavir should only be used as a last resort and with close monitoring in patients who are HLA-B5701-positive.

explanationHtml: The clinical scenario indicates the early onset of diabetic and hypertensive kidney disease; therefore, combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) regimens containing tenofovir should be avoided in this patient. As tenofovir depends largely on renal excretion, administering it in those with renal impairment can worsen kidney damage, so it should be avoided.
question: Evaluation of a patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension has revealed moderately increased albuminuria. He has recently been diagnosed with HIV infection. Combination ART preparations including which of the following drugs should be avoided?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fat redistribution resulting in the classic buffalo hump appearance. Nelfinavir is the most likely cause.

It is a protease inhibitor and its chronic administration can result in fat redistribution and metabolic syndrome.

Note: Atazanavir has the least propensity to cause lipodystrophy and metabolic syndrome.
question: A 36-year-old HIV-positive man on cART is presented with the following finding. What is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml: Zidovudine causes suppression of bone marrow and hence, should be avoided in a patient with a history of anemia. It can worsen the anemia and neutropenia, which may require transfusions.
question: A 54-year-old HIV-positive woman has a Hb of 8gm/dl. Combination ART preparations including which of the following drugs should be avoided?

explanationHtml:
The patient is most likely prescribed a cART regimen including efavirenz.

Many patients treated with efavirenz note a feeling of light-headedness and dizziness following the initiation of therapy. They also complain of insomnia, vivid dreams and nightmares.

These symptoms are self-limiting and tend to disappear gradually after several weeks of therapy. If the sleep problems are persistent, stopping the drug is the only solution.

It is recommended to take efavirenz before bedtime to minimize side effects.

The CNS/ psychiatric adverse effects seen with the use of efavirenz are:

  • Frank psychosis (depression, hallucinations, and/or mania)
  • Impaired concentration
  • Dysphoria
  • Dizziness
  • Vivid dreams
  • Insomnia

*Note: Pearl attached below has been updated according to the NACO ART guidelines 2021. Efavirenz has been replaced by Dolutegravir as per the new guidelines.
question: During his routine counselling, a war veteran on cART for the past 2 weeks tells his therapist that he wishes to discontinue his HIV treatment. He explains that since starting them, he has been having extreme dizziness and intense nightmares leading to repeated wakening in the night. What is the likely cause?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of HIV-2 infection. It is intrinsically resistant to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTI) and also to fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide.

Western blot has a high specificity. It detects specific antibodies against multiple proteins of all 3 major HIV genes - gag, pol, and env.

Persons with HIV-2 will often have an indeterminate western blot pattern showing the presence of Gag bands and Pol bands, but an absence of Env bands. This pattern occurs because HIV-1 and HIV-2 share little similarity in the env gene. Moreover, the presence of gp36 points towards a diagnosis of HIV-2.

In India, NACO provides western blot confirmatory testing only to resolve indeterminate results on previous serological testing and not for routine confirmation after a positive result on screening tests.

Etravirine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) currently approved for the treatment of HIV infection in combination with other agents in treatment-experienced patients.

question: A woman is diagnosed to be positive for HIV in her first trimester. What is the appropriate management?

correctAnswer: C. Start ATT and then ART after 2 weeks
explanationHtml:
In a patient with HIV and TB start ATT first and then start ART as soon as ATT is tolerated (between 2 weeks and 2 months) by the patient. This is done in order to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS):

Patients with HIV-related TB may experience a temporary paradoxical exacerbation of symptoms and radiographic manifestations of TB after starting ATT. This occurs as a result of immune reconstitution due to simultaneous administration of ART and ATT.

It is characterized by high fever, lymphadenopathy, expanding intra-thoracic lesions, and worsening of chest X-ray findings. Diagnosis should be made only after ruling out treatment failure and other infections. For severe cases, prednisone 1-2mg/kg is used for 1-2 weeks and then gradually tapered.

However, in patients with CD4 <50/μL, the benefits of administering ART immediately after initiating ATT outweigh the risks of IRIS, and therefore ART should be started as early as possible.

Note: As per RNTCP guidelines, CBNAAT is the preferred diagnostic technique for testing TB in PLHIV (people living with HIV). Smear microscopy has poor sensitivity in detecting TB in PLHIV due to fewer organisms in sputum, and hence is not preferred.

question: A newly diagnosed HIV patient presented with fever, cough, and hemoptysis. His sputum sample showed acid-fast bacilli. What is the appropriate management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
HIV DNA PCR is the diagnostic test of choice for HIV in a baby born to an HIV-infected mother.

The National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) recommends the use of a qualitative HIV DNA PCR on dried blood spots in children aged <18 months for early infant diagnosis. The first HIV DNA PCR should be conducted at 6 weeks, and if the test is positive, the test is repeated as soon as possible for confirmation of the infection.

In case the first PCR is negative:

  • In a non-breastfed baby- Confirm with second PCR tests at 6 months.
  • In a breastfed baby- PCR should be repeated 6-8 weeks after stopping breastfeeding

A report of HIV positivity is given when 2 PCR tests are positive, and an HIV negative report is given when 2 PCR tests are negative.

Infants are likely to have their mother's antibodies. Therefore, antibody assays like ELISA and Western blot are not preferred to avoid false positive results.
question: What is the diagnostic test of choice for HIV in a baby born to an HIV-infected mother?

correctAnswer: A. Cartridge based nucleic acid amiplification test
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of tuberculosis. Cartridge-based nucleic acid amiplification test (CBNAAT) is the diagnostic test for TB in HIV positive patients.

CBNAAT is a rapid molecular test that detects the DNA of TB bacteria in HIV-positive individuals. It uses sputum or any other biological specimen (except blood and blood-contaminated specimens). It can give a result in less than 2 hours. It can also detect the genetic mutations associated with resistance to the drug rifampicin.

Sputum microscopy has poor sensitivity for detecting TB in HIV-infected individuals due to fewer organisms in sputum.

options.text: Cartridge based nucleic acid amiplification test

question: A 29-year-old HIV-positive woman presents to the OPD with fever, cough, and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray is given below. What is the diagnostic test for this condition in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Only after obtaining a biopsy
explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL). In this condition, glucocorticoids should be administered only after a biopsy has been obtained. This is because steroids have a cytolytic effect on lymphoma cells and hence may lead to nondiagnostic tissue.

On CT, PCNSL is identified as a hyperdense enhancing supratentorial mass. On MRI, vivid homogeneous enhancement, as well as restricted diffusion, is seen.

PCNSL is a type of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. The workup usually includes:

  • HIV testing
  • CSF analysis
  • MRI spine
  • PET/CT to assess the extent of the disease
  • Bone marrow biopsy

question: What is the WHO recommendation regarding the initiation of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). The prophylaxis for PCP is started at <200/mm3 CD4 count according to the CDC recommendation. In PCP LDH is elevated and smear stained with Giemsa stain shows trophic forms with dot-like nuclei and pale blue cytoplasm as well as intracystic bodies of Pneumocystis jiroveci.

Primary prophylaxis of PCP:

Indications
  • CD4+ T cell count <200/uL ( CD4 cell %<15)
  • Recent oropharyngeal candidiasis and prior PCP
  • Any patient with unexplained fever for > 2 weeks.
Drug of choice

Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX), one double-strength tablet daily.

Alternatives- Dapsone/Pyrimethamine + Leucovorin or Atovaqone or Aerosolised Pentamidine

Note : TMP-SMX also provides protection against toxoplasmosis and some bacterial respiratory pathogens. The prophylaxis is discontinued in those patients treated with ART who maintain good suppression of HIV (<50 copies/mL) and CD4+ T-cell counts >200/ μL for at least 3 months.
question: A cachexic man presented with a non-productive cough and shortness of breath. He was diagnosed with HIV 6 months ago but is non-adherent to ART. Serum LDH is 350 U/L. explanationHtml:
Recommended post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is a three-drug regimen that includes lamivudine, tenofovir, and dolutegravir.

A regimen for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis with two ARV drugs is effective, but three drugs are preferred. The PEP must be initiated ideally within 2 hours and certainly within 72 hours.

explanationHtml:
Coronaviruses are enveloped helically symmetrical viruses.

Being enveloped contributes to their lipid solvent susceptibility. This is the reason alcohol-based hand sanitizers and soaps are used. The lipid membrane dissolution and protein denaturation by ethanol lead to membrane disruption and inhibition of metabolism.

The coronaviridiae have a single unsegmented ss (+) RNA, which is the largest genome among RNA viruses. They are about 120- 160 nm in size and contain a helical nucleocapsid. A total of seven human coronaviruses have been identified:

question: Coronaviruses are _____

explanationHtml:
The given clinical vignette showing breathlessness, fever, and cough with a low oxygen saturation and ground-glass opacities on HRCT is indicative of COVID-19 caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE-2) is the specific functional receptor for SARS-CoV-2 in human cells.

ACE2 is expressed in nearly all human organs in varying degrees. In the respiratory system, ACE2 is mainly expressed by the type 2 alveolar epithelial cells in the highest quantity. Hence, the primary target of SARS-CoV-2 is type 2 alveolar cells.

The functional receptor for SARS-CoV (SARS 2002) is also ACE 2.

Note: Dipeptidylpeptidase 4 is the functional receptor for MERS-CoV (MERS 2012).
question: An elderly diabetic man presents with difficulty breathing, cough, and fever. He came back after visiting his son in New York, 10 days ago. His SpO2 is 89%. HRCT shows bilateral, multilobar ground-glass opacification. What is the receptor used by the likely causative organism to gain entry into the cells?

explanationHtml:
Spike protein (marked as 1 in the image) determines the infectious nature and host specificity of SARS-CoV-2.

The spike protein also referred to as the CoV S protein is one of the key components determining virus virulence, tissue tropism, and host range. The coronavirus spike protein mediates coronavirus entry into host cells. Each spike protein has two distinct subunits S1 and S2.

  • S1 subunit is responsible for binding to the specific receptor (ACE 2) on the host cell surface facilitating viral attachment to the surface of target cells.
  • S2 subunit drives the fusion of the viral and host cell membranes.

The host protease enzymes, mainly transmembrane protease serine-type 2 (TMPRSS2) cleave the spike protein. This activates the spike protein to induce virus-cell membrane fusion at the cell surface and allows the entry of coronaviruses into the host cell.

question: Which viral structure determines the infectious nature and host specificity of SARS-CoV-2?

correctAnswer: D. A thalassemic girl got infected following routine blood transfusion.
explanationHtml:
Blood transfusion is not a mode of transmission of SARS-CoV-2.

Option A: Droplet transmission

  • A type of direct transmission
  • Occurs when someone coughs, sneezes, speaks, or spits
  • Virus-containing droplets from the infected person travel shortly in the air directly contact another person’s conjunctiva, oral or nasal mucosa
  • Limited to about 6 feet distance between the source and the host
  • Particle size is 5-10 µm in diameter

Option B: Fomite transmission

  • A type of indirect transmission
  • Objects other than water or food contaminated by infectious agents - clothes, towels, linen, cups, spoons, pencils, books, toys, door handles, taps, etc.
  • Transmission occurs when one touches the contaminated objects and touches his mouth, nose, or eyes

Option C: Airborne - droplet nuclei transmission

  • A type of indirect transmission
  • Droplet nuclei - dried residue of droplets of size <5µm that are generated by the evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air and by a variety of atomizing devices
  • Remain infectious when suspended in the air for some time (typically hours)
  • Transmission occurs when one inhales droplet nuclei/aerosols containing the virus in sufficient quantity

A resident transmitted the virus to his neighbour who entered the same apartment lift after a few hours.

question: Which of the following scenarios is unlikely for transmission of SARS-CoV-2?

explanationHtml:
The incubation period of SARS-CoV-2 infection ranges from 1-14 days so he is most likely to develop the disease after this period. The median incubation period is around 4-6 days.

The incubation period is defined as the time interval between invasion by an infectious agent and appearance of the first sign or symptom of the disease.
question: A relative of a COVID-19 positive man, who came in his contact yesterday, reported to the flu clinic. Within how many days is he most likely to develop the disease?

The outbreak of COVID-19 is an example of a propagated epidemic.

The propagated epidemic results from person-to-person transmission of the infectious agent over a prolonged duration of time. Other examples of this type include hepatitis A and polio.
question: Covid 19 outbreak is a type of which of the following kinds of the epidemic?

explanationHtml:
All of the given symptoms are included in the definition of a suspect case of SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 except convulsions.

As per WHO and MOHFW, a suspect case is defined as:

  1. A person who meets the clinical and epidemiological criteria-
    1. Clinical criteria:
      • Acute onset of fever AND cough; OR
      • Acute onset of any 3 or more of the following: fever, cough, general weakness/ fatigue, headache, myalgia, sore throat, coryza, dyspnoea, anorexia/nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, altered mental status.
    2. Epidemiological criteria: A person present in any of the following settings for 14 days prior to symptom onset-
      • Residing or working in an area with a high risk of transmission of virus OR
      • Residing or travel to an area with community transmission OR
      • Working in any healthcare setting
  2. A patient with severe acute respiratory illness with-
    • history of fever or measured fever of ≥38 C° along with cough
    • onset within the last 10 days
    • requiring hospitalization
  3. An asymptomatic person not meeting epidemiologic criteria with a positive SARS-CoV-2 antigen-RDT.
question: What is not included in the definition of a suspect case of SARS-CoV-2?

correctAnswer: A. An asymptomatic contact of a probable case with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test.
explanationHtml:
An asymptomatic contact of a probable case with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test is considered as a confirmed case, and not a probable case.

Probable case is defined as:

  1. A patient who meets clinical criteria and is a contact of a probable or confirmed case, or linked to a COVID-19 cluster.
  2. A suspect case with chest imaging showing findings suggestive of COVID-19 disease.
  3. A person with recent onset of anosmia or ageusia in the absence of any other identified cause.
  4. Death, not otherwise explained, in an adult with respiratory distress preceding death and was a contact of a probable or confirmed case or linked to a COVID-19 cluster.

Confirmed case is defined as:

  1. A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) including RT-PCR or any other similar test approved by ICMR.
  2. A person with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test and meeting either the probable case definition or suspect criteria.
  3. An asymptomatic person with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test who is a contact of a probable or confirmed case.

question: Which of the following is not considered a probable case of SARS-CoV-2?

correctAnswer: C. A passenger in the same bus as a symptomatic patient for 6 hours and the patient later tested positive
explanationHtml:
A person traveling in the same environment and not having significant exposure to the confirmed case is not classified as a high-risk contact.

A contact of COVID-19 is a person living in the same household or having direct physical contact with the patient/infectious secretions without appropriate PPE or a person who was in a closed environment or at a distance of within 1 meter of a COVID-19 case.

High-risk contacts:

  • Touched body fluids of the patient
  • Had direct contact with the body of the patient during the physical examination without proper PPE
  • Touched or cleaned the linens, clothes, or dishes of the patient
  • Lives in the same household as the patient
  • Comes in close contact (within 1 meter) with the patient without necessary precautions
  • A passenger in close proximity with the symptomatic patient for 6 hours and the patient later tested positive


Low-risk contacts:

  • Shared the same space but does not have a high-risk exposure to the confirmed case.
  • Travelled in the same environment but does not have a high-risk exposure to the confirmed case.

For collecting nasal/nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal specimens for COVID-19 testing, a person’s head should be tilted back 70 degrees.

Guidelines for specimen collection:

  • Use appropriate PPE and maintain proper infection control measures
  • Restricted entry to visitors or attendants during sample collection

question: During the swab collection for COVID-19 testing, the healthcare professional asks you to tilt your head approximately to what degree?

correctAnswer: A. The nasal swab is placed in a different viral transport media tube as the throat swab.
explanationHtml:
The nasal swab is placed in the same viral transport media tube as the throat swab.

Samples that can be used for COVID-19 testing are:

  • Throat and nasal swab
  • Oropharyngeal swab
  • Nasopharyngeal swab
  • Broncho-alveolar lavage
  • Endotracheal aspirate

Combined throat and nasal swabs:

  • Tilt patient's head back 70 degrees.
  • Gently rotate the swab and insert less than one inch into the nostril. Rotate the swab several times against the nasal wall and repeat the same in the other nostril with the same swab.
  • Place the tip of the swab into the transport media tube and cut off the applicator.
  • For throat swab, take a second swab, insert into the mouth and swab the posterior pharynx and tonsillar areas.
  • Place the tip of the swab into the same tube and cut off the applicator tip.

Oropharyngeal swab:

  • Tilt patient's head back 70 degrees.
  • Rub swab over both tonsillar pillars and posterior oropharynx and avoid touching the tongue, teeth, and gums.
  • Use only synthetic fiber swabs with plastic shafts. Avoid calcium alginate swabs and swabs with wooden shafts.
  • Place the swab immediately into sterile tubes with viral transport medium.

Nasopharyngeal swab:

  • Tilt the patient's head back 70 degrees
  • Insert flexible swab through the nares parallel to the palate (not upwards) until resistance is encountered
  • Rub and roll the swab and leave it in place for several seconds to absorb secretions before removing
  • Place the swab immediately into sterile tubes with viral transport medium.

Viral transport mediums:

  • Hanks balanced salt solution with Ca and Mg and heat inactivated fetal bovine serum, gentamicin and amphotericin B (most commonly used)
  • Sterile saline
  • Phosphate buffered saline-glycerol medium
  • Amies medium

Note: Biosafety levels include a specific combination of work practices, safety equipment, and facilities that are designed to minimize the exposure of workers and the environment to infectious agents. There are four biosafety levels.

The given clinical scenario, along with CT showing bilateral multiple patchy consolidation and grid-like thickness of interlobular septa, is suggestive of COVID-19. The gold standard for its diagnosis is the identification of viral genome targets in the respiratory tract materials by reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) during the first week of symptoms.

RT-PCR involves the reverse transcription of the genetic material of the virus (RNA) to complementary DNA (cDNA), followed by amplification of some regions of the cDNA. Four regions of the SARS CoV2 genome are used as targets:

  • RdRp gene (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase)
  • Genes from structural proteins
    • E (virus envelope)
    • N (virus nucleocapsid),
  • ORF1ab gene (open reading frame 1a and 1b)

CBNAAT (cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test) uses small, chip-based, portable, battery-operated devices that detect target genetic material of SARS CoV2. Examples include TrueNat and Cepheid Xpert Xpress SARS CoV-2

Options A and B: Antibody testing- Antibodies of IgA, IgM, and IgG isotypes specific to different virus proteins are detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) or chemiluminescence immunoassays (CLIA). CLIA is more sensitive compared to ELISA.

Option C: Rapid antigen test (RAT)- Antigen-based assays are used as point-of-care tests for early detection of SARS-CoV-2. They are used at the field level for early detection of infection and quick containment. Most of such tests have relatively moderate sensitivity but high specificity. They are used for diagnosis along with RT-PCR.

Routine surveillance in containment zones and screening at points of entry for all symptomatic cases including:

The paper-based Covid-19 test kit developed by CSIR and IGIB and approved by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) is named FELUDA.

FELUDA is an acronym for FNCAS9 Editor Linked Uniform Detection Assay. The name is inspired by a fictitious detective character in novels written by Satyajit Ray.

FELUDA uses CRISPR-Cas9 technology (CRISPR = Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats). The CRISPR technology uses a highly specific CAS9 protein to find and bind to the target Covid signature. This is then coupled with paper-strip chemistry to elicit a visual readout on a paper strip. It is a very affordable, sensitive (96%), and specific (98%) strip test which can detect viral genetic material within 45 minutes.

Ground glass opacity (GGO) is the most commonly seen pattern in chest CT of patients with COVID-19.

Some of the typical features seen in the CT scans of COVID-19 patients include:

  • Ground glass opacities
  • Consolidation
  • Air bronchograms
  • Interlobular septal thickenings
  • Visible intralobular lines (crazy-paving pattern)
  • Reversed halo sign

The image below shows an axial CT scan with multiple patchy areas of pure ground-glass opacities. GGO are hazy areas with slightly increased density in the lungs without obscuration of underlying bronchial and vascular margins.

[[figure-1]]

The image given below shows a CT scan with bilateral GGO in the lower lobe and an air bronchogram (arrow) in the left subpleural area. Air bronchograms appear like air-filled bronchi within a highly attenuated parenchymal background. These are dilated bronchi filled with mucus plugs and do not truly contain air.

[[figure-2]]

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple consolidation areas and interlobular septal thickening (arrows) in both lungs. The pulmonary interstitial structures such as interlobular septa and intralobular lines can thicken and manifest as small linear opacities.

[[figure-3]]

The image given below shows a CT scan with crazy-paving pattern (circled area). It is defined as the presence of GGOs with superimposed interlobular septal thickening giving the appearance of irregular paving stones.

[[figure-4]]

The image given below shows a CT scan with multiple lesions with reversed halo sign (arrows). The reversed halo sign or atoll sign is the presence of a ring-like area of consolidation with a superimposed rounded GGO.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of moderate COVID-19 (SpO2 <94%, RR≥24). Awake proning should be avoided in patients with hemodynamic instability.

Awake proning in moderate COVID disease is recommended for any patient with severe respiratory distress. It improves oxygenation by keeping the alveolar units open. Timely proning of patients with SpO2 < 94% can help reduce mortality.
Steps for self-proning:
  • 1 pillow below the neck
  • 1 or 2 pillows below the chest through upper thighs
  • 2 pillows below the shins
  • Keep alternating between proning, laying on your right, sitting up, and laying on your left, in a lying position, ideally for not more than 30 minutes in each position with an upper limit of 2 hours.
  • One may prone up to 16 hours a day, in multiple cycles, if tolerable.
Avoid proning:
  • Hemodynamic instability
  • For 1 hour after meals
  • DVT, cardiac conditions
  • Fractures of spine, femur, or pelvis

When respiratory distress and/or hypoxemia of the patient cannot be alleviated after receiving standard oxygen therapy, high–flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy (HFNO), or non–invasive ventilation can be considered. Compared to standard oxygen therapy, HFNO reduces the need for intubation.

Patients on HFNO should be closely monitored, and endotracheal intubation should be done if the patient acutely deteriorates or does not improve after a short trial (about 1 hr).

Contraindications to HFNO includes patients with:

  • Hemodynamic instability

  • Abnormal mental status

question: A 67-year-old patient with end-stage renal disease is tested positive for COVID-19. Which anticoagulation agent would you recommended for him?

explanationHtml:
The correct answer is 1, 2, 3, and 4.

  1. Tocilizumab is contraindicated in HIV-positive patients and those with active bacterial or fungal infection.
  2. Bamlanivimab is not authorized for patients with mild COVID-19 pneumonia who are not at a high risk for hospitalization.
  3. Remedisivir is contraindicated in postnatal lactating women.
  4. Convalescent plasma therapy is no longer recommended in the management of COVID patients.

Tocilizumab acts by IL-6 inhibition. It may be considered in moderate-severe COVID patients with progressively increasing oxygen requirements and mechanically ventilated patients not improving despite the use of steroids. Patients should be carefully monitored for secondary infections and neutropenia after treatment with tocilizumab. It is contraindicated in:

  • HIV
  • Active infections (systemic bacterial/fungal)
  • Tuberculosis
  • Active hepatitis
  • Absolute neutrophil count < 2000/mm3
  • Platelet count < 1,00,000/mm3

Bamlanivimab is a monoclonal antibody directed against the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. The FDA has issued an emergency use authorization for bamlanivimab for the treatment of adult and pediatric mild to moderate COVID patients (12 years of age and older weighing at least 40 kilograms) who are at high risk for progressing to severe COVID-19 and/or hospitalization. Possible side effects include anaphylaxis and infusion-related reactions, nausea, diarrhea, dizziness, headache, itching, and vomiting. There is no specific contraindication for this drug.

Remdesivir is an antiviral drug that works by inhibiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It may be considered in moderate and severe hospitalized COVID patients requiring supplemental oxygen/oxygen delivery through a high flow device/ noninvasive ventilation/ invasive mechanical ventilation/ ECMO. It is contraindicated in:

  • AST/ALT > 5 times upper limit of normal
  • Severe renal impairment (i.e., eGFR < 30ml/min/m2 or need for hemodialysis)
  • Pregnancy or lactating females
  • Children <12 years of age

Convalescent plasma therapy is no longer recommended in the management of COVID patients, as per the revised guidelines.

Dexamethasone is generally given to all patients of moderate and severe COVID-19. Patients with severe COVID-19 can develop a systemic inflammatory response that can lead to lung injury and multisystem organ dysfunction.

FDA recently sanctioned emergency use authorization to a combination of nirmatrelvir and ritonavir tablets (Paxlovid) for the treatment of mild-to-moderate COVID-19. It is the first oral antiviral for the treatment of COVID-19.

Nirmatrelvir is a peptidomimetic inhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). Inhibition of this enzyme makes the virus incapable of processing polyprotein precursors and thus prevents viral replication.

Home quarantine for 14 days is advised when a person comes in contact with a COVID-19 positive patient.

The home quarantined person:

question: Your worried friend calls you for advice after attending a family function. He informs you that his aunt, who also travelled to the function in the same car, tested positive for COVID-19. What is your advice for your friend?

Pernio / chilblains are skin lesions on the acral surfaces of the body characterised by the development of erythematous-violaceous or purpuric macules. They may be accompanied by edema and pruritus.

It is usually due to cold exposure or underlying hematological disorders but has also been reported in patients with COVID-19 disease. The underlying mechanism is thought to be an inflammatory process. The lesions appear late (postviral phase) with the patients exhibiting positive IgM/ IgG antibodies for SARS-CoV-2 and negative RT-PCR. However, pernio like lesions can also be seen in early stages of the disease when the patients are still infective.

There are no treatment guidelines but high-potency topical corticosteroids may be helpful if the lesions are causing discomfort. Other cutaneous manifestations include exanthematous rash, livedo reticularis, urticaria, MIS-C etc.

explanationHtml:
The component of the PPE kit to be removed first is the shoe covers.

Preparation for doffing the PPE:

  • To be performed only in the designated area
  • Check for any leak or soiling
  • Doffing room should have two chairs, dirty and clean
  • All the PPE must be discarded in the red bin
  • Hand hygiene must be performed after every step

Steps of doffing the PPE:

  • Engage the observer and ask him to check the PPE - observer should check for any leak, tear, or contamination of PPE. If contaminated, then it should be disinfected with alcohol-based wipes.
  • Disinfect the gloves
  • Remove and discard shoe covers
    • Sit on the dirty chair with legs apart
    • Remove the shoe covers by slowly pulling the outer surface starting from the top and then pull from the toes end. Discard them
  • Disinfect and remove outer pair of gloves
    • While removing the outer gloves, inner gloves should not be torn or contaminated
    • Pinch the first glove on the outer surface at the wrist and pull it inside out
    • Hold this glove in the other hand like a ball
    • Slide the thumb inside the other glove and remove inside out balling around the previous glove, making it into a single bag. Then discard it.
  • Disinfect inner gloves
  • Remove face shield/eye goggle - loosen the screw and remove the face shield by holding it from the back handle. Discard it.
  • Disinfect inner gloves again
  • Remove hood and coverall
    • Slide back the hood by holding it from the top
    • Separate the zip flap and unzip the coverall suit
    • Holding the suit at the arms, slide it off the shoulder slightly, then pull the suit from the side of the waist
    • Roll the arms out one by one
    • By touching the inner surface of the suit carefully roll out each leg. Discard it
  • Disinfect and remove inner gloves as previously described
  • Perform hand hygiene and wear a new pair of gloves
  • Remove and discard N-95 mask
    • Do not touch the exposed surface of the mask
    • Stoop forward and first remove the lower strap
    • Then pull out the upper strap and remove the mask
  • Disinfect gloves
  • Sit on the clean chair and disinfect shoes using alcohol wipes
  • Disinfect and remove gloves
  • Perform hand hygiene
  • Wipe the shoes on sodium hypochlorite soaked doormat at exit
  • Exit the doffing area and take a shower

explanationHtml:
The front of the face shield is considered to be a contaminated area of the personal protective equipment (PPE). Hence, it should not be touched while doffing.

The areas that are considered clean are the parts that will be touched while removing a PPE:

  • Inside and back of the gown including the ties
  • Ties or earpieces of the mask, goggles, and face shields

The areas that are considered contaminated are:

  • Outside front and sleeves of the isolation gown
  • Front of goggles, mask, respirator, and face shield

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis. Intravenous administration of amphotericin B is the first line treatment. Other drugs which are approved for its management include isavuconazole and posaconazole. Surgical debridement is the last line management.

Immunocompromised states are important risk factors including diabetes mellitus and glucocorticoid treatment as well as patients on ventilation.

Diagnosis can be made by culturing the organisms from sterile sites like needle aspirate, pleural fluid, or a tissue biopsy specimen. The biopsy is most sensitive. It reveals characteristic wide, thick-walled, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

It can present as:

  • Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis - (most common) the initial symptoms are nonspecific and include eye or facial pain and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and blurry vision. If untreated it can spread from the sinuses to the orbit, and then to the frontal lobe.
  • Pulmonary mucormycosis - (second most common)
  • Cutaneous mucormycosis - usually results after trauma
  • Gastrointestinal mucormycosis - primarily occurs in premature neonates who have disseminated disease or necrotizing enterocolitis
  • Disseminated mucormycosis

explanationHtml:
This is a case of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), associated with COVID-19 infection.

Diagnostic criteria for MIS-C:

Children and adolescents 0–18 years of age with fever ≥3 days

AND two of these:

  • Rash or bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis or mucocutaneous inflammation signs (palmoplantar erythema, lip hyperemia, periorbital erythema and edema, strawberry tongue, and malar erythema)
  • Hypotension or shock.
  • Features of myocardial dysfunction, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities (including ECHO findings or elevated Troponin/NT-proBNP)
  • Evidence of coagulopathy (PT, PTT, elevated D-Dimers)
  • Acute gastrointestinal problems (diarrhoea, vomiting, or abdominal pain)

AND

Elevated ESR(>40 mm), C-reactive protein (>5 mg/L), or procalcitonin.

AND

No other obvious microbial cause of inflammation including bacterial sepsis, staphylococcal or streptococcal shock syndromes.

AND

Evidence of COVID-19 (RT-PCR, antigen test, or serology positive), or likely contact with patients with COVID-19.

Types of MIS-C:

  • MIS-C with shock/multi-organ dysfunction
  • Kawasaki phenotype
  • MIS-C without shock

MIS-C is treated with IV methylprednisolone. The dose can be increased in patients with shock. If the condition does not improve for 48-72 hours, specialists can be consulted for the addition of biologicals to the treatment regimen.

APOL1 gene increases the risk of collapsing nephropathy in patients infected with COVID-19.

Glomerular lesions are reported in a minority of COVID-19 patients. They are associated with collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and are called COVID-associated nephropathy (COVAN). Such patients present with nephrotic-range proteinuria and acute kidney injury (AKI). It specifically affects individuals of African ancestry who are carriers of this gene variant.

Thrombotic microangiopathy is another uncommon finding among these patients. Histopathology is similar to those seen in other forms of collapsing glomerulopathy. But, tubulointerstitial lesions including microcystic tubular dilatation and tubular injury are typically associated with APOL1- related disease.
